title: Trump Budget Proposal Zeroes Out CDC's Global Health Center, Cuts Gavi Vaccine Funding as U.S. Exits WHO
institution: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) / HHS
status: Proposed and largely implemented for FY2026 -- the administration's FY2026 budget request eliminated CDC's standalone Global Health Center line item and zeroed out Gavi funding; later FY2027 budget materials describe successor global-health funding as held level with FY2026, suggesting the final FY2026 structure was less severe than the original zero-out proposal (see caveat)
date_of_action: 2025-05 (FY2026 budget request released) through 2025-09 (reporting characterizing the Global Health Center as shut down, alongside the ongoing WHO withdrawal)
what_changed: The administration's FY2026 budget request, released in May 2025 and detailed further that summer, eliminated CDC's Global Health Center as a standalone budget line -- funded at $693 million in FY2025 and $711 million in FY2024 -- folding a reduced successor ($239 million under 'CDC-Wide Activities') into a new consolidated Administration for a Healthy America (AHA), an HHS reorganization championed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that also absorbed CDC's chronic-disease programs and some NIH institutes. The New York Times reported in June 2025 that the proposal specifically cut $230 million from CDC vaccine programs, including U.S. contributions supporting polio and measles vaccination and funding for the Gavi vaccine alliance; KFF's budget tracking confirmed the FY2026 request eliminated Gavi funding entirely and cut the broader Global Health Programs Account from $10.0 billion (FY2025) to $3.8 billion. By September 2025, Time reported the CDC's Global Health Center had effectively been shut down and global health funding cut by 67%, framing this alongside the administration's separate, ongoing withdrawal from the World Health Organization (announced by executive order in January 2025, taking formal effect January 2026) and warning from public-health experts that the combined cuts weaken the U.S.'s ability to detect and contain outbreaks before they reach American soil, citing estimates that another pandemic as severe as COVID-19 carries roughly a 50% chance of occurring within the next 20-25 years. The Gavi funding line item became a concrete diplomatic act around June 25-26, 2025, when HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced at Gavi's own pledging summit that the U.S. was withdrawing the roughly $1.2 billion pledge the Biden administration had made to the vaccine alliance, saying Gavi had 'ignored the science' on vaccine safety and 'lost the public trust,' and citing a 2017 observational study of infants in Guinea-Bissau as evidence -- a study public-health researchers have specifically disputed as unrepresentative of Gavi's broader immunization record (Gavi says its programs have vaccinated more than 1.1 billion children in low-income countries over 25 years). The withdrawal contributed to Gavi's pledging summit falling short of its $11.9 billion replenishment target. A December 4, 2025 Gates Foundation Goalkeepers report gave the first concrete real-world read on the cumulative effect of these cuts: global under-5 child deaths, which had fallen every year for decades, were projected to rise in 2025 for the first time this century, from 4.6 million in 2024 to an estimated 4.8 million -- an increase of just over 200,000 -- as global health aid fell 26.9% below 2024 funding levels; Bill Gates said Trump administration cuts were 'part of that picture,' given the U.S.'s historic role as the largest single global-health donor, and warned that up to 16 million additional children could die by 2045 if the funding cuts persist.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Publicly championed the Administration for a Healthy America reorganization that absorbed CDC's Global Health Center, describing it as eliminating 'an alphabet soup' of departments by merging them into AHA; defended the broader HHS budget cuts, including CDC restructuring, in congressional testimony.

estimated_impact.summary: Sharply reduced dedicated federal funding for global vaccine and disease-prevention programs, compounding the separate loss of WHO-coordinated surveillance access, at a moment public-health experts warn U.S. outbreak-detection capacity is already strained.

Precise enacted (as opposed to proposed) FY2026 dollar figures were not independently confirmed in sourcing reviewed.

MODERATE confidence on the September 2025 Time article's 'Global Health Center shut down'/67%-cut framing, which was not independently cross-verified against a second contemporaneous outlet in sourcing reviewed and may describe the proposal's anticipated effect rather than a confirmed final enacted figure -- present it as reported characterization, not a settled number, in debate use. title: CDC orders federally funded health programs to drop harm reduction, adopt 'parental authority' priorities on short deadline
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
status: Complete -- notice issued with a fixed compliance deadline
date_of_action: 2026-06-26 (notice reported) - 2026-07-01 (compliance deadline)
what_changed: The CDC issued a notice to state, territorial, tribal, and local health programs receiving federal funding -- covering immunization, HIV, hepatitis, tobacco, and overdose-prevention work -- requiring them to agree to a new set of priorities within five business days, or by July 1, 2026. The new priorities deprioritize 'housing first,' harm reduction, and safe consumption approaches to substance use (evidence-based strategies with a documented record of reducing overdose deaths) in favor of 'parental authority' framing and abstinence/'public disorder' oriented approaches. The notice referenced an earlier CDC statement that funding could be canceled for non-compliance, though the notice itself did not explicitly and unambiguously tie compliance to funding continuation -- reporting describes the funding link as implied/referenced rather than stated as a formal, guaranteed consequence in this specific document. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has publicly signaled support for the broader policy direction, though the memo itself originated from CDC leadership rather than being personally signed by him. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0273), documenting the earlier antecedent history behind the June 2026 compliance notice above: the administration's draft FY2026 budget, reported April 25, 2025, proposed eliminating the roughly $56 million First Responders-Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (FR-CARA) grant program, which in 2023 alone distributed more than 101,000 naloxone (Narcan) overdose-reversal kits and trained nearly 77,000 people to administer them; some congressional Republicans publicly said they would not take up that specific cut. Trump's July 2025 executive order 'Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets' directed federal funds away from 'harm reduction' and 'safe consumption' programs, and by January 2026 CDC officials were telling overdose-prevention grant recipients in compliance meetings that promoting a 'never use alone' safety message -- guidance that connects people using drugs alone with someone who can call for help if they overdose -- might no longer be permitted, while acknowledging to health departments that the boundary was a 'gray area' they could not clearly define; HHS's own public statement said federal funds could not support harm-reduction efforts that 'primarily serve to facilitate illegal drug use,' while agencies should instead focus funding on naloxone distribution, test strips, and treatment referrals. Separately, in Alaska, local police chiefs and addiction-treatment providers warned in December 2025 that proposed federal cuts -- including a potential 35% reduction to the state's High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) program funding alongside broader Medicaid reductions -- could increase fentanyl flow into the state and reduce treatment access, reversing recent progress on overdose deaths.

primary_proponent.name: CDC leadership (institutional; no single named individual signer identified in reporting)
primary_proponent.role: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
primary_proponent.note: Issued the notice and priorities directly; HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has publicly supported the broader shift away from harm reduction but reporting does not show him as the notice's personal signer -- see caveat.

estimated_impact.summary: Programs across immunization, HIV, hepatitis, tobacco, and overdose-prevention work -- serving state, territorial, tribal, and local populations -- were given roughly one week to abandon evidence-based harm-reduction and housing-first strategies or risk their federal funding, based on a referenced but not fully explicit funding-cancellation threat.
estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar figure or program count has been reported for this specific notice. The funding-cancellation consequence is referenced from an earlier CDC statement rather than stated outright in this notice, per the reporting -- this entry should be framed as 'a implied funding threat with a short compliance window,' not a confirmed funding cutoff, until stronger sourcing on the consequence is found.

confidence_note: Sourced to the Guardian's original reporting (which obtained a copy of the memo) and corroborated by wire/aggregator pickup (AOL). Single-original-source story (one outlet obtained the memo directly) -- solid but not yet corroborated by a second independent outlet with direct memo access, and the funding-consequence detail specifically is softer than the compliance-deadline detail. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0273): the FR-CARA/Narcan budget-cut proposal is HIGH confidence (corroborated across Yahoo/AP, NOTUS, and KFF Health News); the January 2026 'never use alone' compliance guidance and HHS's clarifying statement are HIGH confidence, both directly quoted in the Guardian's reporting; the Alaska HIDTA/Medicaid impact warnings are MODERATE-HIGH confidence, sourced to the Guardian's direct reporting with on-record local officials but not independently cross-checked against a second outlet.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: Immunization, HIV, hepatitis, tobacco, and overdose-prevention programs nationwide faced a one-week deadline with a referenced (not explicit) funding threat for non-compliance.

title: CDC Disbanded Its 34-Year-Old Hospital Infection-Control Advisory Committee Without Telling Committee Members for a Month
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Disbanded since March 31, 2025; as of the most recent reporting reviewed, no confirmation was found that the committee has been reinstated despite repeated calls from professional infection-prevention societies (APIC, SHEA, IDSA, and others) urging CDC/HHS to restore it.
date_of_action: 2025-03-31 (termination effective) through 2025-05-02 (CDC disclosed the termination; committee members were not notified until a virtual meeting in early May, over a month after the effective date)
what_changed: CDC disbanded the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC), established in 1991 to issue national, science-based guidance on preventing healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial resistance in U.S. hospitals, effective March 31, 2025. HHS characterized HICPAC as one of the 'unnecessary government entities and federal advisory committees' identified for termination under a Trump executive order directing agencies to eliminate such bodies. CDC did not disclose the termination publicly until May 2, 2025, and did not inform HICPAC's own committee members until a virtual meeting in early May -- more than a month after the committee had already ceased to exist. At the time of its termination, HICPAC was actively working to update federal guidance on two active issues: return-to-work recommendations for healthcare personnel following COVID-19 infection, and isolation precautions in healthcare settings generally -- both left without a resolution because the committee that would have issued the updated guidance no longer existed. Infection-prevention professional societies -- including APIC (Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology), SHEA (Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America), and IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) -- publicly characterized HICPAC as 'a critical asset to the nation's public health infrastructure' and called for its reinstatement.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.role: Federal health department implementing the executive order directing elimination of 'unnecessary' federal advisory committees
primary_proponent.note: No single named HHS or CDC official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for identifying HICPAC specifically as an 'unnecessary' committee for elimination under the broader executive order.

estimated_impact.summary: HICPAC's elimination removed the federal government's dedicated science-advisory body for hospital infection-control standards -- guidance hospitals nationwide rely on to prevent healthcare-associated infections and slow antimicrobial resistance -- leaving two active guidance updates (COVID return-to-work recommendations, general isolation precautions) unresolved with no committee remaining to complete them. Professional societies warn that without an ongoing federal advisory body, infection-control standards risk becoming outdated as clinical evidence evolves, a risk with direct patient-safety implications given how directly hospital infection-control practice depends on this kind of centralized, science-based guidance.

estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar-cost or quantified health-outcome figure specific to HICPAC's elimination was found in sourcing reviewed -- the impact documented here is the loss of an ongoing federal guidance-setting function and the stalling of two specific in-progress guidance updates, not a modeled or measured infection-rate increase attributable to the committee's absence.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- corroborated across NBC News, Healio, LeadingAge, the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society, and multiple infection-prevention professional societies' own public statements (APIC, SHEA, IDSA), all describing the same March 31, 2025 effective date, the delayed May 2025 notification, and the committee's 1991 founding and role. No sourcing reviewed disputes the basic facts of the termination; the characterization of HICPAC as 'unnecessary' is HHS's own stated rationale under the executive order, not an independent finding.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: Hospitals lose the federal government's dedicated science-advisory body for infection-control standards, with professional societies warning guidance will grow outdated as clinical evidence evolves without an ongoing committee to update it.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Well-corroborated across NBC News, Healio, and multiple infection-prevention professional societies; HHS's 'unnecessary' characterization is its own stated rationale, not an independently verified finding.

title: CDC Injury Center Lost 200+ Staff in April 2025, Eliminating Its Drowning-, Motor-Vehicle-, and Child-Maltreatment-Prevention Teams
institution: CDC National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (Injury Center)
status: Ongoing -- the April 2025 staff terminations were not reversed as of the most recent reporting reviewed; a January 2026 appropriations bill restored level funding to the Injury Center's parent unit (documented in this tracker's related cdc-injury-center-funding-freeze-2025.json entry) after a proposed outright elimination, but no sourcing reviewed confirms the specific specialist teams named here -- drowning, motor vehicle, child maltreatment, rape prevention, traumatic brain injury, falls -- were rehired or reconstituted; restored funding for a unit is not the same as restored staff for a specific team.
date_of_action: 2025-04 (mass layoffs directed by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) through 2025-08-27 (NPR follow-up confirming the drowning team remained eliminated and its FY2026 elimination was proposed in the federal budget)
what_changed: In April 2025, as part of the broader HHS workforce purge directed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., entire specialist teams at the CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (the Injury Center) were eliminated: units focused on motor vehicle crashes, child maltreatment, rape prevention and education, drowning prevention, traumatic brain injury, and falls among the elderly, along with the center's data-analysis branch, a key database-maintenance team, and staff supporting the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (the CDC's emergency-room-based injury-tracking system). The loss of that CDC support staff had an immediate downstream effect at the Consumer Product Safety Commission, which co-administers NEISS's broader All Injury Program: an internal CPSC email dated April 11, 2025 stated that 'due to the recent reductions-in-force and budget cuts across CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control, the [All Injury Program] supported portion of NEISS is coming to an end very quickly,' and Reuters reported the 47-year-old program -- which draws from a representative sample of 100 hospital emergency departments and tracks injuries from motor vehicle crashes, alcohol, adverse drug effects, aircraft incidents, and work-related injuries -- would stop collecting that data effective the same week, cutting the program's overall data collection by as much as 65%. Safe States Alliance director Sharon Gilmartin identified more than 200 positions eliminated at the Injury Center in the cuts. A CDC senior health scientist told OPB/member station reporting, 'A lot of the work we do will not be picked up by anyone else.' Christen Rexing of the Society for Advancement of Violence and Injury Research warned, 'We will not know what is killing us and that's very scary.' Beth Moracco of UNC's Injury Prevention Research Center called the work 'critical...done at such a low cost with such a high return,' and Mark Rosenberg, the Injury Center's former director, said, 'There's nothing partisan about injuries.' Injuries are the leading cause of death for Americans under 45, and car crashes are the second-leading cause of death for children ages 1-12. Among the eliminated units, the drowning-prevention team drew particular attention: Politico reported May 26, 2025 that the team -- which tracked national drowning data, issued safety alerts, and partnered with groups including the YMCA to fund swim lessons for at-risk children -- was cut even as drowning remains the leading cause of death for children ages 1-4. NPR reported August 27, 2025 that the drowning-prevention unit, staffed by just three scientists on a roughly $2 million annual budget, had also partnered with the American Red Cross and specifically served autistic children, who face dramatically elevated drowning risk; the Trump administration's FY2026 budget request separately proposed eliminating the drowning-prevention program altogether, on top of the staff terminations already carried out. Drowning kills more than 4,000 Americans annually and is the leading cause of death for children ages 1-4 and among the leading causes for ages 5-14. This entry documents the staff-elimination action specifically; a related but mechanically distinct action -- OMB's freeze of Injury Center program funding, and a separate FY2026 proposal to eliminate the center's parent unit entirely that was defeated by a bipartisan appropriations campaign -- is documented in this tracker's cdc-injury-center-funding-freeze-2025.json entry; that entry's January 2026 'reversed' resolution restored level funding to the Injury Center as a whole but no sourcing reviewed confirms whether the specific specialist teams named here, terminated months earlier in the April 2025 RIF, were ever rehired.

title: OMB Froze CDC Injury Center Funding for Youth Violence, Gun Injury, Diabetes, and Tobacco Programs
institution: CDC Injury Center / Office of Management and Budget
status: Reversed (partial), plus a separate elimination threat that was also reversed -- CDC staffers confirmed delayed FY2025 funds began being disbursed as of August 2025 following press and congressional pressure; a subsequent White House FY2026 budget request to eliminate the Injury Center's parent unit entirely was defeated by a bipartisan appropriations campaign, with Congress fully funding the center through the rest of FY2026 in a bill signed into law by January 2026
date_of_action: 2025 (freeze in place through mid-2025) through 2025-08-05 (WSJ report and NPR follow-up on disbursement); separately, 2025-05 (FY2026 budget request proposing elimination) through 2026-01 (appropriations bill signed, fully funding the center)
what_changed: Earlier, on April 4, 2025, Trump ordered CDC to cut $2.9 billion in contracts -- about 35% of its contracting budget -- by April 18, 2025, as part of the same broader HHS-wide DOGE contract-cutting directive documented in this tracker's NIH contract-cuts entry (nih-contract-worker-cuts-2025). The CDC-specific directive followed an earlier firing of roughly 2,400 CDC employees, including scientists who had worked on asthma, lead poisoning, violence prevention, and climate-related public health research -- overlapping directly with the Injury Center's youth-violence and firearm-injury-prevention portfolio described below. The Wall Street Journal reported that the White House Office of Management and Budget had frozen funding for at least five CDC Injury Center programs -- youth violence prevention, adverse childhood experiences, firearm injury prevention, injury control research centers, and general injury-prevention activities -- alongside broader CDC chronic-disease funding covering diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and tobacco use, with the amount withheld estimated at up to $200 million. This followed a months-long pattern in which CDC did not receive the roughly $9 billion Congress had appropriated for fiscal year 2025 in full, instead receiving disbursements in small increments approximately every 30 days, sufficient only to cover payroll and other limited expenses. Following the WSJ report and subsequent public and congressional pressure, NPR reported on August 5, 2025 that CDC staffers said the agency had begun disbursing previously delayed funds, including money for overdose-prevention programs; separately, funding previously frozen for rape and domestic-violence prevention programs was also reported as being released around the same time. ABC News and the Trust for America's Health's 2025 public-health-infrastructure report characterized this episode as part of a broader, ongoing pattern of 'red tape and budget constraints' delaying CDC program funding beyond this specific freeze. Update 2026-08-30: beyond the funding-freeze episode above, a separate and more severe threat emerged and was later reversed -- the White House's FY2026 budget request, released May 2025, proposed eliminating the CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (the Injury Center's formal parent unit) entirely, not merely delaying its funding. A coalition of over 50 national organizations, philanthropies, universities, and health agencies, organized as the 'Keep America Safe Coalition' by the Safe States Alliance, campaigned against the proposal by highlighting local program outcomes (suicide-prevention work in Louisiana, infant-mortality reduction in Washington state, trauma-center initiatives in Chicago) to Congress and the public. Bipartisan appropriations leaders -- Reps. Tom Cole (R-OK) and Rosa DeLauro (D-CT), and Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) -- championed retaining the center's funding. Nine months after the elimination proposal, President Trump signed into law an appropriations bill (finalized January 2026) that fully funded CDC for the rest of FY2026 at nearly $9.15 billion, including level funding for the Injury Center (with $25 million specifically for gun-violence-prevention research) rather than the proposed elimination. The bill also added regulatory protections requiring independent review of any future CDC reorganization effort and aimed at preventing the kind of grant-disbursement delays this entry's original OMB-freeze episode documented.

OMB Director Russell Vought has been publicly identified as a chief architect of the administration's broader impoundment strategy -- see this tracker's [[nih-impoundment-gao-finding-trump2]] entry for a related, GAO-confirmed NIH funding impoundment from the same period.

estimated_impact.summary: Delayed federal funding for youth-violence, gun-injury, and chronic-disease prevention programs for months without public explanation, straining state and local programs that rely on the funds, before a partial reversal followed press scrutiny.

title: CDC's Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Team Was Cut Entirely, Then Denied Milwaukee's Request for Help With a School Lead Crisis
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Center for Environmental Health / Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry
status: Not restored as of last verification -- Milwaukee ultimately completed its own lead-abatement work in the affected schools by December 2025 without direct CDC field support
date_of_action: 2025-04 (staff cuts confirmed; Milwaukee's request denied 2025-04-03)
what_changed: In January 2025, a Milwaukee Public Schools (MPS) student was diagnosed with elevated blood lead levels, traced to flaking lead paint in a school basement bathroom; a subsequent citywide inspection found lead hazards present in 99 MPS schools built before 1978, when lead paint was still legal. On March 26, 2025, MPS and the Milwaukee Health Department formally requested CDC assistance -- an EpiAid deployment, the CDC's standard mechanism for sending expert field support to a local health emergency. On April 3, 2025, Dr. Aaron Bernstein, director of CDC's National Center for Environmental Health/Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, wrote to Milwaukee officials that the agency could not help: 'I sincerely regret to inform you that due to the complete loss of our Lead Program, we will be unable to support you with this EpiAid request.' Milwaukee Health Department Commissioner Dr. Michael Totoraitis said the city had only learned of the program's elimination via that email, with no advance notice. The CDC's lead poisoning prevention program had been eliminated as part of the broader HHS restructuring and reduction-in-force actions of early 2025 (see hhs-early-2025-workforce-purge-hiv-office-elimination for the department-wide purge this program's staff were caught up in). Wisconsin Rep. Gwen Moore sent a formal letter to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over the denial. Milwaukee proceeded to manage the lead-abatement effort using city and state resources without direct federal expert support, completing lead-hazard remediation across the affected schools by late December 2025, roughly ten months after the crisis began. Milwaukee was not the only community left without help: CDC's lead branch was also in the early stages of coordinating with a state health department and tribal officials on an American Indian reservation over child lead-poisoning concerns when the elimination brought that collaboration to a standstill too. Kennedy himself later called eliminating the Lead Poisoning Prevention and Surveillance Branch a mistake, before walking the remark back; HHS subsequently said it intended to continue lead-poisoning prevention work under the planned Administration for a Healthy America.

title: CDC Has Had a Senate-Confirmed Director for Only Four Weeks in 15 Months, Missing the Legal Vacancies Act Deadline
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Vacancy resolved as of August 5, 2026 -- the Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz (nominated April 2026) as permanent CDC director, 51-44, ending a roughly year-long gap since Monarez's August 2025 firing; the documented harm from that gap (missed 210-day Vacancies Act deadline, ~80% center-director turnover) is not undone by the confirmation and remains part of this entry's record
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2026-03 (ongoing vacancy), with an early wave of five center/office-head departures on March 25, 2025
what_changed: In the first 15 months of Trump's second term, CDC has had a Senate-confirmed director for only about four weeks total -- Susan Monarez, who was fired in August 2025 following a clash with HHS Secretary RFK Jr. over vaccination policy. The center-director exodus the WSJ later quantified at ~80% had visible early markers well before that February 2026 analysis: on March 25, 2025 -- the day after the White House announced it would nominate Susan Monarez as CDC director -- five center and office heads departed at once (Leslie Ann Dauphin of the Public Health Infrastructure Center, Dr. Karen Remley of the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Sam Posner of the Office of Science, Debra Lubar of the Office of Policy, Performance and Evaluation, and Leandris Liburd of the Office of Health Equity), on top of three other recent departures -- roughly a third of the agency's senior leadership at that point, per CNN and STAT News. CDC did not announce the departures publicly; they were confirmed by the AP through officials not authorized to discuss them. Since then, the agency has cycled through acting leadership; NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya was named acting CDC director in February 2026, holding both roles simultaneously. Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit ec8078a, which marked this record folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): Abraham's own tenure began just two months before that resignation. CBS News reported that CDC appointed Louisiana Surgeon General Ralph Abraham as its new principal deputy director on December 4, 2025; Abraham had previously halted his own state's vaccine-outreach campaigns and, per CBS, halted mass-vaccination campaigns at CDC as well, continuing a record of undermining vaccine confidence into the federal role. CDC's principal deputy director, Ralph Abraham, abruptly resigned that same February 2026 -- just weeks into the role and the second senior CDC departure that month -- further compounding the agency's leadership instability during Bhattacharya's dual-role acting tenure. By late March 2026, the White House had missed the legal deadline under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, which limits how long an acting officer may serve in place of a Senate-confirmed official to 210 days, without nominating a permanent replacement; HHS said Bhattacharya would continue overseeing CDC by performing the 'delegable duties' of the director role. This leadership vacuum coincides with the active nationwide measles outbreak and other public-health developments this tracker separately documents. A Wall Street Journal analysis found the turmoil extends well beyond the top director seat: CDC has lost approximately 80% of its center directors -- the agency's division-level leadership -- since January 2025 amid resignations, forced departures, and clashes with Kennedy, leaving much of the agency's center-level leadership under temporary or acting management as well. The Journal reported the White House was, as of that reporting, preparing to nominate a permanent CDC director after months of workforce turmoil. The White House nominated Dr. Erica Schwartz -- a retired Navy rear admiral and former deputy surgeon general who had overseen the U.S. Coast Guard's healthcare system -- in April 2026; the Senate confirmed her 51-44 on August 5, 2026, making her the first Senate-confirmed CDC director since Monarez and the first Black woman to hold the post. Her confirmation ends the specific vacancy this entry tracks, roughly a year after Monarez's firing and well after the missed 210-day Vacancies Act deadline; it does not reverse the center-director attrition (~80% turnover) or the other leadership churn documented above, which remain part of the historical record regardless of the vacancy's resolution.

title: CDC Shut Down Its 30-Year Maternal-Mortality Data System and Eliminated the Team That Ran It
institution: CDC Division of Reproductive Health, Department of Health and Human Services
status: Data collection remains disrupted as of the most recent reporting reviewed (early 2026); no restoration of the Division of Reproductive Health's staff or the PRAMS data system to pre-cut levels has been identified in sourcing reviewed.
date_of_action: 2025-01 (PRAMS data-collection software abruptly shut down) through 2025-04 (Division of Reproductive Health workforce cut by roughly two-thirds, PRAMS team eliminated)
what_changed: In January 2025, for the first time in three decades, CDC abruptly shut down the software system used to collect data for the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) -- a CDC/state-health-department partnership survey that is the country's most comprehensive source of data on health behaviors and outcomes before, during, and after pregnancy, widely used by researchers to study maternal mortality and its racial/geographic disparities. In late March and early April 2025, HHS workforce reductions cut the CDC's Division of Reproductive Health staff by roughly two-thirds, eliminating the entire team responsible for running PRAMS -- about 20 people, per AP's reporting. Rep. Diana DeGette sent a formal letter to the acting CDC director on March 12, 2025 seeking answers on PRAMS' status; STAT News reported April 1, 2025 that the program remained 'in limbo' with affected staff placed on administrative leave rather than the underlying data-collection function being restored. The AP's broader May 2025 investigation, examining draft and final HHS budget proposals and interviewing current and former federal employees, found PRAMS was one of more than a dozen federal health-tracking programs effectively eliminated during the administration's first 100 days, alongside separate cuts to CDC programs tracking abortion data, lead poisoning (this database's cdc-lead-poisoning-program-dismantled-2025.json), job-related injuries (cdc-injury-center-drowning-team-elimination-2025.json and its NEISS component), sexual violence, and youth smoking. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0423: the same Division of Reproductive Health RIF also eliminated the small team, in place for over a decade, responsible for the U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use -- national clinical guidelines on safely prescribing contraception to women with conditions including heart disease, lupus, sickle cell disease, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and obesity. Clinicians, advocacy groups, and the fired workers themselves told CBS News (reported July 2025) that without staff to maintain and update the guidelines -- which include specific warnings, such as that combined hormonal contraception poses an unacceptable blood-clot risk for women with sickle cell disease -- providers will be left relying on outdated guidance as medical evidence evolves.

title: CDC Laid Off Its Entire Full-Time Cruise Ship Health Inspection Team During a Record Norovirus Year
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Vessel Sanitation Program
status: Not restored as of last verification -- program continued operating with a skeleton staff of Public Health Service officers
date_of_action: 2025-04 (layoffs confirmed in reporting)
what_changed: In April 2025, all full-time CDC employees working for the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) -- which inspects large cruise ships for sanitation hazards and investigates onboard disease outbreaks -- were laid off, part of the broader April 2025 HHS reduction-in-force that cut roughly 2,400 CDC positions overall (see hhs-early-2025-workforce-purge-hiv-office-elimination.json for the department-wide purge). what_changed: On December 5, 2025, Mark Calabria, OMB's chief statistician, told the Council of Professional Associations on Federal Statistics that the administration had reopened review of the 2024 Biden-era update to federal race/ethnicity data standards -- including new checkboxes for 'Middle Eastern or North African' and a reformatted combined 'What is your race and/or ethnicity?' question -- saying 'we just wanted to be able to take a look at the process and decide where we wanted to end up on a number of these questions,' while cautioning the review was not prejudging any outcome. That review produced a formal proposal: on September 10, 2026, the administration published a Federal Register notice proposing to eliminate the census race and ethnicity question entirely, citing its 'sensitive nature' and a 'reduced need for or usefulness of this information,' and to ban a sexual-orientation question -- reversing the approach used on the 2020 census, which asked same-sex and opposite-sex couples to identify as such. The same proposal formalizes a separate, previously-tested change: excluding non-U.S. citizens without a green card from the census count used for congressional apportionment and Electoral College allocation, a practice never before used in U.S. census history (this apportionment-exclusion piece was already tracked, at its earlier field-test stage, in census-2026-test-citizenship-question-2030.json; that entry's 'separate legal dispute' framing is now superseded by this formal proposal). The public comment period runs through October 13, 2026, ahead of a final rule; a congressional report on the proposed 2030 census questions is due by April 1.

primary_proponent.role: Chief Statistician, Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: Publicly announced the reopened review of the 2024 race/ethnicity standards on December 5, 2025; the review he described led to OMB's September 10, 2026 formal proposal to eliminate the race/ethnicity question.

estimated_impact.summary: Civil rights advocates and demographers warn eliminating the race/ethnicity and sexual-orientation questions, combined with the non-citizen apportionment exclusion, would degrade the federal data used to draw voting districts, enforce the Voting Rights Act, and target anti-discrimination and civil-rights enforcement -- while also shifting congressional apportionment and Electoral College weight toward states and districts with fewer non-citizen residents. NPR Illinois's reporting separately names 'federal funding allocation' among the areas the proposal would affect: Census Bureau data of the kind this proposal would stop collecting or would undercount guides several hundred billion to (per the Bureau's own FY2021 accounting) roughly $2.8 trillion annually in federal program funding distributed by formulas that rely in part on race/ethnicity and population-count data, so degrading that data's granularity or accuracy plausibly misdirects some share of that money away from the communities it's meant to reach -- though no single figure isolates the dollar effect of eliminating the race/ethnicity question specifically, as distinct from the broader census-accuracy question.

title: Commerce Department ban on Census Bureau statistical-noise privacy protections
institution: U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis (Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing (order in effect as of June 2026; could be revoked by a future administration before the 2030 census)
date_of_action: 2026-06 (order issued; effects unfolding through 2030 census preparation)
what_changed: The Commerce Department, which oversees the Census Bureau, issued Department Administrative Order (DAO) 216-26, 'Disclosure Avoidance for Statistical Products,' on June 4, 2026, banning 'noise infusion' -- specifically including both differential privacy and the older 'multiplicative noise infusion' technique - one of the bureau's core techniques for anonymizing survey and administrative-record data before public release, mandated by federal law (13 U.S.C. §8) to protect respondents' confidentiality. Noise infusion has been used for decades, and more recently through a differential-privacy system built under former chief scientist John Abowd, to make it mathematically much harder to re-identify individuals in small-area statistics. The order leaves the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis only one remaining privacy option: 'coarsening' data (releasing broader, less-detailed categories) or not publishing some statistics at all. Data experts warn this could make data for many rural counties and small communities unpublishable, and that 2030 census redistricting data preparation - already underway - will need to be redesigned from scratch. The order followed, and is intertwined with, a separate 2025 lawsuit by America First Legal (co-founded by White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller) challenging the bureau's differential-privacy system, and came after a broader thinning of the bureau's statistical expertise amid Trump administration workforce cuts. It was issued with no public technical rationale, no advance opportunity for outside statisticians to review or comment, and no response from Commerce to a reporter's request for specific examples of the harm it claims to be fixing. Separately, the America First Legal lawsuit referenced above was dismissed in February 2026 by a three-judge federal panel as time-barred (plaintiffs waited too long to sue), which also rejected Rep. Byron Donalds's standing theory. When plaintiffs refiled, they dropped the differential-privacy challenge entirely and now focus solely on a different technique, statistical imputation (used to fill in missing population data) -- meaning the June 2026 noise-infusion ban was not compelled by any court ruling; it was a standalone Commerce Department policy action, issued independent of and after the litigation's core privacy claim had already been abandoned by its own plaintiffs. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- no new court filings or Commerce Department statements identified since the prior update.

estimated_impact.summary: Removing the bureau's primary legally-mandated privacy technique, with no substitute of comparable quality, is expected to shrink or eliminate published statistics for small counties, rural areas, and minority communities, and to force a redesign of 2030 census redistricting-data preparation already underway.

estimated_impact.caveat: Commerce's stated rationale is that 'indiscriminate use of noise infusion...ultimately undermined confidence in the department's products and cast doubt on their integrity,' and that coarsening better 'upholds our duty to safeguard the privacy of those who provide information' - i.e., the administration frames this as a pro-privacy, pro-integrity move, not a cut. Independent data-user advocates (Beth Jarosz, Association of Public Data Users; John Abowd, former Census chief scientist) and an anonymous current bureau employee dispute this, calling the change 'cataclysmic' for data production and noting it removed the normal scientific/public review process. Long-running controversy over the differential-privacy system predates this administration - Alabama Republican officials sued to block it in 2021 - so this is a continuation of a genuine, multi-year methodological dispute, not a one-sided fabrication.

title: Commerce Department bans Census Bureau's main privacy technique, forcing coarser or withheld data
institution: Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis (U.S. Department of Commerce)
status: Finalized -- Department Administrative Order 216-26 in effect
date_of_action: 2026-06 (order reported)
what_changed: The Commerce Department issued Department Administrative Order 216-26, banning the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis from using 'noise infusion' -- a widely-used disclosure-avoidance technique that adds small random statistical variation to published data so individuals can't be re-identified while still allowing detailed, granular statistics to be released. The order designates 'coarsening' (releasing less granular, more aggregated statistics, or withholding some datasets outright) as the preferred disclosure-avoidance method instead, and bars noise infusion for any statistical product going forward. Data scientists and demographers warned the change would force the bureau to either publish blurrier, less-detailed data or withhold some datasets entirely, since coarsening and noise infusion aren't interchangeable substitutes for the same privacy goal.

primary_proponent.name: Howard Lutnick
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Commerce
primary_proponent.note: Department Administrative Order 216-26 was issued under his department's authority; reporting attributes the order to the Commerce Department generally rather than quoting Lutnick personally on this specific decision, so this entry follows the schema's standard for using the highest-ranking accountable official when no more specific individual is on record.

estimated_impact.summary: Detailed Census Bureau and BEA statistics used for redistricting, disaster response, housing policy, and economic planning are expected to become less granular or unavailable, since agencies now have to choose between coarser aggregation and withholding data rather than using the noise-based method that let them publish detailed figures while still protecting privacy.
estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar or headcount figure has been reported for this policy -- the harm is a data-quality/availability degradation rather than a budget or staffing cut, so this entry has no quantified 'figures' the way most GSR entries do. Impact is described by data experts and demographers (Census Bureau's own disclosure-avoidance researchers, academics cited by NPR/Science) rather than an independent audit.

confidence_note: Well-corroborated by numerous independent outlets (NPR, Science, Wyoming Public Media, South Carolina Public Radio, FlowingData) and the Commerce Department's own order text/framing as reported. No formal GAO or Inspector General finding on this specific policy has been identified.

title: CFPB Ordered to Stop All Work, Nearly Defunded — Federal Judge Called It 'Hanging by a Thread'
institution: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
status: Ongoing litigation (as anticipated in this entry's prior update, Vought's acting-director authority under the FVRA expired August 1, 2026; CFPB Deputy Director Mark Paoletta became Acting Director that same day); permanent-director nominee Brian Johnson's Senate Banking Committee vote had not been scheduled as of the most recent reporting reviewed, and Vought is reported to be remaining at CFPB in a senior-adviser capacity pending Johnson's confirmation
date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (stop-work order issued) through 2025-12-30 (federal judge's 'hanging by a thread' ruling)
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, newly installed Acting Director Russell Vought (who simultaneously serves as OMB Director) ordered all CFPB staff and contractors to stop working entirely and not return to agency offices. DOGE personnel were given access to CFPB's HR, payroll, and enforcement-records systems around the same time; Elon Musk posted 'CFPB RIP' on social media. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on February 14, 2025 blocking further firings, data destruction, or funding cuts, but by then CFPB's website had already been taken down and staff locked out of buildings and systems. Vought separately moved to cut off the agency's Federal Reserve funding entirely and canceled roughly $100 million in CFPB contracts. Court filings from CFPB leadership itself, filed in March 2025, proposed shrinking authorized staff from 1,174 to 556, sparing only the legal division (which defends the agency in the litigation over its own dismantling) from cuts. CFPB's top enforcement official, Eric Halperin, resigned in February 2025 as the dismantlement began; his principal deputy, Cara Petersen, served as de facto acting enforcement director for the next four months before she too resigned, on June 10, 2025, telling staff it had been 'devastating to see the Bureau's enforcement function being dismantled through thoughtless reductions in staff, inexplicable dismissals of cases, and terminations of negotiated settlements that let wrongdoers off the hook' -- citing the dismissal of major cases against Capital One and Walmart among the terminated actions. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0454: the Associated Press detailed several of those dismissed cases on July 15, 2025. CFPB dismissed its lawsuit against Walmart and workforce company Branch Messenger, which had accused the companies of deceptively steering delivery drivers into high-fee Branch accounts and sought $10 million in restitution for harmed drivers -- dropped within the administration's first weeks. Navy Federal Credit Union, which had already settled CFPB's unfair/deceptive-overdraft-fee accusations by agreeing to refund members $80 million, saw that consent order dismissed at the credit union's own request after the administration took over, with CFPB giving no public reason. The bureau also abandoned its suit against Zelle's parent company (Early Warning Services) and several of the nation's largest partner banks, which had accused them of failing to protect customers from what the lawsuit itself claimed was approximately $870 million in fraud losses accumulated over seven years. On the layoffs themselves, D.C. Circuit rulings moved back and forth over several months: an April 11, 2025 panel order granted a partial stay allowing some layoffs to proceed, and it was under that narrow window, around April 17-18, 2025, that about 1,400 employees who had chosen to remain received reduction-in-force notices -- a reduction that would have left only about 200 of the agency's original ~1,700 staff; NTEU, the union representing CFPB employees, argued the 24-hour, no-notice process made a legally required 'particularized assessment' of each position implausible. The D.C. Circuit reinstated the full preliminary injunction on April 28, 2025, blocking further reductions pending appeal (oral argument was set for May 16, 2025), before a different D.C. Circuit panel lifted that injunction again on August 15, 2025, allowing the RIF to proceed toward the ~200-staff target. Separately, on July 4, 2025, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut the statutory cap on CFPB's annual funding request from the Federal Reserve by roughly half (from 12% to 6.5% of the Federal Reserve's total 2009 operating expenses, adjusted for inflation -- about $823 million to $446 million) -- a cut CFPB told employees by September 2025 could force it to cut jobs just to make payroll. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0506: ProPublica reported August 12, 2025 that many of the same Republican lawmakers who voted for that funding cut had themselves routed thousands of constituent complaints to CFPB for help -- Sen. John Cornyn's office had referred more than 800 constituents to the agency, the most of any current lawmaker from either party, while Reps. Darrell Issa and Rob Wittman's offices had each referred more than 100; Issa's spokesperson said most referrals 'occurred several years ago' and reflected 'a conventional way' to handle constituents' consumer issues. CFPB also rolled back two Biden-era consumer protections in this period: on July 11, 2025, a federal court in Texas vacated CFPB's rule barring medical debt from credit reports, at the Bureau's own joint request with industry plaintiffs in Cornerstone Credit Union League v. CFPB; and effective October 29, 2025, CFPB formally rescinded a separate Biden-era rule that would have required nonbank financial companies with a history of breaking consumer-protection laws to register in a public 'repeat offender' database, followed in early November 2025 by an interpretive rule declaring that state laws in 15 states banning medical-debt credit reporting are preempted by the Fair Credit Reporting Act -- 'salt in the wound,' one consumer advocate said, on top of the rule vacatur three months earlier. By December 2025, more than 30% of CFPB's authorized staff had departed. On December 30, 2025, the same federal judge overseeing the case rejected the administration's argument that Vought could lawfully withhold the agency's funding, ordering him to request continued Federal Reserve funding, which he did -- keeping CFPB funded through at least March 2026. A February 2026 report from Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office estimated that changes imposed after Vought took control of CFPB had cost Americans at least $19 billion in lost financial relief -- $15 billion from two rescinded rules (an overdraft-fee cap projected to save $5 billion/year, and a credit-card late-fee cap projected to save roughly $10 billion) plus nearly $4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and unfulfilled consent orders. In May 2026, CFPB removed roughly 1,700 web pages of consumer advisories, press releases, and testimony predating February 2025 from its public website (The Guardian's later, more precise count -- comparing the current site against Internet Archive Wayback Machine snapshots and a mirror site maintained by a former CFPB employee -- found at least 2,200 pages deleted as of early June 2026; the two figures describe the same underlying deletion campaign rather than separate events, with the most common deleted-page topics being enforcement, mortgages, banking, and rulemaking; CFPB also deleted its blog entirely and removed all press releases predating February 2025). Also in May 2026, acting CFPB Director Russell Vought ordered all remaining CFPB staff -- including roughly 450 workers previously based out-of-state -- to relocate to a new, smaller Washington, D.C. headquarters, ending remote work entirely; the bureau terminated leases on all four of its regional offices (San Francisco, Atlanta, Chicago, and New York). The new headquarters space, at 445 12th Street SW, has capacity for only about 550 workers -- roughly half the bureau's remaining headcount of approximately 1,100 -- a mismatch reporting characterized as designed to drive further attrition beyond the office's stated capacity limit alone. Relocation began June 1, 2026 with a hard compliance deadline of August 31 or termination. In June 2026, Trump nominated Brian Johnson -- a former CFPB deputy director under Kathy Kraninger and current Capital One executive -- to be permanent CFPB Director. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, said: 'Starting in August, Russ Vought can no longer legally serve as Donald Trump's hatchet man at the CFPB. So here comes the next hatchet man to try to finish the job.' Also in June 2026, CFPB removed all prior public reports describing its own supervisory activity. On June 22, 2026, Senate Banking Committee Democrats sent a formal letter to Acting Director Vought demanding an accounting of the deleted content and its legal basis. Senior leadership reported to the new headquarters starting July 6, 2026, with full D.C.-area staff required back five days a week by July 13. The Senate Banking Committee held Brian Johnson's confirmation hearing on July 23, 2026; Johnson declined to endorse eliminating the CFPB and said he keeps an 'open mind' about staffing levels, while deflecting questions about the agency reportedly dropping 42 enforcement cases against presidential donors. Separately, the D.C. Circuit remanded NTEU v. CFPB (the litigation over the Bureau's proposed 2026 reduction-in-force) back to the district court and held the appeal in abeyance, after CFPB and NTEU jointly asked for a stay pending Johnson's confirmation so he could decide whether to proceed with, modify, or abandon the RIF plan. Committee advancement is expected before the August recess, with a full Senate vote anticipated in September 2026 -- meaning Johnson is very unlikely to be confirmed before Vought's August 1 FVRA deadline, raising the practical likelihood that Acting Deputy Director Mark Paoletta becomes acting director in the interim (if Johnson is not confirmed by August 1, 2026, Paoletta would become acting director in Vought's place). Ahead of a Vought oversight hearing, a July 2026 follow-up report from Sen. Warren's office found an additional $7.5 billion in costs in the first half of 2026 -- ~$15 billion cumulative from abandoning the credit-card late-fee cap, ~$7.5 billion from repealing the overdraft-fee cap, and ~$4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and abandoned settlements/consent orders (including the 42 dropped enforcement cases against presidential donors) -- bringing the cumulative total Warren's office attributes to the CFPB rollbacks to up to $26.5 billion. Update 2026-08-17: as this entry's prior update anticipated, Vought's FVRA-based authority to run CFPB expired August 1, 2026, and Deputy Director Mark Paoletta -- CFPB's chief legal officer -- became Acting Director that day. Reporting indicates Vought is expected to remain involved at CFPB in a senior-adviser role even after formally leaving the acting-director post, pending Johnson's confirmation. As of the most recent reporting reviewed, the Senate Banking Committee had not yet scheduled a vote on Johnson's nomination following his July 23 hearing, meaning the 'before the August recess' committee-vote timeline this entry previously anticipated has slipped. Update 2026-08-29: the Senate Banking Committee had not scheduled a vote on Brian Johnson's nomination as of this update, following his July 23, 2026 confirmation hearing. Mark Paoletta continues serving as Acting Director since his August 1, 2026 transition, with Russell Vought reported remaining at CFPB in a senior-adviser capacity -- no material change from the prior update.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Acting Director of CFPB (concurrently Director of the Office of Management and Budget)
primary_proponent.note: Vought was one of the architects of Project 2025, which explicitly called for Congress to abolish the CFPB (p. 837 of the document). He has publicly criticized CFPB staff in interviews, telling The Charlie Kirk Show that 'all they want to do is weaponize the tools of financial law against basically small mom-and-pop lenders and other small financial institutions.' This is the same official whose separate impoundment-related actions (NIH funding, broader OMB spending disputes) are covered in other entries across this project's Government Services Redirected and Cabinet-Level Legal Exposure trackers.

estimated_impact.summary: The presiding federal judge's own characterization is unusually direct for a legal ruling: she wrote that the administration was 'actively and unabashedly trying to shut the agency down' through funding cuts after being blocked from doing so through layoffs, and that CFPB 'is hanging by a thread.' The agency's own reporting states it had returned $19.7 billion to consumers since its 2010 creation as of January 2025 -- the scale of consumer-facing enforcement work now substantially curtailed. Former 13-year CFPB attorney Lisa Rosenthal, who resigned after the stop-work order, described the halted work (protecting victims of predatory payday loans, supervising student loan and auto-financing practices) in terms of what it no longer was: 'This work that I had carried out for these decades and that I cared so deeply about -- this was no longer that work.'

This litigation (NTEU v. Vought and the related Baltimore case) remains ongoing and unresolved as of this entry's last update; the December 2025 ruling addressed only the funding question, not the broader dismantlement question.

title: CFTC Lost 24% of Its Staff, Including Its Entire Chicago Enforcement Team, Following Court-Cleared Federal Purges
institution: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)
status: Ongoing -- staffing reductions (layoffs, buyouts, early retirements) continued into 2026, with the agency at its lowest staffing level in 15 years as of February 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07-17 (initial post-ruling layoffs begin) through 2026-02 (staffing figures confirm 24% cumulative reduction)
what_changed: On July 17, 2025, days after the Supreme Court's July 8, 2025 ruling in Trump v. AFGE cleared the way for agency-wide federal reductions in force, the CFTC -- the independent agency responsible for regulating derivatives, commodities futures, and (since 2023) significant crypto-market enforcement -- began layoffs affecting more than two dozen employees across its enforcement, market oversight, administration, and data divisions. The cuts continued via a combination of layoffs, buyouts, and early retirements through 2026: by February 2026, the agency had 535 employees, down from 636 full-time staff in fiscal 2025 -- a 24% reduction, leaving the CFTC at its lowest staffing level in 15 years. The enforcement division was hit particularly hard: requested funding supported only 108 enforcement positions for the coming year, down from 140 filled positions in 2025 (a 23% drop), and the CFTC's Chicago office -- a historically significant post given Chicago's status as a major U.S. derivatives-trading hub -- went from 20 enforcement lawyers to zero. Update 2026-08-18: the CFTC's own Inspector General, in a January 2026 report, put the reduction at 708 full-time-equivalent staff at the end of fiscal 2024 down to 556 at the end of fiscal 2025 -- a 21% one-year drop, measured on a different fiscal-year-end basis than this entry's existing 636-to-535 (24%) figures from Cryptopolitan's February 2026 reporting (see caveat below on the differing baselines). Enforcement output has fallen sharply alongside the staffing losses: the CFTC brought 58 enforcement actions and collected $17.1 billion in monetary relief in 2024, versus just 11 enforcement actions and $1 billion in the year leading up to January 2026. In July 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren asked the Government Accountability Office to investigate whether the CFTC's workforce reductions -- which she put at 25% since January 2025, a third measurement point distinct from the two fiscal-year figures above -- have contributed to the enforcement decline. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig has publicly defended the smaller staff, saying the agency is leaning on AI and automation to make up for the cuts. Update (2026-08-30 recheck): Politico reporting, cited in Banking Dive's July 23, 2026 coverage of Sen. Warren's GAO request, states the CFTC was offering staff buyouts and early retirement as recently as June 2026 -- a period during which Chairman Michael Selig was publicly describing the agency as actively hiring, a tension not previously captured in this entry's account of Selig's public defense of the staffing situation. Warren's GAO request specifically asks the watchdog to determine whether the cuts complied with federal law, their impact on CFTC's regulatory mandate, and whether they contributed to, detracted from, or had no impact on fraud and waste at the agency -- a fuller framing than previously captured. No GAO findings had been published as of this recheck.

title: CIA Offers Buyouts Agency-Wide and Freezes Hiring to Realign Workforce with New Priorities
institution: Central Intelligence Agency
status: Implemented -- buyout offer and hiring freeze took effect February 2025; broader multi-year workforce reduction plan reported as ongoing. Updated 2026-08-30: the pace of departures is now reported as historic/unprecedented and is overwhelming the retirement-processing system, with new retirees facing months-long waits for their first pension check.
date_of_action: 2025-02-04 (buyout offer announced, February 6 deadline) through at least 2025-05 (multi-year reduction plan reported)
what_changed: On February 4, 2025, the CIA under newly confirmed Director John Ratcliffe offered buyouts to its entire workforce, giving employees until February 6, 2025 to accept -- a two-day window -- in exchange for eight months of pay plus benefits if they chose to resign. The agency simultaneously imposed a hiring freeze and began reviewing already-extended conditional job offers to new recruits, indicating offers not aligned with the agency's new focus were likely to be rescinded. Ratcliffe framed the changes as realigning the CIA toward new priorities, including a greater focus on the Western Hemisphere (targeting drug cartels and other threats not traditionally treated as top-tier adversaries) and covert operations, rather than legacy Cold War-era regional priorities. Beginning around March 7, 2025, the CIA also began terminating some probationary employees (generally those with fewer than two years on the job) citing a review of personnel suitability, following a federal judge's ruling allowing Director Ratcliffe to dismiss employees at his discretion -- a distinct, involuntary action layered on top of the earlier voluntary buyout program. National-security reporting at the time warned that the cuts came as U.S. intelligence had confirmed Russia and China were actively attempting to recruit recently fired or at-risk federal employees with security clearances, using LinkedIn, TikTok, and job postings, raising concern that thinning the intelligence workforce during a period of active foreign recruitment efforts compounded the risk. Reporting in May 2025 indicated this was part of a broader, multi-year plan across U.S. intelligence agencies to reduce the CIA's workforce by approximately 1,200 positions, with several hundred employees already having taken early retirement or the buyout by that point. The Washington Post reported August 20, 2026 that the pace of CIA retirements and resignations by mid/late 2026 had become historic -- current and former officials described it as outstripping anything in recent memory -- and, combined with OPM's own staffing cutbacks, is overwhelming the federal retirement-processing system: new CIA retirees can wait as long as nine months for their first full pension check, receiving only interim payments (60-80% of the eventual benefit) in the meantime. Some employees have reportedly withdrawn retirement paperwork already filed because they can't sustain the income gap. Precise current departure totals remain classified, so this doesn't update the 1,200-position target itself, but it is independent evidence the pace of departures is real and significant enough to strain a downstream federal system outside the CIA's own control. This reporting was corroborated across the Washington Examiner, MSN, and multiple regional reprints of the same wire/syndicated account. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): identified the structural cause behind the pension-processing backlog this entry already documents -- OPM's own workforce, the agency responsible for processing retirement claims government-wide (including CIA retirees'), fell by roughly a third, from just over 3,000 employees in FY2024 to about 1,980 in FY2026, while average retirement-claims processing time rose from 79 days in October 2025 to 109 days by July 2026. Directly-fetched OPM data corroborates the backlog's scale independent of the cause figures: OPM's Pennsylvania retirement operations center had 34,587 pending claims as of October 2025, the highest level since a roughly 36,000-claim peak during the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2022, against a prior (Biden-era) steady-state goal of roughly 13,000 pending claims. The CIA has responded by moving additional personnel into its own Retirement Branch to help work through the backlog; retiree hardship reports describe former officials drawing down savings, taking second mortgages, or delaying planned retirements because they could not afford months without expected income.

title: CISA Lost Roughly One-Third of Its Workforce, Including Election Security and Threat-Sharing Capacity
institution: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing (Kristi Noem was replaced as DHS Secretary by Markwayne Mullin, confirmed March 24, 2026; Mullin says the president has met with a likely CISA director nominee; DHS plans roughly 600 new CISA hires once a director is confirmed, with an initial 329-role 'mission-critical' hiring plan already underway -- about 180 tentative offers were out by the end of June 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2026-06 (rolling cuts across multiple rounds: buyouts, layoffs, forced reassignments)
what_changed: Since January 2025, CISA -- the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency, created in 2018 specifically to coordinate federal response to critical infrastructure attacks -- lost roughly 1,000 employees, about one-third of its workforce, through a combination of buyout offers, early retirements, formal layoffs (reduction-in-force notices), and Management Directed Reassignments transferring CISA staff to ICE, CBP, FEMA, and the Federal Protective Service (refusing a reassignment could be grounds for termination). DHS Secretary Kristi Noem personally halted federal funding for the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) in March 2025, eliminating roughly $8.3 million of its remaining 2025 budget -- MS-ISAC provided threat-sharing services to state and local governments. The cuts disproportionately hit CISA's election security and disinformation-monitoring functions, which had drawn Republican criticism as politically biased 'censorship' under the prior administration. The agency has operated without a permanent, Senate-confirmed director since January 2025. The early 2025 cuts had specific, named costs: by March 4, 2025, NOTUS reported over 100 CISA cybersecurity experts had been laid off, including agents specifically assigned to track Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon, the Chinese state-sponsored hacking campaigns that had already infiltrated U.S. telecom networks and critical infrastructure; by March 8, 2025, CBS News reported the toll had grown to 130+, including top recruits working on CyberSentry, a program built specifically to detect cyberattacks against the U.S. power grid, pipelines, and water systems. On March 5, 2025, former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce testified to Congress that the mass federal firings -- more than 100,000 workers government-wide by that point, including 130+ from CISA -- would set back U.S. cyber defenses against China. Joyce continued sounding this warning publicly: at the Black Hat security conference in August 2025, CISA spokesperson Marci McCarthy defended the staffing purges as a return to the agency's 'core mission,' while Joyce countered that the U.S. had 'backslid' and lost critical national-defense capability, with nearly a third of CISA's workforce gone by that point. Congress's own October 2025 government shutdown compounded the damage months before the separate February 2026 DHS funding lapse described below: the Washington Post reported only about 35% of CISA staff remained active during the October shutdown even as ransomware and Chinese cyberattacks intensified, and Politico reported the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act -- the law providing legal liability protection for companies that voluntarily share cyber-threat data with the government -- lapsed during the same shutdown, prompting some companies to halt that cooperation entirely. Later that month, House Democrats formally accused DHS, under Secretary Noem, of unlawfully reassigning CISA cybersecurity staff to ICE, CBP, and the Federal Protective Service during the shutdown -- the same Management Directed Reassignment mechanism described above -- alleging the diversions violated the Antideficiency Act; a separate New York Times report the same week noted the cuts had also reached the State Department's cyber-diplomacy function. During the shutdown, on November 10, 2025, WIRED reported the Congressional Budget Office itself was hacked by a suspected foreign actor, an incident experts tied directly to the shutdown-driven halt in routine federal patching, monitoring, and device management. In December 2025, Bloomberg reported the administration eliminated CISA's retention-incentive pay program -- a tool used to keep cyber defenders from leaving for better-paying private-sector jobs -- despite the agency already having lost over a third of its staff; the change exposed many remaining employees to pay cuts of up to 25%, a further attrition risk on top of the losses already documented here. The February 2026 DHS funding lapse compounded this attrition: The New York Times reported CISA furloughed more than half of its remaining workforce during the shutdown, leaving fewer than 1,000 employees on duty at the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency during the funding gap; ABC News separately reported that with DHS unfunded for 45 days during that same shutdown, CISA furloughed roughly 60% of its remaining workforce, disrupting vulnerability assessments and further weakening federal cyber defenses at a time when officials were warning of rising Iran-linked cyber threats to critical infrastructure, including power, water, and federal civilian networks. Also in February 2026, acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala moved to reassign two senior career officials -- CIO Bob Costello (CISA's CIO for over four years) and acting Chief Human Capital Officer Kevin Diana -- giving them seven days to accept new roles elsewhere in DHS or resign, following an earlier unsuccessful attempt to oust Costello over a contracting-decision dispute that other political appointees had previously intervened to stop. Kristi Noem was replaced as DHS Secretary by Markwayne Mullin, confirmed by the Senate 54-45 on March 24, 2026. In April 2026, Sean Plankey, Trump's first nominee to lead CISA, withdrew his own nomination, writing 'After thirteen months since my initial nomination, it has become clear the Senate will not confirm me' -- the nomination had been held up by a mix of Democratic senators (Ron Wyden, over a withheld telecom-security report) and Republican senators (Rick Scott, over an unrelated Coast Guard shipbuilding dispute), plus broader holds affecting all DHS nominees. CISA is now led by acting director Nick Andersen. Mullin has since said the president has met with a likely CISA director nominee (not yet named or formally nominated as of this update) and that DHS believes CISA needs roughly 600 new hires, though a full rebuild can't proceed in earnest until a director is confirmed. CISA has begun an initial hiring plan for 329 'mission-critical' roles, with about 180 tentative job offers extended by the end of June 2026 -- the first concrete numbers behind CISA's previously-announced, more general 2026 hiring push, which agency officials had cited the workforce reductions as having hampered preparedness for potential conflict with China. By June 2026, of CISA's authorized 3,292 positions, only 2,324 were actually filled -- a nearly 1,000-position gap. Five of the agency's ten regional directors were serving only in acting capacity, disrupting the primary points of contact state and local governments rely on for federal cybersecurity assistance. Update 2026-07-27: state election officials from both parties told USA Today that, ahead of the 2026 midterms, they no longer expect federal agencies to reliably share election-threat intelligence with them -- a direct downstream consequence of the CISA staffing cuts and reduced regional-director capacity already described above. States say they're increasingly relying on private technology companies and nonprofits to fill the gap in federal threat-sharing coordination.

title: Federal Indigent-Defense Funding Ran Out for Nearly Three Months, Leaving 12,000+ Court-Appointed Lawyers Unpaid
institution: Federal Judiciary -- Defender Services (Criminal Justice Act panel attorney program)
status: Resolved for FY2025 arrears by a later appropriation, but the underlying funding mechanism (annual Defender Services appropriation) remains subject to future continuing-resolution risk
date_of_action: 2025-03 (continuing resolution freezes judicial-branch funding at FY2024 levels) through 2025-10-01 (payments resume) and into 2026 (arrears repayment sought)
what_changed: A continuing resolution Congress passed in March 2025 to fund the government for FY2025 froze all Judicial Branch funding at FY2024 levels. Because Defender Services funding needs grow year-over-year with caseload, that freeze meant the Criminal Justice Act (CJA) panel-attorney program -- which pays private attorneys, investigators, paralegals, expert witnesses, and interpreters appointed to represent criminal defendants who cannot afford counsel -- ran roughly $130 million short of what the judiciary had requested. The program's funds were depleted on July 3, 2025, and payments to CJA panel attorneys and support staff stopped; the Judiciary told them they would be paid once Congress passed a new budget. The lapse dragged on nearly three months -- the longest such pause on record -- worsened by the fall 2025 government shutdown, which delayed the appropriations process that would have restored funding. During the gap, some CJA attorneys refused new indigent-defendant cases or took out loans to stay afloat, straining already-overworked federal public defenders forced to absorb the difference, and delaying some trials. The Judiciary requested $116 million in supplemental funding specifically to cover the missed FY2025 payments, folding that figure into its $1.77 billion total FY2026 Defender Services funding request. Payments resumed October 1, 2025 with the start of the new fiscal year, though some CJA attorneys reported continuing to wait for full back-payment into 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Congress (bipartisan continuing resolution, signed by President Trump)
primary_proponent.role: Legislative and executive branches jointly responsible for the FY2025 funding mechanism
primary_proponent.note: The March 2025 continuing resolution that froze Judicial Branch funding at FY2024 levels, without adjusting for Defender Services' growing caseload costs, directly caused the shortfall; the administration's own role was signing that CR into law and, separately, presiding over the fall 2025 shutdown that delayed the fix.

estimated_impact.summary: Thousands of federally appointed defense lawyers and their support staff went unpaid for nearly three months -- the longest such lapse on record -- straining the constitutional right to counsel for indigent criminal defendants, delaying some trials, and forcing overworked federal public defenders to absorb cases panel attorneys declined to take without pay.
