estimated_impact.caveat: This is a funding-mechanism failure (a flat-funded continuing resolution not scaling with caseload, compounded by a separate shutdown) rather than a targeted policy decision to cut indigent defense specifically -- no sourcing reviewed suggested the administration or Congress intended to defund CJA representation as such. The constitutional/due-process harm (Sixth Amendment right to counsel) is a documented risk this entry's sourcing describes, not a quantified count of dismissed cases or convictions overturned as a direct result.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the funding mechanism, the shortfall amount, the payment lapse's duration, and its effects -- this entry draws directly on the Judiciary's own public statements (U.S. Courts, Defender Services Office) corroborated by CBS News, the Daily Record, Maryland Lawyers Media, Virginia Lawyers Weekly, and the Death Penalty Information Center. The causal chain (CR freeze -> shortfall -> shutdown delay -> nearly 3-month lapse) is consistently reported across all sources reviewed. This entry attributes responsibility to the funding mechanism Congress passed and Trump signed, and to the separate shutdown that delayed the fix -- not to a specific administration decision to target indigent defense, since no sourcing reviewed supports that stronger claim.

title: NOAA Fired Climate.gov's Entire Content Team; the Site Was Later Shut Down Entirely, Then Resurrected by Former Staff

what_changed: On May 31, 2025, NOAA fired the roughly 10-person contract team responsible for producing and publishing new content on Climate.gov, a public-facing NOAA website providing science-based climate information and education to the public for over a decade. The firing eliminated the entire content-production staff, effectively halting new content indefinitely. Rebecca Lindsey, Climate.gov's former program manager, told The Guardian the action was 'a very deliberate, targeted attack,' not incidental collateral from broader NOAA cuts. In June 2026, former NOAA employees launched an independent replacement site recreating Climate.gov's climate-data tools and educational content outside of government control, in response to the shutdown.

title: Administration Strips 'Climate' From Federal Research Funding, Websites, and Course Materials
institution: Multiple federal science and research-funding agencies, government-wide
status: Ongoing -- through at least March 2026, per Grist's NSF grant-title analysis showing the pattern continuing and deepening
what_changed: The Guardian reported on February 21, 2025 that the administration was cutting funding for scientific research that mentioned 'climate,' stripping grants from affected projects both domestically and abroad, altering government websites and course materials to remove the term, and in some cases forcing researchers to remove or retitle studies specifically to avoid the word in order to remain eligible for funding or publication. USA Today's July 2025 reporting found this pattern continuing at NOAA specifically: scientists described being told to avoid the word 'climate' in their work, alongside operational tool cuts including Saildrone ocean-monitoring devices going undeployed and forecasting quality suffering as a result of the broader staffing and budget cuts documented elsewhere in this database. Update 2026-08-17: Grist reported (March 27, 2026) that NSF grant titles mentioning "climate change" fell from 889 in 2023 to 148 in 2025 -- a 77% drop -- with a corresponding rise in the substitute term "extreme weather," evidence the pattern this entry documents continued and deepened through 2025. The same reporting identified a March 2025 USDA Agricultural Research Service memo, obtained by the outlet More Perfect Union, banning more than 100 words and phrases from agency communications and research materials, roughly a third of them climate-related (including "climate change," "global warming," "climate science," and "carbon sequestration," alongside unrelated banned terms like "DEI"). Ethan Roberts, union president at USDA's National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research, and Trent Ford, Illinois's state climatologist, were both quoted describing having personally altered their own language in proposals and public communications to avoid the banned terms. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 41): a March 2026 Wyden/Investigate Midwest review of the same USDA Agricultural Research Service memo found the 110-term banned-word list extended well beyond climate-specific language -- including "clean water," "safe drinking water," "equity," and "microplastics." Sen. Ron Wyden, Reps. Andrea Salinas, Chellie Pingree, and Jill Tokuda, joined by 22 additional colleagues, sent USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins an April 11, 2025 letter -- predating this entry's own 2026-08-08 creation date by nearly four months and missed by both prior rechecks -- warning the banned-word list would harm rural communities facing wildfires, drought, and food insecurity, calling it "an intentional effort to hinder, distort, and improperly steer federal scientific work in the name of political expediency." Separately, Government Executive's own March 2026 reporting on the same NSF grant-title data found "DEI"-related terms have vanished from NSF grants entirely, with "clean energy" and "pollution" also declining, though less sharply than "climate change." A broader, separately tracked mechanism -- an OMB rule proposed June 2026 that would give political appointees final say over federal research grant awards, with an American Meteorological Society scientist specifically warning it could chill hurricane and heat-wave warnings given climate change's politicization -- would escalate this entry's self-censorship pattern into outright political control of funding decisions; that rule's own status and timeline are tracked in this database's separate white-house-200b-research-funding-overhaul-2026 entry, not duplicated here.

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration

primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing this cross-agency language and funding policy; it is documented as a coordinated, government-wide pattern rather than one agency's isolated decision, distinct from (though related to) the agency-specific climate-research funding cuts documented in this database's separate NOAA entry.

estimated_impact.summary: A form of research suppression operating through language control rather than direct funding cuts alone -- researchers whose work touches climate topics faced pressure to retitle or reframe their work to remain fundable, a chilling effect on climate science distinct from (and compounding) direct budget cuts to climate research documented elsewhere in this tracker

title: CMS Rescinded Guidance That Encouraged States to Use Medicaid Funds for Housing, Food, and Other Health-Related Social Needs
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
status: Rescission in effect since March 4, 2025. States' existing approved Section 1115 waivers are not immediately eliminated, but face uncertain odds at renewal; new waiver applications are now evaluated case-by-case without the prior encouraging framework, which multiple outlets reported will likely make them harder to obtain.
what_changed: On March 4, 2025, CMS issued an informational bulletin rescinding Biden-era guidance -- a November 2023 bulletin, a December 2024 bulletin, and an accompanying 2023 Health-Related Social Needs (HRSN) coverage framework -- that had outlined and encouraged states' use of Medicaid Section 1115 demonstration waivers to cover housing assistance, nutrition supports, and other non-traditional "health-related social needs." CMS spokesperson Catherine Howden said the prior guidance "distracted the Medicaid program from its core mission: providing excellent health outcomes," and that ending it would prevent "draining of resources" from services CMS characterized as duplicative of other federal programs such as SNAP and HUD housing vouchers. North Carolina pioneered the HRSN waiver model during Trump's first term, using Medicaid funds to cover security deposits, first month's rent, transportation to medical appointments, wheelchair ramps, and fresh-produce prescriptions; at least 24 additional states had gone on to launch similar programs, with California's CalAIM program (launched 2022) the largest, committing $12 billion over five years and generating approximately 577,000 referrals for benefits, and Oregon's program covering home-delivered meals, rental assistance, and climate-control devices. As of the March 2025 rescission, 18 states had CMS-approved Section 1115 waivers specifically addressing HRSN. CMS's new policy does not immediately terminate those 18 states' existing approved waivers, but reporting at the time noted they could face challenges at renewal, while new state applications are now considered on a rolling, case-by-case basis without reference to the rescinded framework -- a standard multiple outlets reported will likely make approval harder to obtain going forward.

estimated_impact.summary: CMS withdrew the federal guidance and framework that had encouraged states to use Medicaid funds to address housing, food, and other social needs -- a model already adopted or in progress in 25+ states -- replacing it with case-by-case review that multiple outlets reported will make future HRSN waiver approvals harder to obtain, while leaving existing approved programs' renewal prospects uncertain.

title: Trump Unilaterally Withdrew From the Biden-Era Columbia Basin Salmon Agreement With Northwest Tribes, Reviving Two Decades of Dam Litigation

title: Community Health Centers Serving 32-34 Million Patients Faced a Grant Freeze, a Lapsed Federal Fund, and OBBBA Medicaid Cuts All at Once
institution: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA); federally qualified community health centers nationwide
status: Ongoing -- Community Health Center Fund extended only through December 2026 via the Feb. 3, 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act, with no multi-year reauthorization secured; underlying Medicaid-revenue pressure from OBBBA continues
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Medicaid funding freeze and proposed budget cuts first threaten centers) through 2026-02 (short-term Community Health Center Fund reauthorization)
what_changed: Community health centers -- federally qualified clinics serving roughly 32-34 million patients nationally, 90% of them at or below 200% of the federal poverty level -- faced four compounding federal funding and administrative threats across 2025-2026. First, beginning around March 2025, a Trump administration freeze on already-approved federal grants left health centers in at least 10 states experiencing payment delays, on top of a broader Medicaid funding freeze and proposed budget cuts that advocates warned could force closures or service reductions; centers rely on roughly $4.4 billion in annual federal grants (versus the $5.8 billion advocates say is needed) plus Medicaid, which made up 43% of the $46.7 billion in 2023 health-center revenue nationally. Second, HRSA itself -- the $12-billion-a-year HHS agency that administers this and other grant programs to clinics, rural hospitals, and workforce initiatives -- lost about a quarter of its roughly 2,700-person workforce between February and August 2025 across two rounds of cuts (a 7% RIF on February 14, 2025, followed by a larger DOGE-driven reduction on March 27, 2025), including analysts, auditors, grant managers, and nursing consultants; DOGE reportedly cut 40% of staff specifically at HRSA's Bureau of Primary Health Care, the office that directly oversees the Health Center Program funding these clinics, a direct contributor to the payment-processing delays documented above. Third, the Community Health Center Fund -- which provides about 70% of centers' federal funding -- was extended only to September 30, 2025, and then lapsed when Congress failed to pass renewal legislation before the government shutdown began; a temporary extension to January 30, 2026 was included in the continuing resolution that ended the 43-day shutdown in November 2025, and a further extension through December 2026 (with a modest increase to $4.6 billion for FY2026) came via the February 3, 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act -- short-term stopgaps rather than the multi-year reauthorization advocates had sought. Fourth, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid provisions layered a projected $32 billion five-year revenue loss onto the sector, per a Commonwealth Fund estimate, compounding the funding and staffing uncertainty. Trump's proposed FY2026 budget separately called for eliminating HRSA entirely, along with specific programs including rural hospital grants, workforce training, Ryan White HIV/AIDS programs, and emergency medical services for children. An analysis cited by health-center advocates found one in four community health centers could close or reduce services within two years absent increased funding, and concrete harm had already begun by late 2025: a rural New Hampshire community health center shuttered, and a Des Moines, Iowa hospital system laid off dozens of employees and closed a clinic explicitly citing its 'ongoing response to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.' Light-touch update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): beyond the Community Health Center Fund's Dec. 2026 mandatory-funding expiration already documented above, health centers also rely on a separate, smaller stream of annual discretionary Section 330 appropriations that runs on the standard federal fiscal-year cycle and expires September 30, 2026 -- a second, nearer-term funding cliff that requires its own timely congressional action independent of the CHCF extension. No reporting reviewed indicates either deadline has been further extended or resolved since the February 2026 appropriations act.

title: Trump Fires Librarian of Congress and Register of Copyrights; Appeals Court Orders Reinstatement Amid Unsigned-Certificate Chaos
institution: Library of Congress / U.S. Copyright Office
status: Ongoing -- Perlmutter reinstated pending appeal since Sept. 10, 2025; Supreme Court deferred ruling on the administration's stay application as of Nov. 2025
date_of_action: 2025-05-08 (Hayden fired) through 2025-05-10 (Perlmutter fired); litigation ongoing into 2026
what_changed: On the evening of May 8, 2025, Deputy Director of Presidential Personnel Trent Morse emailed Dr. Carla Hayden, the first woman and first African American Librarian of Congress, a two-sentence notice terminating her effective immediately (CBS News, Library Journal, May 2025). Hayden had been targeted since February 2025 by the American Accountability Foundation's 'DEI Watch List,' which also named Register of Copyrights Shira Perlmutter (NPR, June 2025). Trump then named Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche acting Librarian of Congress; on May 10, Blanche executed the removal of Perlmutter and sought to install Paul Perkins, an Associate Deputy Attorney General, as Acting Register of Copyrights, with Brian Nieves as acting deputy librarian (Publishers Weekly, May 2025). On May 12, Perkins and Nieves went to the Library of Congress carrying a White House letter asserting their new roles, but Library General Counsel Meg Williams and staff denied them building-badge access to the Copyright Office; staff called U.S. Capitol Police, and the two officials left voluntarily after being asked to (The Daily Beast, Publishers Weekly, May 2025) -- a more concrete confrontation than some contemporaneous coverage's looser framing that the replacements simply 'never showed up to work.' Perlmutter sued in Perlmutter v. Blanche (filed May 22, 2025), arguing the President has no authority to remove the Register directly and that Blanche, himself installed without the Librarian-appointment process the statute requires, had no authority to remove her either (Authors Alliance, NPR, May 2025). With no Senate-unaffected Register in place, the Copyright Office continued issuing registration certificates but without the Register's signature, prompting law-firm client alerts warning of downstream validity questions for registrants relying on those certificates in infringement litigation (Venable LLP, Copyright Lately, June 2025); the vacancy also left the office's pending AI-related policy guidance -- including its copyright-and-AI report released just before Perlmutter's firing -- without a confirmed Register to see it through (Wired, Deadline, May-June 2025). A district court initially declined to block the removal (IPWatchdog, July 2025), but on September 10, 2025 the D.C. Circuit granted Perlmutter an injunction pending appeal, reinstating her as Register while the case proceeds on the merits (NISO, Patently-O, Roll Call, September 2025). The administration asked the Supreme Court to stay that reinstatement; in November 2025 the Court declined to act on the request, holding it alongside similar administration removal-power fights over an FTC commissioner and a Federal Reserve governor rather than ruling on Perlmutter's case on its own timeline (SCOTUSblog, November 2025).

title: Congress Rescinded $1.1B From Public Broadcasting; CPB Dissolved After 58 Years
institution: Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB)
status: Complete (CPB formally dissolved January 5, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-04 (board members fired) through 2026-01-05 (CPB board votes to dissolve)
what_changed: In March 2025, CPB sued FEMA in federal court, alleging the Trump administration was withholding reimbursement funding CPB needed to pay back public media stations for equipment investments already made under the Next Generation Warning System (NGWS) grant program -- a $136 million program Congress created in 2022 to help rural, tribal, and other underserved public media stations replace and upgrade their emergency-alert equipment, administered by CPB on FEMA's behalf. In April 2025, Trump fired three members of CPB's board of directors; the fired directors argued in subsequent legal action that the dismissal was governmental overreach targeting an entity whose congressional charter specifically guarantees its independence from political control. In July 2025, Congress passed a $9 billion rescissions package (canceling previously appropriated funds) requested by the White House, including $1.1 billion earmarked for CPB through fiscal year 2027 -- the first time in nearly 60 years Congress had voted to not fund CPB. The House vote was 216-213, with all but two Republicans in favor; in the Senate, only Susan Collins (R-ME) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) broke with their party to vote against the package, alongside two House Republicans (Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike Turner). Trump signed the bill and wrote on Truth Social: 'REPUBLICANS HAVE TRIED DOING THIS FOR 40 YEARS, AND FAILED....BUT NO MORE.' CPB announced August 1, 2025 that it would begin winding down, eliminating most staff positions by the September 30 fiscal year-end and retaining a small transition team through January 2026 to handle compliance and music-rights obligations. NPR reported (Aug. 28, 2025) that the NGWS reimbursement delays and stop-work orders were compounding the effect of CPB's own defunding and wind-down: rural broadcasters that had already been awarded NGWS funding were still waiting to be reimbursed for equipment upgrades, even as CPB -- the program's administering entity -- itself faced dissolution; the Office of Management and Budget told NPR the program would continue, and FEMA posted a new $40 million funding announcement that same August inviting states and tribes to apply, but station executives said the delays and CPB's own uncertain future left completed and in-progress emergency-alert upgrades in limbo. Rep. Lisa McClain and Rep. John Delaney sent FEMA a September 9, 2025 letter pressing for answers on the NGWS grants specifically. PBS itself -- a distinct entity from CPB -- announced on September 4, 2025 that it was cutting approximately 15% of its own staff, more than 100 positions including 34 immediate layoffs, citing a 21% hit to overall revenue from the loss of federal funding; PBS CEO Paula Kerger noted that an estimated 70 to 80 of NPR's 246 member stations could also be forced to shut down entirely. When the Senate Appropriations Committee subsequently declined to restore any funding for the following budget year, CPB's board voted to formally dissolve the organization entirely on January 5, 2026, rather than continue to exist in a defunded, vulnerable state -- CPB President and CEO Patricia Harrison described this as protecting 'the integrity of the public media system' by closing on the organization's own terms.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Personally pushed the rescission package and has repeatedly called CPB a 'monstrosity,' arguing public broadcasting -- particularly NPR -- displays 'extreme liberal bias.' OMB Director Russell Vought, who requested the rescissions package on the administration's behalf, told reporters afterward the administration would 'likely' send additional rescissions packages, saying 'there is still a great enthusiasm for these rescissions bills, because Congress wants to be a part of voting for these cuts and making them permanent.'

estimated_impact.summary: CPB funded more than 1,500 local radio and television stations nationwide; roughly 70% of its money went directly to 330 PBS and 246 NPR member stations. NPR President and CEO Katherine Maher estimated approximately 96% of all classical music broadcast in the United States airs on public radio stations specifically. The impact fell most heavily on rural and small-market stations with fewer alternative funding sources: specific documented effects include KCTS in Seattle abandoning long-form journalism ambitions, WFAE in Charlotte closing its community engagement facility, and WPSU in State College, Pennsylvania considering shutting down its radio station entirely. Sen. Susan Collins, despite voting to preserve funding, articulated the underlying tension directly: 'I share the frustration with the biased reporting by NPR, and I would support defunding it. Nevertheless, local TV and radio stations continue to provide important coverage' -- citing Maine-specific examples like the emergency alert network and local high school sports coverage.

title: CPSC's Three Democratic Commissioners Fired, Battery-Safety Standard Withdrawn, Agency Left in Republican-Only Rump
institution: Consumer Product Safety Commission
status: Complete (firings litigated and now final following the June 29, 2026 Trump v. Slaughter ruling)
date_of_action: 2025-05-08 (firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court finalization)
what_changed: On May 8, 2025, President Trump fired three of the CPSC's five commissioners -- Alexander Hoehn-Saric, Mary Boyle, and Richard Trumka Jr., all Biden appointees -- citing 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' without further detail, hours after the three had voted to block DOGE representatives from entering CPSC headquarters to fire staff employees. The CPSC's founding statute allows removal only for 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' and requires no more than three of five commissioners share a political party, structural protections designed to preserve a bipartisan agency that regulates the safety of thousands of consumer products. The fired commissioners sued; a federal judge in Maryland ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, and the Fourth Circuit declined to stay that order, but the Supreme Court granted an emergency stay on July 23, 2025, allowing the firings to proceed while the appeal continued. During the roughly five weeks the three commissioners were absent, the two remaining Republican-aligned commissioners -- Acting Chairman Peter Feldman and Douglas Dziak -- withdrew a previously approved (3-2 vote) e-bike and lithium-ion battery safety testing standard from public comment; lithium-ion battery fires from e-bikes and similar devices have been a rising home-fire and fatality concern nationally. The same two commissioners released a CPSC FY2026 budget request proposing to cut the agency's funding and staffing and to transfer CPSC's functions to the Department of Health and Human Services, led by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's ruling in Trump v. Slaughter -- which held FTC commissioners' for-cause removal protections unconstitutional -- prompted CPSC Acting Chairman Feldman to state publicly that the fired commissioners' 'claims should now fail as a matter of law,' effectively finalizing the terminations. As of this writing the CPSC operates with only two commissioners, both Republican-aligned.

primary_proponent.role: President

estimated_impact.summary: A statutorily bipartisan, five-member consumer-safety commission has operated as a two-member, single-party body for over a year, during which a pending battery-fire safety standard was withdrawn and a budget proposal to shrink and fold the agency into HHS was released.

Slaughter decision confirms 'officials who exercise executive power are accountable to the President' and that the prior for-cause removal protections were themselves unconstitutional -- i.e., that the firings were lawful all along, not merely permitted going forward. The withdrawn e-bike/lithium-battery standard had not been finalized and remains a live issue the agency could revisit; its withdrawal reflects the preference of the two remaining commissioners rather than a formal reversal of prior CPSC safety findings. Consumer-safety groups (Consumer Federation of America, National Consumers League, Public Citizen, which represented the fired commissioners) and the fired commissioners themselves argue the firings undermine the bipartisan design Congress built into the agency; the HHS-transfer budget proposal has seen no visible congressional movement as of mid-2026 per Covington & Burling's analysis, so its practical effect remains prospective rather than realized.

title: CVE Vulnerability-Tracking Program Nearly Shut Down When CISA Let Its MITRE Contract Lapse
institution: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Averted -- 11-month contract extension executed April 16, 2025, through March 16, 2026; CVE board told in January 2026 there would be no funding cliff at that deadline, and a more durable arrangement has since replaced the stopgap, though the underlying contract's terms remain undisclosed even to CVE board members
date_of_action: 2025-04-15 (MITRE warning letter) through 2025-04-16 (CISA contract extension)
what_changed: MITRE, the nonprofit that has run the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) program -- the foundational database used worldwide to catalog and cross-reference software security flaws -- and the related Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) program under contract with CISA since 2018, disclosed on April 15, 2025 that the government did not plan to renew its contract, set to expire the next day. Yosry Barsoum, MITRE vice president and director of its Center for Securing the Homeland, warned in a letter to the CVE board that a lapse would cause 'multiple impacts to CVE, including deterioration of national vulnerability databases and advisories, tool vendors, incident response operations, and all manner of critical infrastructure.' The warning came less than a month after MITRE had marked the CVE program's 25th anniversary. On April 16, 2025, with hours to spare, a CISA spokesperson announced the agency had exercised the contract's option period to 'ensure there will be no lapse in critical CVE services,' extending the $57.8 million agreement for 11 months, through March 16, 2026. Barsoum said on LinkedIn that CISA had 'identified incremental funding to keep the programs operational.' The near-lapse triggered the founding of the independent CVE Foundation, formed to explore alternative governance models less dependent on a single, opaque federal contract. The CVE board was told at its January 21, 2026 meeting there would be 'no funding cliff in March,' and reporting since indicates the stopgap has been replaced by a more durable funding arrangement -- though a source close to the program described the underlying contract as still 'a mystery contract with a mystery number,' opaque even to CVE board members.

estimated_impact.summary: CVE is the backbone identifier system for tracking software vulnerabilities worldwide -- used by security vendors, incident responders, and government agencies alike -- so even a brief lapse risked degrading vulnerability databases, security advisories, and incident-response coordination across critical infrastructure globally, not just within the U.S. government. No health/mortality figure applies: this is a cybersecurity-infrastructure capacity story with no direct health-outcome dimension to source.

title: Defense Health Agency Reviewed Military Hospitals for Closure/Downgrade; Congress Moved in 2026 to Reverse Changes at 41 Facilities

what_changed: Starting in early 2025, the Defense Health Agency began a facility-by-facility review of military treatment facilities (MTFs) across the U.S. military medical system to determine whether each should be closed or downgraded from a full hospital to a clinic. title: DHS Tied Counterterrorism/Homeland-Security Grants to Immigration-Enforcement Cooperation; Courts Blocked It Twice, DHS Kept Trying
institution: U.S. Department of Homeland Security (FEMA Homeland Security Grant Program / State Homeland Security Program)
status: Ongoing litigation -- a federal judge ruled against DHS in September 2025, and again after DHS disabled states' ability to formally accept the funds a court had just ordered released; DHS then imposed new population-estimate and shortened-spending-deadline conditions applying to all states; a coalition of 26 states plus two governors filed a further suit July 23, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island challenging both the immigration-cooperation condition and new voter-data-sharing/election-practice conditions
date_of_action: 2025 (conditions first imposed) through 2026-07-23 (latest multi-state suit filed)
what_changed: DHS's FEMA-administered Homeland Security Grant Program -- post-9/11 funding used by states for items like bomb detectors, security-analyst salaries, and emergency-preparedness capacity -- was conditioned on states cooperating with the administration's immigration-enforcement crackdown. Oregon and 19 other states (a coalition including California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Washington, Wisconsin, and Vermont) sued, arguing DHS was holding emergency-preparedness funding hostage in violation of the Constitution and the Administrative Procedure Act. A federal judge ruled in September 2025 that DHS could not attach immigration-cooperation strings to the grants. After that ruling, Oregon officials found the button to formally accept their already-approved award had been disabled on the federal grant website; states went back to court and won again, treating the disabled button as a defiance of the original order. Nearly $18 million was at stake for Oregon alone in the 2025 round; Portland had received an average of $5 million a year in homeland security grants over the prior two decades. DHS subsequently imposed two new conditions applying to all states regardless of the immigration dispute: states must estimate their populations net of people who had been deported, and the spending deadline for awarded funds was cut from three years to ten months. Separately, in September 2025, Trump ordered National Guard troops deployed to Portland, citing 'violent radical left terrorism' -- a characterization the city disputed -- adding a second front to the same underlying dispute over whether Oregon and similarly-positioned jurisdictions would be treated as partners or adversaries in federal counterterrorism/homeland-security funding. The dispute escalated further in 2026: on July 23, 2026, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield led a coalition of 26 states plus the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania in a new suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island, challenging DHS grant conditions requiring states to assist with federal immigration enforcement, alter election practices, and provide DHS with personal information on registered voters, as well as challenging FEMA's asserted authority to cancel grants at any time -- again on Administrative Procedure Act and Spending Clause grounds. Oregon alone receives roughly $10 million annually through the Homeland Security Grant Program; the 2026 suit put the nationwide funding at issue above $1 billion. Rayfield's office noted it had already won two similar cases in Rhode Island federal court in 2025.

title: DHS Rescinded Its Decade-Old 'Sensitive Locations' Policy, and Nearly Half of Undocumented Adults Report Avoiding Medical Care Out of Fear

status: In effect since January 21, 2025; no reported reversal as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (policy rescinded) through 2025-01-21 (ICE directive announced)
what_changed: Within hours of Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, DHS rescinded the decade-old 'Sensitive Locations' policy that had directed immigration enforcement to generally avoid arrests, searches, surveillance, and questioning at hospitals, health clinics, doctors' offices, schools, and places of worship. ICE announced a new directive on January 21, 2025 eliminating those restrictions on enforcement at what the prior policy termed sensitive or 'protected areas.' Health care providers and researchers subsequently documented a measurable chilling effect: surveys found nearly half of likely undocumented adults in the U.S. had avoided seeking medical care since the rescission, providers reported patients delaying or avoiding hospital emergency-room visits (including for conditions like gunshot wounds, diabetes complications, and high-risk pregnancies) out of fear of encountering immigration enforcement, and clinics reported drops in patient visits and interpreter usage. Health workers documented downstream effects including delayed diagnoses of life-threatening illnesses, children presenting at emergency rooms unaccompanied, and young children showing anxiety symptoms tied to fear of family separation.

title: Trump Budget Proposals Sought to Zero Out Federal Disability-Rights 'Protection & Advocacy' Funding -- and State Agencies Already Cut Services in 2025, Before Any Cut Was Enacted
institution: Health and Human Services (Administration for Community Living); the nationwide network of state Protection and Advocacy (P&A) systems
status: Proposed -- Congress had not enacted the FY2026 cuts as of the sources reviewed; several state P&A agencies had already curtailed services in 2025 due to funding-release delays tied to the broader federal funding freeze, independent of the final appropriations outcome
date_of_action: 2025-04 (leaked HHS budget draft and first state-level service pauses) through 2025-07-31 (formal FY2026 budget proposal)
what_changed: A leaked HHS budget draft reported in April 2025 revealed plans to zero out federal funding for the nationwide network of Protection and Advocacy (P&A) systems -- federally mandated, legally independent disability-rights agencies in every state and territory that investigate abuse and neglect, including in group homes and institutions, and provide free legal representation to people with disabilities -- alongside state councils on developmental disabilities, the lifespan respite program, and University Centers for Excellence in Developmental Disabilities. Even before any budget was enacted, funding-release delays tied to the broader administration funding freeze forced P&A agencies in New Jersey, Mississippi, and Arkansas to pause or limit services in April 2025, including halting intake of new clients. By July 2025, the administration's formal FY2026 budget request confirmed the leaked draft's direction in a more concrete form: it proposed eliminating three of the four major federal grant streams that fund the P&A network outright and cutting the fourth by roughly 60%. The National Disability Rights Network, which represents the state-based P&A agencies, calculated the proposal would cut the system's total federal funding from $148 million to about $69 million -- a roughly 53% reduction -- for a network of 57 agencies nationwide.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services

estimated_impact.summary: A 53% proposed federal funding cut (from $148M to ~$69M) threatens the free legal-advocacy and abuse-investigation function of the only federally mandated, legally independent disability-rights infrastructure in the country, present in every state; real service reductions -- new-client intake halts in at least three states -- had already occurred by April 2025, months before any final budget action, because of funding-release delays alone.

title: Federal Disease Surveillance Cuts Coincide With Emergence of Flesh-Eating Bacteria, Screwworm, and Malaria-Reintroduction Risk
institution: HHS/CDC and USDA disease-surveillance programs
status: Ongoing -- most surveillance reductions remain in place as of mid-2026; the ocean-monitoring-instrument removal was reversed after congressional opposition
date_of_action: 2025 (surveillance program cuts begin) through 2026-07 (reporting on emerging health threats)
what_changed: The Trump administration reduced or eliminated multiple federal disease-surveillance programs beginning in 2025. As of July 1, 2025, CDC's FoodNet (the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, a CDC/USDA/FDA/state partnership covering 10 sites) stopped requiring reporting on six of the eight pathogens it was built to track -- Campylobacter, Cyclospora, Listeria, Shigella, Vibrio, and Yersinia all became optional, leaving only Salmonella and STEC (E. coli) mandatory; Cyclospora surveillance had been mandatory since 1997. The administration also began removing hundreds of deep-sea ocean-monitoring instruments used to track ocean conditions that help predict pathogen proliferation, including Vibrio; this removal was later reversed following congressional opposition. USDA lost 18% of its workforce (more than 20,000 employees) in the first half of 2025. USAID, dismantled entirely in 2025, had provided global disease-surveillance and response funding, including stripping more than $300 million from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization and targeting roughly 80% of global malaria grants for termination, ending a U.S. malaria-prevention investment that had exceeded $9 billion since 2005. These reductions coincided with the emergence or resurgence of multiple disease threats in 2026: a 2026 Cyclospora outbreak that food-safety commentators say the weakened surveillance system was slower to detect and characterize (though some analyses argue the surveillance changes did not directly cause the outbreak itself -- see caveat); Vibrio vulnificus ('flesh-eating bacteria') cases in Florida and detections in New York coastal waters (CDC estimates roughly 80,000 Vibrio infections annually, with about 1 in 5 Vibrio vulnificus wound infections fatal, sometimes within days); the first confirmed U.S. case of New World Screwworm in June 2026, with over a dozen animals infected, threatening the cattle industry; and a CDC warning in May 2026 that 'the country remains susceptible to malaria reintroduction' despite the disease's 1951 eradication in the U.S. Update 2026-08-17: the 2026 Cyclospora outbreak referenced above has a documented scale -- as of mid-July 2026 reporting, over 700 confirmed cases in Michigan alone (the largest cluster), with additional cases in Ohio (177), Illinois (141), New York (120), North Carolina (110), and Texas (48), for a total spanning at least 18 states. Separately, CDC's Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria was dissolved in 2025, a specific staffing/capacity fact not previously captured in this entry that bears directly on the malaria-reintroduction-risk warning already documented above. Update 2026-08-30: the New World Screwworm outbreak referenced above has a documented trajectory since the first confirmed animal case in June 2026 -- monthly counts fell from 30 cases in June (29 in Texas, 1 in New Mexico) to 14 in July (all Texas) to 3 in August (two sheep and one goat, all in the Big Bend area near the Mexican border, with no cattle cases reported that month), a cumulative 47 cases, per trade-press reporting attributing the slowdown to a coordinated USDA/APHIS and state eradication effort. This is presented as evidence of the outbreak's trajectory and current containment status, not a resolution of the underlying surveillance-capacity concern this entry documents -- it rests on a single trade outlet (Oklahoma Farm Report) rather than the multi-outlet corroboration this entry's other figures have, and a direct fetch of USDA APHIS's own case-count page (screwworm.gov) timed out during this recheck, so this addition is flagged MODERATE pending independent primary-source confirmation.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Oversees the HHS restructuring that included the FoodNet reporting changes and broader public-health surveillance reductions; HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard defended the reforms in response to press inquiries. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins separately denied that USDA staffing cuts caused the screwworm's return.

estimated_impact.summary: Public health experts, including former CDC director Tom Frieden and infectious-disease specialists, warn the surveillance reductions have left the country less able to detect emerging disease threats before they spread widely -- a concern illustrated concretely by the near-simultaneous emergence of flesh-eating bacteria in new coastal areas, the first U.S. screwworm case in decades, and a CDC-flagged malaria-reintroduction risk.

estimated_impact.caveat: Agency officials dispute a direct causal link between the staffing/surveillance cuts and the specific emerging threats -- HHS's Hilliard defended the reforms generally, and Agriculture Secretary Rollins specifically denied that USDA cuts caused the screwworm's return. On the 2026 Cyclospora outbreak specifically, at least one political-response piece (Will Campbell for Texas) explicitly argues the surveillance changes did not cause that outbreak, while food-safety trade commentary (Food Safety News, eFoodAlert) argues the weakened system slowed detection and characterization -- present this as a genuinely disputed point, not settled either way. Broadly, the surveillance reductions and the emerging-threat reports are documented as a concerning coincidence by public-health experts, not as a proven causal chain for any single case.

MODERATE confidence on the causal link between the cuts and any specific outbreak (including the 2026 Cyclospora outbreak), since administration officials and at least one independent commentary explicitly dispute that link, while other food-safety commentators argue the opposite -- this is a live, disputed question, not an established fact. Update 2026-08-17: the outbreak case counts and the Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria dissolution are both sourced to Newsweek's July 10, 2026 reporting; the causal-link caveat already in this entry applies equally to these more specific figures -- the outbreak's scale is well-documented, its causal relationship to the FoodNet downgrade remains a disputed, expert-attributed inference, not an established fact. Re-verified 2026-08-30: added the New World Screwworm outbreak's monthly case trajectory (30 in June, 14 in July, 3 in August, 47 cumulative) from a single trade outlet (Oklahoma Farm Report), flagged MODERATE since it could not be independently cross-checked against USDA APHIS's own screwworm.gov case tracker (WebFetch timed out); no other material change to the FoodNet/malaria/Vibrio findings already documented was identified.

section_summaries.what_changed: The administration downgraded mandatory foodborne-pathogen reporting to optional, cut USDA staff by 18%, and eliminated USAID's global malaria/surveillance funding, while flesh-eating bacteria, screwworm, and malaria-reintroduction risk all emerged or resurfaced in 2026.

section_summaries.confidence_note: Facts well-corroborated in detailed CBS News reporting citing CDC data and named officials; causal link to specific outbreaks is disputed by the administration and not independently established.

title: DOE Proposed ~$19-20 Billion in Budget Cuts, Deemed 43% of Its Workforce Non-Essential, and Targeted 47 Energy-Efficiency Regulations for Elimination
institution: Department of Energy (DOE)
status: Ongoing -- FY2026 budget cuts proposed, not yet fully enacted; the 47-regulation deregulatory push formally announced and underway
date_of_action: 2025-01 (first deferred-resignation round) through 2025-05-12 (47-regulation deregulatory announcement)
what_changed: In April 2025, DOE extended an agency-wide hiring freeze and, in an internal reorganization plan, classified 43% of its workforce as non-'essential.' The hiring freeze and reorganization ran alongside a separate voluntary-departure mechanism: more than 2,600 DOE staffers accepted the administration's second round of deferred-resignation offers by April 10, 2025, more than double the 1,217 who took the first round in January 2025, with the Grid Deployment Office (responsible for power-grid maintenance) and the Loan Programs Office (low-interest financing for high-tech energy, nuclear, and transmission projects) among the hardest-hit, alongside the Policy Office and the offices of Manufacturing and Energy Supply Chains and Clean Energy Deployment. At least 114 employees were laid off from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) on May 5, 2025, part of a broader wave of departures and forced exits across the department's clean-energy and research functions. The administration's FY2026 budget proposal sought to cut DOE's budget by roughly $19.3-20.3 billion compared to FY2025 levels, with deep cuts concentrated in the offices funding renewable-energy research and demonstration projects, including NREL's parent office. Separately, on May 12, 2025, DOE announced it would pursue the elimination or reduction of 47 regulations -- what the department itself called the first milestone in 'America's biggest deregulatory effort' -- the large majority targeting consumer-appliance and building energy-efficiency standards (covering products such as refrigerators, water heaters, and furnaces), alongside some administrative/testing-process rules and DOE's own diversity-related grant-recipient requirements. DOE workers and outside experts warned the combination of budget cuts, workforce losses, and the efficiency-standard rollbacks would raise household energy costs, slow clean-energy innovation, and dismantle energy-efficiency programs that had historically saved consumers money on utility bills.

title: DOE Cancels $4.9 Billion Loan Guarantee for the Largest Planned U.S. Transmission Line, Days After a Senator's Personal Appeal to Trump
institution: U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), Loan Programs Office
status: Cancelled -- DOE formally withdrew the conditional loan guarantee July 23, 2025
what_changed: The Department of Energy announced July 23, 2025 that it was cancelling a $4.9 billion conditional loan guarantee for the first phase of the Grain Belt Express, a planned 578-mile, 2,500-megawatt transmission line intended to carry wind and solar power from Ford County, Kansas to Callaway County, Missouri and onward toward eastern markets -- widely described as the largest transmission-line project in active development in the United States. The Biden administration had issued the conditional guarantee in November 2024. title: DOE's nuclear waste cleanup office loses nearly half its workforce, GAO finds
institution: Department of Energy, Office of Environmental Management
status: Ongoing -- 45% vacancy rate at end of FY2025 per GAO, with site-level rates as high as 100%; DOE plans to hire 174 workers in FY2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-04 (first Carlsbad Field Office lease-termination attempt) through 2026-05 (GAO report)
what_changed: The Carlsbad Field Office's eventual collapse to 100% vacancy had an earlier warning sign than the GAO report alone shows: on March 4, 2025, DOGE included the Carlsbad Field Office's 90,000-square-foot Skeen-Whitlock Building lease on a spreadsheet of more than 7,000 federal leases marked for termination, citing roughly $810,000 in annual savings. The office, staffed by about 200 workers, directly manages the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP) -- the only U.S. site licensed to permanently dispose of transuranic nuclear waste, including plutonium-contaminated material, stored in a deep salt formation -- and includes an emergency response center for handling nuclear-material accidents. Following bipartisan New Mexico congressional pushback (Rep. Gabe Vasquez among others) over the national-security and public-safety risk of disrupting the only facility of its kind, GSA reinstated the lease within days, confirming by March 6, 2025 the office was no longer slated for termination. That reversal, however, did not stop the underlying workforce attrition documented below: a Government Accountability Office report found the Department of Energy's Office of Environmental Management -- responsible for cleaning up nuclear contamination from World War II- and Cold War-era weapons programs at sites across the country -- ended FY2025 with a 45% vacancy rate, roughly half its needed workforce. Of 409 staff who left in 2025, 76% (312) departed through the White House's deferred resignation program; nearly half of those departures (180) were in positions GAO classified as mission-critical, spanning engineering, contracting, physical sciences, and IT management. GAO further warned that 35% of DOE-EM's remaining 856 employees will be eligible to retire by the end of 2030, meaning attrition is likely to continue independent of any further resignation programs. title: DOE Dismantles Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, Cancels $3.7B+ in Awarded Projects
institution: Department of Energy (Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations)
status: Complete (office wound down; zero FY2026 funding provided by Congress)
date_of_action: 2025-05-30 (first project terminations announced) through 2026 appropriations (OCED zeroed out)
what_changed: The Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED) was created in 2021 to manage roughly $27 billion in funding for large-scale clean energy demonstration projects -- hydrogen hubs, direct air capture hubs, long-duration energy storage, and industrial decarbonization -- and had committed over $18 billion to about 100 projects by November 2025. On May 30, 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced the termination of 24 OCED projects worth more than $3.7 billion in financial assistance, citing lack of economic viability and misalignment with administration priorities. Internal documents reviewed by Latitude Media showed a broader target list of nearly $24 billion in awards for cancellation across six DOE offices. Staffing followed funding: OCED's roughly 250-person staff was cut to a planned temporary staff of 35, a reduction of about 86%. On November 20, 2025, DOE announced its updated agency-wide organization chart, removing OCED entirely and folding remaining functions into the newly created Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation alongside similarly eliminated offices (Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy, Grid Deployment Office, Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management); reporting at the time put the value of clean-energy awards canceled as part of this specific reorganization at more than $7 billion, on top of the May 2025 $3.7 billion figure above and distinct from the broader ~$24 billion cross-office target list. As part of the same reorganization, DOE's Loan Programs Office was rebranded the Office of Energy Dominance Financing, a change trade press described as centering the office around fossil and nuclear energy financing and de-emphasizing its prior broader mandate supporting clean-energy technologies from any source. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0507): on December 1, 2025, DOE renamed the National Renewable Energy Laboratory the National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Assistant Secretary Audrey Robertson stating the agency was 'no longer picking and choosing energy sources' -- a symbolic rebranding in the same November-December 2025 window as the organizational changes above. On January 22, 2026, the Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced it was de-obligating roughly $29.9 billion of the $83.6 billion in Biden-era loan principal referenced below and revising the remaining $53.6 billion, with $9.5 billion of the total specifically tied to wind and solar energy projects; DOE framed the review as covering $104 billion in Biden-era obligations, including roughly $85 billion the department said was 'rushed out the door' in the final months after the 2024 election. Congress's FY2026 appropriations bill, passed in early 2026, formalized the outcome by providing zero new funding to OCED and directing DOE to report quarterly on the redistribution of the office's remaining obligated and unobligated funds.

title: NLRB Deleted DOGE System-Access Records Before GAO Investigators Could Examine Them
institution: National Labor Relations Board (NLRB)
status: Complete -- GAO report published; the underlying account-access records cannot be recovered
date_of_action: 2025-04-16 (DOGE detail begins) through 2025-08 (access records deleted, after DOGE detail ended and before GAO could examine them)
what_changed: Two DOGE staffers were formally detailed to the National Labor Relations Board beginning April 16, 2025, under agreements running through July 25, 2025, and requested access to seven internal HR systems covering personnel records, payroll, and hiring databases -- a request that prompted an NLRB IT staffer to file a whistleblower disclosure with Congress and the agency's inspector general to open an investigation into a potential data breach. A Government Accountability Office report -- titled 'National Labor Relations Board Detailees Did Not Access IT Systems Between April 16 and July 25, 2025' -- found no evidence the DOGE detailees accessed those systems during that specific window. However, GAO also found that in August 2025, after the DOGE detail had ended but before GAO investigators requested to observe the systems, NLRB deleted the team members' system-access accounts and associated audit-trail records -- eliminating the digital evidence needed to independently verify what access, if any, occurred, and undercutting confidence in the agency's own account. Access logs for sensitive systems are generally subject to a six-year retention requirement under the General Records Schedule; the deleted records were only months old.

primary_proponent.name: National Labor Relations Board
primary_proponent.role: Independent federal agency (IT/records management under agency leadership)
primary_proponent.note: NLRB deleted the DOGE detailees' system-access accounts and associated audit-trail records in August 2025, before GAO investigators could examine them -- a records-retention violation that prevented independent verification of the agency's own no-access finding.

estimated_impact.summary: GAO's finding of 'no evidence of access' during the specific detail window is undercut by NLRB's own deletion of the access records that would have made that finding independently verifiable -- the deletion itself, occurring within a records-retention period that should have preserved the data for six years, is the more significant and independently confirmed problem, regardless of what DOGE staffers did or did not do.

title: DOGE's 'Fraud Review' of $8.6 Trillion in Social Security Payments Found Almost No Fraud, Slowed Claims 25%, and Led to an Unauthorized Server Holding 300M+ Americans' Data
institution: Social Security Administration (SSA); DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
status: Ongoing litigation, now proceeding to discovery after the government's own bid to block it failed -- the Fourth Circuit vacated the injunction limiting DOGE's SSA data access and remanded (April 10, 2026); on remand, the district court lifted its stay and granted plaintiffs' motion for discovery (April 14, 2026); the government's Motion to Rescind that discovery order was denied on June 26, 2026, in an opinion finding SSA and DOGE had made 'serious if not egregious misrepresentations' to the court; SSA reportedly considering rolling back the anti-fraud phone checks; a June 5, 2026 sworn whistleblower declaration separately alleges a DOGE official proposed marking 2.7 million living Social Security recipients as dead to pressure them into self-deporting or expose them to ICE detention, which SSA disputes as ever having been implemented
date_of_action: 2025-03-08 (review publicly reported) through 2026-04-10 (Fourth Circuit ruling); data-access disclosures continuing into 2026
what_changed: Starting in mid-February 2025, Elon Musk publicly laid the political groundwork for DOGE's Social Security fraud review with two separate, since-debunked claims: that 20 million people 'definitely dead' were still marked alive in SSA's Numident database, and, in a March 11, 2025 Fox Business interview, that $500-700 billion in Social Security 'waste' needed to be eliminated. Fact-checkers and SSA's own then-acting commissioner rejected both claims -- SSA data traces the '150-year-olds' figure to a database-structure quirk (SSA's own inspector general found improper payments of all kinds, fraud included, totaled less than 1% of the $8.6 trillion paid out from FY2015-2022), and experts told ABC News Trump and Musk were falsely implying millions of dead Americans were actively receiving benefits rather than merely still appearing as unremoved records. In March 2025, ABC News and other outlets reported that DOGE was searching through $8.6 trillion in Social Security payment records as part of the same stated anti-fraud effort, with DOGE engineer Aram Moghaddassi and Musk separately claiming that up to 40% of phone calls to SSA requesting direct-deposit changes came from fraudsters -- a narrower claim used to justify new anti-fraud identity checks on phone-based claims starting in early April 2025. Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek later confirmed the review's scope in a letter to Congress. The actual results, revealed in internal SSA documents reported by Nextgov/FCW and cited by Sen. Elizabeth Warren in a May 15, 2025 release, contradicted the fraud claims: of more than 110,000 phone claims examined under the new checks, only 2 were found to have a high probability of fraud, and fewer than 1% were flagged as even potentially fraudulent at all -- consistent with SSA's own data showing fraud is a negligible share (a fraction of the already-small 0.3%) of the program's improper payments. The new checks themselves caused documented harm: an internal SSA document from May 2025 found they slowed retirement claim processing by 25% and caused a 'degradation of public service,' with over 140,000 retirement claims left unprocessed for more than 60 days, prompting SSA to consider walking the policy back. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0557), restoring an antecedent the entry had omitted: the unauthorized-cloud-server allegation did not originate with the January 2026 court filing below -- SSA's own Chief Data Officer, Charles Borges, first raised it five months earlier. Borges filed a protected whistleblower disclosure with the Office of Special Counsel and congressional committees in late August 2025, alleging DOGE staff had created a live copy of the nation's Social Security data in a cloud environment that circumvented oversight, putting more than 300 million Americans' records at risk. He resigned August 29, 2025, days after filing, writing in his resignation letter that retaliatory actions against him made it impossible to do his job 'legally and ethically'; he separately filed a Prohibited Personnel Practices retaliation complaint. SSA publicly rejected his claims at the time, calling the alleged data release 'highly irresponsible' to characterize as a security lapse. Separately, and more seriously, court filings beginning in January 2026 revealed that DOGE staff had improperly accessed and shared SSA data well beyond the stated fraud-review purpose: a January 16, 2026 DOJ court filing corrected prior sworn agency testimony and admitted a DOGE employee had copied Social Security records covering more than 300 million Americans onto an unauthorized, inadequately secured cloud server that SSA itself could not fully audit for who had accessed it -- independently confirming, months later, the core factual claim Borges had already made under oath to Congress and OSC. The same filing revealed a DOGE employee had signed an agreement to share SSA data with an outside political advocacy group seeking to find evidence of voter fraud and 'overturn results in certain States,' prompting a Hatch Act referral for two DOGE employees to a federal watchdog. A federal court had issued a temporary restraining order in March 2025 limiting DOGE's SSA data access -- U.S. District Judge Ellen Hollander's order barring DOGE affiliates from accessing SSA's sensitive personal data -- and Acting Commissioner Dudek initially told reporters the order applied so broadly it would force him to shut down the agency; Hollander responded in two same-day letters to counsel calling that characterization 'inaccurate' and then 'patently incorrect,' clarifying the order applied only to SSA staff working on the DOGE data-access effort specifically, and Dudek reversed himself hours later, saying the agency would remain open and continue operating under the TRO. Reporting found DOGE associates continued accessing sensitive data even after that order; a further whistleblower complaint reported in March 2026 alleged a former DOGE associate planned to take sensitive citizen data to a subsequent government-contractor job. On April 10, 2026, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the district court's preliminary injunction restricting DOGE's SSA data access, with the majority finding plaintiffs had not shown 'irreparable harm' -- over a dissent arguing the prior record was 'materially erroneous' given the January 2026 disclosures. Update 2026-08-29: on remand, the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland lifted its stay of the case on April 14, 2026 and granted plaintiffs' motion for discovery -- meaning the case is now proceeding to fact-finding on the scope of DOGE's SSA data access, rather than simply sitting dormant after the Fourth Circuit's ruling. No further ruling or discovery outcome was identified as of this recheck. Update 2026-08-31 (real correction): this entry's prior text stopped at the April 14, 2026 discovery order and found no subsequent ruling. In fact, defendants moved to rescind that order (ECF 215), arguing discovery was improper and citing the DOGE Temporary Organization's then-upcoming July 4, 2026 expiration date. On June 26, 2026, Judge Ellen Lipton Hollander (D. Md.) denied the Motion to Rescind in a 39-page opinion, holding that defendants' own January 16, 2026 Notice of Corrections -- which disclosed that SSA had falsely assured the court of TRO compliance, concealed the DOGE Team's full systems access, and misrepresented that DOGE work was confined to fraud detection -- itself justified the discovery, and declined defendants' request to cap it at five requests for production, five interrogatories, five requests for admission, and zero depositions. The opinion quotes Judge King's concurring and dissenting opinion within the Fourth Circuit's en banc ruling (AFSCME VI, 172 F.4th 361) -- not the court's own holding -- in which he wrote that, given the corrected record, 'we should not accord the defendants any benefit of the doubt or readily trust in anything they say.' The same district court opinion detailed further specifics of the Voter Data Agreement beyond what was previously known: SSA says it first learned of the agreement during an unrelated November 2025 review, and documents produced in a related FOIA suit (Democracy Forward Found. v. SSA, ABA-26-1188, D. Md.) show a member of the SSA DOGE Team separately emailed a password-protected Excel workbook containing personally identifiable information on 971 beneficiaries to DOGE personnel at the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Labor. Separately, and more seriously, plaintiffs' June 5, 2026 'Second Factual Notice' (ECF 233) attached a sworn declaration from former SSA senior executive Jeremiah Schofield, who says he was present when a DOGE official, Jon Koval, laid out a plan to mark roughly 2.7 million living Social Security recipients as dead in SSA's Death Master File -- with the stated purpose, per Schofield, of forcing those individuals to either self-deport or go to a local SSA office to prove they were alive, where ICE could then detain and deport them. Sens. Warren and Blumenthal made the declaration public and sought records and answers from SSA Commissioner Bisignano and the named DOGE-affiliated staff. SSA publicly disputes the account, saying it 'did not add a list of 2.7 million names to the Death Master File' and that the plan, as alleged, was never implemented. Plaintiffs' earlier March 10, 2026 'First Factual Notice' (ECF 208), already reflected in this entry as a March 2026 whistleblower complaint, is clarified by the June 26 opinion to have specifically alleged the departing DOGE associate took restricted SSA databases to a private-sector employer potentially on a thumb drive. As of this recheck, defendants' separate May 1, 2026 Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Jurisdiction remains pending and undecided; no ruling on it, and no outcome of the now-authorized discovery itself, has been identified.

primary_proponent.note: Musk publicly made at least three separate, since-debunked fraud claims to build political support for cutting Social Security: 20 million 'dead' people supposedly still marked alive in SSA's database (February 2025), $500-700 billion in program 'waste' to eliminate (Fox Business, March 11, 2025), and roughly 40% of direct-deposit-change phone calls being fraudulent (used to justify the specific program this entry tracks). SSA's own subsequent data (110,000+ claims reviewed, 2 high-probability-fraud cases found) directly contradicted the phone-fraud figure, and SSA's then-acting commissioner and outside experts separately rejected the dead-people and waste claims. Acting Commissioner Leland Dudek confirmed the review's existence and scope to Congress.

estimated_impact.summary: A fraud-prevention program justified by a since-disproven 40%-fraud claim degraded legitimate service (slower claims, more unprocessed cases) while producing almost no confirmed fraud, and separately resulted in Social Security data for more than 300 million Americans being copied to an unsecured, unauthorized server that the agency could not fully audit -- with at least one documented instance of that access being shared outside SSA for an unrelated political purpose.

title: DOGE Canceled 585 VA Contracts After Backlash Forced It Down From an Initial 875 -- Officials Gave Congress Inconsistent Figures
institution: Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
status: Implemented, with ongoing congressional oversight pressure over transparency and inconsistent figures
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial ~875-contract cancellation list) through 2025-05-16 (Collins gives Congress a differing figure)
what_changed: DOGE, under Elon Musk, moved to cancel roughly 875 VA contracts as part of its cost-cutting campaign. Reporting and VA employees flagged that many targeted contracts covered essential services, including cancer-registry maintenance, sterility certification for medical equipment, air-quality testing, suicide-prevention support, physician recruitment and retention, and safety inspections at VA medical facilities. Frontline Veterans Health Administration employees warned the cuts would imperil safety at the VA's nearly 1,400 hospitals and clinics. Facing that backlash, the VA paused its planned cuts, then announced the termination list had fallen by about a third, to 585 contracts, with an alleged combined value of $1.8 billion; the VA said the reductions would let it redirect more than $900 million to health care, benefits, and services for VA beneficiaries. The VA declined to disclose the full list of canceled contracts despite congressional requests, drawing criticism from senators including Richard Blumenthal and Angus King over the lack of transparency and consultation. VA Secretary Doug Collins subsequently gave Congress inconsistent figures on the scope of the cuts -- telling lawmakers on May 16, 2025 that the VA had canceled more than 440 contracts worth $120 billion, a figure sharply at odds with the earlier 585-contract/$1.8 billion accounting, without a public reconciliation of the discrepancy identified in sourcing reviewed. Update 2026-08-30: identified the specific mechanism behind the cancellation list -- an AI review tool built and operated by a DOGE software engineer with no prior healthcare or government experience, which ProPublica reported was error-prone and, per Government Executive/Nextgov reporting on a June 11, 2025 forum, appeared to select contracts for termination by matching keywords rather than individualized review. House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee Democrats raised the AI tool's use directly at that forum. A concrete example of the tool's effect: Task Order 169, a contract held by Aptive Resources (a veteran-owned and woman-owned small business) supporting VA's Electronic Health Record Modernization program by resolving identity-record anomalies in the VA's master person index, was terminated abruptly and without a transition plan despite having resolved 13,400 such anomalies -- inaccuracies that can otherwise block veterans from receiving medical care, disability compensation, or other earned benefits. At least six contracts directly supporting the EHR-modernization rollout, all held by service-disabled or veteran-owned small businesses, were similarly terminated. Separately, DOGE's broader public accounting of its savings claims, including the VA figures described above, was reported to have quietly removed some previously touted savings figures from its own public tracking website after they were found to be inflated or erroneous, though no source reviewed specifically confirms whether the VA contract figures in this entry were among those quietly revised.

title: DOGE/GSA Moved to Cancel Leases for the Alaska and Hawaii Volcano-Monitoring Observatories, Then Backed Off Under Congressional Pressure
institution: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) -- Alaska Volcano Observatory and Hawaiian Volcano Observatory; General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Alaska lease reversed after congressional intervention; Hawaii's temporary Hilo lease threat was overtaken by a previously-planned, congressionally-funded permanent relocation
date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (leases publicly reported as targeted) through 2026-04 (new permanent Hawaii facility opened)
what_changed: In early March 2025, NOTUS and the Washington Post reported that DOGE/GSA had listed the leases for the Anchorage office housing the USGS Alaska Volcano Observatory and the Hilo, Hawaii office housing the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (which monitors Kilauea) among hundreds of federal office leases slated for termination as part of the administration's real-estate cost-cutting push, with GSA claiming roughly $2.2 million in savings from the Anchorage lease alone. Scientists and local officials warned that ending these leases -- on top of concurrent GSA staffing cuts complicating any relocation of specialized monitoring equipment and servers -- risked degrading real-time eruption-warning capability near active volcanoes in both states; a former observatory scientist specifically flagged the difficulty of moving a recently purchased $500,000 backup generator and critical monitoring servers without risking data loss or monitoring gaps. In Alaska, Rep. Nick Begich's office intervened with the Department of the Interior and GSA, and the Anchorage lease was reinstated by March 18, 2025, according to the Anchorage Daily News and Begich's own office -- though GSA itself did not confirm the reversal on the record to the Anchorage Daily News, leaving the reinstatement independently reported but not agency-confirmed. In Hawaii, the Hilo Ironworks Building lease -- always a temporary arrangement dating to 2018, when the observatory's original Kilauea-summit headquarters was damaged beyond repair by earthquakes -- was listed for termination effective September 30, 2025; that threat did not require a comparable reversal because a new, permanent, non-leased Hawaiian Volcano Observatory headquarters (funded separately through congressional disaster-recovery appropriations after the 2018 damage, shared with the Pacific Island Ecosystems Research Center) opened in Hilo in April 2026, mooting the lease question for that observatory's long-term housing.

primary_proponent.name: General Services Administration, with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
primary_proponent.role: GSA administered the lease-termination list; DOGE's broader federal-real-estate cost-cutting push provided the policy driver
primary_proponent.note: No named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for including the two observatory leases; GSA described itself only as 'reviewing all options to optimize our footprint' when asked for comment.

estimated_impact.summary: Two of the nation's volcano-hazard monitoring facilities were briefly slated for lease termination with no documented relocation plan for specialized, hard-to-move monitoring equipment, at a time when both regions had active volcanic activity (Kilauea eruptions in Hawaii) -- an example of a blanket cost-cutting process moving without an apparent case-by-case safety review.
