title: DOJ Civil Rights Division Lost 70% of Its Attorneys — Voting Section Down From 30 to 3
institution: Civil Rights Division, U.S. Department of Justice
status: Ongoing (departure rate now over 75%; Voting Section led in acting capacity by a former Public Interest Legal Foundation attorney; White House reportedly considering defunding a related election-observer program); a former division attorney's August 2026 whistleblower disclosure to Congress separately alleges predetermined outcomes in three high-profile antisemitism investigations (Harvard, Brown, Columbia) and bar-discipline-driven departures among current attorneys
date_of_action: 2025-01 (initial departures begin) through 2025-10 (Justice Connection's most recent departure count)
what_changed: Since President Trump's January 2025 inauguration, an estimated 250-260 attorneys -- roughly 70% of the division's approximately 365-person attorney roster -- have resigned, accepted the administration's deferred-resignation offer, or been reassigned elsewhere within DOJ. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0278), filling in the growth trajectory between this entry's own snapshots: ABC News reported more than 100 attorneys had already left the division by April 29, 2025, tying the departures directly to the same priority shift documented throughout this entry -- away from voting-rights and policing-reform enforcement toward pursuing culture-war priorities including transgender-athlete policy and 'anti-Christian bias' claims. The priority shift also reached environmental-justice enforcement: on April 11, 2025, the Civil Rights Division terminated a March 2023 interim resolution agreement with the Alabama Department of Public Health covering Lowndes County -- a rural, majority-Black area with a longstanding raw-sewage exposure crisis from inadequate septic infrastructure -- that had required ADPH to prioritize septic and wastewater fixes there based on residents' sewage-exposure risk; DOJ's own press release framed the termination as advancing Executive Order 14151's ban on 'illegal DEI and environmental justice policies.' The agreement had been the first-ever use of federal civil rights law to address an environmental-justice claim, making its termination a specific, named instance of the division abandoning a novel enforcement theory rather than merely reassigning staff away from existing casework. By July 23, 2025, Reuters put the cumulative departure count at 368 staff, a dated data point between the entry's own January-May ~250-260-attorney figure and its October 2025 ~400-person/75% estimate. By October 2025, Justice Connection (a support network founded by former division attorneys) estimated the departure count had grown to nearly 400 people, about 75% of attorneys. The Voting Section specifically -- responsible for enforcing the Voting Rights Act -- fell from an estimated 30 attorneys in January to just 3 by May 2025. The section devoted to ensuring nondiscrimination by recipients of federal funds was left with no attorneys whatsoever, per the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, confirmed in April 2025, sent new mission statements to each of the division's 11 sections shortly after taking office, redirecting the Voting Section's focus from protecting against discrimination toward pursuing voter fraud, and telling the Educational Opportunities Section that its work required 'the full dedication of this section's resources, attention and energy to the priorities of the president.' Career section-chief managers -- in some cases with decades of institutional tenure spanning multiple administrations of both parties -- were removed from leadership roles and reassigned to processing public records requests or complaint intake, which several described as a deliberate push to induce their resignation. By August 2025, DOJ was actively soliciting permanent internal transfers from other CRT sections to refill the most depleted offices (Voting, Employment Litigation, Educational Opportunities), some of which were themselves already down more than 75% of their attorneys. The Voting Section is now led in an acting capacity by Maureen Riordan, previously an attorney at the Public Interest Legal Foundation, a conservative legal group whose stated mission is to 'fight against lawlessness in American elections' -- a notable leadership choice for a section this entry documents was redirected toward pursuing voter fraud rather than voting-rights enforcement. As of March 2026, the White House was reportedly considering ending funding for a separate, longstanding DOJ election-observer program aimed at protecting minority voting rights, according to CBS News sources. Departures across the division have continued to be counted at roughly 75%, consistent with Justice Connection's October 2025 estimate already in this entry, rather than climbing further as of this update. Update 2026-07-26: a DOJ spokesperson has since gone on the record denying the reported consideration of ending the election-observer program's funding, stating the Department 'has no plans to end its monitorship program which is integral to assessing compliance with federal voting rights laws across the country.' This resolves the 'reportedly considering' item from the prior update with an explicit denial, though it does not address or retract the underlying reporting that such defunding had been discussed internally. Reuters reporting (Feb. 2026) found the division's unit prosecuting police and federal-agent misconduct lost roughly two-thirds of its attorneys, from about 40 down to as few as 13, with charges under the civil rights statute most commonly used in federal excessive-force cases falling about 36% to 54 total in 2025 -- the lowest since 2020. Section supervisors reportedly instructed staff early in the administration that law-enforcement-misconduct investigations would proceed only in egregious circumstances (e.g. a death in custody or sexual assault), with state and local authorities expected to lead most other cases. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0462): an earlier, concrete instance of the same leniency-toward-police pattern predates the Reuters staffing report. On July 17, 2025, career prosecutors' successor DOJ leadership recommended a one-day sentence and three years of supervised release for Brett Hankison, the former Louisville officer convicted in November 2024 of violating Breonna Taylor's civil rights by firing blindly into her apartment during the 2020 raid that killed her -- an about-face after DOJ had spent years prosecuting the case through two trials. U.S. District Judge Rebecca Grady Jennings rejected the recommendation on July 21, 2025 as treating the offense as 'an inconsequential crime' and sentenced Hankison to 33 months. DOJ's involvement did not end with sentencing: in November 2025 the department asked the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals to release Hankison from prison pending his appeal, and the court granted the request December 19, 2025, ordering him released on his own recognizance. Former DOJ lawyers cited in the reporting expressed doubt the diminished section could conduct thorough investigations of recent incidents, including the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis -- the same shootings this tracker's prosecution/cabinet-level/bondi-doj-renee-good-widow-investigation-2026.json entry documents DOJ leadership blocking a standard investigation of and instead pressuring an investigation of Good's widow. Update 2026-08-17: in July 2026, Dhillon swore in more than 100 new attorneys and staff to the Civil Rights Division, beginning to refill the roster this entry documents was hollowed out by departures. The division's new composition drew public scrutiny after DOJ published a group photo of the incoming class; commentators (Atlanta Black Star) highlighted the demographic makeup of the new hires as a marker of the division's redirected priorities. Coverage citing DOJ deputy leadership (Jeffrey Morrison, elevated to Deputy Assistant Attorney General by May 2026 and now counsel on the department's Title VI suit against the University of California; Eric Sell, who followed Dhillon from the Center for American Liberty) describes a division now oriented toward Second Amendment cases, litigation against transgender-related policies, and alleged campus antisemitism -- confirming the mission-redirection this entry already documents is now staffed with new personnel aligned to it, rather than remaining merely depleted. Update (2026-08-30 recheck): a whistleblower disclosure from former Civil Rights Division attorney Haley Van Erem, filed through the Government Accountability Project and forwarded to four congressional committees including the House Judiciary Committee (reported Aug. 18-19, 2026), alleges that DOJ and HHS officials departed from longstanding investigative practices in at least three high-profile antisemitism investigations -- Harvard, Brown, and Columbia -- conducted under the administration's Task Force to Combat Antisemitism (led by DOJ official Leo Terrell), claiming the investigations' outcomes were 'predetermined, without regard to the evidence' and that for at least some of them there was 'little to no factual predicate justifying opening them.' Van Erem, who spent nearly a decade in the Special Litigation Section before being reassigned off five active ADA cases onto Title VI investigations on March 21, 2025, left DOJ May 30, 2025, citing unwillingness to continue in what she described as politically motivated investigations. Per Above the Law's coverage, her disclosure separately provides 'the first direct acknowledgment' that some departing Civil Rights Division attorneys' exits were driven by concern that continued participation in the division's current work -- including alleged use of 'poison pill' settlement language designed to force litigation rather than resolution, and opening at least one investigation based on a single news article -- could expose them to state bar discipline.

primary_proponent.name: Harmeet Dhillon
primary_proponent.role: Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights
primary_proponent.note: Personally authored and sent the new mission statements redirecting each section's priorities. At a Federalist Society event, she likened the division's work under Democratic administrations to a 'speeding train' and, addressing the departing attorneys directly, said 'we wish them well in their future endeavors and their passions. They need to pursue them elsewhere. That's not going to be happening at the DOJ.'

estimated_impact.summary: Stacey Young, an 18-year Civil Rights Division veteran who resigned in January 2025 and founded Justice Connection to support current and former staff, described the scale of change as unprecedented in the division's near-70-year history: 'Every presidential administration has its own policy priorities, but I don't think there's any precedent for an administration almost completely refocusing the civil rights division's enforcement priorities the way this one has.' Joseph Rich, who led the Voting Section from 1999-2005 under both a Democratic and Republican administration, raised a specific operational concern about the reduced Voting Section potentially bringing voter-fraud suits 'right in the middle of an election.'

Re-verified 2026-07-20: Riordan's appointment and the reported election-observer defunding consideration both extend this entry's existing pattern (priorities redirected toward voter-fraud pursuit, away from voting-rights protection) with new, specific, named developments rather than changing the basic trajectory already documented. Re-verified 2026-07-26: the DOJ denial is corroborated by CBS News's own follow-up reporting and Election Law Blog's contemporaneous coverage. Re-verified 2026-08-17: the July 2026 swearing-in of 100+ new attorneys and the division's reoriented case priorities are corroborated across Bloomberg Law and Federal News Network reporting; the demographic-composition criticism is a characterization from Atlanta Black Star's coverage of DOJ's own published photo, presented here as commentary rather than an independently adjudicated fact. Re-verified 2026-08-30 (real correction): Van Erem's whistleblower disclosure and its core claims (25-28 page disclosure, House Judiciary Committee referral, the Harvard/Brown/Columbia investigations, the predetermined-outcome allegation) are well-corroborated across CBS News, ABC News, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, jweekly, Higher Ed Dive, and the Government Accountability Project's own press release -- HIGH confidence. The specific 'poison pill' settlement-language and single-article-triggered-investigation details are sourced to Above the Law's fuller writeup of the disclosure and were not independently cross-checked against the disclosure document itself -- MODERATE confidence on those two specific procedural details. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0278): the April 2025 100+-attorney and July 2025 368-staff figures are each HIGH confidence, directly sourced to ABC News's and Reuters's own original reporting respectively. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0462): the Hankison sentencing-recommendation and appeal-release sequence is HIGH confidence, corroborated across WDRB, LPM, CNN, Al Jazeera, The Hill, and Yahoo/wire reporting on the December 2025 Sixth Circuit release order. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0231): the Lowndes County environmental-justice settlement termination is HIGH confidence, directly sourced to DOJ's own press release plus independent reporting (Inside Climate News, 1819 News, Alabama Daily News) all corroborating the same April 11, 2025 date, EO 14151 rationale, and settlement history.

section_summaries.what_changed: Roughly three-quarters of the Civil Rights Division's attorneys have left since January 2025, with the Voting Section gutted from 30 lawyers to 3, and the police-misconduct unit down two-thirds. DOJ's July 2025 recommendation of one day in prison for Brett Hankison, the officer convicted of violating Breonna Taylor's civil rights -- rejected by the sentencing judge, who imposed 33 months -- was a concrete early instance of the same leniency-toward-police pattern; DOJ later helped secure Hankison's release pending appeal. A former attorney's August 2026 whistleblower disclosure to Congress separately alleges the division's Harvard, Brown, and Columbia antisemitism investigations had predetermined outcomes, and that some departures were driven by attorneys' concern over exposure to state bar discipline for the division's current work.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: A division veteran called this shift unprecedented in nearly 70 years; a former Voting Section chief warned of fraud suits timed around elections.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Strongly sourced, including figures from current employees rather than outside inference; the 2026 whistleblower disclosure's core claims are corroborated across five-plus independent outlets, though two specific procedural details rest on a single source.

title: Mass Reassignment of Federal Agents to Immigration Enforcement Collapsed Drug, Trafficking, Child-Exploitation, and Counterterrorism Casework
institution: Department of Justice (DOJ/OCDETF); Department of Homeland Security (Homeland Security Investigations); FBI; ATF
status: Ongoing -- reassignments continued through the reporting reviewed, with no announced reversal
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OCDETF case-transfer order) through 2025-11 (Senate disclosure of reassignment percentages)
what_changed: Starting in mid-2025, the Trump administration redirected thousands of federal law-enforcement agents and prosecutors from their existing casework to immigration enforcement and mass-deportation operations. On July 23, 2025, the Deputy Attorney General ordered the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Force (OCDETF) -- described by former officials as the nation's largest and most effective anti-crime task force -- to transfer all of its 5,000-plus active cases to a newly created Homeland Security Task Force structure that placed far greater emphasis on immigration offenses and human smuggling than on joint law-enforcement efforts against organized crime and drug trafficking. A Reuters analysis of nearly 2 million federal court records found that, as a direct result, federal drug prosecutions fell roughly 10% compared to the same period in 2024 (about 1,200 fewer cases), the slowest pace since at least the late 1990s, while federal money-laundering prosecutions fell 24%. For the first time in decades, nearly half of all people charged with federal crimes in 2025 were accused of immigration violations, and roughly 700 additional federal prosecutors -- more than one in ten nationwide -- were assigned to at least some immigration casework. Reuters quoted federal officials describing high-priority cases stalling as a direct result, including one supervising prosecutor who said a fentanyl-trafficking investigation was at a standstill because the agents leading it had been ordered to focus on deportations instead. The Wall Street Journal and New York Times separately reported the reassignment extended well beyond DOJ: at Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) -- one of the primary federal agencies combating child exploitation, human trafficking, and fentanyl smuggling -- personnel warned the reassignments were dismantling one of the country's most effective child-protection and national-security forces, with key trafficking routes left unstaffed. NYT reported the same pattern hit counterterrorism and sanctions-enforcement work: investigations into the black-market Iranian oil trade used to finance terrorism were delayed by months, and highly trained specialized personnel were reassigned to routine traffic stops and immigrant roundups. Sen. Mark Warner disclosed in November 2025 that 25% to 45% of FBI agents working counterterrorism, cyber, espionage, and child-exploitation cases had been reassigned to immigration enforcement; separate reporting put the reassignment rate at roughly 25% of FBI agents overall and as high as 80% of ATF agents. A subsequent Reuters/NYT analysis of federal data found drug arrests and gun seizures had dropped sharply nationwide as HSI and other agencies pulled agents off narcotics and firearms casework to staff deportation operations, with former officials describing key investigations as stalled or abandoned outright.

primary_proponent.name: Deputy Attorney General (DOJ leadership directing the OCDETF case transfer); DHS leadership (HSI reassignments)
primary_proponent.role: DOJ's Deputy Attorney General ordered OCDETF's case load transferred to the new Homeland Security Task Force structure on July 23, 2025; DHS leadership directed HSI agent reassignments to immigration enforcement documented separately by WSJ and NYT
primary_proponent.note: Reporting reviewed did not identify by name the specific DAG who signed the July 2025 OCDETF transfer order; this entry names the office rather than an unconfirmed individual, consistent with this tracker's convention when sourcing does not clearly identify a more specific individual.

estimated_impact.summary: Federal capacity to prosecute drug trafficking, money laundering, child exploitation, human trafficking, counterterrorism, and sanctions-evasion cases measurably declined as agents and prosecutors were redirected to immigration enforcement, with officials on the record describing specific stalled investigations (a fentanyl case, Iranian oil-sanctions evasion) as direct results.

title: DOJ and DHS Canceled Hundreds of Millions in Public-Safety and Violence-Prevention Grants in 2025, With Most Recipients Still Unreimbursed Months Later
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (Office of Justice Programs) and U.S. Department of Homeland Security (Center for Prevention Programs and Partnerships / FEMA)
status: Ongoing -- most DOJ grant recipients remained unreimbursed as of November 2025 reporting; the lead legal challenge to the DOJ cancellations (Vera Institute v. DOJ, D.C. Cir. No. 25-5248) remains pending on appeal with no ruling identified as of this 2026-08-31 recheck; DHS's CP3 office continued operating in reduced, redirected form rather than closing outright; a stipulated injunction barring DOJ from re-obligating the terminated grant funds has been repeatedly extended and remains in effect through at least September 1, 2026, with a further extension decision pending a status report due August 28, 2026 whose outcome was not identified as of this recheck; both officials who led the original 2025 cuts, AG Bondi and DHS Secretary Noem, have since left their posts, replaced by AG Todd Blanche (confirmed by the Senate August 8, 2026) and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (confirmed March 23, 2026), though neither successor is reported to have altered the underlying cancellations or CP3's reduced posture; a May 2026 one-year retrospective found affected organizations still had not recovered, including at least one full nonprofit closure
date_of_action: 2025-02 (CP3 cuts and workforce reductions begin) through 2025-11 (NPR follow-up documenting unreimbursed DOJ grantees)
what_changed: Two parallel cancellation waves hit federal public-safety and violence-prevention grantmaking in 2025. At DHS, in a single week in late February/early March 2025, the department cut roughly $20 million from more than two dozen programs tied to its Center for Prevention Programs and Partnerships (CP3) -- the office responsible for terrorism and targeted-violence-prevention grants -- including counterterrorism and school-shooter-prevention initiatives; the roughly $90 million CP3 had awarded to community groups and law enforcement since 2020 was placed in jeopardy. Affected programs included a Boston Children's Hospital intervention team for violent youth behavior, the Eradicate Hate prevention umbrella group, research into far-right-extremist disengagement, a national threat-compilation database for law enforcement, and hate-crimes training programs; one recipient told ProPublica that programs based in 'sanctuary states' resisting deportation cooperation were specifically targeted. FEMA's separate Nonprofit Security Grant Program, which funds physical security upgrades at religious institutions including synagogues, was also frozen amid the same review. On March 3, 2025, CP3 dismissed roughly 20% of its workforce through probationary-employee terminations; Director William Braniff resigned the same night, calling the terminations 'wrongful.' DHS's own framing, in a July 2025 press release, characterized $18.5 million in canceled CP3 grants as eliminating 'wasteful, misdirected spending' rather than shutting the office down, and DHS materials indicate CP3 continued operating afterward in a reduced form -- a more precise characterization than some contemporaneous reporting describing the office as fully 'shut down.' A ProPublica investigation published June 4, 2025 found DHS had installed Thomas Fugate, a 22-year-old with a one-year-old undergraduate degree and no counterterrorism background, to lead CP3's remaining work. On June 27, 2025, House Homeland Security Committee ranking members Bennie Thompson and Seth Magaziner sent a letter demanding Fugate be called to testify on current threats to the homeland. The Daily Beast then reported (published on or around July 8, 2025) that police had investigated Fugate in 2020, at age 18, over threatening text messages he allegedly sent a romantic rival in a teenage love triangle; DHS denied any police investigation occurred, calling it a parental matter, but the Cedar Park (TX) City Attorney's Office told Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in a letter that an investigation involving Fugate over 'alleged injury to a child' had in fact taken place -- Fugate was not charged either way. By July 22, 2025, DHS itself walked back Fugate's public profile, telling reporters he was only a 'Special Assistant' who never held CP3's director role or exercised operational control over it, contradicting DHS's own earlier framing (and much contemporaneous reporting) of him as the office's head; Fugate gave an interview describing himself as 'low-level' staff. Separately at DOJ, the Office of Justice Programs (OJP) abruptly canceled roughly 350-373 grants worth more than $800 million on April 22, 2025, terminating funding mid-cycle for programs supporting crime victims, opioid-abuse and trauma recovery, rural law enforcement, disability services, and legally mandated functions including prison-rape-elimination-act audits. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0203): among that April 22 wave, 69 of 145 community violence intervention (CVI) grants -- worth $158 million of more than $300 million DOJ had awarded to CVI programs -- were abruptly terminated, hitting groups in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Washington D.C., and Baltimore that trained outreach workers to de-escalate conflict, connected at-risk people to social services and employment, and ran hospital-based programs for gun-violence victims; a Council on Criminal Justice analysis found more than 550 organizations affected, almost all nonprofits. Five organizations -- the Vera Institute of Justice, the Center for Children and Youth Justice, Chinese for Affirmative Action, FORCE Detroit, and Health Resources in Action -- sought a preliminary injunction and reversal in a lawsuit filed May 2025; in July 2025, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta denied the injunction and dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction and failure to state a constitutional claim, while separately calling DOJ's conduct 'shameful' and likely to harm vulnerable communities. Plaintiffs appealed to the D.C. Circuit the next day (case no. 25-5248); the appeal was argued October 14, 2025, and no ruling had been issued as of this recheck (docket last updated June 22, 2026) -- the case remains open on appeal, not finally resolved as this entry previously implied. Six months after the cancellations, NPR reported in November 2025 that most affected organizations still had not been reimbursed for money already spent under the canceled grants, forcing layoffs, draws on reserve funds, and reduced services; organizations that appealed the cancellations reported no response, and several had filed additional lawsuits. DOJ told NPR the government shutdown then underway -- which began roughly five months after the cancellations -- was hindering its ability to process appeals and reimbursements, though the cancellations themselves predated the shutdown by months. Circuit appeal (No. 25-5248) remained pending with no ruling identified as of this recheck. Update 2026-08-31: neither of the two officials who directed the original 2025 cuts remains in office. Markwayne Mullin, confirmed by the Senate 54-45 and sworn in March 24, 2026; Noem moved to a newly created role as special envoy for a security initiative called the Shield of the Americas. No reporting identified in this recheck indicates either successor has revisited the CP3 cuts or the DOJ grant cancellations themselves. Separately, the stipulated injunction in Vera Institute v. DOJ barring DOJ from re-obligating or further diminishing the terminated grant funds -- entered July 21, 2025 and previously described in this entry's prior recheck only via a since-superseded February 25, 2026 status report extending it to May 5, 2026 -- has in fact been extended multiple additional times since, most recently (per an April 30, 2026 joint status report) to July 10, 2026 and (per a July 8, 2026 joint status report) currently through September 1, 2026; the parties' next joint status report, due August 28, 2026, was to determine whether the injunction is extended further, but no report content or ruling was identified as of this recheck. title: DOJ Career-Staff Purge Guts Environment Division Enforcement Capacity
institution: U.S. Department of Justice — Environment and Natural Resources Division (ENRD), with related reassignments touching the Civil Rights and National Security Divisions
status: Ongoing and formalized — beyond the sustained attorney exodus documented through mid-2026, the division itself was renamed in June 2026 with an explicit mission shift away from environmental enforcement, and Trump has since used the pardon power to unwind Clean Air Act criminal cases the division's remaining attorneys had prosecuted
date_of_action: 2025-01-27 (initial reassignments) through 2025-03-25 (formal DOJ-wide reorganization memo), with effects documented into 2026
what_changed: In the days immediately following Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, DOJ began reassigning senior career officials across multiple divisions -- national security, civil rights, and public corruption staff were transferred into a newly created Sanctuary Cities Enforcement Working Group, often into roles outside their expertise. The Environment and Natural Resources Division (ENRD) was hit hardest: all four Environmental Enforcement Section chiefs, including section chief Tom Mariani (who had led the section since 2016), were told they were being involuntarily transferred to the working group; Mariani chose retirement instead, leaving in February 2025. The division's civil-rights-focused work was also frozen -- DOJ reportedly halted all Civil Rights Division cases pending review. Separately, career staff working on environmental-justice and diversity initiatives were placed on administrative leave, incoming Honors Program job offers to new attorneys were rescinded, and DOJ requested a list of probationary employees from the White House, raising concerns about a broader mass-firing push. On March 25, 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal memorandum cementing a sweeping DOJ-wide reorganization, including further ENRD reassignments to the Office of Sanctuary Cities. Follow-up reporting over a year later (Inside Climate News and E&E News, July-August 2026) found the damage was substantial and lasting: ENRD, which began 2025 with roughly 400 attorneys, had lost at least a third of its lawyers, representing more than 260 combined years of legal experience among just the 11 senior attorneys and managers interviewed; and DOJ's civil environmental lawsuits referred by EPA fell to just 16 in Trump's first year back in office, a 76% drop from the first year of the Biden administration. A separate, October 2025 Bloomberg Law report adds a concrete budget-request figure to this attrition: the administration's FY2026 budget request sought $90 million for ENRD, a 22.5% drop from FY2025, and proposed cutting division staffing from 641 to 449 positions, including 79 attorney positions. The same report quotes former Environmental Enforcement Section head Tom Mariani putting the section's own headcount at roughly 120 lawyers in February 2025, down to 65-70 by October 2025 -- a steeper, more specific decline than the single-digit-months-later 'at least a third' figure this entry already cites from the later Inside Climate News/E&E News reporting, and consistent with it. Section-level detail from the same Inside Climate News/E&E News reporting, not previously broken out in this entry: the Environmental Crimes Section fell from 42 attorneys to roughly 21 (a 50% cut), and the Environmental Enforcement Section dropped to less than half its prior size -- both steeper than the division-wide 'at least a third' figure, consistent with section chiefs and senior staff being disproportionately targeted in the initial 2025 reassignments. In June 2026, DOJ formally renamed ENRD to the Energy and Natural Resources Division, per the department's own press release, explicitly reorienting its stated mission toward 'advancing U.S. energy dominance' rather than environmental protection -- confirmed directly against justice.gov, whose ENRD landing page now carries the new name. On July 3, 2026, Trump pardoned nine people convicted of Clean Air Act violations for installing 'defeat devices' that bypass diesel-engine emissions controls (part of a larger 11-person pardon batch that included non-CAA cases), calling the recipients victims of Biden-era 'persecution' for 'fixing their car'; this followed DOJ's own earlier 2026 directive ordering federal prosecutors to drop pending defeat-device prosecutions, meaning the division's remaining attorneys are now unwinding cases their own predecessors built rather than only losing capacity to bring new ones. Separately, Law360 reported August 19, 2026, citing court filings, that a top deputy in the renamed division left the agency; the deputy's identity and reason for departure were not accessible in sourcing reviewed (Law360's full report sits behind a paywall), so this is noted as an unconfirmed-detail data point rather than asserted as fact.

title: DOJ and FBI National-Security Ranks Gutted by Departures Just as U.S. Braced for Iranian Retaliation; DHS Dissolved Its WMD-Countering Office the Same Month
institution: Department of Justice (National Security Division), Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Homeland Security
status: Reported as a completed set of departures/reorganizations as of mid-2025 reporting; sourcing reviewed for this entry did not identify a walk-back or reversal of the DOJ/FBI departures or the CWMD dissolution
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2025-06, surfacing publicly in reporting dated 2025-06-16 (CWMD dissolution) and 2025-06-24 (DOJ/FBI staffing losses)
what_changed: As the U.S. braced for possible Iranian retaliation following the June 22, 2025 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear sites, NBC News reported that political departures and forced-outs had hollowed out the national-security ranks of both DOJ and the FBI. DOJ's National Security Division -- the division responsible for nationwide visibility into terrorism and counterintelligence threats -- had its Law and Policy section's staff drop by as much as two-thirds, while its Counterintelligence and Export Control section lost roughly one-third of its workforce. At least 20 FBI national-security personnel departed in the three months preceding the report. Robert Wells, head of the FBI's National Security Branch, was forced out shortly after Trump took office in January 2025; David Scott, the FBI's counterterrorism chief, left in May 2025. Four ousted National Security Division officials alone represented close to 100 years of combined institutional experience, according to a former senior DOJ official who said 'the senior ranks of the FBI and DOJ's national security teams have been decimated.' Former DOJ counterintelligence chief David Laufman said the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran 'heightened the risk of Iranian retaliation in the homeland' and warned the losses could 'adversely impact' the FBI's ability to prevent Iranian attempts within the United States, given the National Security Division's role providing nationwide visibility into the threat landscape during exactly this kind of crisis. Separately, the New York Times reported the same week that DHS and the FBI had redirected national-security and counterterrorism resources toward immigration enforcement even as Iran-retaliation risk rose. DHS's FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification, published June 16, 2025, formalized the complete dissolution of the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction (CWMD) office -- the DHS component responsible for coordinating federal defense against chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and high-yield-explosive threats, including biosurveillance and detection-equipment procurement -- eliminating all 286 of its positions and redistributing its $409.4 million budget across other DHS components: policy functions to the DHS Office of Strategy, Policy, and Plans; the National Biosurveillance Integration Center to the Office of Health Security; operational programs including BioWatch to CISA's Infrastructure Security Division; R&D to the U.S. Coast Guard; and $142.9 million in federal assistance programs to CISA. This dissolution is a distinct action from, and predates, the roughly one-third CISA workforce reduction documented separately in this tracker (see cisa-cyber-workforce-cuts-trump2.json) -- CWMD was a standalone DHS office with its own chemical/biological/radiological/nuclear mission, not a CISA program, though CISA absorbed some of its functions and budget in the dissolution.

estimated_impact.summary: At the exact moment U.S. officials were warning of heightened Iranian retaliation risk following the June 2025 strikes on Iran's nuclear sites, DOJ's National Security Division and the FBI's national-security ranks had already lost a large share of experienced staff, and DHS had formally dissolved its dedicated office for countering chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear threats -- a convergence former officials say directly weakened the government's capacity to detect and respond to exactly this kind of crisis.

title: Two-Thirds of the DOJ Unit That Defends Trump's Policies in Court Have Quit
institution: U.S. Department of Justice — Civil Division, Federal Programs Branch
status: Ongoing as of July 2025 reporting -- no reversal, staffing-restoration effort, or updated attrition figure identified in later sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2024-11 (post-election departures begin) through 2025-07-14 (Reuters' cumulative reporting)
what_changed: Reuters reported July 14, 2025 that roughly 69 of the 110 attorneys who staffed DOJ's Federal Programs Branch -- the Civil Division unit responsible for defending nearly every federal policy and executive action against legal challenge, including the bulk of the lawsuits filed against the second Trump administration -- had left since the November 2024 election, a roughly two-thirds attrition rate. The departures included at least 10 of the branch's 23 supervisors, experienced litigators who in many cases had served across multiple presidential administrations regardless of party; former officials described this level of turnover mid-administration as unprecedented for the unit. Departing attorneys gave two overlapping reasons: at least three said they left specifically over fear of being sanctioned for refusing department pressure to skew facts in court filings or otherwise violate professional ethics rules, while others described broader demoralization and exhaustion from continuously defending an unusually large volume of litigation against the administration's own policies -- work several described as being asked to defend actions they personally viewed as unconstitutional. This is a distinct, narrower thread from the department-wide attorney attrition already documented in doj-workforce-collapse-trump2.json (which separately cross-references the Civil Rights Division and ENRD exoduses); the Federal Programs Branch's specific role -- as DOJ's primary in-court defender of the administration's own actions -- makes its attrition rate a direct measure of institutional strain on the government's litigation capacity precisely where that capacity is most tested by legal challenges to the administration itself.

title: DOJ Reassigned the Senior Attorneys Running Its 60-Year-Old Program Accrediting Non-Lawyers to Help Indigent Immigrants, Freezing Its Core Functions
institution: Department of Justice / Executive Office for Immigration Review
status: Ongoing -- as of late April 2026 reporting, the program had not approved a single new accreditation application since the March 2026 reassignments, and Illinois-based immigration advocacy organizations independently described the office as being 'quietly gutted'; applications continue to accumulate (40-60 per week) with no staff authorized to process them, and no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2026-03 (senior attorneys reassigned)
what_changed: CBS News reported DOJ abruptly reassigned the handful of senior attorneys who operate the Recognition and Accreditation program -- a more than 60-year-old program, administered by DOJ's Executive Office for Immigration Review, that accredits non-attorneys working for largely faith-based legal-aid organizations (such as Catholic Charities and Jewish Family Services) so they are legally authorized to assist low-income immigrants with matters ranging from naturalization petitions to representation in immigration court. The reassignment orders came from Jamee Comans, Acting Assistant Director for DOJ's Office of Policy, which administers the program. Most of the reassigned attorneys were told they would now work as entry-level law clerks in immigration courts -- a role typically reserved for people fresh out of law school -- while only two support staff remained in the accreditation office, neither with legal authority to approve or renew accreditation applications. A DOJ official told CBS the program 'isn't ending or being abolished' and 'will continue,' but confirmed the office kept receiving 40-60 new applications per week even after the reassignment, with no staff able to act on them, creating a growing backlog.

title: DOJ Fired More Than 100 Immigration Judges in 2025, Even After Congress Funded Hiring More to Cut a 4-Million-Case Backlog
institution: Department of Justice, Executive Office for Immigration Review
status: Ongoing through 2025; no reversal or reinstatement identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025 (firings continuing throughout the year); a 17-judge round announced July 2025, days-to-weeks after Congress's mega-spending bill appropriated funding to add judges
what_changed: Throughout 2025, the Justice Department's Executive Office for Immigration Review fired more than 100 of the roughly 750 immigration judges who had been in place at the start of the second Trump administration, most without a stated cause. In one round, 15 immigration judges serving in California, Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, New York, Ohio, Texas, Utah, and Virginia were told on a Friday they would be placed on leave with termination effective July 22, 2025, with two more judges in Chicago and Houston fired separately around the same time. The firings came despite -- and shortly after -- Congress passing a mega-spending bill appropriating more than $3 billion for DOJ immigration-related activities, including funding to hire additional immigration judges, in an explicit effort to reduce the nearly 4 million-case immigration court backlog; Congress had authorized up to 800 immigration judge positions. Matt Biggs, president of the IFPTE union representing immigration judges, called the firings 'outrageous and against the public interest,' saying 'you can't enforce immigration laws when you fire the enforcers.' Among those fired: Ila Deiss, a Massachusetts immigration judge since 2017 with consistently excellent performance reviews who was on pace to resolve roughly 1,000 cases that year, fired without advance notice or an explanation; DOJ separately fired a forensic accountant, identified in NPR's reporting by the surname Feinstein, who had worked seven years with stellar reviews at DOJ's U.S. Trustee Program investigating bankruptcy fraud -- her firing came the same summer her husband's ICEBlock app, which tracks the movement of ICE agents, drew national attention, raising the question of whether the firing was retaliatory, though DOJ did not state a reason. NPR's broader reporting described a Justice Department workforce reshaped by hundreds of firings across roles -- prosecutors, immigration judges, forensic accountants -- amid a documented pattern of officials removed for resisting political pressure or clashing with the administration, without always being told why.

primary_proponent.note: DOJ's Executive Office for Immigration Review, which conducts the firings, operates under Bondi's authority; no individual official was named in reporting as personally directing each specific judge's removal.

estimated_impact.summary: Removing more than 100 of roughly 750 immigration judges -- a workforce Congress was simultaneously funding to expand, not shrink -- directly undercuts the stated goal of reducing a nearly 4 million-case immigration court backlog, with several fired judges (including at least one on pace for roughly 1,000 case resolutions that year) having no performance-based reason given for their removal.

title: DOJ Sued 21 States to End In-State College Tuition for Undocumented Students, Winning 5 and Losing at Least 1
institution: Department of Justice / state higher-education tuition policy nationwide
status: Ongoing, mixed outcomes -- 5 states (Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois) resolved on terms favorable to DOJ; a Minnesota federal judge ruled in March 2026 that state's Dream Act may stand; litigation against additional states continued through at least September 2026
date_of_action: 2025-04-28 (EO 14287 signed) through 2026-09 (litigation ongoing against additional states)
what_changed: Following Trump's April 28, 2025 executive order 'Protecting American Communities from Criminal Aliens' (and the related EO 14218, 'Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Open Borders'), the Department of Justice began a sustained litigation campaign against states that let undocumented students pay in-state college tuition rates or receive state financial aid, arguing the practice unlawfully discriminates against U.S. citizens from other states who pay higher out-of-state rates. DOJ filed its first suit against Texas on June 4, 2025; Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Trump-aligned Republican, signed a consent agreement the same day the suit was filed, immediately ending the state's 24-year-old law -- a turnaround fast enough that the Texas Tribune and other observers raised questions about coordinated state-federal collusion rather than adversarial litigation. DOJ then expanded the campaign through the rest of 2025 and 2026, ultimately suing 21 states including Minnesota, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Illinois, California, Virginia, Nebraska, New Jersey, Kansas, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland, Colorado, New York, Connecticut, Vermont, Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington. Five states -- Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, and Illinois -- resolved on terms favorable to DOJ, ending their programs. The campaign was not uniformly successful: a federal judge in Minnesota ruled in March 2026 that the state's Dream Act could stand, rejecting DOJ's challenge. As one documented financial-scale example, DOJ's own complaint against Arizona stated that 432 people without legal immigration status received in-state tuition at Arizona State University in fall 2025 alone, totaling $10.5 million in reduced tuition at that single school in a single semester. Advocacy groups estimated roughly 500,000 undocumented students nationally could lose access to affordable in-state tuition if the campaign succeeds everywhere it has been filed.

primary_proponent.note: Signed the two executive orders (14218, 14287) directing DOJ's campaign against state in-state-tuition policies for undocumented students; DOJ under Attorney General Pam Bondi executed the resulting lawsuits.

estimated_impact.summary: The campaign threatens affordable college access for an estimated 500,000 undocumented students nationally; five states have already ended their programs under DOJ pressure, while at least one (Minnesota) successfully defended its policy in court, and Texas's same-day consent agreement raised distinct state-federal collusion concerns beyond the underlying policy question.

title: DOJ Cuts Over 4,000 Jobs at FBI, ATF, DEA, and National Security Division While Immigration Enforcement Gets More Funding
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (FBI, ATF, DEA, National Security Division)
status: Documented via DOJ's own management-unit records, obtained by Reuters under FOIA and reported April 23, 2026; no reversal or correction identified as of this entry
date_of_action: Cuts accumulated across fiscal year 2024 through early 2026; reported 2026-04-23
what_changed: Justice Department management-unit records obtained by Reuters under the Freedom of Information Act show the Trump administration cut more than 4,000 employees from several of the DOJ's top law-enforcement components even as the administration publicly vowed to get tough on crime. The FBI's total employee count dropped more than 7% since fiscal year 2024, a loss of about 2,600 people. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) lost about 14% of its staff. The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) lost about 6% of its staff. The National Security Division, which handles intelligence and terrorism matters, lost nearly 38% of its staff -- the steepest cut of any of the components named. One notable exception to the pattern: the arm of DOJ handling immigration enforcement secured billions of dollars in additional funding over the same period, as the administration pushed to increase deportations -- making this both a staffing cut at the named components and a funding redirection toward immigration enforcement specifically.

primary_proponent.role: Then-Attorney General (served 2025-2026, removed by Trump April 2, 2026)

title: DOJ's September 2025 Reorganization Disbanded the 43-Year-Old OCDETF Anti-Cartel Task Force and Nearly Eliminated the 1964 Community Relations Service and Office for Access to Justice, Cutting About 275 Positions
institution: Department of Justice (OCDETF, Community Relations Service, Office for Access to Justice)
status: OCDETF permanently disbanded, cases transferred to Homeland Security Task Forces -- no reversal reported as of the reporting reviewed. CRS and Office for Access to Justice layoffs were initially allowed to proceed by a federal judge, then partially reversed by DOJ in January 2026 (13 of 15 CRS employees and Access to Justice's terminated staff reinstated 'as a matter of administrative discretion') following a bipartisan congressional funding deal; litigation over CRS's underlying legality continues.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OCDETF case-transfer order) through 2026-01 (DOJ rescinds CRS and Access to Justice layoff notices)
what_changed: In September 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi approved the most sweeping Justice Department reorganization in two decades, disbanding three units: the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETF), the Community Relations Service (CRS), and the Office for Access to Justice -- cutting about 275 positions and eliminating or involuntarily reassigning roughly 140 employees. The reorganization built on an order the Deputy Attorney General had issued July 23, 2025, directing OCDETF -- established under President Reagan in 1982 as the Attorney General's centerpiece program for coordinating multi-agency drug-cartel and organized-crime investigations -- to transfer all of its 5,000-plus active cases to newly created Homeland Security Task Forces, a structure created by a Trump executive order on his first day in office that did not become fully operational until September 2025 (see the separately tracked doj-dhs-agent-reassignment-immigration-2025 entry for the immediate casework consequences of that July transfer order). DOJ ordered OCDETF operations shut down by September 30, 2025, and its last employees departed through a Reduction in Force on October 31, 2025, ending a 43-year program that, per its own final report, had conducted more than 37,200 investigations, dismantled or significantly disrupted over 21,100 criminal enterprises, convicted more than 321,000 defendants, and seized $13.4 billion in cash and property and over 870,000 weapons -- including the investigation that led to the conviction of Sinaloa Cartel leader Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzman. Congress had directed $547 million annually to OCDETF for the two prior fiscal years and included that funding rate in the continuing resolution then in effect; Republican-led appropriations reports had called eliminating the program 'infeasible,' and veteran House appropriator Harold Rogers told a September markup that 'our commitment to the work of the task forces can't be underestimated,' but DOJ disbanded it regardless, characterizing the move as a reorganization rather than a closure. Thomas Padden, OCDETF's acting director during the closure, wrote that the replacement structure -- which places far greater emphasis on immigration offenses than joint investigations of organized crime and deprioritizes financial investigations -- leaves the country 'more vulnerable to organized crime threats'; former Rep. Matt Cartwright, D-Pa., who had chaired the House Appropriations subcommittee overseeing DOJ funding, called the unilateral fund repurposing illegal under the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, saying he 'could not imagine DOJ taking this kind of unilateral action' in his 12 years on the subcommittee. The Community Relations Service (CRS) -- a DOJ agency created by Title X of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, nicknamed 'America's Peacemaker,' that mediates racial and ethnic conflict and had deployed to incidents including the unrest following George Floyd's 2020 killing -- was slated in DOJ's FY2026 budget summary to close all offices by the end of FY2025 with no FY2026 funding. DOJ issued Reduction-in-Force notices to 13 of CRS's remaining 15 employees, and on October 30, 2025, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani (Boston) declined to issue a temporary restraining order blocking the October 31 terminations sought by the Ethical Society of Police and two NAACP branches, who alleged the dismantling violated the Civil Rights Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, and separation of powers. Talwani found the plaintiffs 'have made a strong showing that they are likely to succeed on the merits, where Defendants concede that only Congress, and not the executive branch, may eliminate a Congressionally created agency,' but held they had not shown irreparable harm sufficient for injunctive relief while the case proceeded. The Office for Access to Justice -- established in 2010 to expand legal aid and promote fairness in the criminal justice system -- was hit the same way, with RIF notices issued September 29, 2025. Both reversals came in January 2026: on January 9, DOJ rescinded the layoff notices to 13 of CRS's employees, reinstating them 'as a matter of administrative discretion' without saying whether they would resume CRS duties (plaintiffs asked the court to assess the impact); DOJ separately reinstated the Office for Access to Justice's terminated employees around the same time. Both reversals followed, within about a week, a bipartisan congressional spending deal that would fund the Access to Justice office and give CRS $20 million in fiscal 2026 -- funding the administration's own budget proposal had zeroed out. No comparable reversal has been reported for OCDETF, whose closure and case transfer to the Homeland Security Task Force structure remains in effect.

title: DOJ withholds $88 million in appropriated anti-trafficking victim services funding
institution: DOJ Office for Victims of Crime (OVC), Office of Justice Programs
status: Ongoing (as of Nov. 2025 letter; funds not yet released)
what_changed: On October 1, 2025, DOJ's Office for Victims of Crime allowed grants funding more than 100 anti-trafficking victim service providers to lapse without issuing new grants, cutting off services for at least 5,000 trafficking survivors nationwide; the lapse coincided with that day's federal government shutdown, which separately affected services for over 17,000 survivors. As of a November 14, 2025 letter, OVC had still not released any notice of funding opportunity for the $88 million Congress appropriated to these programs (authorized under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act) in FY25 -- 45 days after the lapse. A coalition of 45 national anti-trafficking and anti-violence organizations plus 22 state and local organizations (Freedom Network USA, Polaris, International Rescue Committee, Kids in Need of Defense, and others) wrote directly to Attorney General Pam Bondi, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Maureen Henneberg (Office of Justice Programs), and Acting OVC Director Katherine D. Schmitt, urging DOJ to release the FY25 funds and, in the interim, offer non-competitive one-year awards to existing FY22 grantees so survivors don't lose access while a new funding-opportunity process runs (which the letter itself estimates can take multiple months). An earlier, separate letter -- signed by 74 advocacy and faith-based groups and reported October 3, 2025 -- had already warned lawmakers that the freeze would strip survivors of housing, counseling, and legal support.

title: DOJ's Attorney Corps Nearly Cut in Half Since January 2025, With Its Entry-Level Recruitment Pipeline Frozen and a Growing Public Archive of Resignation Letters
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) -- department-wide attrition, distinct from this tracker's Civil Rights Division- and Environment Division-specific entries
status: Ongoing (Justice Connection's own more granular full-year count, published April 2026, has not been updated with a fresher figure since; DOJ has not published its own current attorney headcount)
date_of_action: 2025-01 (hiring freeze, Honors Program cancellation) through 2025-11 (Justice Connection's ~5,500-departure estimate, farewell-letters archive reporting)
what_changed: President Trump's January 20, 2025 government-wide federal hiring freeze immediately triggered cancellation of the Attorney General's Honors Program -- DOJ's 'premier' entry-level attorney recruitment pipeline, in place since 1953 and typically responsible for more than 100 hires per year from top law schools. Accepted job offers were revoked, with rescission emails citing the freeze directly; the program was later reopened for the 2025-26 recruiting cycle, but the initial cancellation disrupted a full incoming class and, per legal-trade reporting, left the program with diminished appeal to law students and law-school career offices. By June 21, 2025, Trump himself stated that more than 4,000 DOJ employees had accepted voluntary-departure packages under the department-wide 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation program, with officials signaling further rounds of workforce reductions were expected -- a documented mid-year checkpoint between the initial January 2025 hiring freeze and the fuller attrition below. Over the following months, DOJ's overall attorney corps -- an estimated 10,000 people before January 2025 -- was, per Washington Post reporting, 'nearly cut in half' by September 2025 through resignations, retirements, reassignments, and terminations; the Appellate Section specifically lost more than 40% of its attorneys since February 2025. Replacement hiring filled only a fraction of the resulting vacancies, and reporting found new hires skewed toward candidates with more overtly political or ideological alignment with the administration, including hires drawn from Republican congressional offices and conservative advocacy groups rather than DOJ's traditional recruitment channels. The understaffing forced DOJ attorneys to repeatedly seek case-schedule delays across multiple active litigation matters, per the ABA Journal. Justice Connection, a support network for departed DOJ staff founded by former DOJ Civil Division attorney Stacey Young, separately estimated in reporting through November 2025 that roughly 5,500 people -- not exclusively attorneys -- had left the department via resignation, transfer, buyout, or termination since January 2025; by November 23, 2025, Young said the cumulative purge had 'eclipsed 5,000 employees.' Justice Connection also maintains a public 'farewell messages' page (thejusticeconnection.org/farewell-messages) that had grown, by that point, into a chronicled archive of DOJ resignation letters, including from senior officials, describing political interference, retaliation, and pressure to pursue cases some departing attorneys viewed as targeting the administration's perceived critics rather than legitimate law-enforcement priorities. This entry documents DOJ's department-wide attorney attrition and recruitment-pipeline collapse; two narrower threads already tracked in this database document specific divisions in more depth -- the Civil Rights Division's roughly 75% attorney exodus (see doj-civil-rights-division-exodus-trump2.json) and the Environment and Natural Resources Division's career-staff purge (see doj-enrd-career-staff-purge-2025.json), and -- added 2026-09-12, round-4 backlog cluster c0450 -- the Civil Division's Federal Programs Branch, which lost roughly two-thirds of its attorneys defending the administration's own policies in court by July 2025 (see doj-federal-programs-branch-exodus-2025.json) -- all three consistent with, and contributing to, the department-wide pattern documented here. Update 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0733): a November 26, 2025 Washington Post analysis found the pattern extending to DOJ's ability to secure indictments at all -- federal grand juries had begun declining to return charges prosecutors sought, and judges had admonished DOJ prosecutors for misconduct at least three times since November 2025, a marked departure from historical norms (as a baseline, DOJ secured indictments in all but six of roughly 130,000 federal cases charged in 2016). Lindsey Halligan's installation as interim U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia and grand juries' partial rejection of her case against James Comey (see halligan-comey-vindictive-prosecution-2025-2026.json) were the Post's lead example of this broader trend, not an isolated incident. A December 17, 2025 Reuters analysis, citing Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, found the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia's criminal-complaint dismissal rate had risen to 21% over an eight-week span in mid-2025, compared to a 0.5% rate over the prior decade, and tied the pattern to more than 2,900 DOJ attorney departures from January through November 2025 -- a separate count, on a different measurement window, from the Washington Post and Justice Connection figures already documented above. Reuters also documented a dismissed gun case after an unlawful backpack search lacking probable cause, improper public statements by FBI Director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche that courts cited in vindictive-prosecution rulings, and federal courts quashing DOJ subpoenas for bad faith. Former federal prosecutors quoted by Reuters attributed the pattern to institutional-knowledge loss from the mass departures documented above, combined with political pressure to bring cases before they were ready. Update (2026-08-17 recheck): Justice Connection published its own detailed "By the Numbers" accounting on April 7, 2026, covering the full period from January 2025 through January 2026 -- a later, more granular count than the Washington Post/ABA Journal "nearly cut in half" figure this entry originally led with. Justice Connection's own count puts DOJ's attorney corps at 12,955 as of December 31, 2024 (a larger baseline than the ~10,000 figure the Post used) and documents 3,402 attorney departures between January 2025 and January 2026 -- "over a quarter of its legal machinery in a year," per the group's own framing, not a figure it characterizes as nearly half. The breakdown: 1,421 departures from DOJ headquarters (including 338 in leadership roles), 1,356 from U.S. Attorneys' Offices (including 260 leaders), and 370 from the Executive Office for Immigration Review. The average departing employee had 16.6 years of federal service (over 22 years among departing leaders), and 2,069 of the 3,402 resigned before becoming eligible for retirement -- consistent with departures driven by working conditions rather than planned retirements. This is a later, more precise count from the same organization already cited in this entry, not a contradiction from a new or less credible source; it should be read alongside, not as flatly replacing, the earlier Washington Post/ABA Journal reporting, since the two also cover different measurement windows (a September 2025 snapshot vs. a full January 2025-January 2026 year). Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 34): identified a formal, dated policy response to the recruitment-pipeline collapse that this entry's existing Honors Program discussion had not captured. On March 13, 2026, DOJ headquarters sent U.S. Attorneys' offices nationwide a memo titled "Suspension of Attorney One Year Experience Requirement," waiving the department's longstanding requirement that newly hired federal prosecutors have at least one year of legal practice experience -- permitting hiring directly from law school with only a law degree and active state bar membership. The suspension, which cites an "exigent hiring need for attorneys across the department," remains in effect through February 28, 2027. Job postings reflecting the change appeared in multiple U.S. Attorneys' offices with documented attrition, including Minnesota, Southern Florida, Montana, Alaska, and Louisiana. Harvard Law School affiliates and former federal prosecutors quoted in press coverage said the policy could expand access to public-service legal careers but risks oversight and mentorship gaps for prosecutors trying cases without prior practice experience. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): DOJ leadership imposed a new caseload floor on the prosecutors it has retained -- in the weeks before a July 14, 2026 Bloomberg Law report, the deputy attorney general's office told all 93 U.S. Attorney's offices that Assistant U.S. Attorneys must maintain at least 25 open matters at all times, with DOJ leadership monitoring case-management databases to flag prosecutors falling below that line for possible transfer. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels defended the floor as 'the bare minimum' -- noting hundreds of AUSAs already juggle 100+ open matters -- and framed it as a tool to push out 'low productivity AUSAs.' Former DOJ official Mark Yancey and other critics warned the quota risks pressuring prosecutors, especially those handling long-running white-collar, corruption, or national-security matters that can occupy a full docket for months, into bringing weak or premature charges to hit the number. This is a direct operational consequence of the attorney-corps attrition this entry documents -- a formal productivity mandate imposed on the shrunken remaining workforce rather than a new departure or hiring datapoint.

title: Trump Halted Labor Department Contractor Civil-Rights Enforcement on Day One, Killing a Near-Complete BAE Systems Sexual-Harassment Case
institution: Department of Labor / Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP)
status: Complete -- enforcement office's core function halted; underlying investigations, including BAE Systems, not resolved

what_changed: On January 20, 2025 -- his first day back in office -- Trump signed an executive order revoking Executive Order 11246, the 1965 order requiring federal contractors to comply with anti-discrimination and affirmative-action obligations, and directed the Department of Labor office enforcing it to stop most of its work. Acting Labor Secretary Vincent Micone followed on January 24 with an order directing DOL staff to 'immediately cease and desist' enforcing contractor compliance under the revoked framework. This effectively shut down the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs' active enforcement docket, including a nearly-complete two-year investigation into BAE Systems -- a defense contractor holding roughly $8 billion in annual federal contracts for weapons, vehicles, and cybersecurity tools -- over findings that male managers at a Norfolk, Virginia Navy shipyard had demanded oral sex and other sexual contact from female employees in exchange for promotions and overtime pay, and that Black women had been paid and promoted at lower rates than men. Investigators had been preparing to propose a resolution requiring BAE to make seven-figure payouts to affected workers and adopt reforms, or risk losing its federal contracts; that resolution was never presented as a result of the halt.

title: Labor Department Lost 20% of Its Staff to Buyouts While Cutting $577 Million in Anti-Child-Labor and Wage-Enforcement Grants -- Then Warned Remaining Staff They Could Face Criminal Charges for Talking to Reporters
institution: U.S. Department of Labor, including its Bureau of International Labor Affairs (ILAB)
status: As of May 2025 reporting, further reductions-in-force were anticipated following a February 2025 White House order for agencies to draw up 'reorganization' plans; DOL did not confirm departure figures or comment on operational impact when asked by The Guardian.

what_changed: By early May 2025, nearly 2,700 Department of Labor employees -- about 20% of the department's workforce -- had left via retirement, early retirement, deferred-resignation buyouts, or the government-wide 'Fork in the Road' program, according to Guardian reporting drawing on department employees. In March 2025, DOL cut $577 million in international labor grants, eliminating years of ongoing work and research and canceling roughly $237 million in funds not yet disbursed; these grants funded core functions including researching and combating forced and child labor abroad and enforcing basic labor-rights standards tied to U.S. free trade agreements. The cuts hit DOL's Bureau of International Labor Affairs (ILAB) especially hard: staffing there was cut by more than a third through buyouts and retirement incentives, with one ILAB employee estimating about half the bureau's staff had taken buyout offers following the grant cuts and threats of further terminations. Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer's office separately exempted OSHA and MSHA safety inspectors specifically from the broader federal resignation program, an acknowledgment that cutting those safety-critical roles carried risks the administration wanted to avoid -- a protection not extended to ILAB or other affected offices. Last month before the Guardian's report, Jihun Han, chief of staff to Secretary Chavez-DeRemer, sent a staff-wide email warning employees they could face criminal charges for speaking to journalists about agency business. A Bureau of Labor Statistics employee told the Guardian the cuts were 'catastrophic,' warning that 'all of the core aspects of working life can no longer be assumed' given the department was already 'chronically underfunded for a long time.' A DOL spokesperson said the department could not confirm the number of employees who had taken retirement or resignation offers or were on administrative leave, and did not comment further on operational impact.

title: Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency Budget Cut Two Years Running, Slashing Recovery Missions for Missing Servicemembers
institution: Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA)
status: Ongoing -- FY2026 cuts already implemented and reducing recovery missions; FY2027 budget capped lower still; new Pentagon oversight (Anthony Tata, assigned June 2026) has pledged to seek roughly $40 million in restored funding via the FY2027 NDAA, but that bill itself remains stalled in the Senate (a July 14, 2026 cloture vote failed) with no House-Senate conference yet convened, so the restoration is not close to secured; DPAA nonetheless conducted its first China recovery mission in 13 years, July-early September 2026, alongside the ongoing budget squeeze
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Hegseth-era Pentagon-wide cost-cutting first put DPAA's budget at risk) through 2026 (FY2026 cuts implemented; FY2027 funding capped)
what_changed: As part of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's broader Pentagon-wide cost-cutting purge that began in February 2025, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency -- the agency responsible for recovering and identifying America's missing servicemembers from past conflicts -- saw its budget cut across two consecutive fiscal years. The FY2026 budget request was $171.3 million for Operation and Maintenance, an 11% reduction from the previously planned $191.4 million, including the loss of 26 civilian billets; the agency's total budget fell from $185 million in FY2025 to $167 million as enacted for FY2026, with FY2027 projected to be capped at $160 million. The funding shortfall forced DPAA to cut its recovery and investigative teams operating in Vietnam from 27 to seven and in Laos from 13 to five, and reduced planned field missions from 105 to 66 -- a 59% reduction. In June 2026, Anthony Tata was assigned Pentagon oversight of DPAA and sought to reassure affected families that he had Trump and Hegseth's full support, pledging to work toward restoring roughly $40 million of the cuts through a bill then pending before Congress. A July 26, 2026 South Texas Public Radio / American Homefront Project report ('Time is passing') adds a Cambodia-specific figure this entry did not previously capture: recovery/investigative teams there were also cut, from three to one, alongside the Vietnam and Laos cuts already documented. As of that report, no restoration funding had been secured -- Sen. Fischer's push (a bill she introduced in the Senate, distinct from the general FY2026/FY2027 NDAA cycle) remained pending, and Tata's outreach to Congress had not yet produced enacted relief. Separately, CRS's DPAA budget primer (updated 2026-03-09) shows the enacted FY2026 NDAA authorized and Congress appropriated DPAA's full agency-wide budget at $171.8 million, matching the administration's original request exactly -- indicating that a $19 million above-request add Sen. Fischer secured at the Senate Armed Services Committee markup stage in July 2025 did not survive to final enactment. (This $171.8 million CRS figure is DPAA's total appropriated budget across all accounts; it is not directly comparable to the $167 million O&M-specific figure already cited in this entry from DPAA's own O&M budget justification, and this entry does not attempt to reconcile the two beyond noting neither reflects the requested restoration.) Fischer's FY2027 NDAA push for the $40 million restoration referenced in this entry was confirmed still pending as of a June 11, 2026 press release, in which she urged 'swift passage through the Senate' -- consistent with this entry's existing framing that the restoration is sought, not secured. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 32): the FY2027 NDAA vehicle carrying Fischer's restoration provision remains unenacted and is now specifically stalled -- the House passed its own version (H.R. 8800) 219-206 on July 22, 2026, but the Senate's companion bill (S. 4784, reported by the Senate Armed Services Committee 18-9 on June 15, 2026) failed a cloture vote on July 14, 2026 after Senate Democrats blocked floor consideration over objections to the Iran war and the bill's overall defense-spending growth, unrelated to the DPAA provision itself. No House-Senate conference has been established as of this update, meaning the $40 million DPAA restoration remains contingent on a broader defense-policy fight that has nothing to do with POW/MIA recovery specifically. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): despite the funding squeeze, DPAA recovery teams conducted a previously undocumented mission in China from roughly July through early September 2026, with an investigative team in Hunan province and field recovery operations in Guangxi province -- DPAA's own announcement describes it as the agency's first recovery mission in China in 13 years. The mission is part of renewed U.S.-China cooperation on MIA recovery that resumed in January 2024, which has since covered Hunan, Guangxi, and Liaoning provinces and included the identification of a World War II 'Flying Tiger' pilot; roughly 678 U.S. personnel remain unaccounted for in China across conflicts from World War II through Vietnam. No source reviewed confirms an outcome (a specific identification or recovery) resulted from this China mission specifically, and the Senate's cloture-vote stalemate on the FY2027 NDAA and the $40 million restoration remained unresolved as of this update -- no further procedural movement was identified beyond the July 14, 2026 failed cloture vote and Leader Thune's subsequent motion to reconsider.

title: USAID/CDC Staff Removals Slowed Response to an Unidentified Deadly Illness Cluster in DRC's Equateur Province -- Cause Never Definitively Confirmed
institution: USAID (in dismantlement) / CDC global health security programs
status: Outbreak clusters resolved/contained by spring 2025; underlying cause never definitively confirmed

what_changed: Beginning in January 2025, two clusters of an unidentified illness caused a wave of deaths in the Bolomba and Basankusu health zones of DRC's Equateur province, eventually totaling roughly 2,969 reported cases and 66 deaths across both clusters. Wired reported that the USAID and CDC staff who would normally work directly with DRC's health ministry to identify and contain such an outbreak had been removed from their DRC posts as part of the agency's dismantlement, and that a separate January 2025 executive order required CDC to cease collaboration with the WHO -- reducing U.S. visibility into and support for the response. USAID had also supported the physical logistics of outbreak response, including training health workers on proper viral-sample storage/shipment and funding the transport of samples from remote areas to central labs; with that support degraded, identifying the cause took longer than it otherwise would have. WHO and CDC investigators ultimately could not definitively confirm a single cause; leading hypotheses included bacterial meningitis and chemical or food-borne poisoning, with one thread of the investigation tracing part of the Bolomba cluster to three children who died after eating a bat carcass. The clusters were brought under control by late March 2025 without ever being conclusively attributed to a single pathogen or cause.
