title: Department of Education Dismantled via Interagency Transfers, Without Congressional Approval
institution: U.S. Department of Education
status: Ongoing (Supreme Court allowed dismantling to continue via McMahon v. New York, July 14, 2025, pending lower-court challenges; Congress has not abolished the department and continues funding it); as of an August 24, 2026 White House event, the administration continues to publicly frame the dismantlement as substantially accomplished while using additional devolution mechanisms -- unrestricted state waivers -- alongside the interagency-transfer strategy already documented
date_of_action: 2025-03 (executive order) through 2026-06 (special education and civil rights transfers, the last core offices remaining)
what_changed: Following a March 2025 Trump executive order directing the department's effective abolition and return of control to the states, Education Secretary Linda McMahon -- following a strategy explicitly drawn from Project 2025, written in part by her now-deputy chief of staff Lindsey Burke -- began signing what would eventually total 14 interagency agreements transferring the department's functions elsewhere, since only Congress can formally eliminate the department itself. K-12, higher education, and workforce training oversight moved to the Department of Labor. On March 21, 2025, Trump separately announced that the Small Business Administration would take over management of the department's $1.6 trillion student loan portfolio; the plan drew immediate legal challenge, and a federal judge blocked the transfer on May 27, 2025, ruling the Higher Education Act assigns that responsibility to the Education Department's Federal Student Aid office and that only Congress could reassign it -- the SBA plan was never carried out, and the portfolio instead began transferring to Treasury in March 2026 as described below. McMahon sought to lay off roughly 1,400 of the department's 4,200 employees in March 2025 (litigated but largely proceeded), halving the department's staff to roughly 2,000. The layoffs' effects were visible within a day: AP News reported more than 300 Federal Student Aid staff were cut, including two dozen from its technology division -- the entire team responsible for the FAFSA systems -- and StudentAid.gov suffered an hours-long outage on March 12, 2025 that blocked students nationwide from completing the federal financial-aid application; laid-off staff, still technically employed through March 21 but with limited system access, struggled to help diagnose the outage, with roughly 70 employees stuck on an hours-long troubleshooting call. The Washington Post reported April 14, 2025 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0236, added 2026-09-10) that the disruption continued past that initial outage: universities nationwide described ongoing delays accessing student records and calculating aid packages, with financial-aid platforms crashing multiple times in the weeks after the layoffs and FSA support lines unresponsive or overwhelmed -- a downstream, university-side view of the same staffing collapse the entry already documents from the agency side. The Guardian reported the FSA cuts also gutted the office's compliance function specifically, eliminating the team responsible for policing for-profit-college fraud and abuse in the $1.6 trillion loan program; consumer advocates drew a direct parallel to the late-1980s student-loan crisis, when weak oversight of for-profit schools helped drive a 41% default rate before Congress tightened compliance requirements. An Education Department Inspector General report found 135 of the department's divisions were left with zero employees after the layoffs, and fewer than 20 retained more than five staff. The March 2025 cuts included a reduction-in-force that laid off nearly half of the Office for Civil Rights' staff and shuttered 7 of its 12 regional offices; during the period OCR was short-staffed (March-September 2025), the office received over 9,000 discrimination complaints and dismissed roughly 90% of them without full review. The Supreme Court allowed the dismantling to proceed via McMahon v. New York, decided July 14, 2025 -- an unsigned emergency-docket order staying a Massachusetts district court's May 22, 2025 injunction that had ordered the laid-off employees reinstated, with Justice Sotomayor dissenting, joined by Kagan and Jackson (correcting this entry's prior 'August 2025' date, which was imprecise) -- while litigation continues in lower courts. title: Education Department Rescinds Disparate-Impact Standard From Title VI Civil Rights Enforcement
institution: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
status: Final rule, effective July 24, 2026
date_of_action: 2026-07-24 (final rule effective)
what_changed: Citing Executive Order 14281, the Department of Education finalized a rule rescinding disparate-impact provisions from its regulations implementing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, effective July 24, 2026. Disparate-impact provisions had allowed investigators to find a school policy violated federal civil rights law based on its disproportionate effect on students of a particular race or ethnicity -- demographic outcome data alone -- even without a facially discriminatory policy or proof of discriminatory intent. Under the rescinded standard, federal investigators could challenge practices like discipline policies, tracking/placement decisions, or resource allocation that produced racially disparate outcomes, regardless of intent. The new rule clarifies that Title VI 'prohibit[s] intentional discrimination and do[es] not prohibit conduct or activities that have an unintentional disparate impact,' meaning investigators must now prove a school district specifically intended to discriminate -- a substantially higher evidentiary bar. Roughly 60 civil rights and education organizations publicly condemned the change, warning it 'will hurt Black, Latino, Asian American, and Native American students, other students of color, and other marginalized students who face higher rates of discrimination.'

title: SAVE Student-Loan Plan Dismantled Over 18 Months, From Application Freeze to Full Termination for 7.5 Million Borrowers
institution: Department of Education
status: Finalized -- SAVE plan ended; borrowers given 90 days from the July 1, 2026 servicer-notice start date to select a new plan
date_of_action: 2025-02-24 (online IDR/consolidation applications pulled down) through 2026-07 (90-day replacement-plan selection window begins)
what_changed: On February 18, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the Biden-era SAVE (Saving on a Valuable Education) income-driven repayment plan -- which had reduced payments to as little as 5% of a borrower's discretionary income and offered forgiveness after 10 years for borrowers who originally borrowed $12,000 or less -- exceeded the Education Secretary's statutory authority, and directed the lower court to broaden its injunction to block the entire SAVE rule, calling into question the legality of related income-contingent plans (PAYE, REPAYE) as well. Late on February 24, 2025, the Education Department responded by pulling down the online application for all income-driven repayment (IDR) plans and Direct loan consolidation entirely -- not just SAVE -- cutting off enrollment access for borrowers who wanted to switch plans regardless of which IDR plan they were pursuing. By mid-March 2025, the Department had closed applications across every IDR plan and restricted eligibility for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, leaving millions of borrowers unable to access repayment calculators or determine their new payment obligations; some reported being unable to determine whether to take a second job or plan for default. Roughly 7.5 million borrowers who had been placed into interest-free forbearance since July 2024 while the litigation proceeded then saw that forbearance end when interest resumed accruing on their loans August 1, 2025, with the White House characterizing the SAVE plan itself as 'illegal' and borrowers facing a roughly 1.5-million-application backlog as they tried to move onto other repayment plans. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0516: Bloomberg reported August 11, 2025 that, amid this resumption, only about a third of the roughly $1.6 trillion in outstanding federal student debt was actively being paid down, with millions of borrowers skipping bills -- some citing inability to afford payments after covering housing and groceries, others refusing to pay as a form of protest -- despite the risk of credit damage and wage garnishment. On July 18, 2025, Politico reported the Department would deny roughly 460,000 of those backlogged applicants -- about a third of the 1.5 million total -- specifically because they had requested the plan with the lowest available monthly payment, with the Department stating loan servicers could not process those requests since SAVE was no longer a legal option; a December 2025 court filing later put the confirmed denial figure at 327,955 IDR applications rejected in August 2025 alone, citing an 'unforeseen ambiguity' about which plan denied borrowers should be enrolled in instead, with 802,730 IDR applications still pending as of the end of November 2025. The underlying litigation concluded with a court ruling that SAVE was unlawful, and in late March 2026 the Education Department formally directed the same 7.5 million borrowers to prepare to exit SAVE, ending their forbearance for good. Starting July 1, 2026, loan servicers began issuing notices giving borrowers 90 days to select a new repayment plan; the Department's chosen replacement option, a new income-driven plan called the Repayment Assistance Plan, ties payments to income and household size with fixed 10-25-year terms, but results in higher monthly payments for most affected borrowers than SAVE had. Borrowers exiting forbearance without selecting a new plan in time would resume payments automatically under a plan that could be substantially costlier than what they had budgeted for during the intervening period of relief.

title: Education Department Announced, Then Reversed, Social Security Benefit Seizures for Defaulted Student Loans -- Now Delayed Again to Mid-2026
institution: U.S. Department of Education (with Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service, via the Treasury Offset Program)

On August 17, 2026, Sen. title: Trump Administration Explored Selling the $1.6-1.77 Trillion Federal Student Loan Portfolio to Private Investors, Over Bipartisan Legal Objections
institution: Department of Education; Department of the Treasury
status: Ongoing exploration -- as of February 2026, ED confirmed talks with stakeholders but said no final decision or action had been taken on a sale; separately, a March 2026 interagency agreement began shifting portfolio administration itself from ED to Treasury in stages, with Sen. Warren saying as of May 2026 that ED/Treasury still could not explain the plan's purpose or implementation
date_of_action: 2025-10-07 (Politico first reports talks) through 2026-02-23 (Under Secretary Kent confirms exploration continuing, no final decision)
what_changed: On October 7, 2025, Politico reported that senior Education and Treasury Department officials, under Secretary Linda McMahon and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, had held talks -- including approaching finance-industry executives as potential buyers -- about selling portions of the federal government's student loan portfolio (reported variously as $1.6 trillion face value, against a roughly $1.1 trillion 2024 FSA fair-value estimate) to private investors. Under the plan, private buyers would gain ownership and collection rights over the loans while the loans' original federal terms would nominally remain unchanged, though critics disputed whether that protection could survive a change of ownership in practice. On November 16-17, 2025, more than 40 congressional Democrats led by Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Ron Wyden sent a formal letter to McMahon and Bessent opposing the sale, arguing it could strip borrowers of legally guaranteed protections -- including income-driven repayment, Public Service Loan Forgiveness, disability discharge, and borrower-defense/fraud-based relief -- and that federal law (the Higher Education Act of 1965) permits the Education Secretary to sell Direct Loans only with Treasury consultation and only if the sale imposes no net cost to the federal government, a condition the lawmakers argued would be difficult to meet given loans are generally worth more to a public lender collecting under federal terms than to a private buyer. By late November 2025, reporting on the same exploration cited an updated $1.77 trillion portfolio figure. On February 23, 2026, Under Secretary Nicholas Kent responded to Sen. Warren's inquiry confirming the department had met with stakeholders 'to discuss ideas' but stated ED 'has not taken any final actions or made final decisions regarding selling all or part of the student loan portfolio' -- leaving which loans might be sold, to whom, on what timeline, and under what terms all undecided as of that response. Update 2026-08-30 (correction -- a related development this entry had missed): in March 2026, separate from the private-sale question, ED and Treasury announced an interagency agreement (IAA) transferring administration of the federal student loan portfolio from ED to Treasury in three stages, as part of the administration's broader effort to dismantle the Education Department (only Congress can formally abolish it, so officials are relocating its functions via inter-agency agreements instead). The first stage, beginning in early 2026, shifted management of defaulted loans -- about $180 billion, roughly 11% of the $1.7 trillion portfolio -- to Treasury; the agreement calls for Treasury to eventually take over all federal student loans. Sen. Warren followed up with an April 2, 2026 letter and, in a May 4, 2026 release, said ED's and Treasury's responses 'cannot articulate a clear purpose or plan' for the IAA and failed to provide implementation details on timing, cost, or Treasury's plans for forced collections on defaulted loans. This IAA is the administrative mechanism determining who would actually control the portfolio if a private sale proceeded, making it directly relevant to this entry's subject; no reporting found ties the two tracks together as parts of one announced plan, and they are presented here as related but distinct actions.

title: EEOC Loses Quorum for Nine Months After Trump Fires Two Democratic Commissioners
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
status: Resolved as a quorum matter (quorum restored October 7, 2025 with Senate confirmation of a third commissioner); the underlying legal challenge to the firings was voluntarily dismissed July 6, 2026 after the Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter ruling foreclosed it
date_of_action: 2025-01-28 (firings) through 2025-10-07 (quorum restored); related litigation resolved 2026-07-06
what_changed: On January 28, 2025, President Trump fired EEOC Commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels, both Democratic appointees, along with General Counsel Karla Gilbride -- in the agency's 60-year history, no commissioner had ever before been removed before the end of their term. Burrows's term was not set to expire until 2028, Samuels's not until 2026. Title VII requires three commissioners for the EEOC to have a quorum; without one, the agency could continue routine case processing but could not initiate formal rulemakings or issue, modify, or revoke formal guidance. The agency operated without a quorum for over eight months. In April 2025, Samuels sued Trump, the EEOC, and Chair Andrea Lucas, arguing her termination before the end of her statutory term was unlawful. Quorum was restored October 7, 2025, when the Senate confirmed Brittany Panuccio as a third commissioner, giving the EEOC a 2-Republican (Lucas, Panuccio), 1-Democrat (Kalpana Kotagal) composition, with Lucas subsequently named permanent Chair on November 5, 2025. With quorum restored, the EEOC gained the votes needed to pursue the policy changes documented elsewhere in this dataset, including the EEO-1 data-collection rescission proposal. Samuels's lawsuit remained pending until the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter on June 29, 2026, substantially expanding presidential removal power over independent-agency officials and overturning the 91-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent that had previously insulated such agencies from at-will removal. Concluding the ruling foreclosed her claim, Samuels voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit on July 6, 2026.

title: EEOC Moves to End 60 Years of Mandatory Workplace Demographic Data Collection
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
status: Ongoing (written comment period closed August 24, 2026 as scheduled; EEOC has not yet issued a final rule and must review the full comment record first)
date_of_action: Early 2025 (removal of Democratic commissioners clears the path) through 2026-06-09 (OMB review of the rescission proposal concludes); final rule still pending as of the last-verified date
what_changed: Early in his second term, President Trump removed the EEOC's Democratic commissioners, eliminating what would have been a blocking minority against a reorientation of the agency's civil rights enforcement priorities under Chair Andrea Lucas. On May 14, 2026, the EEOC submitted a proposed rule to the White House's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) titled 'Rescission of EEO-1, EEO-2, EEO-3, EEO-4, EEO-5, and Reporting Requirement Under Title VII, the ADA, GINA, and the PWFA.' The proposal would eliminate the mandatory annual and biennial workforce demographic data collections that have applied since 1966 to private employers with 100 or more employees, unions, state and local governments, and public school systems, covering employee race, ethnicity, and sex data across job categories. OIRA concluded its review on June 9, 2026, clearing the way for the proposal to be published in the Federal Register for public comment. As of the last-verified date, the EEOC had not opened its EEO-1 filing portal for 2025 data, leaving employers uncertain whether any further demographic data collection will occur before a final rule is issued. The move follows the EEOC's 2025 decision to rescind the option for employers to report non-binary employees on the form, and a separate, still-pending EEOC proposal to rescind a 1979 regulation permitting voluntary affirmative action plans. Re-verified 2026-07-19: the proposed rule had still not been published in the Federal Register as of this update. The EEOC's own regulatory agenda projects publication in July 2026 with a comment period running into September 2026, and the Commission held a Sunshine Act-noticed meeting on July 17, 2026 that included the draft rescission rule -- both signs publication remains imminent, but no notice-and-comment period had formally opened as of this writing. Update 2026-07-26: On July 21, 2026, the Commission voted 2-1 along party lines to advance the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, authorizing publication in the Federal Register and opening a 30-day public comment period (narrower than the September 2026 window earlier projected in the EEOC's own regulatory agenda); a public hearing on the proposal is scheduled for August 11, 2026. Employers remain subject to EEO-1 filing obligations for the 2026 cycle in the meantime. At the August 11, 2026 public hearing, roughly 22 witnesses testified; per National Law Review and Ogletree Deakins coverage, most urged the Commission to retain or reform the EEO-1 framework rather than eliminate it outright, with both employer-side and employee-side speakers warning that rescinding standardized reporting would not actually reduce employers' data burden, since the same information could still be sought via investigations, subpoenas, and litigation on a case-by-case basis. The EEOC took no formal action at the hearing itself. Nearly 1,500 public comments had been submitted on the NPRM as of the hearing date; the written comment period runs through August 24, 2026, after which the Commission will review comments before any final rule. Correction 2026-08-29: this entry's prior text described the proposal as covering EEO-1 through EEO-5, based on the May 14, 2026 OIRA-submission title -- but the NPRM as formally published in the Federal Register on July 23, 2026 (91 FR 46332, 'Removal of Reporting Requirements') covers EEO-1 through EEO-6. EEO-2 and EEO-6 have not actually been collected since 1981 and 1993 respectively, so their formal rescission is largely a procedural formality rather than a change to real-world data collection -- the practical stakes remain concentrated in EEO-1 (private employers), EEO-3, EEO-4, and EEO-5 as before. Separately, written comments on the NPRM closed August 24, 2026 as scheduled, with roughly 1,500 comments already submitted as of the August 11 hearing; no final rule had been issued as of this update, and the Commission must review the full comment record first.

title: EEOC Under Lucas Abandoned Disparate-Impact Enforcement, Rescinded Transgender Protections, and Pivoted to Investigating DEI as 'Reverse Discrimination'
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC)
status: Ongoing and expanding -- active subpoena enforcement litigation (Nike) and investigations (Coca-Cola, others) continue; disparate-impact enforcement and the transgender-harassment guidance rescission remain in effect
date_of_action: 2025-11 (Lucas named chair, 2-1 GOP majority) through 2026-05 (ongoing enforcement expansion)
what_changed: After Trump designated Andrea Lucas as EEOC Chair, giving the commission a 2-1 Republican majority, Lucas redirected the agency's civil rights enforcement priorities in two connected ways. First, EEOC pivoted toward investigating employer diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs as unlawful 'reverse discrimination' against white and male employees: in December 2025, Lucas posted a video calling on white men to report workplace discrimination based on race or sex, and the agency subsequently opened investigations into Coca-Cola (for hosting a women's networking/mentorship event) and Nike (for race-restricted mentorship and leadership programs), among others. Lucas personally filed a Commissioner's Charge against Nike on behalf of a class of white employees alleging systemic race discrimination via its DEI programs; in February 2026, EEOC filed a federal subpoena-enforcement action against Nike after the company resisted document requests. Lucas articulated the standard as: 'It doesn't matter if you call that DEI or belonging or "EO" or anything: If it functions like that, it's illegal.' Second, and simultaneously, EEOC rolled back protections historically used to find discrimination against traditionally protected groups: on January 22, 2026, the commission voted to rescind its 2024 Enforcement Guidance on Harassment in the Workplace, which had addressed harassment against transgender employees (including misgendering and facilities access) alongside other protected categories; EEOC had separately, in 2025, moved to dismiss nearly every discrimination lawsuit it had previously filed on behalf of transgender plaintiffs, prompting a lawsuit from FreeState Justice alleging an unlawful 'Trans Exclusion Policy' denying transgender workers access to EEOC's charge-investigation process. Most significantly, Lucas announced EEOC will no longer process complaints alleging disparate-impact discrimination -- the legal theory, in place for over 50 years, that facially neutral employment practices producing disproportionate harm to a protected group can constitute unlawful discrimination even without proof of intentional bias -- a legal tool historically used to challenge practices disadvantaging people of color, women, disabled people, and pregnant workers.

estimated_impact.summary: The combined effect is a structural inversion of the agency's historical enforcement focus: EEOC is simultaneously expanding investigative and subpoena power against employers' DEI programs (creating new legal exposure for companies with diversity initiatives) while eliminating the disparate-impact theory and transgender-specific harassment protections that have been primary tools for finding discrimination against traditionally protected groups -- narrowing, not just redirecting, the categories of harm the agency will pursue.

title: U.S. Energy Information Administration Lost 40% of Its Staff to Buyouts, Canceling Its International Energy Outlook
institution: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Department of Energy
status: Ongoing -- remaining staff were, as of reporting reviewed, still assessing which of the agency's other reports could continue
date_of_action: 2025-04 (buyout departures) through 2025 (canceled International Energy Outlook)
what_changed: More than 100 EIA employees -- about 40% of the agency's roughly 350-person staff -- left or accepted the Trump administration's deferred-resignation buyout offers by mid-April 2025, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. EIA is the federal government's independent statistical agency for energy data, publishing weekly, monthly, and annual reports on oil and gas output, crude and fuel inventories, and price forecasts that traders, energy companies, and foreign governments rely on as authoritative benchmarks -- reports that can and do move global oil prices on release. title: Household Electricity Bills Rose 10%+ Under Trump's Energy Policy, Hitting Coal-Dependent West Virginia Hardest

title: EPA Moved to Eliminate the 30-Year-Old Energy Star Program; Bipartisan Congressional and Industry Pushback Forced a Transfer to DOE Instead -- Then the Administration Proposed Killing It Again a Year Later
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Office of Atmospheric Protection; later transferred to the Department of Energy (DOE)
status: Program preserved via interagency transfer, not eliminated -- fully moved to DOE by June 2026 with a congressionally mandated funding floor, but the administration's FY2027 budget (April 2026) proposed eliminating the EPA office that had housed it for a second consecutive year

what_changed: In May 2025, Paul Gunning, director of EPA's Office of Atmospheric Protection, told staff at an internal meeting that 'the Energy Star program and all the other climate work, outside of what's required by statute, is being de-prioritized and eliminated.' Energy Star, launched in 1992, is a voluntary labeling program that has helped identify energy-efficient appliances, buildings, and electronics for over three decades and is credited by the EPA's own historical figures with saving consumers and businesses more than $500 billion in energy costs over its lifetime; the FY2026 President's Budget proposed zero dollars for the program. More than 1,000 companies and organizations -- including appliance manufacturers, 14 HVAC associations, 19 HVAC manufacturers, and energy-management and real-estate firms -- signed letters to Congress opposing elimination, and more than 20 U.S. senators sent a letter (May 28, 2025) urging EPA to reverse course, arguing elements of the program are protected by statute and cannot be unilaterally terminated. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin subsequently indicated the agency would not fully eliminate the program. Rather than being shut down, Energy Star was moved internally to EPA's Office of Radiation and Indoor Air starting around November 2025, then transferred entirely out of EPA to the Department of Energy under a March 2026 interagency agreement, with the move completed by June 2026. In January 2026, Congress funded Energy Star at $33 million for FY2026 -- a $1 million increase over the prior year -- and for the first time attached a mandatory minimum annual spending level to the program, an explicit legislative check against future unilateral elimination attempts. Despite that outcome, the administration's FY2027 budget request, released in April 2026, again proposed eliminating EPA's Office of Atmospheric Protection -- the second consecutive year it targeted the office, though Energy Star itself was by then housed at DOE rather than EPA.

title: EPA Canceled $2.8 Billion in Environmental Justice Grants -- Including a Flood-Protection Grant to an Alaska Village Devastated by a Typhoon Months Later -- Then a Federal Judge Ruled the Cancellation Unlawful
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
status: Court-ordered relief, partial and contested -- a federal judge ruled the mass cancellation unlawful in June 2026 and ordered EPA to resume administering the program through its original September 2026 expiration, while a separate D.C. Circuit appeal over jurisdiction to hear related claims proceeded on its own track
date_of_action: 2025-04-29 (mass cancellation revealed in a court filing) through 2026-07-24 (federal judge orders EPA to resume administering the program)
what_changed: A court filing revealed on April 29, 2025 that EPA was canceling 781 grants under the Biden-era Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program (also referred to as the Environmental and Climate Justice Program), a roughly $2.8 billion fund created by the Inflation Reduction Act to help low-income and minority communities address pollution and climate-related risk; by mid-May 2025, EPA had canceled more than 600 grants totaling over $2.7 billion. Sen. Ed Markey and California Attorney General Rob Bonta publicly condemned the mass termination. Among the canceled grants was a $20 million award to the Native Village of Kipnuk, Alaska, revoked May 2, 2025, that would have funded protection for homes and infrastructure against the Kuskokwim River's riverbank erosion. Roughly five months later, in October 2025, the remnants of Typhoon Halong produced a record storm surge that devastated Kipnuk, washing away dozens of homes -- the same infrastructure the canceled grant would have helped protect. EPA publicly defended the cancellation even after the storm. A coalition of nonprofits, tribes, and local governments -- including Baltimore, Nashville, and San Diego -- sued over the terminations on multiple fronts: one suit reached the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit on a jurisdictional question after a district court found it lacked jurisdiction to hear the claims, while a separate case before U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel in South Carolina reached the merits directly. On June 12, 2026, Gergel ruled EPA's termination of the program 'arbitrary and capricious and unlawful' and voided the cancellation, but stopped short of ordering full reinstatement, noting that would likely require rehiring EPA staff the administration had already fired to administer the grants -- which he called impractical. On July 24, 2026, in a follow-up order, Gergel clarified that EPA must nonetheless 'comply with its statutory obligations to administer' the program through the end of September 2026, the date the grants were originally scheduled to expire under the Biden administration. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0235): a separate but related EPA environmental-justice program was frozen even earlier. NPR reported April 14-15, 2025 that EPA's Office of Environmental Justice and External Civil Rights had frozen roughly $350 million awarded to more than 22 tribes and nonprofits nationwide -- part of nearly $1.6 billion in Community Change Grants distributed for infrastructure projects including housing renovation, solar installation, and climate-resilience work -- often without formal notice; some grantees discovered the freeze only when funds vanished from the federal payment system, and Alaska Native villages including Tyonek received no notice at all. One example: the Tebughna Foundation's $20 million award to renovate or replace 20 asbestos- and lead-contaminated homes in the Native Village of Tyonek, Alaska (also connecting them to solar power), was among the frozen grants. This Community Change Grants freeze is a distinct EPA program from the ~$2.8 billion Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program this entry's title and central narrative concern, though both were administered by the same EPA office and hit in the same broader rollback of Biden-era environmental-justice funding.

title: EPA Issues Reduction-in-Force Notices to 22 Remaining Environmental Justice Staffers, Completing a Two-Year Wind-Down of the Function
institution: Environmental Protection Agency
status: Finalized as to this round -- RIF notices issued; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-02-06 (initial administrative leave) through 2026-02 (RIF notices to the final 22 remaining EJ staffers)
what_changed: EPA's dismantlement of its Environmental Justice function played out as a multi-stage, 'roller coaster' process (E&E News's own description) over roughly a year. On February 6, 2025, EPA placed nearly 170 employees of its Office of Environmental Justice and External Civil Rights (OEJECR) on administrative leave agency-wide. Less than a month later, around March 7, 2025, EPA reinstated dozens of those employees -- reporting suggested this followed new White House guidance and reflected that some of the office's work was legally required -- reassigning the recalled staff to other duties, chiefly managing Community Change Grants and maintaining relationships with communities, tribes, and local/state partners. That reprieve did not hold: on March 12-13, 2025, as part of the same week Administrator Lee Zeldin announced a sweeping 31-rule deregulatory package, EPA shut down all 10 of OEJECR's regional Environmental Justice Divisions and placed 168 employees back on administrative leave. On April 22, 2025, EPA issued formal Reduction in Force (RIF) notices to nearly 200 of those employees, with the agency stating that a total of 280 EJ staffers -- both in Washington and across the regional offices -- would be laid off effective July 31, 2025, while another 175 employees whose roles included statutory functions were reassigned to other EPA offices rather than terminated, undertaken to comply with executive orders eliminating environmental-justice programs across the federal government. Finally, in February 2026, EPA issued RIF notices to the 22 EJ staffers still remaining after the 2025 wave -- among the last people at the agency doing this work in any form -- completing the function's elimination. According to InsideEPA, many of the 22 employees targeted in this final round were staff with disabilities. The American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Council 238, which represents EPA employees, publicly condemned the final round; council president Justin Chen said the union was 'outraged by the EPA's decision to issue RIF notices to 22 environmental justice employees whose work ensures that communities disproportionately burdened by environmental hazards receive the protections they are entitled to.'

title: EPA Tried to Claw Back $20 Billion in Congressionally-Appropriated Climate Grants Over Unsubstantiated Fraud Claims -- Courts Blocked It Twice
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF)
status: Blocked by courts -- EPA Administrator Zeldin has 7 days from the Aug. 5, 2026 D.C. Circuit ruling to seek Supreme Court review; not yet final
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Zeldin, FBI, and Treasury order Citibank to freeze the grantee accounts) through 2026-08-05 (D.C. Circuit rules against EPA); Solar for All sub-program: 2025-08-07 (terminated) through 2026-06-02 (states' suit dismissed on jurisdictional grounds)
what_changed: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin sought to freeze and then terminate roughly $20 billion in Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund grants -- awarded to eight National Clean Investment Fund and Clean Communities Investment Accelerator nonprofit entities to fund clean-energy financing, including in communities that had lacked access to green financing -- out of a $27 billion program Congress established in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. In February 2025, Zeldin, together with the FBI and Treasury Department, ordered Citibank to freeze the grantee nonprofits' accounts, citing possible fraud, waste, and abuse; EPA's stated justification also relied on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's repeal of the underlying IRA statutory section as separate legal authority to claw the funds back. A federal district judge (Tonya Chutkan) issued an injunction in April 2025 blocking the freeze, ruling that the government's 'vague and unsubstantiated assertions of fraud are insufficient.' EPA appealed; on August 5, 2026, a divided U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (6 of 10 judges) upheld the injunction, ruling EPA lacked authority to reclaim funds already disbursed to grantee accounts. No EPA Inspector General, DOJ, or FBI investigation had produced a substantiated fraud finding as of the ruling, more than 17 months after the initial freeze. Separately, on August 7, 2025, EPA terminated the remaining $7 billion Solar for All sub-program -- the third GGRF pillar alongside NCIF and CCIA, which had made 60 awards to states, tribes, territories, and nonprofits (roughly $5.5 billion to 49 state-level awardees, over $500 million to six tribal awardees, and about $1 billion to five multistate awardees) to fund low-income residential solar access -- citing the same One Big Beautiful Bill Act repeal of GGRF's authorizing statute as its legal basis; only about $53 million of the $7 billion had actually been spent at termination. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0558): one of the six tribal Solar for All awardees was the Hopi Tribe in Arizona, which had been approved for a $25 million grant to install solar panels and battery storage connecting roughly 600 previously unelectrified homes; after the termination, the tribe was left with a far smaller Tribal Electrification Program grant sufficient to power only about 100 homes, forcing Hopi officials to decide which families would remain without electricity. Twenty-three states sued EPA in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington in October 2025 to reinstate the Solar for All funding, but on June 2, 2026 Judge Tiffany Cartwright dismissed the suit for lack of jurisdiction, holding the states' claim was effectively a Tucker Act money-damages claim belonging in the Court of Federal Claims rather than a district-court APA challenge -- a markedly different legal outcome from the NCIF/CCIA fight, where Chutkan's injunction was upheld on appeal. Grantee nonprofits separately sued in the Court of Federal Claims to recover their withheld Solar for All funds.

title: EPA Employees Suspect Broken Elevators, Extreme Heat Meant to Drive Them Out
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA headquarters, William Jefferson Clinton Federal Building)
status: Ongoing as of July 2025 reporting -- EPA denies intentional degradation, blaming deferred maintenance; no independent facility-condition investigation or GSA repair timeline identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-06 through 2025-07 (reported conditions persisting roughly three weeks before July 11, 2025 CBS News report)
what_changed: By July 2025, EPA headquarters employees had endured roughly three weeks of degraded working conditions they suspected were being used, or at minimum tolerated, as a tool to pressure them into resigning rather than being formally laid off. Multiple employees reported getting stuck in malfunctioning elevators, and some described elevators suddenly dropping between floors. During a Washington, D.C. heat wave with outdoor temperatures above 100 degrees, indoor air conditioning failed in parts of the building, with employees sharing photos of desk-mounted temperature/CO2 monitors showing indoor readings above 80 degrees. Some employees were relocated to a basement area adjacent to a firing range used by federal law-enforcement officials for target practice, raising employee concern about elevated indoor lead exposure from ammunition residue. EPA leadership publicly attributed the conditions to ordinary deferred maintenance, telling CBS News the prior administration had 'didn't invest in buildings that were partially empty, due to work-from-home habits' -- a framing that blames pre-2025 remote-work patterns rather than any current decision. The conditions arrived amid a broader EPA workforce contraction: hundreds of employees had already accepted the government-wide 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation offer, and separately, roughly 140 employees had been placed on administrative leave weeks earlier (in a still-ongoing episode this database documents separately, see zeldin-dissent-letter-retaliation-2025-2026.json) after signing a June 30, 2025 'Declaration of Dissent' letter criticizing the administration's treatment of agency science and staff -- a distinct accountability concern (First Amendment retaliation against named dissenters) from the facility-conditions story documented here, which concerns the general workforce rather than the letter's specific signatories.

A future recheck should look for a GSA facility-condition assessment or an OSHA/inspector-general complaint, either of which could supply a quantified figure this entry currently lacks.

title: EPA's Environmental-Justice Screening Tool and NOAA's Billion-Dollar Disaster Database Both Discontinued
institution: Environmental Protection Agency; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Both discontinuations are final as of this entry -- EJScreen taken offline, the NOAA disaster database retired with no updates beyond 2024
date_of_action: 2025-02 (EPA's EJScreen taken offline) through 2026-05 (NOAA announces retirement of its billion-dollar disaster database)
what_changed: EPA's EJScreen -- a mapping and screening tool combining environmental and demographic indicators to identify communities facing higher combined environmental and socioeconomic burdens -- was taken offline by the Trump administration between February 3 and February 5, 2025; a nonprofit, the Public Environmental Data Project, has since built a replica to keep the underlying data accessible. Separately, NOAA announced it will retire its 'Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters' database, which had tracked the frequency and cost of major U.S. weather and climate disasters for decades -- the agency will keep historical data through calendar year 2024 available but will not add further updates, as part of a Trump 2026 fiscal year budget proposal cutting NOAA's overall budget by $1.52 billion, concentrated in climate-related research, data, and grant programs. Separately, CDC removed multiple web pages addressing health disparities among LGBTQ+ youth, and USDA (which oversees the Forest Service) removed pages referencing climate change, as part of the same broader wave of federal data and web-content removal reported across agencies in 2025-2026. (Note: the parallel removal of USDA's 30-year Household Food Security Survey is documented separately in this tracker's usda-food-security-survey-cancellation-2025.json entry and is not duplicated here.) Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0686): the Federation of American Scientists and other data scientists published a 'Dearly Departed Datasets' list around late October 2025 cataloguing federal datasets killed off, stripped of variables, or made harder to access under the second Trump administration, sorting them into categories (fully terminated, variables deleted, access tools removed, or preserved by outside groups after federal discontinuation). Specific examples beyond the EPA/NOAA/CDC/USDA items above included: figures on transgender inmates removed from Bureau of Justice Statistics inmate data, three gender-identity questions removed from the National Crime Victimization Survey, a race-and-ethnicity column removed from a federal workforce dataset, and a Census Bureau dataset on the relationship between income inequality and disaster vulnerability. The report found the number of fully-terminated datasets 'in the dozens, out of the hundreds of thousands' the federal government produces, and warned that continued loss of federal staff and expertise (following the year's broader workforce reductions) put additional datasets at ongoing risk. No specific administration official was named or quoted defending the removals catalogued in this report.

primary_proponent.role: EPA, NOAA (Commerce Department), and HHS/CDC leadership each independently discontinued or removed tools/data within their own agencies
primary_proponent.note: Reporting reviewed does not identify one official personally ordering all three actions; each agency's leadership (EPA, NOAA under Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's broader NOAA budget cuts, and CDC under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) is responsible for the removal within its own domain.

estimated_impact.summary: Each tool served a distinct, widely-used public function: EJScreen was used by researchers, journalists, and local governments to identify environmental-justice burdens; the NOAA disaster database was the standard reference for the cost and frequency of major U.S. weather and climate disasters, used by researchers, insurers, and policymakers; the CDC pages provided health-disparity data specific to LGBTQ+ youth. Outside groups have moved to independently preserve the EJScreen and NOAA disaster data specifically because federal versions were discontinued.

title: EPA Eliminated Its Scientific Research Office, Placing the Successor Directly Under the Administrator's Political Control
institution: Office of Research and Development (ORD), Environmental Protection Agency
status: Complete (formally eliminated; Congress notified February 2026 that closure is finalized)
date_of_action: 2025-03 (plan first reported) through 2026-02-13 (EPA formally notified Congress of ORD's elimination)
what_changed: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced in May 2025 that the agency's Office of Research and Development -- described by AFGE Council 238 President Justin Chen as 'the heart and brain of the EPA' -- would be eliminated and its scientists redistributed into other EPA program offices. On July 18, 2025, EPA formally announced ORD's elimination and the creation of a replacement, the Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solutions (OASES). Unlike ORD, which operated as its own independent division, OASES was placed directly under the EPA Administrator's office -- a structural change critics say subjects scientific research directly to political oversight rather than insulating it. Notably, 'research' does not appear anywhere in the new office's name, which former ORD senior science adviser Andy Miller said reflects what the reorganization was actually designed to eliminate: 'the kind of work that points out that there are still problems.' More than 300 ORD staff, including senior scientists, had already left via deferred-resignation offers before the formal announcement. As many as 1,155 of ORD's 1,540 positions -- chemists, biologists, toxicologists, and other scientists across 10 facilities nationwide -- were identified as at risk of layoff in documents reviewed by Democratic staff on the House Science Committee. EPA notified Congress on February 13, 2026 that the office's elimination was finalized, roughly nine months after Zeldin first announced the plan; the agency has not disclosed which offices remaining former-ORD employees were transferred to, or when OASES's top leadership positions would be permanently filled. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0128): the plan was reported on before Zeldin's formal May announcement -- the New York Times reported on March 17, 2025 that EPA planned to lay off up to 1,155 ORD scientists, chemists, and toxicologists as part of a proposed 65% cut to the agency's budget, the same at-risk-positions figure later confirmed in the documents reviewed by House Science Committee Democratic staff and cited above. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0293: Reuters reported May 1, 2025 that the reorganization had already effectively grounded Kolibri, a shoebox-sized EPA-developed sensor that attaches to a drone and flies into wildfire smoke plumes to measure airborne pollution -- research a University of Idaho wildland-fire science professor said no one else in the world was doing. Internal documents reviewed by the House Science Committee at that time put the at-risk share of ORD's roughly 1,200-person staff at up to 75%, tied to Trump's proposed 65% cut to EPA's budget -- broadly consistent with, though not identical to, the more precise 1,155-of-1,540 figure documented above from the same congressional document review. Wired separately reported in May 2025 that the reorganization specifically threatened the future of IRIS (the Integrated Risk Information System), ORD's program for assessing chemical health risks and a longstanding target of the chemical industry precisely because its independent findings support environmental regulation; IRIS staff were told to reapply for fewer roles, and the program's leader stepped down around the same time. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0646): that IRIS staffing collapse produced a concrete example by October 2025. IRIS had completed a scientific assessment of PFNA, a 'forever chemical' linked to lower birth weights, liver damage, and male reproductive harm, in mid-April 2025, but EPA had not released it; of 55 scientists who had worked on recent IRIS assessments, only 8 remained in the office, per a ProPublica investigation published October 13, 2025. The report's release would affect an estimated 26 million Americans who get drinking water from systems containing PFNA, detected in 28 states, and could set national cleanup standards and establish corporate liability. The withholding coincided with EPA's own May 2025 rescission of enforceable drinking water limits for PFNA and three other PFAS chemicals (see pfas-drinking-water-rollback-trump2.json), which advocates called a suspicious pairing suggesting the report's findings were being suppressed to avoid justifying stricter standards. On October 17, 2025, Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) wrote to Zeldin demanding to know why the report remained unpublished, who ordered the delay, and when it would be released, calling it part of 'a growing pattern of interference with the Agency's scientific work'; EPA's press office did not respond to her letter, and an EPA spokesperson had previously told ProPublica only that the report would be published 'when it was finalized.'

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.role: EPA Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced and defended the reorganization, framing the mass layoffs using the government euphemism 'reduction in force' and stating it would ensure the agency could 'better fulfill that mission while being responsible stewards of your hard-earned tax dollars.' An EPA spokesperson separately described the restructuring as reflecting 'an unwavering commitment to gold-standard science' through 'integration of scientific expertise directly into EPA's offices' -- the administration's stated rationale is that embedding scientists in program offices improves rather than diminishes the agency's science capacity, a claim directly disputed by the researchers and former officials quoted below. This is the same EPA Administrator whose actions are covered in several deregulation-tracker entries in this project (endangerment finding rescission, MATS mercury standards, etc.) -- this entry covers the elimination of the scientific research infrastructure underlying those separate regulatory actions, not the regulatory actions themselves.

estimated_impact.summary: Independent scientists outside EPA identified specific, concrete functions at risk: ORD maintained toxicology databases used by state and local governments, industry, and nonprofits to assess chemical risks, and its atmospheric/hydrologic models are used by researchers worldwide to study pollutants like particulate matter and ozone. Allen Burton, an environmental scientist at the University of Michigan, specifically warned the closure could delay or prevent new methods for assessing risks from chemical mixtures (which can differ meaningfully from individual-substance risk, a core ORD research function). Rep. Zoe Lofgren, ranking Democrat on the House Science Committee, called it a 'travesty' with 'generational impacts on Americans' health and safety.'

title: EPA Terminated $15 Million in PFAS Farmland-Contamination Research Grants, Then Quietly Restored Two of the Ten Studies Without Explanation

title: FAA Air Traffic Controller Shortage — Chronic Structural Crisis, Acutely Worsened by 2025 Shutdown
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation
status: Ongoing, unresolved (FAA released a new workforce plan in 2026; current administrator says full staffing may never be reached under the existing structure; a congressionally funded controller pay raise remains undisbursed months after enactment)
date_of_action: Structural decline since 2013; acute crisis point during the Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown
what_changed: IMPORTANT ATTRIBUTION NOTE: unlike most entries in this tracker, this is predominantly a chronic, multi-administration structural problem, not a single action taken by the current administration. GAO's own December 2025 report traces the roots to the 2013 budget sequester (which froze hiring), the 2018-2019 shutdown (35 days, further hiring/training delays), and COVID-19 (FAA Academy training suspended 4 months in 2020, reduced-rate training through 2022). The controller workforce declined about 6% since 2015 even as flight volume rose ~10%; the FAA employed 13,164 controllers at the end of FY2025, and 19 of the 30 largest facilities are staffed below 85% of FAA's own targets. What IS specific to the current administration: months before the shutdown, the chronic shortage produced an acute, widely covered crisis at Newark Liberty International Airport in late April-May 2025. On April 28, 2025, controllers handling Newark-area airspace -- relocated from the New York TRACON to the Philadelphia TRACON in July 2024 to address N90's own chronic understaffing -- lost radar and radio contact with 15-20 aircraft for about 90 seconds after a burnt copper wire severed the radar-data feed from a Long Island FAA facility; at least five controllers subsequently took 45 days of trauma leave, and the resulting staffing shortage, compounded by further outages on May 9 and May 11, contributed to over 1,000 flight disruptions. Update 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0332): one of those controllers, Jonathan Stewart, 45, went on the record with the Wall Street Journal May 16, 2025, describing averting a May 4, 2025 near-miss between two aircraft -- a business jet out of Morristown and a small jet from Teterboro -- flying nose-to-nose at the same altitude; because the facility's radar had failed days earlier, Stewart said he resorted to manually writing down the aircrafts' callsigns to keep track of them. He told the Journal, 'I don't want to be responsible for killing 400 people.' The Philadelphia TRACON facility handling Newark-area airspace was staffed at just 24 of the 38 controller positions the FAA says it needs (63%) at the time of his account, and delays of up to seven hours, with as few as 1 to 3 fully certified controllers on duty against a required 14. United Airlines cut 35 daily Newark flights in response. The outages were not confined to Newark: on May 12, 2025, the FAA's Denver Air Route Traffic Control Center lost both its main and backup radio transmitters for about 90 seconds, cutting radio contact with up to 20 aircraft over Colorado and neighboring states (controllers relayed instructions via the 121.5 MHz emergency frequency; no loss of separation occurred; the FAA later attributed it to overlapping transmitter and circuit failures). Testifying before the Senate Appropriations Committee on May 15, 2025 about the episode, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the FAA resorts to buying replacement parts for its outdated, decades-old equipment on eBay and 3D-printing others when none can be found -- disclosing that a GAO review found 76% of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems were unsustainable or potentially unsustainable -- and unveiled a modernization plan (fiber/wireless/satellite upgrades, 618 replaced radars, six new control centers) targeting 2028 completion at an estimated $12.5 billion. The outages continued even after that testimony and plan: on May 19, 2025, the Newark-area TRACON (the same relocated Philadelphia facility) lost radio contact with aircraft for about two seconds, again with no loss of separation, underscoring that the announced modernization had not yet reached the equipment actually causing the failures. The 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 shutdown further disrupted hiring and training pipelines and forced acute flight reductions (see the related, separate entry on the FAA's 10% traffic cut at 40 airports). Current FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Congress in December 2025 that towers would 'never' reach full staffing under the agency's existing structure, stating plainly: 'The system is designed to be chronically understaffed.' Separately, a 2025 proposal to build a second controller training academy (to relieve the bottleneck at the single Oklahoma City academy) was blocked in Congress amid cost and oversight objections, despite FAA and safety experts' warnings that one campus cannot produce enough certified controllers quickly enough. The FAA's new 2026 workforce plan, released in May 2026, resolved the staffing gap partly by lowering the goal itself: full-staffing target dropped from the 14,633 controllers the agency had forecast needing in 2024 to 12,563, a reduction of more than 2,000 positions from the prior target -- the FAA frames this as a modernization-driven reassessment of actual need, not merely redefining the shortfall away, but the effect is that a large share of the 'gap closing' reflects a lower bar rather than more controllers hired. As of June 2026, the FAA was roughly 3,000 certified controllers below even its original, higher target (about 10,800 actual against a ~13,800 historical goal). The staffing shortfall had concrete summer-2026 consequences: the FAA capped Chicago O'Hare at 2,708 scheduled daily operations from May 17 through October 24, 2026, a nearly 15% cut from airline-planned schedules, with New York and Southern California TRACONs also cited as most strained. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to the core FAA civilian-controller narrative; a July 21, 2026 DoD Inspector General report on military air-traffic-controller shortages concerns a separate workforce (military, not FAA/DOT) and is not folded into this entry. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 34): Congress funded an additional 2.8% pay increase for controllers (enacted April 2026, intended to bring 2026 controller compensation in line with the 3.8% raise military personnel received), but as of mid-to-late August 2026 -- roughly four months later -- the raise had still not reached controllers' paychecks. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has tied disbursement to the union agreeing to broader schedule/staffing-utilization reforms, telling reporters 'if we can figure out how we can engage with...the union leadership on the basic watch schedule questions...there's no reason we can't unlock it this year'; the FAA's 2026-28 workforce plan argues controllers' average 'time on position' during 8-hour shifts (currently ~4 hours) could rise past 5 hours through modernized scheduling. A statute reportedly gives the FAA Administrator 'sole discretion' over whether operational improvements justify releasing the retroactive raise -- meaning Bedford is using an already-enacted, congressionally funded pay increase as leverage for a separate policy concession from NATCA, rather than a simple implementation delay. NATCA did not respond to the reporting outlet's requests for comment on the delay or on Bedford's remarks.

Update 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0332): added named controller Jonathan Stewart's on-record Wall Street Journal account of the May 4, 2025 near-miss and the Philadelphia TRACON's 63% (24/38) staffing level at the time -- HIGH confidence, the Journal's original reporting corroborated by CNN, CBS News New York, and multiple wire/local reprints.

title: FAA Cut Flights 10% at 40 Major Airports After Unpaid Controllers Began Missing Work
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation
status: Complete (implemented and later lifted after shutdown ended)
date_of_action: 2025-11-05 (announced); ramped from 4% to 10% between Nov. 7-14, 2025
what_changed: During the 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown -- the longest in U.S. history -- air traffic controllers, deemed 'essential' employees required to work without pay, began missing shifts in increasing numbers as the shutdown dragged on, compounding the FAA's already-chronic staffing shortage (see related structural staffing entry). The buildup was visible well before the formal reduction order: as early as Oct. 10, staffing shortages left some control towers unmanned (nearly 6,000 delayed flights nationwide that day); by Oct. 27-31, roughly 13,000 controllers and 50,000 TSA officers were working without pay, and ground delays hit major hubs including New York, Washington, Newark, Houston, Austin, and Dallas-Fort Worth (over 4,200 delays Oct. 23, nearly 7,000 Oct. 31); by Nov. 4, the shutdown's 31st day, nearly half of U.S. air traffic centers were short-staffed and 90% of controllers in the New York region were unavailable. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford then announced a mandatory flight-capacity reduction at 40 'high-volume' airports nationwide, ramping from 4% on Nov. 7 to 10% by Nov. 14, affecting an estimated 3,500-4,000 flights daily. Both officials described the move as unprecedented -- Bedford, with 35 years in aviation, said he 'could not recall a similar situation.' Duffy publicly warned the cuts could escalate to 15-20% if the shutdown continued, and separately said he could 'shut the whole airspace down' if it dragged on further. The order also restricted private jets from high-traffic airports to preserve capacity for commercial aviation. The reduction produced immediate, measurable disruption: over 1,000 flights canceled the first day, more than 2,900 cancellations and 10,000+ delays the following Sunday, nearly 2,200 cancellations in a single day by the second weekend, and over 40 emergency staffing alerts issued nationwide since the order took effect. On Nov. 12, as cancellations continued (over 2,000 Monday alone after nearly 3,000 the prior Sunday, with delays topping 6,400 nationwide), Trump escalated the pressure directly on the workforce: he publicly demanded controllers 'get back to work, NOW!!!,' threatened to dock pay from those who missed shifts, and offered a $10,000 bonus to those who stayed on the job -- prompting controller unions to warn that workers were being used as political pawns in the shutdown fight.

The scale of disruption was immediate and large: over 12,000 American Airlines customers alone had flights canceled on the first day of the reduction.

title: FBI Told to Stop Investigating Confrontations Involving Immigration Agents, Shifting Oversight to ICE's Own Investigative Arm
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation / DHS Homeland Security Investigations
status: Guidance reportedly distributed and in effect per internal emails reviewed by CBS News; DOJ and DHS have publicly denied any policy change
date_of_action: 2026-07 (guidance distributed to FBI agents)
what_changed: The New York Times reported, and CBS News independently confirmed via internal emails reviewed by its reporters, that FBI agents around the country were told in mid-July 2026 that the FBI would no longer investigate confrontations involving immigration agents -- including assault-on-a-federal-officer cases that can arise from violent encounters between ICE agents and members of the public. Under the change, responsibility for these investigations would shift to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), which is itself a component of ICE -- meaning cases involving potential misconduct by immigration agents would be investigated by an arm of the same agency employing those agents, rather than by the FBI as an independent investigative body. FBI and HSI personnel were advised the FBI would defer on all assault-on-federal-officer inquiries involving DHS agents to HSI, according to the emails CBS reviewed. The Justice Department and DHS both publicly denied that any policy change had occurred, despite the written guidance already having been distributed to FBI and ICE personnel.

title: FBI Scaled Back Staffing and Scrapped a Tracking Tool for Domestic Terrorism Investigations
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation / Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing and escalated -- a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee report from Ranking Member Gary Peters (D-MI), released 2026-07-30, documents a broader institutional pullback beyond the March 2025 DTOS reassignments already in this entry: roughly 15,000 positions cut across DOJ and the FBI combined, and 1,300 DHS personnel cut from roles involved in preventing, countering, and responding to terrorism. The report also found the administration has skewed its domestic-terrorism focus almost exclusively toward left-wing groups while removing from public view a DOJ study showing far-right extremist attacks have outpaced all other categories of domestic terrorism since 1990; AG Bondi's December 4, 2025 directive formalizing an 'Antifa-aligned extremists' investigative priority is the primary-source mechanism behind that finding. No final decision on formally disbanding DTOS itself has been independently confirmed in sourcing reviewed for this recheck.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (initial reassignments and tool scrapping); 2025-04 (congressional oversight letter)
what_changed: FBI leadership transferred roughly 16 agents and intelligence analysts out of the Bureau's Domestic Terrorism Operations Section (DTOS), which supports domestic-terrorism investigations run out of all 55 FBI field offices and would have hundreds of employees if fully staffed, Reuters reported (citing sources familiar with the matter) on 2025-03-21. The FBI also scrapped a tool used to track domestic terrorism cases. Senior FBI officials discussed disbanding the section entirely, though no final decision had been announced as of the reporting. Agents were being redirected instead to assist the administration's immigration enforcement crackdown, while attacks on Tesla property were newly classified and prioritized as domestic terrorism. Domestic terrorism investigations have in recent years disproportionately involved violence tied to right-wing and anti-government ideologies, and FBI Director Kash Patel has been a public critic of the Bureau's domestic-terrorism investigative effort. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent a formal oversight letter to DHS Secretary Kristi Noem and Director Patel on 2025-04-08 documenting a broader institutional pullback beyond the FBI reassignments alone: DHS had also dismantled a national database tracking domestic extremism and hate crimes and cut funding for domestic-terrorism-prevention programs supporting community groups and local law enforcement. Durbin's letter cited FBI's own data showing a 357% increase in domestic terrorism investigations between 2013 and 2021 (from 1,981 to 9,049 cases) as the backdrop against which the cuts were occurring, and urged DHS and the FBI to reverse the resource reallocations. ProPublica reported May 31, 2025 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0366, added 2026-09-10) that the DHS prevention cuts documented above also eliminated hate-crime hotlines and halted extremist-threat tracking specifically, and that states -- Michigan among them -- were attempting to fill the resulting gap with their own programs, though ProPublica found many state efforts were unprepared or inactive given the scale of the federal pullback. NBC News reported June 16, 2025 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0392, added 2026-09-10) that the cuts documented above specifically include elimination of the $18 million Targeted Violence and Terrorism Prevention (TVTP) Grant Program, which had funded local efforts like school-based threat assessments and mental-health interventions credited by experts with helping identify radicalized individuals before attacks; the administration's budget submission said the program 'does not align with DHS priorities.' A senior DHS official, speaking anonymously out of fear of being fired, told NBC News: 'That line should be quoted after every future mass casualty event in this country.' Update 2026-08-17: A Senate HSGAC report from Ranking Member Gary Peters, released 2026-07-30 ("Peters Report Finds Trump Administration Has Dismantled Critical Counterterrorism Infrastructure and Weaponized What Remains Against Political Opponents"), documents roughly 15,000 positions cut across DOJ and the FBI combined and 1,300 DHS personnel cut from counterterrorism-related roles, a larger institutional pullback than the ~16-agent DTOS reassignment this entry originally documented. The report also found the administration's domestic-terrorism enforcement focus has shifted almost exclusively to left-wing targets, and that a DOJ study showing far-right extremist attacks have outpaced all other domestic-terrorism categories since 1990 was quietly removed from the department's website. Several outlets covering the report describe DTOS's entire remaining staff as having been reassigned, but that specific claim could not be independently confirmed against the report's own text or another primary source in this recheck; it is not asserted as fact here. Update 2026-08-30 (correction -- a primary source for the report's 'skewed toward left-wing groups' finding, missed until now): Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a domestic-terrorism directive on December 4, 2025, predating the Peters report by nearly eight months, that explicitly prioritizes investigation of 'Antifa-aligned extremists' -- defined in the memo to include those holding 'extreme viewpoints on immigration, radical gender ideology, and anti-American sentiment' -- and directs DOJ to prioritize grant funding to state/local law enforcement for domestic-terrorism programs tied to that focus. The memo also orders Joint Terrorism Task Forces to use 'all available investigative tools' to map suspected networks, requires the FBI to compile and update every 30 days a domestic-terrorist-organization list, establishes a cash-reward tip line, and orders a retrospective five-year review of agency files for Antifa-related intelligence to be transmitted to the FBI for potential new prosecutions. This directive is the concrete administrative mechanism behind the ideological-skew finding this entry already cites from the Peters report, not merely a restatement of it.

title: FBI Lowered Agent Training Standards and Diverted Agents From Fraud, Corruption, and Counterintelligence Casework to Street Patrols and Violent-Crime Duty
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation
status: Ongoing as of the reporting reviewed -- the reduced training standards and workforce cuts were implemented; the DC-deployment diversion and broader violent-crime pivot were active as of September 2025, with no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-08 (training-standards and mission-shift reporting) through 2025-09 (DC-deployment casework diversion documented)
what_changed: The New York Times reported August 21, 2025 that the FBI, under Director Kash Patel and Deputy Director Dan Bongino, planned to cut new-agent training at the Quantico academy from 18 weeks to 8 weeks and eliminate the bachelor's-degree requirement for new recruits, with the shortened curriculum set to begin with an October 2025 class. The changes came as the bureau anticipated losing more than 5,000 employees -- agents, analysts, and other staff -- by September 2025 through severance and early-retirement packages offered under the administration, and as the FBI's specialized-agent workforce was separately reported to be shrinking from roughly 13,000 to 11,000 over the same period. Retired FBI senior counterterrorism official Chris O'Leary called the changes the latest example of 'generational destruction' at the bureau, warning: 'When you lower the standards, your mission effectiveness goes down with that, because not only does the capability of each individual agent decline, but your reputation, both domestically and globally, takes a hit.' Separately, MSNBC reported August 19, 2025 that the bureau was executing a broader mission shift, with a planned 15% workforce reduction (about 5,800 of roughly 37,000 employees) accompanying a redirection of agents toward violent-crime investigations, immigration enforcement, and nightly anti-crime foot patrols in Washington, D.C. alongside D.C. police -- work outside the bureau's traditional investigative role -- at the expense of terrorism prevention, espionage/counterintelligence, white-collar fraud, public corruption, child sex crimes, and cybersecurity casework. Patel described the goal as letting 'good cops be cops'; retired FBI agent Rob D'Amico said 'This is putting the nation in jeopardy -- they seem to be making national security threats secondary,' and one unnamed senior agent said the changes were 'effectively making the FBI a national police force.' The New York Times reported September 15, 2025 that Trump's deployment of National Guard troops and federal agents in Washington had concretely diverted FBI staff from financial-fraud, corruption, and counterintelligence casework specifically to support the D.C. surge, slowing those investigations and prompting resignations; prosecutors told the Times the diversion left D.C. courts flooded with weak street-crime cases, many of which were thrown out by grand juries. This grand-jury pattern is independently corroborated at the case level: D.C. grand juries refused to indict defendants at least six to seven times over the following weeks, including declining a felony assault indictment against Sean Dunn (the 'sandwich thrower' case, tracked separately in this database's pirro-sandwich-thrower-failed-prosecution-2025.json), Alvin Summers, and Sidney Lori Reid, among others -- a pattern reporting characterized as an unusual judicial check given prosecutors ordinarily control grand jury outcomes.

title: Leaked 115-Page Assessment Found FBI 'Internally Paralyzed by Fear' Under Director Kash Patel, Amid a Pattern of Patel Disclosing Sensitive Investigation Details on Social Media
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
status: Ongoing -- no formal response or corrective action from FBI leadership identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-02 through 2025-08 (assessment's coverage period) through 2025-12-01 (report leaked)
what_changed: The New York Post obtained and reported on December 1, 2025 a 115-page internal assessment -- compiled by a national alliance of retired and active-duty FBI special agents and analysts, drawing on confidential accounts from 24 FBI sources, and prepared for the Senate and House Judiciary Committees -- covering the first six months of Director Kash Patel's tenure (February 21 through August 21, 2025). The report described the FBI as 'internally paralyzed by fear,' with plummeting morale and a 'rudderless ship' in which managers were afraid to take initiative without Patel's explicit personal approval. It characterized Patel himself as 'in over his head,' leading a 'chronically under-performing' agency, and cited concerns from foreign law enforcement partners that the leadership turmoil could cause long-term damage to international law-enforcement cooperation. Sen. Dick Durbin issued a public statement responding to the report. Separately, the same period saw a documented pattern of Patel publicly disclosing sensitive operational details on social media before or during active investigations: in one specific instance, the Secret Service accused Patel of compromising an active covert investigation into a planned attack on a White House-linked UFC event (which numerous high-ranking officials attended) by publicly announcing the plot had been foiled while the operation, including still-at-large suspects, remained active -- FBI Deputy Director Matthew Quinn confirmed the operation's active status at the time. In a related development the same season, the FBI launched a new 'Rapid Response' social-media account in November 2025 that took an unusually combative public posture, immediately engaging in public disputes with commentators including Tucker Carlson, amplifying Deputy Director Dan Bongino's own frequently partisan public statements, and defending the Bureau's January 6 pipe-bomb investigation against outside criticism -- a marked departure from the FBI's traditionally reticent public-communications posture. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0579): the pattern of premature public disclosure during active investigations predates the November/December 2025 developments above by roughly two months. On September 11, 2025, hours after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was fatally shot at Utah Valley University, Patel publicly announced 'the subject for the horrific shooting... is now in custody' -- then retracted the claim less than two hours later, saying authorities had the wrong person, while Utah law enforcement officials were simultaneously holding a news conference stating the gunman remained at large, producing hours of public confusion before the actual suspect, Tyler Robinson, was arrested roughly 33 hours after the shooting. Patel also drew criticism for dining at an exclusive New York restaurant hours after the assassination while continuing to post premature investigative updates; former FBI officials characterized both the dining choice and the social-media conduct as 'grandstanding' that undermined public confidence in the bureau during an active national-security-sensitive investigation.
