title: FDA Suspended a 40-Lab Bird Flu Milk-Testing Exercise After Eliminating Its Food Safety Lab, Then Suspended Grade-A Milk Testing Outright
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Testing suspended as of April 2025; no confirmed restoration identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's addition
date_of_action: 2025-04-03 (VLIRN exercise suspension notice) through 2025-04-23 (grade-A milk testing program suspension reported)
what_changed: As part of the broader 2025 HHS staffing reductions (which cut roughly 3,500 FDA employees overall), the FDA eliminated its Human Food Program's Moffett Center food-safety laboratory in Illinois, including a key quality-assurance officer. On April 3, 2025, the FDA-backed Veterinary Laboratory Investigation and Response Network (VLIRN) informed its roughly 40 member laboratories -- a mix of federal, state, and private labs across the country -- that a planned nationwide exercise to confirm those labs' ability to detect H5N1 avian influenza in milk had to be suspended because of the Illinois lab's elimination and the loss of the quality-assurance function it provided. Three weeks later, CBS News and other outlets reported the FDA had gone further, suspending its own testing program for grade 'A' milk and other dairy products -- the routine surveillance testing distinct from the VLIRN inter-laboratory readiness exercise -- citing the same food-safety-division staffing cuts.

title: FDA vaccine/biologics division leadership purge and COVID vaccine access restriction
institution: FDA — Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER)
status: Ongoing -- leadership churn spread upward to the Commissioner's office itself: Marty Makary resigned as FDA Commissioner on May 12, 2026 (amid MAHA-movement backlash after Trump moved to lift a ban on flavored e-cigarette sales), with Kyle Diamantas installed as Acting Commissioner the same day; within that same single business week, acting CDER director Tracy Beth Hoeg (in the role since December 3, 2025) and acting CBER director Katherine Szarama both departed (May 15, 2026), replaced by CDER deputy director Michael Davis and CBER's Karim Mikhail respectively -- Davis is the sixth person to lead CDER since Trump took office. Diamantas declined the permanent Commissioner job; Trump nominated White House Domestic Policy Council deputy director Dr. Heidi Overton for the Senate-confirmed post on August 19, 2026, drawing "strong concerns" from Senate HELP Committee Chairman Bill Cassidy. No permanent CBER or CDER director had been named alongside the Overton nomination as of this recheck, though FDA had signaled it intended to announce both together.
date_of_action: March 2025 - April 2026
what_changed: CBER, the FDA division that regulates vaccines, gene therapies, and blood products, went through six different directors across it and its sister division (CDER) since January 2025. Longtime CBER director Peter Marks resigned in March 2025 amid reported disagreements with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over vaccine policy. Vinay Prasad was installed as CBER director in May 2025. In July 2025 Prasad was forced out after backlash over his handling of Sarepta Therapeutics' Duchenne muscular dystrophy gene therapy, then reinstated roughly two weeks later after Commissioner Marty Makary intervened. Upon returning, Prasad fired the official in charge of vaccine safety/surveillance and took direct control of that function himself, and went on to push out at least seven other agency leaders during his second tenure. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 cluster c0286): the May 2025 framework did not emerge without warning -- on April 30, 2025, Makary told CBS News the FDA was reconsidering whether to approve updated COVID-19 boosters for the coming winter at all, citing a "lack" of new clinical-trial data and declining public trust in the vaccines, a month-earlier signal of the risk-stratified approach that followed. By early August 2025, as COVID-19 cases were rising across 26 states, the guidance had gone further than an age/risk cutoff alone, also dropping the standing recommendation for children and pregnant people specifically -- groups for whom health authorities had previously recommended vaccination regardless of individual risk factors. title: FDA Loses ~3,500 Staff in April 2025 Purge -- Pharma Industry Warns of Delays, Though Drug-Review Deadlines Largely Held
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Implemented -- April 2025 terminations, effects assessed through 2025
date_of_action: 2025-03 (industry warnings begin) through 2025-04 (HHS terminates ~3,500 FDA employees)
what_changed: Starting in March 2025, multiple pharmaceutical companies' SEC filings warned that Trump-administration budget and staffing cuts at the FDA could delay drug research, review, and commercialization -- an early, industry-side signal distinct from the agency's own later, larger staffing action. In April 2025, HHS terminated approximately 3,500 FDA employees as part of the department-wide reduction, this time hitting support and policy staff broadly across the agency rather than the narrower food-safety/device/tobacco-specific cuts already documented in this tracker's separate February 2025 entry. Despite the cuts, an analysis of 2025 performance data found FDA reviewers largely met their statutory PDUFA (Prescription Drug User Fee Act) deadlines for new drug application reviews. The more concrete, documented impact was a decline in FDA responsiveness to non-essential inquiries, with Endpoints News reporting some meetings between drug developers and FDA reviewers were missed or postponed due to reviewer shortages. The Wall Street Journal reported April 18, 2025 that biotech companies were experiencing broader guidance delays as a result: Daré Bioscience CEO Sabrina Johnson said FDA delays forced the company to postpone the planned mid-2025 Phase 3 clinical trial of its Sildenafil Cream product, pivoting instead toward bringing a compounded version of the drug to market -- a concrete case of a company altering its drug-development plans (a trial start, not an approval decision) in direct response to FDA slowdown, consistent with this entry's narrower defensible claim above rather than a delayed statutory approval itself. One specific named casualty of the same April 2025 action: the FDA's Division of Learning and Organizational Development, which trained both agency staff and outside doctors, nurses, and pharmacists on opioid safety, medication-error prevention, and other regulatory-science topics, was eliminated in full, with all 30-plus employees laid off and the division's continuing-education accreditation function -- required for professional licensing credits -- discontinued entirely.

title: FDA Cut 170 Inspection-Support Staff, Curtailing Routine Food and Drug Safety Inspections -- Foreign Inspections Later Fell to a Decade Low
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Implemented -- 2025 staffing cuts confirmed to have caused a sustained, measurable drop in foreign inspection volume through at least November 2025
date_of_action: 2025-04 through 2025-05 (staffing cuts and planning disclosures) through 2025-11 (foreign-inspection-volume impact reported)
what_changed: As part of the broader 2025 HHS-wide staffing reduction, the FDA cut roughly 170 staff from its Office of Inspections and Investigations -- the administrative and management support staff who coordinate and schedule the agency's food and drug safety inspectors, distinct from the inspectors themselves, who were not directly targeted. CBS News and NPR reported in April-May 2025 that FDA leadership was planning to cut back on routine 'surveillance inspections' -- proactive, scheduled checks not tied to a specific safety complaint -- reserving remaining inspection capacity for higher-priority cases such as facilities already flagged for safety risks or follow-up visits confirming a prior violation had been corrected. A companion CBS News report the same week, citing multiple federal health officials, described a more structural tentative plan under consideration: handing off most routine food-facility inspections entirely to state and local officials, building on an existing arrangement in which FDA already contracts with 43 states and Puerto Rico to perform roughly a third of routine inspections; FDA would retain direct responsibility only for higher-risk categories such as infant-formula manufacturers and foreign facilities. The plan was described as not yet final and potentially requiring congressional approval and funding, and an FDA spokesperson pushed back on record, stating 'the claim that the FDA is suspending routine food safety inspections is false' and that the agency 'remains committed to ensuring critical programs and inspections continue.' Leaked draft White House FY2026 budget documents around the same time proposed a 17% cut to FDA's budget (to $6.5 billion) that included shifting all routine food-facility inspections to states, though the leaked figures were not independently confirmed as final. HHS stated the layoffs, ordered by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., would not directly cut FDA's inspector headcount, but acknowledged the loss of administrative and logistical support staff would likely cause delays and disruption to inspection scheduling and travel approvals. Internal emails and draft contracting documents obtained by CBS News in April 2025 showed FDA finalizing plans to replace most of the work of the more than 50 laid-off travel-logistics and inspector-spending-oversight staff with private contractors -- who would be issued FDA laptops and badges -- directly contradicting what those same employees had been told in their layoff notices, that their work was 'unnecessary or virtually identical to duties being performed elsewhere in the agency.' By late April and into May 2025, HHS reversed a portion of the cuts, reinstating more than 20 of the roughly 60 travel staff along with food-safety scientists and lab staff in Chicago and San Francisco, attributing the original terminations to inaccurate HR data used to select employees for layoff. By November 2025, the Louisiana Illuminator reported that foreign food-safety inspections had fallen to their lowest level in more than a decade, an outcome FDA insiders and reporting attributed to the combined effect of the staffing cuts, slowed travel approvals for inspectors, and reduced logistical support -- compounding an inspection shortfall that had already failed to meet the agency's own foreign and domestic inspection targets since 2018.

title: FDA Refused to Even Review Moderna's mRNA Flu Vaccine Despite a 40,000-Person Trial Showing Stronger Protection for Older Adults
institution: Food and Drug Administration
status: FDA approval resolved August 5, 2026 (branded mFlusiva, after reversing its refusal-to-file decision twice within days in February 2026), but practical access is not fully resolved -- a separate court-ordered freeze on ACIP (in effect since March 16, 2026) blocks the recommendation that normally triggers guaranteed no-cost insurance coverage
date_of_action: 2026-02-03 (FDA's refusal-to-file letter)
what_changed: Moderna submitted an application in December 2025 for FDA approval of its new mRNA flu vaccine for adults 50 and older, supported by a clinical trial of more than 40,000 people that found the new vaccine somewhat more effective than a standard flu shot. Rather than reviewing the application on its merits, the FDA issued a 'refusal-to-file' letter dated February 3, 2026 -- declining to even begin substantive review. FDA vaccine director Dr. Vinay Prasad's letter stated the agency did not consider the trial 'adequate and well-controlled' because Moderna compared its vaccine to a flu shot Prasad's letter characterized as not the 'best-available standard of care,' rather than rejecting the vaccine's efficacy or safety data itself. Moderna disputes this characterization, saying it ran the trial in the manner regulators had previously discussed and agreed to. Notably, drug regulators in Canada, Europe, and Australia accepted the same application for substantive review rather than issuing a refusal-to-file. Update 2026-08-17 (correction -- this entry's original 'contested and unresolved' framing is now outdated): just eight days after the February 3, 2026 refusal-to-file letter, FDA reversed course on February 18/19, 2026 and agreed to review the application under an amended, age-stratified regulatory pathway Moderna proposed -- standard approval for adults 50-64, accelerated approval (contingent on a postmarketing study) for adults 65 and older. FDA then accepted the amended Biologics License Application and set a PDUFA goal date of August 5, 2026. On that date, FDA approved the vaccine, branded mFlusiva, for all adults 50 and older -- the first mRNA-based flu vaccine ever approved. FDA and Moderna reviewers identified no new or serious safety concerns; the trial's roughly 27%-better efficacy finding versus a standard flu shot was not disputed at any point in this episode, consistent with Prasad's original refusal-to-file letter objecting only to the trial's comparator-vaccine choice, not to safety or efficacy data. The episode remains a legitimate accountability entry -- FDA's vaccine division initially blocked substantive review of a well-supported vaccine application for a flu-vulnerable population while peer regulators abroad accepted the identical data -- but the outcome was ultimately approval, not suppression, following public and regulatory scrutiny of the initial refusal. Update 2026-08-30 (correction -- the 'Resolved' framing needs a caveat): FDA approval does not, by itself, guarantee mFlusiva reaches patients at no cost. A separate, unrelated action -- U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy's March 16, 2026 preliminary injunction in American Academy of Pediatrics v. Kennedy (D. Mass., No. 1:25-cv-11916), which stayed all 13 sitting ACIP members' appointments and barred HHS/CDC from convening ACIP meetings or votes -- has left the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices unable to formally recommend mFlusiva as of this update. An ACIP recommendation is the statutory mechanism that normally triggers mandatory no-cost commercial insurance coverage under the ACA, Medicare billing-code assignment, and state vaccine-program funding access; without one, mFlusiva entered the market licensed by FDA but in a coverage 'regulatory limbo,' per contemporaneous analysis. Moderna expects supply at select retailers ahead of the 2026-27 flu season regardless, but the ACIP freeze -- not addressed anywhere in this entry's prior text -- bears directly on how many people in the approved population can actually obtain it affordably.

estimated_impact.summary: A refusal-to-file is procedurally more severe than a rejection after review -- it prevents the FDA from ever substantively evaluating a 40,000-person trial's safety and efficacy data for a vaccine that showed improved protection for older adults, a population at elevated risk from flu, at the same time peer regulators internationally accepted the identical application for review.
estimated_impact.caveat: This entry documents the refusal-to-file decision and its immediate reception; FDA's institutional rationale (comparator-vaccine standard-of-care requirements) is not without precedent in FDA regulatory practice generally, and this entry does not resolve whether Moderna's trial design was in fact non-compliant with FDA's own prior guidance -- that dispute is unresolved as of this entry's addition.

title: FDA Blocked Publication of Its Own Studies Finding COVID-19 and Shingles Vaccines Safe
institution: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
status: Documented via reporting first published May 2026; no reversal or republication identified as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-10 (two COVID-19 vaccine studies withdrawn after acceptance) through 2026-02 (Shingrix/shingles vaccine conference-abstract submission blocked)
what_changed: In October 2025, FDA scientists were directed to withdraw two COVID-19 vaccine safety studies that had already been accepted for publication in medical journals, based on data drawn from millions of patient records and finding serious side effects to be rare. In February 2026, top FDA officials declined to approve submission of study abstracts on the safety of Shingrix, the recombinant shingles vaccine, to a major drug-safety conference. Andrew Nixon, a spokesman for the Department of Health and Human Services (which oversees FDA), defended both actions: on the COVID-19 studies, he said they 'were withdrawn because the authors drew broad conclusions that were not supported by the underlying data'; on the blocked shingles research, he said 'the design of that study fell outside the agency's purview.' Independent experts who reviewed the withdrawn studies disputed that characterization -- Caleb Alexander, a drug-safety and methodology expert at Johns Hopkins University, said after reviewing the reports that 'there is nothing inherently problematic regarding these reports.'

title: RFK Jr. Cancels FDA's Public Flu-Vaccine Advisory Meeting, Strain Selection Made Behind Closed Doors Instead
institution: Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (VRBPAC), Food and Drug Administration
status: Implemented -- the March 13, 2025 public meeting was never rescheduled; the FDA's 2025-2026 strain recommendation was issued without it
what_changed: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ordered the cancellation of VRBPAC's March 13, 2025 public meeting, at which the committee's outside experts were set to recommend which influenza strains should go into the 2025-2026 season's flu vaccines -- the annual, decades-old process manufacturers rely on to begin roughly six months of production lead time. Panel members were notified late on February 26 with no explanation given, and no rescheduled date was ever set; VRBPAC member Dr. Paul Offit told reporters he'd received no reason for the cancellation either. It was the second vaccine-related advisory disruption within the same two weeks, following a postponed CDC vaccine meeting the week before. Rather than reconvene the public committee, Acting FDA Commissioner Dr. Sara Brenner and a closed-door interagency group of FDA, CDC, and Defense Department scientists decided the strain composition internally, aligning with the WHO's own recommendation, and the FDA published its selections without the normal open, externally-reviewed VRBPAC process. The FDA maintained the decision would not delay 2025-2026 season vaccine availability.

what_changed: Republican commissioner Sean Cooksey resigned from the FEC effective January 20, 2025 to become counsel to Vice President JD Vance. title: Trump's Attempt to Fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook Blocked by Supreme Court, Fed Independence Preserved
institution: Federal Reserve Board of Governors
status: Blocked once by the Supreme Court (June 29, 2026), but not a closed matter -- Trump opened a second, renewed removal attempt August 5, 2026, following the Court's own prescribed due-process steps (notice, opportunity to respond, deadline); Cook's attorney formally rejected the allegations August 26, 2026; as of this update Trump had not yet made a final removal decision on this second attempt, and the underlying 'for cause' merits question from the first attempt remains separately unresolved
date_of_action: 2025-08-25 (attempted firing) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling)
what_changed: In August 2025, President Trump attempted to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook -- the first attempted removal of a sitting Fed governor in the central bank's 111-year history -- citing mortgage-fraud allegations against her from before she joined the Fed, raised by FHFA Director (and later Director of National Intelligence) William Pulte. Cook, who denied the allegations and was never charged, sued, arguing her removal was not 'for cause' as the Federal Reserve Act requires and that she was denied due process. A federal district court blocked the firing with a preliminary injunction; the D.C. Circuit declined to lift it; and on June 29, 2026 -- the same day it ruled against FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter in the companion case Trump v. Slaughter -- the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in Trump v. Cook that Cook could remain in her position while her lawsuit proceeds. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for a majority that included conservative Justice Kavanaugh alongside the Court's three liberals, held that accepting the administration's position 'would in effect transform the Federal Reserve's for-cause protection into at-will employment' and stressed that 'not only the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve's design.' The Court explicitly carved the Federal Reserve out of the broader independence-narrowing logic it applied to the FTC, CPSC, NCUA, and other agencies the same day. Cook remained in her seat throughout, participating in the Fed's September 2025 rate-setting meeting. Trump responded on Truth Social that the ruling was 'strictly procedural' and vowed further action; Pulte stood by his fraud allegations. Re-verified 2026-07-19: no further procedural movement identified since the June 29, 2026 Supreme Court ruling; the case remains before the lower courts on the underlying 'for cause' merits question, unchanged from the prior update. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no further procedural movement identified; the case remains before the lower courts on the underlying 'for cause' merits question, unchanged from the July 19, 2026 update. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 50, real correction): Trump opened a second removal attempt against Cook, this time explicitly following the Supreme Court's own June 29 roadmap requiring notice, an opportunity to respond, and a deadline before removal can take effect. On August 5, 2026, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino sent Cook a letter stating the President was 'considering' removing her, citing the same pre-Fed mortgage-fraud allegations as the first attempt (now recharacterized as 'gross negligence'), and set an August 26, 2026 deadline for her to respond with evidence or argument through the Director of Presidential Personnel. Cook's attorney, Abbe Lowell, responded on or before the August 26 deadline with a five-page letter calling the allegations 'unfounded and untrue,' arguing 'an inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing' (referencing the property-listing/vacation-home-designation basis for the fraud claim). Corroborated across CBS/CNBC, Axios, SCOTUSblog, The Hill, ABC News, UPI, and the Washington Post. As of this recheck, no final removal decision had been announced following the August 26 deadline -- the dispute has moved from the courts (first attempt) to this renewed executive-branch process (second attempt), and the entry's prior framing of the underlying 'for cause' merits question as the sole open thread needs updating to reflect this parallel, currently more active track.

date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (presidential memorandum) through 2025-04-30 (agencies still tracking daily office occupancy)
what_changed: On January 20, 2025, Trump's first-day presidential memorandum directed federal agencies to end remote-work arrangements and require full-time in-person work, with OPM recommending agencies reach full compliance within 30 days. The rollout hit employees hired or relocated for remote positions especially hard: the Washington Post reported some workers received just days' notice to report to offices hundreds or even thousands of miles from where they lived -- one HHS employee working remotely from the Southwest since 2023 was told via an email titled 'Return to In-Person Work Guidance for March 17, 2025' that she needed to report that Monday. Employees described scrambling to book flights, arrange childcare, or sell homes, with some assigned to offices that had already been shut down amid the administration's mass federal-lease cancellations; others faced commutes of nearly two hours each way with no clarity on what would happen if they couldn't comply, and some were told to report to offices that had already lost their lease. Separately, CNN and NPR reported the offices employees were ordered back into often lacked basic infrastructure to receive them -- shortages of desks, computer monitors, parking, Wi-Fi, and even toilet paper were widely documented; in one case reported in this cycle of coverage, a USDA remote employee was directed to a reporting location that turned out to be a storage unit. Reuters reported similar conditions on March 16, 2025, documenting a cockroach infestation at a NASA facility employees were ordered back into, IRS staff forced to share training rooms in a way that left them unable to discuss sensitive taxpayer information privately, and immigration agency employees working out of storage rooms. Wired's April 8, 2025 follow-up reporting on the mandate's rollout described some employees facing commutes of up to two hours each way solely to sit in an office and take the same Zoom meetings they had previously taken from home, reinforcing outside characterizations of the rollout as producing disruption without a clear productivity rationale. Some federal employees and outside observers characterized the mandate's chaotic, under-resourced rollout as a de facto pressure campaign to induce resignations, working in tandem with OPM's January 28, 2025 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation offer to all roughly 2 million federal employees (a separate, related action this database references but does not duplicate in full here). Pew Research Center calculated federal civilian headcount fell 10.3% in 2025 overall, with 348,219 quits, retirements, and layoffs against only 116,912 new hires -- a figure reflecting the combined effect of the RTO mandate, the deferred-resignation program, and other workforce-reduction actions rather than the RTO mandate in isolation.

title: Survey of 300+ Fired Federal Workers Finds 95% Report Ongoing Mental Health Harm, Nearly a Year After Court Found Firings Unlawful
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and government-wide probationary workforce
status: Harm ongoing/documented; Judge Alsup declined to order reinstatement, reasoning fired workers had 'moved on with their lives and found new jobs' -- the same May 2026 survey's own data (21% still unemployed, 7% underemployed, 49% of the employed earning significantly less as of Jan. 31, 2026) directly contradicts that assumption, and of the ~157 respondents who were reinstated via separate legal challenges (not Alsup's ruling), 115 described inadequate communication about the process. As this documentation emerged, OPM separately proposed (reported July 2026) reducing the morale/satisfaction questions on its own government-wide employee survey and giving agencies more control over public disclosure of results
date_of_action: 2025-02 (OPM directive to mass-fire probationary employees) through 2026-05 (survey results published)
what_changed: In February 2025, the Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies to mass-terminate probationary employees -- workers typically in their first one to two years in a position or newly promoted role, who have fewer job protections than tenured federal staff. More than 25,000 probationary employees were fired government-wide as a result. The mental-health toll was documented almost immediately, not just in the 2026 retrospective survey below: in March 2025, NBC News interviewed 20 federal workers -- many of them military veterans -- who described panic attacks, weight loss, sleepless nights, and suicidal ideation in the weeks after losing their jobs, with some visiting emergency rooms after breakdowns; several described being harassed on social media on top of the job loss itself, and suicide-prevention specialists among the fired workers said the firings had left them questioning their own worth. In September 2025, U.S. District Judge William Alsup ruled that OPM had unlawfully directed agencies to carry out these terminations. In May 2026 -- more than a year after the initial firings and roughly eight months after the court's unlawfulness finding -- a group of former fired probationary employees conducted and published a survey of more than 300 of their fired colleagues. The survey found that 95% of respondents reported continuing mental health effects, including depression and sleep disruption, and that nearly half described PTSD-like symptoms; about a quarter said they had started new medication to cope. The survey's release pushed back specifically against the narrative that affected workers had 'moved on' in the year-plus since being terminated. That pushback was aimed squarely at Alsup's own stated reasoning for declining to order reinstatement: he had reasoned that many fired workers had 'moved on with their lives and found new jobs.' The survey's employment data (drawn from the same 300+ respondents across 43 states and 14 federal agencies) contradicts that assumption directly -- as of January 31, 2026, 21% of respondents remained unemployed, another 7% had found only part-time work, and 49% of those who were employed reported earning significantly lower salaries than before their firing. Separately, of the survey's ~157 respondents who had been reinstated -- through other legal challenges distinct from Alsup's ruling, which did not itself order reinstatement -- 115 said communication about the reinstatement process had been inadequate, and many described returning without any assurance of job security. About 82% of all respondents said they now have zero trust in their former agency's leadership. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 49): as this survey data was drawing attention to the firings' psychological toll, OPM moved in the opposite direction on its own government-wide morale measurement -- a pattern with an earlier antecedent than this update initially captured. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0538): OPM had already fully canceled the 2025 FEVS in August 2025, after months of postponement, despite a federal statute requiring the survey be conducted annually (Government Executive, Federal News Network, August 2025). OPM's stated rationale was to remove questions on diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, and gender identity added under the Biden administration, adding a new question about poor performers instead, and said it would field a revised survey in 2026 -- the same 'reworked' framing that later produced the reduced-question, agency-disclosure-control proposal reported the following July. The Washington Post characterized the cancellation as removing one of the few institutional tools for measuring civil-service morale and accountability at a moment when mass firings and relocations had already depressed it. Reported July 10, 2026, OPM proposed reducing the number of questions on the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) -- the government's own annual instrument for measuring federal workforce morale and job satisfaction -- while giving individual agencies more control over whether and how their results are publicly disclosed. The proposal emerged amid a broader context of roughly 317,000 federal employees having left government (through firings or buyouts, including the DOGE-driven departures documented elsewhere in this database) by the time DOGE's operations concluded July 4, 2026. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0241): this 317,000 figure traces back at least as far as Reuters reporting from late November 2025, in which Trump's OPM director confirmed the government would shed 317,000 workers over the course of 2025 alone -- consistent with, not a revision of, the July 2026 cumulative figure above. That same reporting specified only about 68,000 replacement hires against the 317,000 departures, and described OPM as working with the White House budget office to 'institutionalize' DOGE's workforce-reduction approach into standing personnel policy ahead of DOGE's own wind-down -- i.e., making the reduction mechanism durable past DOGE itself, not merely a one-time purge.

primary_proponent.name: Office of Personnel Management leadership (directive originated under then-Acting OPM Director Charles Ezell)
primary_proponent.role: Federal government's central human-resources agency, which directed the probationary firings later found unlawful
primary_proponent.note: OPM's directive is the originating action; this entry documents the human-impact evidence that emerged more than a year later, distinct from the agency-specific staffing entries elsewhere in this tracker (e.g., IRS, CISA, NPS) that document firings' operational effects rather than firsthand psychological impact on the workers themselves.

estimated_impact.summary: The survey's testimonials describe lasting psychological harm well beyond the initial job loss: respondents reported ongoing nightmares, new medication use, and a sense that the firings 'will reverberate through my life for years,' as one respondent put it. The scale (300+ respondents drawn from a pool of 25,000+ terminated workers, with 95% reporting continuing effects) suggests the psychological impact was not a short-term disruption but a durable harm, more than a year after the terminations and roughly eight months after a federal court found the underlying directive unlawful.

estimated_impact.caveat: This is a self-selected survey of fired workers conducted by a peer advocacy group of fellow fired employees, not an independent, randomly sampled clinical study -- the 95%/PTSD figures likely reflect a population motivated to respond because they experienced significant harm, and should be read as documenting the existence and severity of harm within an affected, engaged subset rather than as a precise government-wide psychological-impact rate. The underlying legal question (whether the mass firing was lawful) has already been resolved against OPM by a federal court; the survey's own employment and reinstatement data (21% unemployed, 49% of the employed earning less, majority of reinstated respondents reporting poor communication) is the closest available evidence on the remedy question, though it still reflects the same self-selected respondent pool rather than an independent audit of all ~25,000 fired workers or of OPM/agency reinstatement records.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the survey's existence, methodology (300+ respondents across 43 states and 14 federal agencies, conducted by former fired federal workers), and headline findings (95% ongoing effects, ~50% PTSD-like symptoms, ~25% new medication), corroborated by Federal News Network and Government Executive's direct reporting on the survey release, with the underlying Alsup ruling and 25,000-worker firing scale corroborated by earlier NPR and Washington Post reporting. The March 2025 NBC News reporting (20 fired workers interviewed directly, veteran-specific detail) independently corroborates that the harm described in the 2026 survey was present and reported within weeks of the firings, not a delayed or survey-artifact effect. MODERATE confidence on generalizing the survey's percentages to the full population of ~25,000 fired workers, given the self-selected respondent pool noted above. Re-verified 2026-08-30: Nonprofit Quarterly's coverage of the same May 2026 survey release adds the employment/reinstatement figures and Alsup's specific 'moved on with their lives' rationale, corroborating and quantifying what the entry's prior text described only qualitatively; single-outlet sourced for these specific figures, so flagged MODERATE confidence on the exact percentages pending a second outlet, though HIGH confidence that the underlying survey and its release are real (multiply corroborated above). Real correction, GSR recheck batch 49 (2026-09-01): the OPM FEVS-question-reduction proposal is sourced to The Mindful Federal Employee (a single outlet, reporting July 10, 2026), which itself cites separate, more current survey figures (95% new mental-health symptoms, one in four started psychiatric medication, only 5% fully recovered one year out) attributed to independent researchers without naming the underlying survey by name -- these figures are consistent with but not confirmed as the identical May 2026 survey already documented in this entry, so presented here as corroborating context rather than a fifth data point layered onto the existing figures. MODERATE confidence on the FEVS proposal itself pending a second outlet. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0538): the August 2025 full cancellation of the 2025 FEVS is HIGH confidence, corroborated across The Washington Post, Federal News Network, Government Executive, and Bloomberg Law, all describing the same OPM announcement and its stated DEI-question-removal rationale; Government Executive's framing ('despite law requiring it') is its own characterization of the statutory requirement, not independently verified against the statute's text for this entry.

title: Roughly 250,000-335,000 Federal Employees Left Government in 2025 -- Overwhelmingly Through Resignations and Buyouts, Not Mass Firings, Per OPM's and Independent Agencies' Own Tallies
institution: Office of Personnel Management (government-wide, all civilian agencies)
status: Largely complete for the 2025 cohort as of the most recent government-wide tallies reviewed (OPM's own November 2025 count and the Washington Post's January 2026 agency-by-agency breakdown); this entry tracks the cumulative, government-wide total distinct from this tracker's separate per-agency entries (IRS, DOJ, SSA, USAID, Education, etc.)
date_of_action: 2025-01-28 (OPM's original 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation memo) through 2026-01-10 (Washington Post's Jan.-Nov. 2025 agency-by-agency departure breakdown)
what_changed: On January 28, 2025, OPM sent all federal civil-service employees a memo titled 'Fork in the Road,' offering deferred resignation (continued pay and benefits through September 30, 2025 in exchange for leaving) to anyone unwilling to work under the new administration's terms -- the opening move in a year-long, government-wide workforce reduction carried out mainly through voluntary programs (deferred resignation, buyouts, early retirement) rather than the individual reduction-in-force actions this tracker's per-agency entries separately document. By August 2025, more than 154,000 federal employees -- over 6% of the civilian workforce -- were being paid under the deferred resignation program despite not working, a figure first reported by the Washington Post and confirmed by administration officials; Senate Democrats estimated the program's mismanagement had cost $21.7 billion, a figure the administration disputed. By October 2025, more than 250,000 federal employees had exited government through retirements and buyouts, with OPM facing a backlog of over 35,000 pending retirement claims that the concurrent government shutdown further delayed. In November 2025, OPM itself announced the year's cuts had reached 317,000 departures, surpassing the administration's own 2025 workforce-reduction goal. By January 2026, the New York Times put the cumulative civilian workforce reduction at approximately 249,000 employees, or about 10% of the federal civilian workforce, attributing it to purges, forced resignations, and early retirements combined with terminated programs, frozen grants, and agency dismantlement. Days later, the Washington Post's own agency-by-agency analysis, using newly available federal workforce data, found roughly 335,000 employees had left between January and November 2025 -- a somewhat higher total than either the NYT or OPM's own November count -- and, significantly, found the departures were driven overwhelmingly by resignations, retirements, and buyouts rather than mass involuntary purges. The Post's breakdown found the steepest proportional losses at the Department of Agriculture (more than a third of USDA's food inspectors left), the Social Security Administration (more than a quarter of its IT management staff gone), and additional heavy losses at Treasury/IRS, USAID, the Education Department, and HHS, while enforcement-focused agencies like ICE grew during the same period.

primary_proponent.name: Office of Personnel Management leadership, under President Trump's broader workforce-reduction directive
primary_proponent.role: Federal government's central human-resources agency
primary_proponent.note: OPM authored and issued the original January 28, 2025 'Fork in the Road' memo that structured the deferred-resignation program underlying most of this entry's cumulative departure figures; OPM also self-reported the November 2025 317,000-departure milestone as exceeding its own 2025 target.

estimated_impact.summary: Between roughly a quarter and a third of a million federal civilian employees left government service in 2025 -- a scale of workforce reduction achieved mainly through voluntary exit programs rather than mass firings, concentrated heavily at a handful of agencies (USDA, SSA, Treasury/IRS, USAID, Education, HHS) while enforcement agencies like ICE grew, and estimated by Senate Democrats to have cost $21.7 billion in mismanagement even before accounting for the lost institutional expertise the Post's reporting documents (a third of USDA's food inspectors, a quarter of SSA's IT management staff).

The Washington Post's reporting specifically found the departures were 'overwhelmingly' voluntary (resignations, retirements, buyouts) rather than mass involuntary RIFs -- an important nuance distinct from this tracker's separate per-agency entries, some of which do document specific involuntary reduction-in-force actions at individual agencies.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on each individual figure, all sourced to OPM's own data, the Washington Post's and New York Times' independent reporting, or Senate Democrats' publicly stated estimate (labeled as an estimate, not adjudicated fact). MODERATE confidence in reconciling the different totals against each other, since they use different date ranges, methodologies, and in OPM's case, self-reported figures without independent verification identified in sourcing reviewed -- this entry presents them side by side rather than resolving them into one number.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: A quarter to a third of a million federal workers left in 2025, overwhelmingly voluntarily rather than through mass firings, with the heaviest proportional losses at a handful of agencies; Senate Democrats estimate the deferred-resignation program alone cost $21.7 billion in mismanagement, disputed by the administration.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Every individual figure is well-sourced (OPM's own data, WaPo, NYT); the different totals from different outlets and dates are not directly reconcilable and are presented as a sequence of estimates rather than one number.

title: FedRAMP Approved Microsoft's Government Cloud Despite Reviewers Calling It Unassessable and 'a Pile of Shit,' Citing How Embedded It Already Was Across Government
institution: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP), General Services Administration
status: Finalized December 26, 2024 -- GCC High was authorized despite unresolved security concerns; ProPublica's March 2026 investigative report brought the authorization decision and reviewers' internal doubts to public light over a year after the fact; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: FedRAMP's review ran roughly three years (ending initial talks October 2023), then resumed under a new team in summer 2024; GCC High was authorized December 26, 2024. ProPublica's investigation into the authorization -- including reviewers' documented lack of confidence -- was published and widely reported in March 2026, roughly 14 months after the authorization itself, not concurrent with it.
what_changed: A ProPublica investigation found federal cybersecurity reviewers concluded Microsoft's Government Community Cloud High (GCC High) -- cloud infrastructure widely used across federal agencies to store sensitive government data -- lacked proper documentation of how it encrypts data in transit, a basic security requirement that competitors Amazon and Google routinely documented for their own competing federal cloud products. FedRAMP spent 480 hours and conducted 18 technical deep-dive reviews over roughly three years and still concluded it had a 'lack of confidence' in GCC High's overall security posture; one FedRAMP reviewer was quoted describing the product as 'a pile of shit.' Despite these unresolved concerns, FedRAMP authorized GCC High anyway. ProPublica's reporting found the authorization decision was shaped by how deeply embedded Microsoft's cloud products already were across the federal government -- rejecting the authorization would have been highly disruptive -- and by internal deference to Microsoft evident in memos, logs, and interviews, even as Microsoft had separately suffered major prior breaches. ProPublica's reporting also connects the deference and the review's ultimate outcome to FedRAMP's own staffing cuts, which reduced the program's capacity to hold a vendor as large as Microsoft to the same documentation standard applied to smaller competitors. Update 2026-08-30 (moderate -- more specific figures on the staffing-cuts connection, same underlying ProPublica investigation): FedRAMP's own authorization package reportedly appended a cover report acknowledging GCC High's deficiencies and 'unknown risks,' concluding that 'not issuing an authorization would impact multiple agencies that are already using GCC-H' and that authorizing with conditions was a 'better value' than withholding it. Coverage of the same investigation puts a specific number on the staffing cuts already referenced here: FedRAMP was reduced to roughly 28 employees -- its lowest staffing and funding level in a decade -- attributed to DOGE-driven budget cuts that left the program focused on issuing authorizations at record pace rather than conducting the kind of meaningful security review this episode illustrates.

primary_proponent.name: FedRAMP / General Services Administration
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency responsible for authorizing cloud products for government use
primary_proponent.note: Sourcing reviewed did not identify a single named individual FedRAMP or GSA official who made the final authorization decision; ProPublica's reporting attributes the outcome to institutional dynamics (Microsoft's market embeddedness and FedRAMP's own reduced staffing capacity) rather than one identified decision-maker.

estimated_impact.summary: Sensitive federal government data across numerous agencies now sits on cloud infrastructure that the government's own technical reviewers, after years of dedicated review, said they could not verify meets basic security standards -- a documented instance of federal cybersecurity oversight yielding to a vendor's market entrenchment and the reviewing program's own reduced capacity, rather than resolving the underlying security gap.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the review's findings (the encryption-documentation gap, the 480-hour/18-review process, the 'pile of shit' quote, and the 'lack of confidence' conclusion) and the authorization decision itself are drawn from ProPublica's own investigation, including internal memos, logs, and interviews, and independently corroborated by Boing Boing, Let's Data Science, and Bruce Schneier's security-industry commentary. MODERATE confidence on the specific causal role of FedRAMP staffing cuts in the outcome, since that connection is ProPublica's own analytical framing rather than an on-record admission from FedRAMP that staffing capacity drove the authorization decision. Primary-source confirmation directly from ProPublica's own article establishes the authorization was finalized December 26, 2024; the investigative report that surfaced it publicly ran about 14 months later, in March 2026. This is a factual correction to the entry's timeline, not a change to the underlying findings, which remain HIGH confidence as before. Re-verified 2026-08-30: the ~28-employee/decade-low-funding figure and the authorization cover report's 'better value' language are drawn from Techdirt's write-up of the same ProPublica investigation rather than independently checked against ProPublica's own article text in this pass -- MODERATE confidence on those specific figures, though consistent with the staffing-cuts causal link already in this entry.

title: FEMA Cancelled $3.6B in Disaster-Resilience Grants, Then Was Ordered by a Federal Court to Restore Them a Year Later
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Reversed by court order and subsequent agency action -- FEMA reinstated the program in March 2026 with $1B in new funding, after a federal judge's December 2025 order
date_of_action: 2025-04 (program termination) through 2026-03 (reinstatement)
what_changed: In April 2025, the Trump administration ended FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program, which funded predisaster projects -- floodwalls, elevated infrastructure, fire-resistant building retrofits, and similar hardening work -- for hundreds of communities nationwide. The termination halted $3.6 billion in funding that had already been awarded to specific, in-progress projects but not yet paid out, and separately refused to award another $882 million in grants that had been planned for the following fiscal year. Twenty states, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James among others, sued the administration, arguing FEMA lacked legal authority to cancel a program funded and directed by Congress, that the cancellation undermined already-underway projects, and that it left disaster-prone communities more vulnerable to floods, fires, and storms. In December 2025, a federal judge in Massachusetts sided with the 22 states and D.C. that had joined the suit by that point, ordering FEMA to restore the canceled funding. In March 2026, FEMA announced it would reinstate the program -- rebranded as the 'Building Resilient Communities and Infrastructure' program -- making $1 billion available for states, local governments, territories, and tribes to pursue hardening projects against wildfires, floods, earthquakes, and hurricanes, though at less than a third of the originally canceled $3.6 billion figure.

primary_proponent.name: FEMA leadership (Trump administration)

primary_proponent.note: This action predates and is distinct from FEMA's separately documented staffing collapse ([[fema-capacity-collapse-texas-floods-trump2]]) and partisan-approval-gap pattern ([[fema-disaster-aid-partisan-approval-gap-trump2]]) already in this tracker -- BRIC's cancellation is a specific funding-program termination, not a staffing or approval-timing issue, though all three reflect the same broader disaster-response degradation under this administration.

estimated_impact.summary: The cancellation directly threatened hundreds of already-planned, partially-underway community resilience projects nationwide for nearly a year, until a federal court intervened; the eventual reinstatement restored the program in principle but at less than a third of the originally terminated funding level.
