title: FEMA Capacity Collapse — Staff Exodus and Spending Bottleneck Delayed Texas Flood Response
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing institutional instability, now independently confirmed by GAO -- Cameron Hamilton's August 2026 Senate confirmation resolved the leadership-vacancy thread, but a GAO report published August 4, 2026 found FEMA at risk of 'critically low' staffing for the 2026 hurricane season, with its DHS-provided surge workforce down to about 240 available personnel versus roughly 600 in 2025, and no updated workforce plan in place since FEMA rescinded its 2022-2026 strategic plan in May 2025
date_of_action: Staff departures throughout 2025; acute failure documented July 4-10, 2025 during Texas floods
what_changed: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0434, inserted first as causal-prequel context predating every other fact in this entry): Kerr County's own flood-warning infrastructure had been left unfunded for nearly a decade before the July 2025 disaster, compounding the federal capacity failures documented below rather than existing independently of them, since the county's earliest funding requests targeted federal money the state administered. Kerr County first requested roughly $1 million in federal Hazard Mitigation Grant Program funding for a flood warning system in 2017; Texas's state emergency-management department denied it, and a second attempt following 2017's Hurricane Harvey was also denied, with the state directing available federal hazard-mitigation money toward more densely populated areas like Houston instead. Separately, at the state legislative level, a bill that would have created a $500 million grant program to help rural counties fund emergency alert systems -- spurred by prior wildfires -- failed in the Texas Senate earlier in 2025, months before the flood; Republican state Rep. Wes Virdell, who voted against it, said afterward 'in hindsight, watching what it takes to deal with a disaster like this, my vote would probably be different now,' while maintaining his specific objection had been the bill's lack of transparency rather than opposition to funding warning systems themselves. Texas lawmakers separately passed on other flood-specific protections (siren systems, drainage upgrades, rural support) earlier in 2025, prioritizing tax cuts and drought measures instead. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0318: internal FEMA memos reviewed by Reuters showed that since February 5, 2025, FEMA staff had been barred from travel unrelated to disaster deployment, and since early March 2025 had been required to get speaking engagements and presentation materials approved by the Office of External Affairs and Office of Chief Counsel; few such requests were approved, forcing the National Hurricane Program to cancel or move online training sessions for emergency managers in storm-prone areas. Organizers of the April 2025 National Hurricane Conference in New Orleans canceled several FEMA-led sessions -- including one aimed at helping emergency managers make evacuation decisions during hurricanes -- after FEMA staff dropped out due to the travel restrictions. Lynn Budd, president of the National Emergency Management Association, said states needed more time and resources to compensate, noting FEMA provides local/state jurisdictions expertise 'that the states simply don't have at this time.' Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0518: youth outreach was cut too -- FEMA emailed the 15 students on its 13-year-old Youth Preparedness Council on January 16, 2025 that their culminating Washington summit that summer was canceled, then, after months of silence, emailed them again on August 1, 2025 that the program itself would be terminated early; FEMA told the students the move was meant 'to ensure FEMA is a lean, deployable disaster force that is ready to support states as they take the lead in preparedness and disaster response.' Starting March 24, 2025, Trump implemented sweeping changes to FEMA's hiring policies, forcing thousands of employees to reapply for their jobs through the Department of Homeland Security; more than 200 probationary workers were let go in the same period. Two days later, on March 26, 2025, Noem told reporters discussing border security that "we're going to eliminate FEMA" -- an offhand remark made without further detail, four months before her more formal July 9, 2025 call (see below) to eliminate the agency 'as it exists today,' showing the elimination framing was already administration rhetoric from the earliest days of the hiring-policy overhaul rather than a position that emerged only after the Texas floods. Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit ec8078a, which marked these records folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): the elimination rhetoric traces back even earlier than the March 24 hiring overhaul -- Trump had already said in January 2025 that FEMA "should go away" -- and by May 6, 2025, Noem told lawmakers directly that Trump wanted to abolish FEMA outright and replace it with block grants sent directly to states, a cost-and-control-shifting mechanism that recurred later in the November 2025 FEMA Review Council dispute (see below), where Noem's own counter-proposal likewise sought to shift half of recovery costs onto states. Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling more of the same dropped commit-ec8078a fold, continuing where the prior addition above stopped): the abolish-FEMA rhetoric had a concrete early test case: on April 25, 2025, Trump denied federal disaster relief to Arkansas following March tornadoes and storms that killed over 40 people across Arkansas, Mississippi, and Missouri, rejecting the request despite it coming from Republican Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Arkansas's own congressional delegation. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0363): two more denials followed the same pattern. On May 23, 2025, FEMA Acting Administrator David Richardson denied North Carolina Governor Josh Stein's request to extend the 100% federal cost-share (a Biden-era commitment) for Hurricane Helene debris removal and emergency protective measures, reverting the state to the standard 90% share -- a 10-percentage-point cut on a Category 4 storm that had killed over 230 people; Stein was granted 30 days to appeal. Then, after a stalled monsoon system caused flash flooding in Gila and Mohave Counties, Arizona (including the town of Globe) on September 25-27, 2025 with preliminary damage estimated around $33 million, FEMA denied Arizona's major-disaster-declaration request, finding the damage 'not of such severity and magnitude as to be beyond the capabilities of the state and affected local governments'; Governor Katie Hobbs, who had declared a state of emergency, appealed on January 16, 2026, and FEMA denied that appeal too, on July 2, 2026, reaffirming the same finding. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0400: the denial pattern was not partisan -- Reuters reported June 17, 2025 that Trump had declined hazard-mitigation funding requests from six disaster-hit states, all with Republican governors, including Iowa's Kim Reynolds, Mississippi's Tate Reeves, Missouri's Mike Kehoe, and Oklahoma's Kevin Stitt, following March 2025 disasters in their states; Trump had signed major disaster declarations greenlighting some other funding for these states, but their specific hazard-mitigation requests remained undecided, and Reuters found the administration had not approved a single hazard-mitigation request in over a year at that point. The same reporting profiled Lake Lure, North Carolina, still working to rebuild its dam and tourism economy after Hurricane Helene, where the uncertainty created by Trump's FEMA-shrinking plans -- on top of the cost-share reduction to Helene recovery already documented above -- left the town's rebuilding timeline in limbo; one local business owner asked, 'There's got to be some federal help, right?' Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0387: Trump gave that push a specific timeline and mechanism at a June 10, 2025 Oval Office briefing, saying 'we want to wean off of FEMA, and we want to bring it down to the state level' and that the administration would begin phasing the agency out after the 2025 hurricane season, with disaster-aid funding distributed directly from the president's own office rather than through FEMA. Noem said at the same briefing that the administration would form a council 'over the next couple of months' to plan the agency's future -- the origin of the FEMA Review Council fight documented later in this entry. Jeremy Greenberg, head of FEMA's National Response Coordination Center, resigned in mid-June 2025, just weeks into hurricane season, joining a wave of senior departures as Trump pushed states to 'wean' off federal disaster aid. A ProPublica investigation published June 30, 2025 found Trump had stalled billions in FEMA grant funding, missed legal disbursement deadlines, and begun dismantling core preparedness programs; Noem's new requirement that she personally review any FEMA expenditure over $100,000 (also documented below in the Texas flood context) was already slowing operations agency-wide at that point, even as states rely on FEMA for up to 99% of their emergency budgets in some cases. In July 2025, as California sought $40 billion in wildfire recovery aid, Trump's feud with Governor Newsom became entangled with proposals to raise disaster-aid eligibility thresholds and cut preparedness grants; separately, internal memos reported by CNN on July 28, 2025 revealed plans to cut nearly $1 billion from FEMA's disaster-preparedness and security grants, including the $500 million Urban Areas Security Initiative, with FEMA officials themselves acknowledging the cuts would leave cities more vulnerable. That October, FEMA froze $300-320 million in preparedness grants (reported with slightly different figures by CNN on Oct. 2 and ABC News on Oct. 21, likely the same freeze), requiring states to recertify population counts excluding deported migrants before releasing funds -- a requirement that followed a court ruling blocking the administration from redirecting FEMA money away from Democratic-led states. On October 20, 2025 -- over three months after the July 4 Texas floods -- the Texas Tribune reported FEMA had denied or delayed the majority of Kerr County residents' aid requests, approving only 22% of applications, with many rejected over technicalities like missed calls or incomplete paperwork, forcing nonprofits to fill the gap. The following day, FEMA employees and former staffers protested outside agency headquarters, accusing Noem of slashing programs, forcing FEMA to cooperate with ICE, and delaying aid as staffing and funding collapsed. On November 10, 2025, NPR reported FEMA had pulled $14 million in promised funding for a tsunami-proofing project at Columbia Memorial Hospital on the Washington coast after officials abruptly canceled the BRIC disaster-mitigation program mid-construction, leaving the hospital without resources to survive a Cascadia earthquake and tsunami; a similar case surfaced in Oregon by December 31, 2025 (CBS News), where a coastal hospital scrambled to build a tsunami shelter after the same BRIC cancellation hit its project mid-stream, even as courts had separately ruled the BRIC cuts unlawful. On November 29, 2025, AP reported new detail on the FEMA Review Council fight already documented below: the Trump-appointed council's own draft had concluded FEMA should be elevated and given more independence, but Noem intervened with a competing draft that would keep FEMA under DHS, slash its disaster role, and force states to cover half of recovery costs -- cutting the council's own 160-page proposal down to under 20 pages in the process, a more specific and more adversarial picture than this entry's existing 'draft report...recommending workforce be cut in half' framing alone conveyed. (Five additional discovery-backlog records in this same dropped fold describe National Weather Service staffing cuts during May-December 2025 tornado/hurricane/winter-storm events; NWS staffing is a distinct agency from FEMA and is already tracked in this database's own dedicated entries -- nws-staffing-losses-trump2.json, noaa-wide-staffing-collapse-spring-2025.json, and nws-weather-balloon-launch-cuts-trump2.json -- so those five records are not duplicated into this FEMA-specific entry.) Throughout 2025, FEMA underwent a wave of staff departures -- about 18% of the agency's permanent full-time employees had left as of June 2025, including 24 senior-level staffers, per GAO. In May 2025 alone, 16 senior officials departed, taking with them a combined 200+ years of disaster-response expertise. On May 24, 2025, Acting Administrator David Richardson abruptly rescinded FEMA's 2022-2026 strategic plan, calling it disconnected from the agency's core mission, and ended the Office of Resilience Strategy. In early June 2025, Reuters reported that Richardson told staff during a briefing he had not known the U.S. has a hurricane season (which runs June 1-Nov 30); DHS later said the remark was a joke, though some employees called it poorly timed given already-low morale amid the ongoing purges. Separately, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem implemented a rule requiring her personal sign-off on any FEMA expenditure over $100,000 -- for an agency whose disaster costs routinely run into the billions, officials described this threshold as effectively 'pennies.' This bottleneck had direct, documented consequences during the deadly July 4, 2025 Texas Hill Country floods: FEMA's disaster survivor call-center contract funding lapsed on July 5, and it took Noem five days -- until July 10 -- to approve renewed funding, during which most survivor calls went unanswered (an internal memo documented the call-answer rate collapsing from 99.9% to 20%, with survivors waiting over 90 minutes). NPR reported in August 2025 that this documented 10-20% call-answer rate directly contradicted Acting Administrator Richardson's own claim to Congress that most survivor calls had been handled during the crisis. Noem also did not authorize deployment of FEMA's Urban Search and Rescue teams until more than 72 hours after the flooding began. Ken Pagurek, head of FEMA's Urban Search and Rescue branch, resigned on July 23, 2025, citing the delayed deployment caused by Noem's $100,000 sign-off requirement as a direct factor in his decision. Acting FEMA Administrator David Richardson did not travel to Texas for a full week after the disaster, telling a House committee he had stayed in Washington to 'kick down the doors of bureaucracy' -- and separately acknowledged he had been camping with his sons over the July 4 weekend when the floods hit. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0442: Politico reported July 10, 2025 that Richardson had made no public appearances or statements at all since the flooding began, even as Noem personally toured the disaster zone and spoke to the press -- a total public-visibility gap, distinct from the week-long physical absence from Texas already documented above, that former FEMA officials told Politico broke with the agency's own precedent for how its administrator engages during a major disaster response. The Washington Post separately reported in September 2025 that FEMA staff could not reach Richardson for nearly 24 hours during the acute phase of the disaster, a communications gap that further delayed critical rescue-deployment decisions on top of the sign-off bottleneck itself. Even as FEMA was actively responding to the ongoing Texas disaster, Noem publicly said on July 9, 2025 that FEMA should be 'eliminated as it exists today,' criticizing the agency's response times and bureaucracy and calling instead for a state-led disaster system -- remarks made during a federal disaster-system reform meeting held while FEMA personnel were still deployed to the flood response. Separately, by July 4, 2025, FEMA officials said they were being blocked from communicating directly with Congress and local agencies, with internal memos requiring all inquiries to go through political appointees as Noem tightened control over the agency's external communications. The following month, Reuters reported that Trump officials began reassigning FEMA personnel to help ICE hire 10,000 new agents, warning staff they could be terminated if they refused the reassignment -- a redirection of disaster-response staff toward immigration enforcement that came at the height of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season. On the 20th anniversary of Hurricane Katrina, August 31, 2025, 180 FEMA employees wrote to Congress warning that the administration's cuts and inexperienced leadership could cripple the agency in a future crisis; days later, more than 190 employees signed a related letter after Noem ordered FEMA staff to publicly praise Trump's leadership even as the agency reeled from mass resignations, contract delays, and the Texas flood response failures. On September 2, 2025, Noem announced an IT security breach at FEMA and purged 23 employees, blaming FEMA's IT team for "failure" and "incompetence," while saying no sensitive citizen data had been stolen. Around the same time, a GAO report found that 2,500 FEMA employees -- including 24 senior leaders -- had quit since January 2025, a harder figure than the informal 18% departure estimate cited above, leaving the agency understaffed heading into peak hurricane and wildfire season. Richardson resigned in November 2025 after six months in the role, the second of three different acting administrators to lead FEMA within the year. In January 2026, FEMA abruptly stopped renewing contracts for its Cadre of On-Call Response/Recovery (CORE) employees -- term-limited hires who can hold senior disaster-response roles -- then paused the cuts in late January as a major winter storm affecting roughly half the country's population approached; FEMA managers confirmed in early February 2026 that the CORE staff reductions would resume once the storm passed, though no specific restart date was given. FEMA supervisors had told staff in mid-January 2026 to prepare for roughly 1,000 disaster-worker dismissals that month, and a coalition of federal employee unions (led by AFGE), nonprofits, and local governments sued FEMA in late January/early February 2026 to block the workforce cuts, arguing they violated the law and would leave the agency unable to meet its statutory disaster-response obligations; U.S. District Judge Susan Illston indicated in February 2026 she would likely deny a preliminary injunction after FEMA offered to rehire some of the affected on-call responders. Around the same period, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who has overseen FEMA's cuts, received a draft report from the Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council recommending the agency's workforce be cut in half. During the February 2026 DHS funding lapse, DHS halted nearly all employee travel department-wide, including FEMA disaster-response deployments, according to internal emails The Washington Post obtained -- disrupting FEMA's ability to send personnel to respond to active or anticipated disasters during the lapse; a separate internal FEMA email obtained by The Washington Post warned that national continuity operations were 'significantly constrained' during the same shutdown, limiting the agency's ability to maintain critical continuity-of-government functions. A second documented instance of the same DHS approval bottleneck emerged around the same time: CNN reported FEMA failed to renew a $200,000 contract for a tornado-tracking mapping tool used by rescue teams to identify storm damage paths. The contract expired in February 2026 and remained stuck in the DHS approval process even as deadly tornadoes struck the Midwest and Plains, forcing rescue teams to rely on news reports and manual searches to locate the hardest-hit areas instead of the mapping tool. By March 2026, FEMA's overall staffing had fallen further, from roughly 26,000 employees in January 2025 to about 21,100 -- an approximately 19% decline -- with 18 of the agency's 38 senior leadership positions vacant, including deputy administrator and chief of staff. A CNN KFile investigation published March 20, 2026 found Gregg Phillips -- installed to lead FEMA's Office of Response and Recovery, a key role directing federal disaster-response operations, despite limited emergency-management experience -- has a documented history of promoting conspiracy theories and using violent rhetoric, including saying in January 2025 he would 'like to punch' then-outgoing President Biden 'in the mouth,' and repeatedly claiming on podcasts to have been involuntarily 'teleported,' including once to a Georgia Waffle House 50 miles away. Rep. Tim Kennedy cited Phillips's 'violent statements' and 'deeply troubling bigoted comments about immigrants' as evidence he was 'wildly unfit for his role'; Phillips defended the teleportation claims in a follow-up CNN report the following month, saying 'haters gonna hate.' Robert Fenton (FEMA's Region 9 administrator) took over as senior official performing the duties of administrator; Trump nominated Cameron Hamilton as permanent administrator. Facing the 2026 hurricane season, FEMA began a limited hiring campaign: it rehired 14 staff Secretary Noem had fired for signing the 'Katrina Declaration,' and DHS approved roughly 300 near-term new hires with hopes of filling up to 700 vacancies. Fenton told reporters FEMA has about 30-40% of its disaster workforce available at any given time, which he characterized as normal availability rather than a crisis-level shortfall; NOAA's 2026 Atlantic hurricane season outlook predicts a below-normal season (8-14 named storms, 3-6 hurricanes). Hamilton previously served as acting FEMA administrator from January-May 2025 before being fired for telling Congress he did not believe eliminating FEMA was in the public interest. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0353: Reuters reported the firing came one day after that testimony, and that DHS officials had attempted to revoke Hamilton's building access hours before he testified but backed off to avoid public fallout; the ouster followed reported clashes between Hamilton and Trump adviser Corey Lewandowski. At his June 17, 2026 confirmation hearing, Hamilton pledged to be 'fair and reasonable' in assessing disaster-aid requests -- a notable pledge given the separate, related pattern this tracker documents in the FEMA disaster-aid partisan-approval-gap entry. Update 2026-07-26: Hamilton's nomination for permanent FEMA Administrator advanced out of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on an 8-4 vote, roughly a month after his confirmation hearing, and now awaits a full Senate floor vote whose timing before the August recess is not yet clear. Update 2026-08-17: The Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton as permanent FEMA Administrator on 2026-08-07, by a 51-47 vote as part of an en bloc package confirming more than 70 Trump nominees together -- FEMA's first Senate-confirmed administrator under this administration. His nomination had advanced out of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on an 8-4 vote in late July 2026, per this entry's prior update. Hamilton previously served as acting FEMA administrator from January-May 2025 before being fired for telling Congress he did not believe eliminating FEMA was in the public interest; his confirmation resolves the entry's prior 'four different acting/nominated administrators within roughly a year' leadership-instability framing going forward, though it does not reverse the staffing decline (~26,000 to ~21,100 employees, Jan. 2025-March 2026) or the vacancy rate among senior leadership positions documented elsewhere in this entry. Update 2026-08-31 (real correction, GSR recheck batch 45): a Government Accountability Office report (GAO-26-108427, 'FEMA Workforce: Staff Reductions and Lack of Planning May Impact Mission Readiness,' published August 4, 2026) independently confirmed and sharpened this entry's staffing-decline trend with nonpartisan-watchdog figures more current than any previously cited here. GAO found FEMA averaged about 25,134 employees in FY2025, down to about 21,742 by May 2026; more than 4,300 employees separated in FY2025 alone, a 55% increase in departures over FY2024; 58 Senior Executive Service personnel departed between January 2025 and January 2026, versus roughly 13 per year historically; and only 4% of FEMA's incident management workforce was available to deploy in November 2024, cited by GAO as prior context for why concurrent-disaster capacity matters. Most directly relevant to the 2026 hurricane season this entry already tracks: GAO found FEMA anticipated only about 240 personnel available through the DHS Surge Capacity Force for 2026, down from about 600 in 2025 -- a roughly 60% reduction in the external federal support FEMA can draw on during a large or concurrent disaster. GAO's core finding is that FEMA made its workforce-reduction decisions 'without assessing whether it had the necessary staffing capacity to meet its mission,' and that the agency has continued to lack a documented workforce plan for future incidents, including the 2026 hurricane season, since rescinding its 2022-2026 strategic plan in May 2025 -- a structural gap this entry already documented as of that rescission but that GAO now confirms persisted unaddressed fifteen months later. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0309, placed here ahead of the September-dated cluster c0574 addition below to keep this tail section in chronological order): two individual-survivor aid-access barriers, distinct from the staffing/spending-bottleneck mechanisms already documented above but part of the same capacity-collapse pattern. Wired reported May 6, 2025 -- the same day Noem told lawmakers Trump wanted to replace FEMA with state block grants, already documented above -- that FEMA would stop sending workers door-to-door in disaster zones to help survivors register for aid, shifting instead to fixed assistance centers and coordination with local officials; the change aligned with the broader elimination push already underway at that point. The Guardian reported August 22, 2025 that FEMA had begun requiring an email address to apply for federal disaster aid, with FEMA framing it as streamlining communication while critics warned it would exclude elderly, disabled, rural, and low-income survivors without reliable internet access -- a barrier compounding the loss of door-to-door outreach three months earlier and the closure of field offices. Both predate, and offer a mechanism for, the Kerr County 22%-aid-approval-rate finding this entry already documents from October 2025: fewer outreach channels and an added digital-access requirement for exactly the population -- flood survivors in a rural area -- most likely to be excluded by them. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0574): an Associated Press analysis of decades of federal disaster-declaration data, published September 9, 2025, quantified the delay pattern this entry documents in individual episodes as a systemic trend: major disaster declarations took under two weeks on average in the 1990s and early 2000s, rose to about three weeks over the past decade under presidents of both parties, and reached nearly 34 days on average during Trump's current term as of the analysis -- up from a 24-day average during his first term and nearly four times George H.W. Bush's average. Separately, a distinct flood-mitigation-grant dispute emerged in Washington state, apart from the BRIC-program tsunami-shelter cancellations at Columbia Memorial Hospital already documented above: the administration attempted to cancel roughly $182 million in FEMA hazard-mitigation funding for the state, prompting Attorney General Nick Brown and other states to secure a court order requiring FEMA to take concrete steps toward reversing the cancellation, while a separate $31 million in disaster-prevention grants sat awaiting Secretary Noem's personal approval for months. The stalled funding covered projects to elevate flood-prone homes, relocate residents, and build levees and floodwalls, including specific levee/floodwall construction in Aberdeen and Hoquiam; the dispute intensified after a December 2025 storm forced evacuation orders for more than 100,000 Washington residents and damaged nearly 4,000 homes, after which the administration went on to deny the state's request for future flood-preparedness funding entirely.

estimated_impact.caveat: GovFacts' broader analysis of whether cuts affected the flood response itself is careful to note that specific FEMA deployment numbers for the July 2025 disaster weren't fully public at time of writing, and frames the staffing-to-outcome link as 'plausible' rather than definitively proven for every aspect of the response -- the call-center funding lapse specifically, however, is documented via internal agency records, not just inference. title: FEMA Disaster Aid Approvals Skewed Toward Republican-Led States
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing pattern -- most recent documented denial episode July 2026, no reversal or independent (GAO/IG) audit announced as of this writing
date_of_action: 2025-2026 (pattern); most recent documented episode 2026-07 (four-state blizzard aid denial)
what_changed: An E&E News/POLITICO analysis of roughly 2,500 major disaster declaration decisions dating back to the Reagan administration found that under Trump, Democratic-led states have had disaster aid requests approved at a 23% rate, compared to 89% for Republican-led states -- the lowest approval rate for Democratic-led states of any president since Reagan (every prior president approved at least 67% of their requests). The same analysis found Democratic-led states waited an average of 80 days for a decision versus 39 days for Republican-led states, and documented at least $250 million in specific state disaster requests blocked or left pending, including $34 million to Washington, $41 million to Colorado, and $46 million and $83 million in separate Illinois storm-damage requests. The pattern produced a concrete, dated episode in July 2026: Trump denied Major Disaster Declaration requests from New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island -- a combined $227 million sought after a February 2026 blizzard that buried New York City, Long Island, and the Mid-Hudson region, with Rhode Island separately citing record snowfall and cold -- after all four states' damage assessments exceeded FEMA's own threshold for triggering aid. The denials came two days after Trump approved disaster declarations for six Republican-led states; Trump has publicly touted having granted over $846 million in disaster relief to Republican-led states. White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson defended the pattern, saying Trump "provides a more thorough review of disaster declaration requests than any Administration has before him." This is a distinct mechanism from a separate, later legal fight over FEMA's Homeland Security Grant Program: on July 24, 2026, a coalition of 23 Democratic-led states, two Democratic governors, and DC sued DHS in Rhode Island federal court alleging it illegally conditioned that separate grant program on states adopting specific election policies (hand-marked paper ballots, manual audits, the SAVE program) -- a related pattern of FEMA/DHS funding being used as leverage, but a different funding stream and a different specific demand than the major-disaster-declaration approvals this entry tracks. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no new denial episode identified since the four-state February 2026 blizzard denial already documented. The July 24, 2026 lawsuit over FEMA grant conditions (noted in this entry as related context) is now more precisely quantified: DHS/FEMA plan to withhold 20% of the plaintiff states' federal disaster grant funding, at least $148 million, if they don't adopt the demanded election-system changes -- filed by the attorneys general of California, Illinois, New Jersey, and Rhode Island, joined by 19 other states, the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania, and DC. A follow-up E&E News/POLITICO investigation, drawing on emails and 150+ pages of documents submitted to FEMA by New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island, found that FEMA's own field offices had verified damage estimates exceeding the threshold for aid before Trump personally overrode those agency-level findings to deny the requests -- a former FEMA official said they could not recall another instance of a declaration being denied for a state that met FEMA and NOAA standards. The same reporting found that in Trump's first term, by contrast, he approved 93% of Democratic-led states' disaster requests versus 89% of Republican-led states' -- no partisan gap -- underscoring that the current pattern is specific to this term. Separately, an AP analysis of FEMA data (reported by PBS NewsHour and Fortune, July 16, 2026) using a different dataset/methodology found Trump approved 80% of Republican-governor requests versus about 60% of Democratic-governor requests, and more than three-fourths of requests from states that voted for him in 2024 versus less than half from states that didn't -- a real, differently-sized partisan gap from the E&E/POLITICO figures already cited here, not a duplicate of them; both analyses agree a gap exists and that it's unprecedented (the AP piece separately notes no other president has shown a comparable partisan divide), but the specific percentages differ by dataset and shouldn't be merged into one number. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 35): two new developments extend the pattern. First, a new denial episode: in July 2026, FEMA denied federal fire-management-assistance grants for two major Oregon wildfires, prompting Oregon's Democratic senators (Wyden and Merkley) to publicly press FEMA for an explanation -- Oregon has separately been denied a hazard-mitigation grant (after atmospheric-river flooding, appealed by the state in April 2026) even after its underlying public-assistance request for the same disaster was approved, showing the partisan-adjacent denial pattern recurring across different FEMA grant types (major disaster declarations, fire-management assistance, and hazard mitigation), not just the flagship major-disaster-declaration approvals this entry's headline figures track. Second, the separate Homeland Security Grant Program election-conditions dispute (tracked here only as related context, not this entry's core subject) has grown a second, distinct legal front: on August 17, 2026, Harris and El Paso Counties (Texas), Nashville/Davidson County (Tennessee), and Columbus (Ohio) filed a new lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia -- separate from the July 24, 2026 lawsuit by 23 Democratic-led states/DC already documented here -- arguing DHS/FEMA cannot use counterterrorism-grant funding as leverage to force local election-administration changes (hand-marked paper ballots, 5%-minimum manual ballot audits, SAVE-system citizenship verification), with up to 20% of an award withholdable for noncompliance and a full award potentially at risk.

Also added a second, independent AP analysis (via PBS/Fortune) that corroborates a partisan gap exists but reports different specific percentages (80/60 vs. this entry's existing 89/23) -- presented as a distinct, differently-sourced figure rather than merged with the existing E&E/POLITICO numbers, per this tracker's standard for not conflating similar-but-distinct figures from different sources. title: FEMA Shut Down All National Fire Academy Training for Nearly Three Months Amid DOGE-Driven Budget Review
institution: FEMA -- National Fire Academy
status: Reversed -- classes resumed June 2, 2025, after nearly three months closed
date_of_action: 2025-03-07 (classes cancelled) through 2025-06-02 (classes resume)
what_changed: On March 7, 2025, FEMA abruptly cancelled all in-person classes at the National Fire Academy (NFA) in Emmitsburg, Maryland -- along with the co-located National Disaster and Emergency Management University and the Center for Domestic Preparedness in Anniston, Alabama -- as part of a Department of Government Efficiency-driven review of FEMA's spending intended to align it with administration priorities; instructors were told to cancel all future travel, and the suspension was initially described as indefinite, with FEMA saying it would support only 'mission-critical' functions during the review. The NFA provides free, federally funded training that firefighters, EMS providers, and other first responders nationwide travel to Maryland to attend. Lawmakers from both parties pressed FEMA and DHS leadership for an explanation and received none for weeks; the Congressional Fire Services Institute and fire-service leaders warned the shutdown 'undermines first responder public safety' and posed 'an equal threat to public safety' given elevated wildfire risk nationally. FEMA reopened the NFA, NDEMU, and the Center for Domestic Preparedness on June 2, 2025 -- nearly three months after the closure -- following what the agency described as a comprehensive review determining that certain courses 'provide effective training to enhance national readiness for state, local, tribal and territorial emergency managers and first responders.'

title: Trump Used Rescissions to Cancel Billions in Bipartisan Foreign Aid, Gutting Pacific-China-Countering, Myanmar, and Africa Programs
institution: State Department / USAID successor functions
status: Finalized -- rescissions enacted; underlying programs terminated
date_of_action: 2026 (rescissions process, reported April 2026)
what_changed: Extending the original 2025 USAID dismantlement documented separately in this tracker (usaid-dismantlement-trump2.json), Trump pursued a formal rescissions process to permanently claw back billions in previously appropriated, congressionally directed foreign aid funding: first winning party-line approval from the GOP-controlled Congress to cancel a package of spending, then unilaterally expanding the cuts without giving lawmakers the statutory window to object. The New York Times's review of new data found the cuts hit once-bipartisan programs particularly hard: a U.S. initiative helping Pacific island nations counter Chinese influence lost $92 million -- more than half its budget -- and funding to prevent and respond to atrocities committed by Myanmar's military junta was eliminated entirely, directly affecting aid to Rohingya refugees in Myanmar and Bangladesh, forcing UN agencies, international NGOs, and local aid groups to scale back healthcare, food aid, and education programs. Nearly 90% of U.S. economic aid to Africa was cut.

title: Visa Renewal Slowdown for Foreign Doctors From 'National Security Risk' Countries Is Costing Rural Hospitals Physicians
institution: State Department / USCIS visa processing
status: Partially narrowed but core harm ongoing -- USCIS exempted physicians already present in the U.S. from Proclamation 10998's visa-renewal hold, first reported in early May 2026 (about three months before this entry's original write-up), but doctors from the 39 designated countries who are currently abroad remain blocked from returning, the exemption's application procedure is undocumented, and hospitals in several states were still reporting cancelled clinics and disrupted coverage as of reporting reviewed for this recheck; separately, a DHS rule taking effect September 15, 2026 will end open-ended 'duration of status' admission for J-1 physicians, capping their stay at four years and adding new extension filing requirements for the same visa population
date_of_action: 2026 (reported April 2026)
what_changed: Politico reported that Trump officials are slow-walking visa renewals for foreign-born doctors from countries the administration labels national security risks, leaving many physicians unable to continue working legally as their visa status lapses during the delay. Hospitals -- particularly in rural and underserved areas that rely heavily on foreign-trained physicians to fill positions U.S. medical graduates often don't take -- are already losing doctors to missed start dates, interrupted fellowships, and lapsed renewal deadlines caused by the processing slowdown, not by any finding of individual wrongdoing or security risk specific to the affected physicians. The slowdown stems from Presidential Proclamation 10998 (issued December 16, 2025, effective January 1, 2026), which imposed a full entry suspension for nationals of 19 countries and a partial suspension for 20 more (39 total), including Nigeria, Venezuela, and Cuba; USCIS paused visa renewals and status updates for people from those countries even though the underlying travel ban does not apply to visa holders already in the U.S. By early May 2026, USCIS quietly exempted physicians already present in the U.S. from the renewal-processing hold, updating its website and having DHS confirm that medical-physician applications would continue processing -- but the exemption does not extend to physicians from the 39 countries who are currently outside the U.S., who remain blocked from returning, and immigration attorneys have described the exemption's own application procedure as unclear and not made public. Update 2026-08-30: a separate, distinct policy change affecting the same J-1 physician population this entry already tracks (17,000+ visa holders) takes effect September 15, 2026: a DHS final rule, published July 16, 2026, eliminates 'duration of status' admission for J-1 (and F-1/I) visa holders. J-1 physicians will move from open-ended admission tied to their training program's length to a fixed admission period capped at four years, generally matching the residency/fellowship end date in SEVIS; those needing longer than four years to complete training -- mid-residency physicians in longer programs, or those planning a fellowship afterward -- are flagged by immigration counsel as most exposed. Physicians who travel internationally after September 15, 2026 will receive a fixed-end-date I-94 and become subject to new extension-of-status filing requirements, though DHS will allow those already admitted under the prior framework to remain through their program end date (up to four years from the rule's effective date) without filing, and a timely extension filing permits continued work for up to 240 days while pending. This is a new administrative-friction layer distinct from the Proclamation 10998 renewal freeze already documented, but affects an overlapping population and could recreate status-lapse risk for the same physicians the freeze already disrupted.

primary_proponent.note: Sourcing reviewed did not identify a single named official personally directing the slowdown; the policy is attributed to a broader national-security-driven visa-screening posture toward doctors from specifically designated countries.

estimated_impact.summary: A visa-processing slowdown targeting doctors from designated countries -- not individualized security findings against specific physicians -- is directly reducing physician staffing at hospitals, with the effect concentrated in rural and underserved communities that depend most heavily on foreign-trained doctors to fill positions that would otherwise go unfilled.

The in-country physician exemption reduces but does not eliminate the described harm -- physicians abroad remain blocked, and the exemption's mechanics are not publicly documented. The September 15, 2026 duration-of-status rule change (added 2026-08-30) had not yet taken effect as of this recheck, so its practical impact on J-1 physicians is not yet observable -- it is documented here as a dated, near-term development to watch, not a realized harm.

CORRECTION (2026-08-17 recheck): the entry's original status/estimated_impact framing -- 'no resolution or policy change identified in sourcing reviewed' -- missed that USCIS had already exempted in-country physicians from the freeze, reported starting early May 2026, roughly three months before this entry's original write date (2026-08-06). That reporting existed at write-time but was not reflected in original sourcing. This recheck corrects the status to reflect the partial exemption while preserving the entry's core finding that the underlying harm (visa-status lapses disrupting hospital staffing) continues for physicians outside the U.S. Update 2026-08-30: added the September 15, 2026 J-1 duration-of-status elimination rule, corroborated across AHA, AAMC, and multiple immigration-law-firm client alerts (Mondaq, Reddy Neumann Brown, Phillips Lytle) all describing the same DHS final rule and effective date -- a real, dated, near-term development affecting the same J-1 physician population, distinct from the Proclamation 10998 freeze this entry was built around.

title: Forest Service Chief's Own Internal Memo Contradicted Agriculture Secretary's Public 'Fully Staffed' Claims — 5,000 Firefighting Positions Vacant
institution: U.S. Forest Service, Department of Agriculture
status: Ongoing, with a genuine mixed 2026 update -- the Forest Service met its 2026 seasonal wildland-firefighter hiring goal (crediting recent pay raises), even as permanent-staff attrition (~6,000 lost since January 2025) and consolidation continue, and the 2026 fire season itself has been severe
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial layoffs) through 2025-08 (peak fire-season staffing crisis and reorganization announcement)
what_changed: In February 2025, the Trump administration laid off approximately 700 Forest Service employees who support wildland fire operations -- human resource managers, ecologists, and trail-crew workers who hold 'red card' fire-response certifications even though their primary jobs are not firefighting. Many were subsequently rehired, but the administration then pushed remaining staff toward deferred-resignation and early-retirement offers; ultimately at least 1,800 fire-qualified ('red-carded') employees left the agency, out of 4,800 total Forest Service departures in 2025 (more than 13% of the agency's total workforce). Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0205): the layoffs' operational impact was visible within weeks. A ProPublica investigation published April 8, 2025 found the agency's remaining support divisions similarly hollowed out beyond the February layoffs and reinstatements: the IT position overseeing the software firefighters use to request equipment sat unfilled after its posting was removed following the inauguration, legal-department cuts threatened the environmental-review capacity prescribed burns depend on, and hiring slowdowns from insufficient onboarding capacity delayed getting new firefighters into the field, on top of training-program and prescribed-burn cancellations. By mid-June 2025, a Guardian investigation -- quoting five anonymous federal firefighters, all of whom said their agencies were not ready for the season ahead, and Sen. Patty Murray, who separately cited an estimated 7,500 USFS employees pushed out that year (a larger, contemporaneous Senate estimate that doesn't precisely reconcile with this entry's other departure counts but points the same direction) -- found crews going without power for weeks after maintenance-worker cuts, paychecks arriving late or halved because HR retained less than a quarter of its prior staffing, and purchase-card access revoked for basic supplies including chainsaw fuel, printer ink, radios, and fire shelters; a USFS squad leader said newly hired firefighters had gone without healthcare for months. Chief Schultz told senators the agency had hired 11,000 firefighters that summer, about 900 fewer than the prior season, with 37 incident management teams, five fewer than the year before. Separately, Murray said $97 million in congressionally appropriated funding for state, local, tribal, and volunteer wildfire-reduction work went undistributed, and fire ecologist Hugh Safford said the administration's Forest Service research budget request was zero dollars; Schultz told senators the agency's forest-health and mitigation grants were halved to redirect more than $43 million toward the deferred-resignation program, with the grants eliminated entirely in the following year's budget request. The same week, Trump's June 16, 2025 executive order directing Interior and the Forest Service to merge wildland firefighting operations (see wildland-fire-service-suppression-policy-2026.json) added a further layer of uncertainty firefighters said undercut confidence heading into peak season, even among those who supported consolidation in principle -- agency leaders had reportedly told staff the merger wouldn't happen until the following year. Internal Forest Service data reviewed by ProPublica, High Country News, and Capital & Main found at least 5,000 firefighting positions vacant as of mid-July 2025 -- directly contradicting the agency's own public claim of having exceeded its 2025 hiring goal (11,364 firefighters on board by end of July). USDA spokesperson Cat McRae disputed the vacancy data as reflecting 'outdated org charts and unfunded positions'; ProPublica confirmed its analysis had already excluded unfunded positions. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0472): the same vacancy dispute drew parallel, independent corroboration and a formal congressional response. A Reuters investigation published July 21, 2025 -- citing more than a dozen active and retired Forest Service employees -- reported that roughly 5,000 employees, about 15% of the agency's workforce, had left in the preceding five months, with retired USFS fire chief Riva Duncan describing firefighters "answering phones at the front desk, or cleaning toilets at campgrounds or mowing the lawn at administrative sites" due to short-staffing elsewhere in the agency. On August 14, 2025, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, sent Secretary Rollins a formal letter demanding "a detailed and comprehensive accounting of current staffing and staffing changes at the Forest Service, including firefighting jobs" since January 2025, citing a follow-up ProPublica report that described as much as 27% of firefighting roles as vacant as of July 17, 2025 -- the same underlying internal data already discussed above, expressed as a percentage rather than a raw count -- as directly contradicting the agency's public "fully staffed" claims. Days after that public dispute, a memo Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz sent to agency leadership -- obtained by High Country News -- stated plainly: 'As expected, the 2025 Fire Year is proving to be extremely challenging... we know the demand for resources outpaces their availability,' and directed that all red-carded employees, including IT and HR staff, be made available for fire assignments. At an internal spring planning meeting, one employee was told directly, 'Help is not on the way' -- a phrase the employee said they had 'never been told before' in their career. The agency subsequently took the unusual step of waiving a statutory 1,039-hour cap on seasonal-employee work hours (raising it to 1,560 hours) and asked 1,400 firefighting-qualified former employees to return; as of August 12, only 100 had accepted. Separately, USDA announced a reorganization eliminating the Forest Service's nine regional offices and consolidating them into five 'hub' locations, with Secretary Brooke Rollins acknowledging up to half of affected staff may not relocate. For the 2026 fire season, the Forest Service set a goal of 11,300 wildland firefighters onboard by mid-July and reported 11,816 onboard as of July 6, 2026 -- 104% of goal, which Chief Tom Schultz attributed to recent pay raises improving seasonal recruitment. This is a genuine, verifiable improvement on that specific metric, distinct from the broader permanent-workforce attrition: the agency has still lost close to 6,000 permanent staff (rangers, timber technicians, and others who also held fire-response 'red card' certifications) to layoffs, buyouts, and early retirement since January 2025, and outside observers (including Washington's public lands commissioner) warn this erodes surge capacity in a severe fire year even with seasonal hiring goals met. As of mid-July 2026, more than 17,000 personnel were assigned to 46 large, uncontained fires nationwide, with over 3.6 million acres burned for the year. Update 2026-07-26: the 2026 fire season's severity escalated further -- on July 18, 2026, the country reached 'Preparedness Level 5,' the highest level on the scale measuring how taxed wildfire resources are nationally, only the third time since 2010 that threshold has been reached this early in the season (after 2021 and 2024). This reinforces, rather than changes, the entry's existing point: seasonal hiring goals being met doesn't resolve the separate concern about permanent-staff attrition eroding surge capacity in a severe fire year. Update 2026-07-28: NPR reported that fire-prevention work itself, not just firefighter staffing, declined sharply in 2025 -- prescribed burning fell to about 900,000 acres, roughly half of the 1.6 million-plus acres burned in each of 2023 and 2024, and total vegetation-management work (which reduces the dense underbrush that fuels catastrophic fires) fell to 2.6 million acres in 2025 from more than 4 million acres in 2024, a decline of almost 1.5 million acres. This directly connects the staffing losses already documented in this entry to a concrete reduction in the preventive work meant to reduce wildfire severity, distinct from firefighting-response capacity alone. Update 2026-08-17: By mid-August 2026, the fire season had grown into one of the most severe on record -- more than 100 wildfires were burning across 15 states, with 6.4 million acres burned nationwide through August 12, the most for that date on record, and crews had responded to over 46,500 wildfires for the year. The Forest Service's elite interagency hotshot crews, reserved for the most difficult assignments, were down roughly 15% in available numbers. Frontline strain reached the point that Washington state requested National Guard personnel and 250 active-duty Army soldiers to supplement firefighting capacity, and the season produced 12 firefighter entrapments -- the highest year-to-date total since 2006. The administration's response has been to stand up a new U.S. Wildland Fire Service intended to consolidate operations across agencies, an efficiency bet not yet tested against a season this severe. USDA continues to maintain frontline firefighter numbers exceed prior administrations' levels; the separate, disputed permanent-staff attrition this entry documents (roughly 5,800-6,000 lost since January 2025 depending on source) remains the underlying strain outside observers point to.

primary_proponent.note: Publicly maintained the Forest Service was 'fully equipped and operationally ready to protect people and communities from wildfire' even as her own agency's Chief, Tom Schultz, was privately telling leadership the opposite in writing. A USDA spokesperson later attempted to reconcile the two statements by saying Schultz's memo referred to a broader pool of red-carded employees who could be 'called on to bolster' response as fire activity increases, while Rollins's statement referred only to full-time firefighters -- a real distinction, though one that doesn't fully resolve why the agency disputed the underlying vacancy data as inaccurate while its own Chief was independently describing a resource shortfall in nearly identical terms.

estimated_impact.summary: This is one of the more directly self-contradicting cases in this tracker: the dispute isn't primarily outside advocates versus the administration, but the Agriculture Secretary's public statements versus her own Forest Service Chief's internal, contemporaneous memo -- both documented, both on the record. Frontline accounts corroborate the operational strain described in Schultz's memo: a California Forest Service survey found 26% of engine captain positions and 42% of engineer positions vacant, and wildland firefighters described being assigned non-firefighting duties like trail-building and lawn-mowing due to short-staffing elsewhere in the agency.

title: Forest Service Plans to Close 57 of 77 Research Stations, Including a Key Pacific Northwest Wildfire Smoke Lab, Ahead of Fire Season
institution: U.S. Forest Service (USDA)
status: Ongoing -- closures announced and reported as proceeding as of June 2026, ahead of the 2026 Western fire season
date_of_action: 2026-03-31 (closure list announced) through 2026-08 (senators demand transparency ahead of an Aug. 19 response deadline)
what_changed: The Forest Service announced plans to close 57 of its 77 research stations across 31 states, merging remaining functions into a single organization headquartered in Fort Collins, Colorado, as part of a broader agencywide restructuring that also moves Forest Service headquarters from Washington, D.C. to Salt Lake City and replaces nine regional offices with 15 state-level offices. title: Internal Forest Service Report Found Trails Nationwide Being Abandoned, 'Unpassable Trails, Unsafe Bridges' After Staffing Purge
institution: U.S. Forest Service, Department of Agriculture
status: Ongoing -- December 2025 internal report documents 2025 conditions; a further FY2027 budget proposal would deepen the trail-funding cut going forward
date_of_action: 2025-12 (internal report completed) with a 2026-03 congressional follow-up and a 2026-04 forward-looking budget proposal
what_changed: An internal U.S. Forest Service Trail Program Status Report, completed in December 2025 after interviews with nearly 300 district-level staff across every Forest Service region and obtained by The Washington Post, found trails across the National Forest System's roughly 158,000-164,000-mile network being abandoned and rapidly deteriorating as staffing losses compound. Some ranger districts lost up to 100% of their dedicated trail crew staff during 2025, part of the agency's broader loss of nearly 6,000 employees to firings, resignations, and retirements documented separately in forest-service-firefighter-shortage-trump2.json (that entry covers the same staffing purge's impact on fire-response capacity; this entry covers its impact on recreation-trail infrastructure specifically). The report found the Forest Service maintained 22% fewer trail miles in 2025 than the prior year, with the share of trails meeting agency maintenance standards falling to its lowest level in 15 years, and stated plainly that 'lost skills are weakening the agency's ability to implement technical projects and oversee partner, volunteer, and contractor work,' producing 'unpassable trails, unsafe bridges, and negative environmental impacts.' One concrete documented safety consequence: the Madison Gulf Bridge, which carries the Appalachian Trail across the Peabody River in New Hampshire's Androscoggin Ranger District, was closed to pedestrian traffic after an inspection found it unsafe. In March 2026, Rep. Kim Schrier (D-WA) and Rep. Andrea Salinas (D-OR), joined by 21 House colleagues, sent a formal letter to Forest Service leadership demanding answers, writing that 'USFS trail maintenance operations have been hamstrung by layoffs, hiring restrictions, budget cuts and other policies that make it harder for staff to do their jobs and meet agency objectives' -- citing, among other local examples, the closure of the Denny Creek Trailhead in Washington's Enchantments area due to staffing shortages. Separately, the administration's April 2026 FY2027 budget request proposed cutting the Forest Service's dedicated trails line item specifically from $22 million to $8 million (a 64% reduction, per Washington Trails Association's analysis of the broader 31% cut to the agency's Recreation, Heritage and Wilderness account) -- a forward-looking proposal distinct from, but compounding, the staffing-driven 2025 maintenance decline this entry's internal report documents.

title: Pentagon's $1.2B Fort Bliss Migrant-Detention Camp Contract Went to a GOP Megadonor Whose Prior Company Pleaded Guilty to Hiring Undocumented Workers
institution: Department of Defense
status: Contract awarded and active as of this entry's last-verified date; no DOD Inspector General review, congressional inquiry, or named official identified in reporting as having personally approved the award
date_of_action: 2025-07 (contract announced)
what_changed: In July 2025, the Department of Defense announced a $1.2 billion contract to build a 5,000-bed migrant detention facility at Fort Bliss, Texas -- among the largest immigration-detention buildouts of the administration. The prime contractor is Virginia-based Acquisition Logistics, with subcontractors Disaster Management Group and Amentum. Disaster Management Group, whose portion of the work ProPublica estimated at 'hundreds of millions' of dollars, is co-owned and led as CEO by Nathan Albers, a self-described 'big-time Republican donor' who has contributed more than $150,000 to Republican campaigns in the year before the award, attended election-night 2024 festivities at Mar-a-Lago, and co-chaired a Trump National Golf Club fundraiser with Eric Trump. Albers previously co-owned TentLogix, a temporary-structures company that pleaded guilty in 2019 to a scheme to hire and conceal undocumented workers -- a 2016 audit had found 96 undocumented employees on its books, co-founder Gary Hendry (Albers's former brother-in-law) served time in prison, and the company forfeited more than $3 million before filing for bankruptcy in 2020. A Disaster Management spokesperson told ProPublica that Albers had been cleared in DHS's investigation of TentLogix and had parted ways with the company as a minority, non-operating owner once he learned of Hendry's conduct. Since 2020, Disaster Management Group has won more than $500 million in federal contracts, primarily for Afghan refugee housing, and only began federal lobbying in late 2024 -- spending $210,000 on immigration-related issues with no prior lobbying history -- shortly before securing the Fort Bliss subcontract. Neither the White House nor DOD identified which official approved or oversaw the award; the White House referred ProPublica's questions to DOD, which did not name a responsible official.

what_changed: In March 2025, the FTC removed approximately 300 blog posts from its website, most authored during Chair Lina Khan's tenure, covering AI, consumer protection, and the agency's lawsuits against tech companies including Amazon and Microsoft. On October 20, 2025, three additional AI-specific posts were found removed: 'AI and the Risk of Consumer Harm' (Jan. 3, 2025, warning of AI's potential for surveillance, fraud, and discrimination), 'Consumers Are Voicing Concerns About AI' (Oct. 2023), and 'On Open-Weights Foundation Models' (July 10, 2024, addressing open-source AI models). Reporting flagged the deletions as raising compliance concerns under the Federal Records Act (which requires agencies to preserve records documenting government activity) and the Open Government Data Act (which requires agencies to publish their data as open data by default).

title: FTC Cuts Workforce 10%, Loses Bipartisan Independence After Supreme Court Upholds Commissioner Firings
institution: Federal Trade Commission
status: Complete (workforce reduction implemented in 2025; commissioner-firing litigation permanently resolved by the Supreme Court on June 29, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-03-18 (commissioner firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling); staff reduction implemented through 2025
what_changed: On March 18, 2025, President Trump fired the FTC's two Democratic commissioners, Rebecca Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya, without citing any statutory cause, instead stating their continued service was 'inconsistent with my Administration's priorities.' This left the five-seat Commission with only its two sitting Republican members. Slaughter and Bedoya sued; Bedoya later resigned and dropped his claim, but Slaughter's case proceeded, with a district court initially ordering her reinstated. Separately, on May 15, 2025, Chairman Andrew Ferguson testified to Congress that the FTC was implementing a 10% workforce reduction, bringing headcount to approximately 1,100 employees (down from 1,221), the agency's lowest staffing level in a decade. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the FTC's for-cause removal protections for commissioners are unconstitutional, permanently allowing the president to remove commissioners at will and explicitly overruling the 1935 precedent Humphrey's Executor v. United States, which had protected the independence of the FTC and similar agencies for 90 years. Re-verified 2026-07-19: the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Chair Andrew Ferguson and Mark Meador) as of this update, with legal commentary noting little short-term incentive to restore a five-member bipartisan structure -- no material change to the entry's core claims. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Ferguson and Meador); no new nominations or structural changes identified since the prior update. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change -- the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Ferguson and Meador); no new nominations or structural changes identified since the prior update. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Ferguson and Meador); no new nominations, resignations, or structural changes identified since the prior update.

On the commissioner firings, the administration's position, upheld by the Supreme Court majority, is that the FTC 'unquestionably exercises executive power' and must therefore be fully accountable to the president; Chief Justice Roberts's majority opinion carved out a possible exception for the Federal Reserve. Critics, including Justice Sotomayor's dissent (joined by Kagan and Jackson) and former commissioner Slaughter, argue the ruling eliminates meaningful independence not just at the FTC but across the broader universe of agencies Congress designed to be insulated from single-party control, and that FTC policy will become more responsive to political and campaign considerations going forward. Legal scholars are split on how far the precedent extends beyond the FTC itself.

title: State Department Froze Fulbright/Gilman/Critical Language Funding; Entire Oversight Board Resigned Over Political Vetting of Recipients
institution: State Department -- Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs / Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board
status: Split status, corrected 2026-08-17: the funding question is resolved -- the FY2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act (P.L. 119-75) was signed into law February 3, 2026, enacting $273.4 million specifically for Fulbright ($667 million for State Department educational/cultural exchange programs overall), rejecting the administration's proposed near-total elimination. The political-vetting dispute and Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board vacancy remain unresolved -- no replacement board members had been named as of the State Department's own June 17, 2026 board page, more than a year after the June 2025 mass resignation.
date_of_action: 2025-02-13 (ECA funding pause begins) through 2025-06-12 (Fulbright board mass resignation)
what_changed: On February 13, 2025, the State Department's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (ECA) paused disbursements for its exchange programs -- including Fulbright, the Gilman International Scholarship, IDEAS, and the Critical Language Scholarship program -- initially described as a 15-day pause but extended well beyond that window, leaving over 10,000 students and professionals in active exchanges without stipends for housing, food, and travel, both in the U.S. and abroad; funding began to be restored in the following months. Separately, State Department officials led by Darren Beattie, Under Secretary for Public Diplomacy and Public Affairs, intervened to reject more than 20% of the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board's selected finalists for the 2025-2026 academic year -- a last-minute override the board called unauthorized -- and subjected an additional roughly 1,200 already-selected foreign recipients to a new, unauthorized ideological review process that could still result in their rejection, spanning fields from architecture and biology to medical science and music. On June 12, 2025, 11 of the board's 12 presidentially-appointed members resigned en masse, writing that the administration had 'injected politics and ideological mandates' into award decisions and that senior administration officials had refused to respond to the board's repeated legal objections, raised both verbally and in writing. Trump's FY2026 budget proposal separately sought to eliminate nearly all Fulbright funding; a July 2025 House committee draft instead included $287.8 million for the program, and the appropriations process ultimately resolved the same way -- Congress passed and Trump signed the FY2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act (P.L. 119-75) on February 3, 2026, enacting $273.4 million for Fulbright specifically (a modest trim from the July draft figure, still a $5 million cut to Title VI/Fulbright-Hays combined year over year) within $667 million for State Department educational/cultural exchange programs overall -- a $74 million (10%) reduction from FY2025 but a large restoration relative to the administration's request to all but eliminate the program. title: Fish and Wildlife Service Loses Over 1,500 Staff; Zero New Species Listed as Endangered
institution: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
status: Ongoing (staffing and budget cuts continue and a further round is proposed for FY2027; the zero-new-listings streak this entry was built around ended July 21, 2026, when FWS finalized endangered status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the term's first new listings after roughly 18 months at zero; 400+ species remain in the backlog)
date_of_action: 2025-01 to 2026-02 (staffing reductions); ongoing effects on listing backlog through the last-verified date
what_changed: Between January 2025 and February 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service saw a net reduction of 1,538 employees, according to Office of Personnel Management data compiled by the Congressional Research Service, with independent analyses from the Center for Biological Diversity estimating the cuts included more than 500 biologists specifically. The Interior Department separately proposed a FY2026 budget cutting the agency's Endangered Species Act listing-activity funding by 36% year-over-year, part of an overall reduction in FWS's average annual appropriations from roughly $1.94 billion (2017-2025 average) to approximately $1.6 billion for FY2026; the same budget proposed eliminating funding for the State and Tribal Wildlife Grant program entirely. The Service also discontinued its Refuge System Strategic Growth Policy and, according to conservation groups, has effectively stopped conducting the annual Florida panther population count last performed in 2015. As of reporting in April 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service had added zero new species to the federal endangered or threatened species list during Trump's second term, compared to 22 species added during the entirety of his first term, a gap the Center for Biological Diversity described as the longest period without a new listing decision since the Endangered Species Act was implemented. A backlog of more than 400 species remains pending final agency listing decisions. Recent Federal Register activity through mid-July 2026 continues the zero-new-listings pattern with specific examples: on June 16, 2026, FWS found listing 'not warranted' for two petitioned species (Sangre de Cristo peaclam, black-backed tanager); on July 14, 2026, FWS issued 90-day findings (a preliminary step, not a listing decision) for 10 more petitioned species including the Cascade red fox and plains spotted skunk; and on the same day, FWS rejected -- for the second time -- a petition to list long-tailed macaque monkeys. None of this recent activity constitutes an actual new listing, consistent with the entry's core finding. Separately, in June 2026 FWS announced a partnership with Colossal Biosciences to collect and cryopreserve cell/tissue samples from every species on the endangered list -- a genomic-preservation initiative distinct from, and not a substitute for, the listing process itself. CORRECTION 2026-07-26: on July 21, 2026, FWS finalized endangered-species status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the Florida Keys mole skink, Key ring-necked snake, and rim rock crowned snake -- effective August 20, 2026. These are the first new species listings of Trump's second term, ending the zero-listings streak that was this entry's central, headline finding; the listing process itself took 14 years from initial proposal to finalization, so this reflects the conclusion of a long-pending case rather than a change in the administration's overall listing pace. Separately, FWS finalized an Endangered Species Act regulatory change in July 2026 removing the 'blanket rule' option that had automatically extended full endangered-level protections to newly listed threatened species by default, a change conservation groups argue weakens protection for future threatened listings even as it doesn't affect already-endangered species like these three. The 400+ species backlog and FY2026 budget/staffing cuts already documented in this entry are unaffected by this correction and remain current. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no new species listings or budget/staffing changes identified beyond the July 21, 2026 Florida Keys listings (effective August 20, 2026) already documented above; the 400+ species backlog remains the entry's current standing figure. CORRECTION 2026-08-30: this entry's FY2026 budget/staffing figures were missing the agency's own forward-looking FY2027 budget request, submitted to Congress in April 2026 (predating this entry's original write-up but never previously incorporated). That request proposes cutting FWS's total discretionary funding a further 20% ($1.65 billion enacted FY2026 to a requested $1.33 billion for FY2027) and its total employee count a further 10% (6,513 to 5,861), on top of the 1,538-employee reduction already documented above, and would zero out discretionary funding entirely for five FWS accounts including the Cooperative Endangered Species Conservation Fund and the State and Tribal Wildlife Grant program (whose FY2026 elimination this entry already noted). Notably, in P.L. 119-74 (the enacted FY2026 Interior appropriations law), Congress directed FWS to maintain staffing levels sufficient to fulfill its statutory responsibilities -- a direct tension with the administration's own FY2027 staffing-cut proposal that CRS's analysis flags explicitly. No FY2027 appropriations had been enacted as of this recheck, and no new species listings were identified beyond the three Florida Keys reptiles already documented.

The Interior Department has simultaneously expanded hunting and fishing access at dozens of refuge sites during the same period, which it points to as evidence of continued investment in the Refuge System even amid budget reductions. Conservation groups and independent researchers, including an Oregon State University economist who studies Endangered Species Act effectiveness, counter that empirical research supports listing and dedicated recovery investment as effective tools for preventing extinction, and that delayed listings carry a real biological cost as at-risk populations continue to decline while awaiting review. The Center for Biological Diversity itself notes that staffing and budget reductions at FWS are 'consistent with what other Republican administrations have done,' while characterizing the scale of this administration's cuts as going significantly further.
