title: IMLS Dismantlement Permanently Blocked by Federal Court — A Rare Full Reversal
institution: Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS)
status: Reversed — federal court permanently blocked the dismantlement; agency fully restored via binding DOJ settlement
date_of_action: 2025-03-14 (executive order issued) through 2026-04-09 (binding settlement agreement finalized)
what_changed: On March 14, 2025, Trump issued Executive Order 14238 directing the elimination of IMLS -- the only federal agency dedicated to the nation's libraries and museums. The administration moved quickly: by March 31, all but 12 of the agency's roughly 70-75 employees were placed on administrative leave, with a reduction-in-force notice set for May 4; nearly all IMLS board members were dismissed; and beginning April 1, the agency's Acting Director (Keith Sonderling, who stated he would act 'in lockstep' with the administration) began terminating previously-awarded, congressionally-appropriated grants nationwide, including Grants to States, National Leadership Grants, and Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian grants. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0203): Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency was directly involved in the dismantlement's early days -- DOGE representatives visited IMLS's Washington offices alongside Sonderling on March 20, 2025, and on April 3, 2025, DOGE publicly congratulated Sonderling for 'cancelling $25M in wasteful DEI grants' from the roughly $180 million the Grants to States program (the largest single source of federal library funding, distributed by population-based formula) had awarded in FY24. The termination notices, which began going out to states including California, Connecticut, and Washington on April 3, 2025, had immediate on-the-ground effects: Maine's State Library issued layoff notices to 13 employees (about 30% of its staff) whose positions were funded through the grant, and temporarily closed; Mississippi libraries lost funding for services including Hoopla digital media access. IMLS's union estimated total grant terminations at well over a thousand nationwide. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog cluster c0703): a November 11, 2025 American Alliance of Museums survey found IMLS was the most commonly cited federal grantmaker (ahead of NEH and NEA) among museums reporting lost federal funding since Trump took office, with two-thirds of affected museums saying the lost funding had not been replaced -- see the museum-sector-wide survey findings in aam-survey-museum-funding-cuts-2025.json; the survey's publication predates the same month's court ruling and December reinstatement described below. Unlike most entries in this tracker, this story does not end in unreversed loss: the American Library Association and AFSCME sued (ALA v. Sonderling), and 21 state attorneys general separately sued in Rhode Island v. Trump. On May 1, 2025, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking further staff terminations. In November 2025, the U.S. District Court for Rhode Island ruled the dismantlement actions 'arbitrary and capricious and contrary to federal law,' and IMLS reinstated all previously terminated grants that December. On April 6, 2026, the administration withdrew its appeal of that ruling, and on April 9, 2026, ALA, AFSCME, and the Department of Justice signed a binding settlement agreement ensuring IMLS remains intact and continues its congressionally mandated work going forward -- closing the litigation with the agency fully restored, not merely paused.

This is the same official covered in this project's Cabinet-Level Legal Exposure tracker for a related action at the Department of Labor, where a federal court similarly blocked his agency's actions -- a recurring pattern across Sonderling's various acting-director roles during this period.

During the roughly 8-month period before reinstatement, real, documented harm occurred at the institutional level: the Dubuque Museum of Art in Iowa had already begun hiring and training staff against a $74,979 grant that was frozen: the Science Center of Iowa's planned internship program, backed by a $196,046 grant, was jeopardized. IMLS awarded $266 million in grants to museums and libraries in 2024, the baseline scale of funding that was disrupted before being restored.

title: Immigrant Student Enrollment Collapsed Nationwide Under Trump's Deportation Push, Straining School Budgets and Closing Newcomer Programs
institution: Local public school districts nationwide (Miami-Dade, Denver, Houston ISD, San Diego Unified, and others) -- driven by Department of Homeland Security immigration enforcement policy
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- reporting describes a multi-year (2023-2025) decline still in progress, not a single resolved event
date_of_action: 2023-2025 (reporting published November 2025)
what_changed: Public school districts across the U.S. reported sharp, multi-year drops in immigrant student enrollment, driven by deportations, families self-deporting, and a steep decline in new arrivals under the Trump administration's border and immigration-enforcement policies. Miami-Dade County Public Schools enrolled about 2,550 students from another country so far this school year -- down from nearly 14,000 last year and more than 20,000 the year before, per Miami-Dade School Board member Luisa Santos; the collective decline erased roughly $70 million from the district's annual budget. Denver Public Schools enrolled 400 new-to-country students this past summer, compared with 1,500 the previous summer. Houston Independent School District shuttered its Las Americas Newcomer School, dedicated to children new to the U.S., after its enrollment fell to 21 students from 111 the year before. At Perkins K-8 in San Diego, Principal Fernando Hernandez had not enrolled a single newcomer student this school year as of the reporting; the school separately serves a student body roughly one-third of whom experience homelessness. Superintendent Bart Reeves (Albertville City Schools) and Daniel Mojica (director of Chelsea's Parent Information Center) were also quoted describing the same pattern in their districts. A companion finding from a separate, independently-conducted survey published the same month (Physicians for Human Rights, Nov. 19, 2025; 691 health care workers across 30 states, surveyed March-August 2025) found 84% of respondents reported significant or moderate decreases in pediatric patient visits since the administration's January 2025 immigration executive orders -- indicating the same fear-driven withdrawal from public institutions documented in schools extends to health care access for immigrant families' children.

title: Surge in Immigration-Detention Habeas Corpus Cases Is Pulling Prosecutors Off Criminal Casework Nationwide

title: Trump Ordered U.S. Withdrawal From 66 International Organizations, Including the UN Population Fund and the Climate-Treaty Framework
institution: Executive Office of the President; U.S. Department of State
status: Ordered -- agencies directed to effectuate withdrawal 'as soon as possible'; implementation across 66 distinct bodies ongoing
date_of_action: 2026-01-07 (memorandum signed), following a review mandated by Executive Order 14199 (Feb. 4, 2025)
what_changed: On January 7, 2026, Trump signed a Presidential Memorandum, 'Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions, and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States,' directing U.S. withdrawal from 66 international bodies -- 35 non-UN organizations and 31 UN entities -- following a State Department review mandated by Executive Order 14199 (Feb. 4, 2025). The memorandum determined it 'contrary to the interests of the United States to remain a member of, participate in, or otherwise provide support to' the listed organizations and directed all executive departments and agencies to effectuate the withdrawals 'as soon as possible.' The list spans climate, population/health, gender, and multilateral-economic bodies: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC, the treaty underlying the Paris Agreement process) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the International Renewable Energy Agency and International Solar Alliance, the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), UN Women, the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, and multiple UN regional economic commissions, among others. The withdrawal formalizes, at the institutional/treaty level, funding cuts to some of these bodies that had already begun during 2025: UNFPA -- the main multilateral agency for sexual/reproductive health, maternal health, and gender-based-violence prevention in humanitarian settings -- lost its entire U.S. contribution (the U.S. was its largest single donor, $286 million in 2024, out of roughly $377 million in total 2025 funding suspended) during 2025, ahead of this formal January 2026 withdrawal. The UNFCCC secretariat, whose 2024-2025 operating budget was about $96.5 million (roughly 22% funded by the U.S., about $7.5 million in 2024), and the IPCC, which the U.S. supplied roughly 30% of historical voluntary contributions to (~$67 million cumulatively, though zero in 2025), both lose their largest historical funder. Philanthropist Michael Bloomberg separately pledged in January 2025 to have Bloomberg Philanthropies cover the UNFCCC's resulting funding gap, an early instance of private philanthropy substituting for withdrawn federal climate-diplomacy funding. Critics, including Nina Schwalbe of the Georgetown Center for Global Health Policy and Politics, called the withdrawal 'a ridiculous and dangerous, thoughtless and malicious action'; commentators argued it cedes U.S. influence over international climate, health, and economic-development norms to other powers as those bodies continue operating without U.S. participation. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0793): the same list also included two counterterrorism/violent-extremism-prevention bodies -- the Global Community Engagement and Resilience Fund (GCERF), which funds community-level extremism-prevention programs across dozens of countries, and the 30-nation Global Counterterrorism Forum (GCTF). Reuters reported GCERF's Geneva-based executive director, Dr. Khalid Koser, said the decision came as a surprise, without explanation, and reflects a deeper ideological shift away from multilateral, prevention-focused counterterrorism programs toward purely security-focused measures. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0811): on January 27, 2026, a separate, dedicated withdrawal process -- the U.S.'s exit from the Paris Agreement itself, distinct from the UNFCCC parent-treaty withdrawal above -- became formally effective, one year after Trump announced it via Executive Order 14162 on his first day in office (Jan. 20, 2025) and the required one-year notice period under the Agreement's own exit clause ran out. Per Harvard's Environmental and Energy Law Program tracker, this made the U.S. the only country to have withdrawn from the Paris Agreement twice (having also done so in Trump's first term before rejoining under Biden), leaving it grouped with Libya, Yemen, and Iran as the treaty's only non-signatories. Amnesty International warned the withdrawal risked triggering a global 'race to the bottom' on climate commitments.

title: Treasury Watchdog Finds ICE Didn't Meet Data-Safeguarding Standards Before Signing Taxpayer Data-Sharing Deal; Judge Separately Found 47,000 Unlawful Disclosures

title: Understaffed IRS's Technical 'Glitch' Left $51 Million in Political Donations Undisclosed, With No Fix Timeline
institution: Internal Revenue Service
status: Unresolved as of this entry's addition -- no fix timeline given
date_of_action: 2025-H2 (donations affected) through 2026-02 (error discovered) and 2026-03 (reported unresolved)
what_changed: The Center for Political Accountability (CPA), a campaign-finance watchdog, found that a technical error at the IRS left $51 million in political donations undisclosed for the second half of 2025, affecting major state-level election groups from both parties -- including the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Republican State Leadership Committee, and the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, whose combined missing disclosures totaled $41 million of the $51 million figure. CPA researchers discovered the discrepancy in February 2026, after the standard January 31 deadline for the prior year's donor and spending lists to become public had passed. As of The Guardian's March 2026 reporting, the IRS had given no clear timeline for fixing the error. The IRS began 2025 with about 102,000 employees and finished the year with roughly 74,000 -- a reduction of about 28,000, or 27%, following a series of firings and layoffs driven by DOGE (documented in more detail in this tracker's irs-workforce-collapse-trump2.json entry) -- which The Guardian's reporting connects to the agency's reduced capacity to identify and fix the disclosure error.

title: IRS Lost 27% of Its Workforce and a Third of Its Auditors — Independent Watchdogs Project $600B in Lost Revenue
institution: Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
status: Ongoing (2026 filing season completed under reduced staff; FY2027 budget request proposes a further ~4,800-employee cut, concentrated almost entirely in enforcement)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial probationary firings) through 2026-04 (most recent GAO/TIGTA reporting)
what_changed: Beginning February 2025, the IRS workforce was cut by approximately 27%, falling from roughly 102,000 employees in January 2025 to about 74,000 by December 2025 -- a reduction of nearly 28,000 people, primarily via probationary-employee terminations (~7,300), deferred-resignation buyouts (~4,700), and further attrition. The cuts were not evenly distributed: Taxpayer Services (which processes returns, answers phones, and handles correspondence) lost about 21-22% of its staff; the agency's IT function lost 27%; and revenue agents -- the specialists who conduct complex audits of high-income individuals, partnerships, and large corporations -- lost roughly 3,600 people, about 31% of the entire auditing workforce. Within the IT-function losses, one dramatic episode stands out: on March 31, 2025, roughly 50 senior IT executives -- most at the Senior Executive Service level, largely associate chief information officers with expertise spanning cybersecurity, modernization, applications, contracts, networks, and data-center operations -- were placed on administrative leave and had their system access cut off immediately, in the middle of tax-filing season. The decision was made by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency and carried out by then-acting IRS Commissioner Melanie Krause; CNN reported the sidelined officials were seen internally as possible 'blockers' to a separate, controversial push to share IRS taxpayer data with immigration enforcement authorities. The IRS's chief information officer, Rajiv Uppal, and chief technology officer, Kaschit Pandya, were not among those dismissed. Of the roughly 50, 26 eventually departed via Treasury's deferred-resignation offer, while the other 22 remained on administrative leave. Uppal himself resigned two weeks later regardless: on April 14, 2025 -- the eve of the April 15 tax-filing deadline -- he told staff by email he would depart effective April 28, 2025, with Pandya, who had already been working closely with DOGE and assumed many CIO responsibilities, serving as acting CIO. Former IRS officials and governance experts warned the leadership churn and uncertainty, arriving at the height of filing season, risked disrupting tax-revenue collection itself. The cuts extended to physical infrastructure as well as headcount: in late February 2025, the General Services Administration sent the IRS a letter proposing to terminate or not renew leases on more than 110 (some reporting says up to 120) Taxpayer Assistance Centers -- the walk-in offices where taxpayers get in-person help with identity theft, audits, and other complex issues -- right at the height of tax-filing season. After pushback from taxpayers, tax professionals, and lawmakers, the IRS agreed to keep TAC offices open through the 2025 filing season, but the closures resumed afterward: by September 2025 the IRS confirmed it would close nine specific centers across six states (Pennsylvania, Iowa, New York, Kentucky, California, and West Virginia), effective November 30, 2025. Congress separately cut the IRS enforcement budget by 8% for FY2026 (the lowest inflation-adjusted level since 1988) and cut $1.1 billion (12%) from the IRS's base budget overall, rescinding most of the remaining Inflation Reduction Act funding that had been allocated to rebuild the agency; the base budget is now about 40% below its 2010 level after inflation. The IRS responded by lowering its own phone-service target from 85% to 70% of calls answered, and an independent analysis by the Center for Taxpayer Rights found call wait times on the main line increased more than 70% between February 2025 and February 2026. A March 2026 GAO audit found the IRS's staffing reductions 'were not targeted or strategic' and that the agency still lacks an updated strategic workforce plan. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0476): a TIGTA report, reported by FedScoop around July 26, 2025, gave an earlier (May 2025) snapshot with division-level breakdowns not otherwise named in this entry: as of May 2025 the IRS had already fallen from ~103,000 to 77,428 staff (a 25% loss), with the Small Business/Self-Employed division down 35%, Human Capital down 28%, and Tax Exempt and Government Entities down 25% -- distinct divisions from the Taxpayer Services, IT, and revenue-agent breakdowns already documented above from the later year-end data. The same report found nearly 300 employees had been separated via formal reduction-in-force actions specifically, as distinct from the far larger numbers who left via deferred resignation or retirement. Notably, IRS Commissioner Frank Bisignano simultaneously serves as the Senate-confirmed Commissioner of the Social Security Administration -- see the related SSA entry in this tracker -- splitting his attention across both agencies during this period. The IRS's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, seeks $9.8 billion in discretionary funding, down $1.4 billion from the $11.2 billion Congress enacted for FY2026, and proposes eliminating roughly 4,800 more positions (about 17% of remaining staff) on top of the 27% already lost in 2025. Nearly all of the proposed staffing reduction falls on enforcement -- examinations and collections -- which would see an 18% budget cut, while taxpayer-service funding would see a small 3% increase. The IRS's own budget documents describe the enforcement-side cuts as yielding roughly $778 million in savings once implemented. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- the FY2027 budget request remains a proposal, not enacted; no new congressional action identified since the prior update. Re-verified 2026-08-05: despite Bisignano's 'less people and better results' framing, internal documents reported by NOTUS show the IRS has been rushing to backfill critical staffing gaps, hiring roughly 2,000 employees as of January 2026 -- a partial rehire that still leaves the agency at a net ~28% workforce reduction from its January 2025 level, and that reporting characterizes as evidence of operational strain the agency's public statements had downplayed. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0132): the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) -- the statutorily independent office within the IRS, quoted throughout this entry, that helps individual taxpayers resolve problems and reports directly to Congress -- was itself targeted for a roughly 25% staff cut, losing 430 of its approximately 1,900 employees in an initial phase of reductions reported in March 2025, on top of more than 90 TAS employees who had already left via deferred resignation or earlier layoffs. Former National Taxpayer Advocate Nina Olson (2001-2019) said the cuts 'will have devastating consequences to the taxpayers that are in need of help.' The reduction directly shrank the capacity of the same watchdog office whose independent reporting on IRS-wide staffing and filing-season risk is cited elsewhere in this entry. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, clusters c0134/c0136): internal IRS emails reveal that senior IRS lawyer Joseph Rillotta warned agency officials in February 2025 that citing 'poor performance' as the justification for the roughly 7,000 probationary terminations that month was false -- no performance assessments had been conducted -- and amounted to fraud; the warning went unheeded, and termination letters citing performance issues went out February 20, 2025. Judge Alsup, ruling on the multi-agency probationary-firings case that also covered Treasury (the IRS's parent department), found in his March 13, 2025 preliminary injunction that the stated justification was 'a lie' and ordered reinstatement; the Supreme Court stayed that reinstatement order on April 8, 2025 on standing grounds, without addressing the merits of the fraud finding, and separate litigation -- including a California case alleging one of the largest employment-fraud schemes in U.S. history -- remained pending as of the reporting reviewed. In the interim, employees who had been reinstated under the since-stayed order were left in administrative limbo: CNN reported in May 2025 that reinstated IRS staff faced lapsed health insurance, unprocessed pension paperwork, and denied workers'-compensation claims amid a decimated HR function, with some describing emergency-room bills and delayed cancer screenings during the gap. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0200): one office was singled out early and disproportionately. When the RIF wave began in early April 2025, the IRS's Office of Civil Rights and Compliance -- which investigates discrimination complaints and audits/investigations bias -- was cut far more severely than the agency-wide rate: nearly 80% of its roughly 176 employees received RIF notices (a 75% net reduction), well above the agency-wide 27% rate documented above, with the remaining staff folded into the Office of Chief Counsel. Fox News, Government Executive, and CPA Practice Advisor all reported the office as an early, specific RIF target rather than swept up incidentally in the broader cuts. In August 2025, IRS Commissioner Billy Long told the office's employees the RIF notices were being reversed, with a memo stating the action served as 'cancellation of your prior RIF notice of separation' -- a reversal Federal News Network reported was specific to this office, not the broader workforce reduction documented above. Real-correction update 2026-08-18: this entry's prior rechecks (through 2026-08-13) described the FY2027 budget request's proposed further cuts as 'a proposal, not enacted,' without noting that the House Appropriations Committee had already voted to advance it, months earlier. On April 24, 2026, the House Appropriations Committee approved the FY2027 Financial Services and General Government funding bill in a 34-28 vote, setting IRS funding at $10.2 billion -- higher than the administration's own $9.8 billion request but still roughly 8.5% below the $11.2 billion FY2026 enacted level, with close to $1.4 billion of the reduction concentrated in enforcement. An amendment offered by FSGG Subcommittee Ranking Member Steny Hoyer (D-MD) that would have restored $1.8 billion to enforcement funding failed. The bill has not yet passed the full House or been taken up by the Senate as of this update, so it remains short of enactment -- but a committee-level vote already exists, which is a materially different posture than 'a proposal' alone, and this entry's five prior re-verification passes (2026-07-20 through 2026-08-13) did not catch it despite the vote predating all but the first of those. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0773): heading into the 2026 filing season, the agency had cycled through seven different commissioners or acting commissioners over the course of 2025 alone -- an unprecedented churn rate Brookings separately described as historically unmatched. One of those seven, Gary Shapley -- a Musk- and congressional-Republican-backed IRS Criminal Investigation official -- was installed as acting commissioner April 15, 2025 while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was traveling abroad, then removed just three days later, on April 18, after Bessent objected to not being consulted on the appointment and complained directly to Trump; Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender was named acting commissioner in his place, and Shapley remained at IRS Criminal Investigation. Bessent said 'trust must be brought back to the IRS,' framing Faulkender's installation as a corrective. On January 2, 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Sen. Angus King led 15 senators in a letter to Treasury Secretary/Acting IRS Commissioner Scott Bessent and IRS Chief of Taxpayer Services Ken Corbin warning the agency was not ready for the upcoming filing season given the combination of that leadership churn, the workforce cuts already documented above, and the tax-law changes the agency had to implement simultaneously. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0640): the furlough action itself, which the c0241 back-pay item below references but this entry had not yet described -- on October 8, 2025, as the shutdown entered its second week, the IRS furloughed more than 34,000 employees, 46% of its remaining staff, leaving about 39,870 employees (53.6%) on the job. The furlough suspended most taxpayer services, including phone assistance and the statutorily independent Taxpayer Advocate Service, while retained staff focused on the 2025 filing season and implementing the administration's tax law; audits and collections activity also halted. The IRS had announced September 29 that furloughs would begin if the shutdown exceeded five business days. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0241): during the Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown, the IRS rescinded its prior promise to guarantee full back pay to its furloughed workers, citing new guidance from Russell Vought's OMB. The reversal followed an OMB draft legal opinion questioning the legality of automatic back pay for furloughed employees -- despite a 2019 law Trump himself signed into effect requiring it -- and came on the heels of Trump's own public threat, the same month, to withhold pay from federal workers he said 'don't deserve' it. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0250): CNBC reported April 17, 2025 that the staffing losses were already producing concrete, named case-level consequences for wealthy-taxpayer enforcement: one IRS agent described three 'enterprise' cases -- two involving business partnerships and one involving a wealthy sports team owner, together representing millions of dollars in potential additional tax -- that were dropped for lack of staff to continue them when he departed. A subsequent Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) report, covered by CBS News and Yahoo Finance in 2026, confirmed the pattern with agency-wide, post-hoc FY2025 outcome data distinct from the modeled $600B Yale Budget Lab projection above: after losing about 30% of its auditors, the IRS opened roughly 43,000 examinations of taxpayers earning over $400,000 in FY2025, down 26% from the prior year; the Global High Wealth program (auditing the wealthiest taxpayers) had 27% fewer employees as of January 2026 than before the FY2025 cuts; audits of new business partnerships fell 30%; and audit revenue collected fell 35%, or about $3.5 billion, in FY2025 -- a real, watchdog-confirmed dollar figure of enforcement revenue actually lost, not merely a future projection.

primary_proponent.name: Frank Bisignano
primary_proponent.role: IRS Chief Executive Officer / Commissioner (concurrently SSA Commissioner)
primary_proponent.note: Publicly defended the cuts before the Senate Finance Committee, stating the agency can achieve 'less people and better results,' and that the IRS cut phone-center 'idle time' by nearly 50%. Committee Democrats, led by Ranking Member Ron Wyden, disputed this characterization directly in the same hearing. Bisignano told senators he treats running both SSA and IRS as managing 'two large organizations,' sometimes working 14-hour days across both.

estimated_impact.summary: The Yale Budget Lab modeled the specific 2025 staffing reductions (broken down by IRS operating function, using the agency's own budget-activity categories) and projected the cuts will reduce federal revenue collection by almost $600 billion over the 2026-2035 window -- a striking figure since the IRS collects 96% of all federal revenue, meaning even modest enforcement-capacity losses compound into large fiscal effects. The National Taxpayer Advocate (an independent office within the IRS that reports directly to Congress) has been notably even-handed in its assessments -- praising the 2025 filing season as one of the most successful in recent memory, while explicitly warning that the more severe 2026 season risks are now 'markedly different' given the compounding effect of workforce loss, budget cuts, and simultaneous major tax-law changes from the 2025 reconciliation bill.

title: LIHEAP Heating Assistance Program Staff Eliminated, Funding Delayed for Millions

what_changed: In April 2025, the Trump administration fired the entire federal staff team responsible for administering LIHEAP -- the ~$4.1 billion program that helps roughly 6 million low-income households pay heating and cooling bills, serving all 50 states, D.C., U.S. territories, and federally recognized tribes. Six months later, when the October-November 2025 government shutdown (the longest in U.S. history at 43 days) hit, LIHEAP's annual funding allocation -- normally distributed to states by early November -- was delayed with no dedicated federal staff left to expedite the process once Congress acted. The $3.6 billion in delayed funding was finally released to states on November 28, 2025, over two weeks after the shutdown ended (Nov. 12) and roughly a month later than the program's normal early-November distribution. Trump's FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026 and documented in more detail elsewhere in this tracker (trump-fy2027-budget-defense-tradeoff-2026.json), again proposed eliminating LIHEAP entirely, even as utility costs continued to rise and the program retained bipartisan congressional support.

title: DOGE Moved to Eliminate Nearly All Staff at the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a Bush-Era Foreign Aid Agency
institution: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
status: Partially reversed -- MCC survived as an agency after congressional/outside pushback, but more than half its programs were slated for cancellation and its workforce was sharply reduced; a leaner, more geopolitically-focused agency emerged rather than the full shutdown DOGE initially ordered
date_of_action: 2025-04-23 (DOGE staff briefing) through 2025-08 (agency confirmed surviving with a reduced portfolio)
what_changed: In late April 2025, Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) informed Millennium Challenge Corporation leadership that the agency's programs would be closed and its staff minimized, with employees told in an internal meeting that the workforce-reduction plan called for eliminating all employees except the agency's acting CEO -- a position MCC is statutorily required to maintain. Staff were told they could be placed on administrative leave as soon as May 5, 2025, roughly a week after DOGE first arrived at the agency. MCC, created by Congress in 2004 under President George W. Bush, provides time-limited grants to developing countries -- including Ukraine, El Salvador, and Nepal -- conditioned on governance and policy reforms, distinguishing it structurally from USAID (tracked separately in this database) even though both are independent foreign-aid agencies targeted by the same DOGE-driven downsizing campaign. Senate Foreign Relations Committee Ranking Member Jeanne Shaheen and House Foreign Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gregory Meeks both issued statements condemning the move. Following that pushback, the shutdown plan did not fully proceed: reporting from August 2025 found MCC would survive as an agency, but more than half of its existing programs were slated for cancellation, and the agency's own public statements said its 'resulting portfolio will clearly align with the Trump Administration's America First foreign policy.' MCC's inaugural Trump-era CEO, Sean Cairncross, departed after roughly four months in the role, with coverage describing his brief tenure as focused on executing the downsizing before moving to a different administration post. By FY2026, MCC's own figures show it planning to award $287.3 million in new contracts against an annual budget of $830 million -- a functioning but substantially narrowed agency compared to its pre-2025 scope.

title: 446 Hospitals Across 44 States Found at High Risk of Closing or Cutting Services Because of Republican Medicaid Cuts
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services / hospitals nationwide reliant on Medicaid funding
status: Ongoing -- risk assessment based on funding changes already enacted (OBBBA) and being implemented (work-requirements rule documented separately in this tracker). Updated 2026-08-17: several individually-named hospitals disputed the risk analysis's methodology as applied to them, and separately, confirmed maternity/OB service closures at specific hospitals since publication show the risk has begun materializing in at least some cases, not just as a projection. Updated 2026-08-30: Public Citizen's own report adds concrete scale figures (beds, patients, workers, and a decade-scale dollar figure) not previously in this entry, and confirms -- with its own breakdown of the full 446-hospital set, not just the smaller Harvard subset already cited -- that the risk skews urban: 267 of 446 (60%) are in urban areas.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OBBBA Medicaid funding provisions signed into law) through 2026-04 (hospital risk analysis published)
what_changed: Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit ec8078a, which marked these 3 records folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): the hospital-closure risk this entry documents was reported in concrete, specific terms within days of OBBBA's July 4, 2025 enactment, well before the November 2025 Harvard analysis below quantified it systematically. The Guardian reported July 4, 2025 that the law's roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts threatened healthcare access for 17 million Americans, with rural areas in Kentucky, Arizona, and Idaho facing hospital shutdowns, job losses, and collapsing health programs as automatic cuts triggered in states including North Carolina. AP reported the same week that over 300 rural hospitals were at risk of closure, with hospitals in Nebraska and Kentucky warning they might shut down or reduce services despite remaining lifelines in remote areas. The New York Times reported July 6, 2025 that the cuts specifically threatened North Carolina's Medicaid expansion and plans to reopen a rural hospital in Martin County, with over 660,000 low-income North Carolina residents at risk of losing coverage as the law's work requirements and funding cuts took effect. An earlier analysis, published November 17, 2025 by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health's Healthcare Quality and Outcomes Lab (researchers Jose Figueroa and Thomas Tsai) in collaboration with the New York Times, examined data on more than 4,400 U.S. hospitals from the American Hospital Association, Medicare's Healthcare Cost Report Information System, AHRQ, and the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, and identified 109 hospitals -- those serving 25%+ Medicaid patients, financially distressed, and already caring for vulnerable populations -- as facing the greatest risk from OBBBA's Medicaid cuts. 85% of those 109 highest-risk hospitals are in urban areas, and are therefore ineligible for the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund OBBBA created to cushion rural hospitals from the same cuts; the researchers noted these urban safety-net hospitals disproportionately serve low-income and racial-minority patient populations. A new analysis, published by Public Citizen on March 31, 2026 (identified by name via HFMA's follow-up reporting; the original entry cited it only as 'an analysis' via NBC News's coverage), found that 446 hospitals across 44 states and Washington, D.C. are at high risk of closing or cutting services as a result of Medicaid funding reductions enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), the same law whose work-requirements provisions are documented separately in this tracker (medicaid-work-requirements-cms-rule-2026.json). Public Citizen's methodology flagged hospitals with a 20%+ Medicaid payer mix and negative net margins over 2022-2024. Many of the at-risk hospitals already operate at a financial loss and rely heavily on Medicaid reimbursement to remain viable; NBC News reported the cuts put jobs, maternity care, mental health services, and general local access to treatment at risk in the affected communities, particularly in rural and underserved areas where Medicaid patients make up an outsized share of hospital revenue. Trump himself connected these funding pressures directly to military spending priorities: speaking at a private White House Easter luncheon in April 2026, NBC News reported he said the federal government could not fund Medicaid, Medicare, and child care because military spending had to come first, arguing those responsibilities should shift to the states. At least four individually-named hospitals on or near the flagged list publicly disputed the risk assessment as applied to them, per HFMA's follow-up reporting: Northwest Mississippi Regional Medical Center's CEO said the analysis's 2022-2024 data window captured a temporary financial disruption from the hospital's May 2023 reacquisition by the county, not its actual trajectory; Minden Medical Center (Louisiana) said flatly it was not at risk of closing; Welch Community Hospital (West Virginia) said the analysis ignored that it is a state-operated facility funded by legislative appropriations rather than exposed to the federal Medicaid cuts the same way; and Metropolitan Hospital Center (NYC Health + Hospitals) pointed to record patient-care revenue and staff expansion as evidence it was securely positioned rather than at risk. None of these four rebuttals were independently adjudicated in sourcing reviewed -- they are hospital self-assessments, not a third-party re-analysis -- but they are documented here for balance given the risk analysis is itself already presented as a projection rather than a confirmed count. Separately, since the risk analysis's publication, at least three hospitals have confirmed actual Medicaid-cuts-linked service closures rather than projected risk: St. Mary's Sacred Heart Hospital (Lavonia, GA) closed its labor-and-delivery unit and OB/GYN center in fall 2025; Centra Southside Community Hospital (Farmville, VA) closed labor-and-delivery and OB/GYN surgical services; and Greene County General Hospital (Linton, IN) ended obstetrics services in January 2026. A broader 2026 rural-hospital report (Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform) found 139 rural hospitals have closed labor-and-delivery units since 2020 (a 13% drop nationally), with OBBBA's Medicaid cuts cited as an accelerating pressure on top of pre-existing rural obstetric-unit attrition, not the sole cause -- the report does not attribute the full 139-hospital figure to OBBBA specifically, and this entry does not either. Additional detail from Public Citizen's own report, not previously broken out in this entry: the 446 at-risk hospitals collectively operate 68,986 beds, served approximately 6.6 million patients in 2024, and employ approximately 275,458 direct patient-care workers; 267 of the 446 (60%) are in urban areas, and five states -- Connecticut (36%), California (31%), New York (31%), Massachusetts, and Washington -- each have more than a quarter of their hospitals on the at-risk list. Public Citizen frames the underlying cause as OBBBA's roughly $1 trillion reduction in federal Medicaid funding over the next decade. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0317), filling in earlier antecedent detail predating even the July 2025 enactment-week reporting already documented above: on May 8, 2025 -- while the House/Senate bill was still being negotiated -- NPR/KFF Health News profiled Spencer Hospital in Iowa, one of the few remaining rural hospitals still operating an inpatient psychiatric unit, whose CEO Brenda Tiefenthaler said she intended to keep the 14-bed unit open despite it losing about $2 million a year against the hospital's roughly $120 million total budget; 40% of the unit's patients are covered by Medicaid, versus about 12% of the hospital's inpatients overall, illustrating concretely how disproportionately Medicaid-dependent specialty units like inpatient psychiatric care are exposed to the cuts this entry documents. On June 13, 2025, before the bill's final text was set, Reuters reported the pending Senate proposal contained an estimated $785 billion in Medicaid cuts over 10 years -- a figure that grew to the roughly $1 trillion decade-scale cut in the law as actually enacted July 4, 2025. A concrete state-level example: the Kentucky Hospital Association estimated the state could lose $11-12.3 billion in federal Medicaid funding -- nearly $5 billion more than the next-highest state -- putting 35 hospitals, mostly rural, at risk of closure and threatening coverage for roughly 200,000 Kentucky residents; Gov. Andy Beshear said the law effectively reduces Kentucky's Medicaid reimbursement system to standard Medicare rates, among the lowest in the country, and warned it would force women in affected areas to travel hours for maternity care. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0424), two more antecedent reports from the same OBBBA-enactment-week and immediate-aftermath window already documented above, this time centered on children specifically rather than hospitals as institutions. CBS News reported July 1, 2025 -- while the bill was still before Congress -- on six-year-old Kennedy Beaver of North Carolina, who has Noonan syndrome and relies on Medicaid, including the state's CAP/C (Community Alternatives Program for Children) waiver, to access care for medically fragile children; her family said they would have to ration her treatment if the proposed cuts passed. North Carolina officials warned at the time that 600,000 state residents could lose coverage -- a figure in the same range as, but from an earlier and separately-sourced estimate than, the 660,000-North-Carolinian figure NYT reported July 6, 2025 and already cited above; both describe the same state-level exposure rather than two different cuts. Separately, NPR reported September 9, 2025 that OBBBA cuts Medicaid by nearly $900 billion over a decade -- a figure in the same order of magnitude as, but sourced independently of, Public Citizen's later ~$1 trillion decade-scale estimate already cited above -- and that children's hospitals are among the hardest-hit, with Phoenix Children's Hospital warning it stood to lose hundreds of millions of dollars annually, jeopardizing clinics, mental health staffing, and child-abuse screening programs that rely on supplemental Medicaid payments. NPR noted children make up nearly half of all Medicaid enrollees nationally. Neither report was previously represented in this entry, which until now documented rural, urban safety-net, and psychiatric-unit exposure but not pediatric-specific hospital systems or a named medically-fragile-child case.

title: House GOP's Medicaid Provider-Tax Cap Threatened Nursing-Home Funding -- Final OBBBA Carved Out an Exemption, But Broader Cuts Still Risk Long-Term Care Access
institution: U.S. House of Representatives / Congress (OBBBA reconciliation legislation)
status: Enacted (OBBBA signed July 4, 2025) -- nursing-home-specific provider-tax and staffing-mandate carve-outs secured during House-to-Senate negotiation, while the law's broader ~$900B-$1T Medicaid cuts proceed
date_of_action: 2025-05-12 (Washington Post reports the House GOP provider-tax proposal) through 2025-07-04 (OBBBA signed, final provider-tax/staffing-mandate terms confirmed)
what_changed: The Washington Post reported May 12, 2025 that House Republicans were pushing to limit states' Medicaid "provider tax" -- a financing mechanism nearly every state uses to draw down additional federal matching funds, which states then use in part to help pay for long-term care -- warning the change could drastically reduce Medicaid funding for nursing homes, which cover more than 60% of nursing-home stays nationally. The House passed its version of the reconciliation bill May 22, 2025 along party lines, including the provider-tax limits as part of what CNN and Healthcare Dive reported as roughly $700-900 billion in Medicaid cuts over ten years; nursing-home operators publicly said they were bracing for steep losses as the bill moved to the Senate. During Senate negotiation, the nursing-home and long-term-care industry secured two specific carve-outs relative to the original House proposal: the bill's new provider-tax caps -- which phase most providers' allowable rate down from 6% to 3.5% in Medicaid-expansion states by fiscal year 2032 -- exempted nursing homes and intermediate care facilities specifically, freezing their rates at the current safe-harbor level (up to 6%) rather than phasing them down; and a separate, unrelated Biden-era CMS rule setting federal minimum nursing-home staffing levels was delayed by 10 years. The Senate-passed version, with these nursing-home-specific provisions intact, cleared the House largely unchanged and was signed into law as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) on July 4, 2025. Despite the industry-specific carve-outs, health-policy analysts (Commonwealth Fund, Penn LDI) warned the law's broader Medicaid reductions -- eligibility/work-requirement changes and other funding cuts documented separately in this tracker's medicaid-work-requirements-cms-rule-2026.json and medicaid-hospital-closure-risk-2026.json entries -- still threaten long-term-care quality and access, since nursing-home Medicaid revenue depends on the overall program's health, not the provider-tax mechanism alone; one nursing-home industry leader was quoted calling the carve-outs "band-aids" that would "soon prove ill-equipped to stop OBBB's damage."

primary_proponent.note: The provider-tax cap and staffing-mandate delay were negotiated into the reconciliation bill's Medicaid title between the May 2025 House passage and the Senate's version; Trump signed the final law July 4, 2025. Sourcing reviewed did not identify a single named member of Congress as personally responsible for the nursing-home-specific carve-outs specifically, as distinct from the bill's Medicaid title generally.

estimated_impact.summary: The carve-outs mean nursing homes avoided the more severe, industry-specific funding threat initially proposed in May 2025, but analysts warn the underlying $900 billion-plus, decade-long Medicaid reduction the OBBBA still enacts leaves long-term-care access and quality exposed through other channels (eligibility redeterminations, state budget pressure, and the broader funding cuts documented in this tracker's related entries).

title: CMS Narrows Medical Frailty Exemption Beyond Statute in Medicaid Work-Requirement Rule -- Cancer and HIV Patients Left Unexempted
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: In effect -- interim final rule published June 1, 2026; national enforcement deadline January 1, 2027; several states (Nebraska, Montana, Arkansas) already implementing ahead of that deadline; public comment period on the rule remains open
date_of_action: 2026-06-01 (CMS interim final rule published)
what_changed:
Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit 99d1af6, which marked these records folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): The work-requirement provision that CMS's June 2026 rule ultimately implements has a documented 2025 legislative history directly relevant to this entry's exemption-narrowing question. CBO's first score of a House GOP Medicaid overhaul, in May 2025, estimated 10.3 million people losing coverage by 2034 (7.6 million becoming uninsured), with savings of roughly $625 billion tied to work requirements, citizenship-status restrictions, and eligibility-rule rollbacks (The Hill, May 14, 2025). The House passed its version on May 22, 2025, setting the 80-hours-per-month work/education/training/volunteer-service threshold that CMS's 2026 rule later enforces nationwide for childless adults; CBO estimated 7.6 million people would lose coverage under that House text, with roughly $280 billion in resulting savings redirected toward other tax provisions in the bill (New York Times, May 22, 2025). By August 31, 2025, reporting on the enacted law (which cut a reported $911 billion from Medicaid) noted that HHS -- the CMS's parent department, then led by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- had been given broad statutory discretion to define who qualifies as 'medically frail' for exemption purposes (Mother Jones, Aug. 31, 2025); this is the same statutory exemption category CMS's June 2026 interim final rule narrowed with its added functional-capacity threshold, the core subject of this entry. Reporting the same week the law's work-requirement provision passed also warned that it echoed earlier, smaller-scale state work-requirement pilots in Georgia and Arkansas, where thousands of otherwise-eligible people -- including caregivers, gig workers, and students -- lost coverage due to confusing reporting rules and administrative red tape rather than actual failure to work (NBC News, July 5, 2025), directly foreshadowing the bureaucratic-mechanism critique in this entry's estimated-impact section. A November 2025 New York Times explainer published ahead of the rule's implementation likewise projected the requirement would cut coverage for 'nearly five million people' -- matching the CBO figure cited above -- and specifically noted that most people expected to lose coverage were already working or otherwise exempt, but would be cut off due to reporting/paperwork failures, while states would face costly new compliance and verification systems to administer the requirement (New York Times, Nov. 3, 2025).

Added 2026-09-09 (brief context; these describe OBBBA's Medicaid provisions and fiscal impact as a whole rather than the work-requirement/medical-frailty mechanism this entry specifically documents, so are noted briefly as backdrop rather than given full treatment): as the bill moved from the House to a harsher Senate rewrite in June 2025 and on to signature, CBO's estimates of the bill's overall scope grew -- from the House-stage figures above up to roughly $1.1 trillion in Medicaid cuts and 11.8 million people losing coverage under the Senate's June 2025 text (New York Times, June 29, 2025), a claimed $1 trillion-plus in cuts with ACA subsidies also ending that the Washington Post reported could leave at least 17 million Americans without coverage across both programs (July 1, 2025), and a final overall CBO deficit estimate near $3.4 trillion through 2034 with 10 million more people uninsured (Associated Press, July 21, 2025). A separate CBO distributional analysis published in August 2025 found the law would cost the poorest 10% of Americans roughly $1,200/year in net resources while the richest 10% gained roughly $13,600/year, and that about 2.4 million people would lose SNAP food-assistance benefits (NBC News, Aug. 12, 2025). Other coverage flagged risk to home- and community-based Medicaid services relied on by an estimated 4.5 million disabled Americans despite administration assurances those services would not be cut (New York Times, July 21, 2025); an administration David Sacks acknowledged the bill's Medicaid cuts totaled roughly $880 billion at a point when other messaging described the cuts as targeting 'fraud' only (Rolling Stone, May 27, 2025); and the administration's separately proposed FY2026 budget -- a distinct legislative vehicle from the reconciliation bill that became OBBBA -- separately proposed $163 billion in Medicaid cuts and new work requirements, which CBO estimated could leave at least 8.6 million people uninsured by 2034 (ABC News, May 17, 2025).

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law July 4, 2025, required Medicaid expansion-population adults aged 19-64 to complete at least 80 hours per month of qualifying work, education, job training, or volunteer service to keep coverage, with a statutory exemption for individuals who are 'medically frail.' On June 1, 2026, CMS -- under Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz -- published an interim final rule implementing the requirement nationwide. Rather than applying the statute's medical-frailty categories as written, CMS added an additional functional-capacity requirement: individuals must affirmatively demonstrate that their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to perform the 80 hours of required activity, a threshold not present in the underlying statute. In practice, advocates and reporting say this leaves out people with early-stage cancer who are undergoing radiation treatment but are still nominally capable of some work, and people with HIV who are stable on treatment but technically employable -- both groups are not automatically exempted under CMS's narrower reading, and must instead navigate state reporting/paperwork processes to prove exemption eligibility or ongoing compliance. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the work-requirement provisions would cause roughly 5 million people to lose Medicaid coverage, out of a program covering about 68 million low-income Americans, and that the requirements account for roughly a third of the $900 billion in Medicaid savings scored under OBBBA overall (i.e., roughly $300 billion of that total tied to work-requirement-driven disenrollment). Nebraska became the first state to implement the requirement on May 1, 2026; Montana and Arkansas followed by July 1, 2026 (Arkansas delayed enforcement to January 2027), with additional states phasing in through the January 2027 national deadline. Update 2026-08-02 (detail): Per CNN's June 6, 2026 reporting on the same rule, the medical-frailty exemption requires more than a diagnosis -- enrollees must submit documentation, such as a signed statement from a medical professional, affirmatively showing their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to meet the 80-hour work standard. A cancer patient in active chemotherapy who remains physically able to sit at a desk part-time may not qualify for the exemption on that documentation standard alone, regardless of diagnosis.

primary_proponent.name: Dr. Mehmet Oz
primary_proponent.role: CMS Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Oz publicly framed the rule as reducing loneliness and building 'skills and independence through work,' stating: 'This rule helps Americans build skills and independence through work, education, job training, or community service, creating new opportunities for themselves and their families.' CMS's specific choice to add a functional-capacity threshold beyond the statute's medical-frailty categories -- the discretionary regulatory action this entry documents -- was made under his administration of the agency.

estimated_impact.summary: Health-policy advocates and reporting describe the rule's core mechanism as bureaucratic rather than substantive: eligible, low-income people who are already working, studying, or too sick to reliably navigate monthly reporting requirements lose coverage not because they fail to meet the underlying policy goal, but because they fail the paperwork. People undergoing active cancer treatment or living with HIV -- conditions advocates argue should self-evidently qualify as medically frail -- are not automatically exempted under CMS's narrower functional-capacity standard.

estimated_impact.caveat: CMS and the administration argue the requirement is a legitimate work-promotion policy applying only to a defined expansion population, that statutory exemptions remain available for parents, pregnant individuals, former foster youth, and Native American/Alaska Native beneficiaries, and that some coverage loss reflects genuinely ineligible enrollees being removed rather than eligible people being wrongly cut off. The specific accountability question this entry documents is narrower: whether CMS's discretionary choice to layer an additional functional-capacity threshold onto the statute's medical-frailty exemption -- rather than applying Congress's own listed categories -- was a reasonable implementation choice or an administrative narrowing of an exemption Congress wrote more broadly. That legal/administrative question was not resolved as of this entry's sourcing.

title: Trump Administration Cut, Then Moved to End, a Federal Subsidy That Had Kept Medicare Part D Drug-Plan Premiums Down
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing -- the underlying Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration is set to expire after 2026, meaning 2027 premiums will not benefit from the subsidy at all
date_of_action: 2025-08 (reported ~40% cut affecting 2026 premiums) through 2026-07 (announced full end of the demonstration after 2026)
what_changed: The Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration is a temporary CMS program, funded at roughly $9.8 billion, that had reduced the average standalone Medicare Part D prescription-drug-plan premium by about 40% in 2025. In early August 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration had cut the subsidy in a way that would still let 2026 average premiums rise sharply even as CMS negotiated with insurers to limit the increase -- CMS's own later figures put the resulting 2026 subsidy-driven premium reduction at roughly 27%, down from the prior year's 40% offset, meaning the effective subsidy value had already been scaled back for 2026 even before the program's later full termination. In July 2026, CMS announced it would let the demonstration expire entirely after 2026, eliminating the subsidy for 2027 premiums altogether. Reporting on the full expiration indicates it will most affect people enrolled in standalone Part D plans (as opposed to Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage, which have more pricing flexibility to absorb the loss) -- an estimated 11 million+ Americans face increased premiums, with about half of Part D enrollees seeing some increase and some paying as much as an additional $20 per month. Officials and reporting describe the change as likely to push more seniors toward Medicare Advantage plans, which the administration has otherwise favored, rather than remaining in traditional Medicare's standalone drug-plan option.

title: Trump's Foreign Aid Freeze Halted a U.S.-Funded Anti-Fentanyl Cargo-Screening Program at Mexico's Busiest Port
institution: U.S. foreign aid programs (State Department/USAID-administered), implemented via UNODC-WCO Container Control Programme
status: Partially reversed after congressional pushback -- UNODC received a waiver restoring the specific port-screening program, but its continuation remained subject to a 90-day policy review, and other related anti-narcotics cooperation with Mexico stayed frozen
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (global foreign aid freeze ordered) through 2025-02-24 (Reuters reporting on the disruption and subsequent waiver)
what_changed: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, Trump ordered a sweeping freeze on foreign aid. Within weeks the freeze stalled U.S. funding for the Container Control Programme, a joint initiative of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the World Customs Organization that trained and equipped Mexico's Navy to screen cargo for fentanyl-precursor chemicals and other contraband at the Port of Manzanillo, Mexico's busiest container port. The U.S. had provided roughly $800,000 to launch the program at Manzanillo in 2023, and a planned expansion to two additional major ports -- Lazaro Cardenas and Veracruz -- was put on hold by the funding cutoff. The freeze also paused other U.S.-funded anti-narcotics cooperation with Mexico, including training for Mexican authorities to locate and dismantle clandestine fentanyl labs and U.S. donations of drug-sniffing canines. Following complaints from U.S. lawmakers, UNODC received notification of a waiver restoring the port-screening program, though State Department officials disputed characterizations that the freeze had 'stalled' it, and the program's longer-term continuation remained subject to a 90-day policy review. title: MSPB Loses Quorum for 8 Months After Trump Fires Whistleblower Board Chair Cathy Harris
institution: Merit Systems Protection Board
status: Resolved against Harris (the Supreme Court denied her petition for certiorari on June 30, 2026 -- one day after Trump v. Slaughter -- leaving the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 ruling upholding her firing as the final word in her individual case; the Board's quorum was separately restored in October 2025 via an unrelated confirmation, so the practical quorum crisis had already ended, but the removal-power precedent from the D.C. Circuit's 2-1 ruling is now permanent since the Supreme Court declined further review)
date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (firing) through present; the Board's quorum was separately restored in October 2025 via a new member's confirmation, independent of Harris's litigation
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, President Trump fired MSPB Chair Cathy Harris via a one-sentence email without citing any cause, three years before her Senate-confirmed term was set to expire in 2028. Harris sued; a district court granted a temporary restraining order reinstating her on February 18, and on March 4, Judge Rudolph Contreras granted summary judgment finding the firing unlawful. The government appealed, and a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed her reinstatement on March 28. The full en banc D.C. Circuit voted 7-4 to vacate that stay and reinstate Harris on April 7, but two days later, on April 9, Chief Justice Roberts granted the government's emergency application for a stay, again removing Harris and leaving the Board without the quorum needed to issue decisions. The quorum gap's practical stakes for ordinary civil servants were illustrated in July 2025, when Mary Comans, FEMA's chief financial officer, sued the administration over her own March 2025 termination -- she was fired along with three colleagues after Elon Musk's DOGE team publicly claimed a $59 million New York City migrant-shelter payment had gone to 'luxury hotels' -- with her complaint explicitly noting that MSPB's lack of quorum left her, like other terminated federal employees, with no functioning venue to appeal. In December 2025, a 2-1 D.C. Circuit panel (Judges Katsas and Walker, both Trump appointees) ruled on the merits that Congress cannot restrict the president's authority to remove NLRB or MSPB members who 'wield substantial executive power,' with a dissenting judge warning the majority's reasoning implies 'no independent agencies may lawfully exist in this country.' The Board separately regained a functional quorum in October 2025 through the unrelated Senate confirmation of a new member, James Woodruff. On March 17, 2026, Harris petitioned the Supreme Court for review, arguing her case is legally distinct from the FTC's Slaughter case because MSPB is purely adjudicatory, does not set policy, and structurally resembles multimember bodies with roughly 150 years of established constitutional standing. A group of Senate Democrats filed an amicus brief in April 2026 urging the Court to hear her case. The June 29, 2026 Trump v. Slaughter ruling did not directly resolve Harris's petition but substantially weakens her argument by holding broadly that agencies exercising 'executive power' must have removable leadership. Correction 2026-07-19: the Supreme Court denied Harris's petition for certiorari on June 30, 2026, one day after deciding Trump v. Slaughter -- this entry's prior 'remains formally unresolved' status is now out of date. The denial leaves the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 2-1 panel ruling (Katsas and Walker) as the final word on Harris's individual removal; the Supreme Court's order gave no reasoning beyond the standard denial, consistent with how it typically treats cert denials, so the underlying legal question (whether purely adjudicatory bodies like MSPB warrant different treatment than the FTC) was not resolved on the merits, only left undisturbed as decided below.

title: National Archives Loses Its Archivist and Digital Access Office Amid Deep Budget Cuts
institution: National Archives and Records Administration
status: Resolved as to leadership -- the Senate confirmed Bradford P. Wilson as Archivist of the United States on August 7, 2026 (Roll Call Vote No. 225, 119th Congress, 2nd Session, an en bloc confirmation of 74 nominations together, 51-47), ending an 18-month vacancy in the confirmed position; FY2026 budget cuts and office eliminations documented below remain in effect independent of the leadership question
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Archivist Colleen Shogan fired) through 2026 (ongoing reorganization, office eliminations, and records-center closures)
what_changed: In February 2025, President Trump fired Archivist of the United States Colleen Shogan without citing cause, an unprecedented removal of the position's confirmed leader. Deputy Archivist William Bosanko briefly became acting archivist before announcing his resignation along with several other senior staff. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was then named acting archivist while continuing his separate Cabinet role, a dual appointment a U.S. senator later suggested may have violated federal law given how long Rubio held both positions simultaneously; during Rubio's tenure, the director of the Eisenhower Presidential Library was separately forced to resign in September 2025 after refusing to hand over a museum sword for a royal gift (tracked in its own entry, eisenhower-library-director-forced-out-sword-2025.json, since no source confirms Rubio personally directed that ouster). Jim Byron subsequently served as senior adviser performing archivist functions before departing in April 2026, when GSA head Edward Forst was named acting archivist. Separately, NARA's FY2026 budget request set the agency's funding at $414.7 million, nearly $60 million less than projected FY2025 spending, eliminating 136 full-time positions agency-wide. The proposal included full elimination of NARA's 50-person Office of Innovation, which runs the agency's online records catalog, digital access initiatives, and the public 'citizen archivist' transcription project, with NARA stating those functions would be 'transferred elsewhere' rather than continued directly. In June 2025, NARA issued reduction-in-force notices affecting roughly 100 employees (about 3% of staff), which two NARA employees said effectively 'wiped out' the Office of Innovation and the division supporting field offices and presidential libraries; the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library was briefly forced to close in February 2025 after probationary employees were terminated. The FY2026 proposal also cut funding for NARA's Electronic Records Initiative by roughly 33%, even as the agency faces a growing volume of incoming digital records, with only about 3% of its roughly 12 billion textual paper pages digitized as of the most recent count. In 2026, NARA also announced it would vacate three federal records centers (Chicago, San Francisco/San Bruno, and Seattle) and sunset its free public History Hub reference forum to save an estimated $370,000 annually. On March 2, 2026, Trump nominated Bradford P. Wilson to be the permanent Archivist of the United States; as of this update, Wilson's confirmation was still pending in the Senate. In the interim, GSA Administrator Edward Forst was named acting archivist under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act in April 2026, telling GSA staff he would 'dually serve' in both roles -- meaning NARA's day-to-day acting leadership is held by an official whose primary job is running a different agency. Re-verified 2026-07-26: Wilson's nomination received a hearing on June 17, 2026, but as one of 11 nominees split across two panels rather than a dedicated AOTUS hearing, with only a few minutes of questioning devoted to him specifically -- notable given the position's usual dedicated-hearing custom, per the Society of American Archivists' own monitoring of the nomination. No confirmation vote had occurred as of this update; Forst continues serving as acting archivist. Update 2026-08-17: the Senate confirmed Bradford P. Wilson as Archivist of the United States on August 7, 2026, as part of an en bloc vote covering 74 nominations together (51-47), per the Senate's own roll call and nominations-confirmed records. This resolves the entry's central open leadership question -- NARA now has a Senate-confirmed archivist for the first time since Colleen Shogan's February 2025 firing, ending the sequence of acting/dual-hatted leaders (Bosanko, Rubio, Byron, Forst) that this entry has tracked. Independent confirmation of Wilson's swearing-in date and formal transition from acting archivist Edward Forst was not found as of this update; the confirmation vote itself is the sourced fact. The FY2026 budget cuts, Office of Innovation elimination, and records-center closures documented above are unaffected by this leadership resolution and remain the entry's standing findings.

title: NASA Closed Its Largest Research Library and 100+ Goddard Labs -- Including One Critical to the Roman Space Telescope -- Over Objections From Its Own Union and Congress
institution: NASA, Goddard Space Flight Center
status: Ongoing -- library closed Jan. 2-3, 2026; broader 13-building/100+-lab consolidation targeted for completion by March 2026
date_of_action: 2025-11 (consolidation plan advanced) through 2026-01 (library closure) and 2026-03 (target completion of building closures)
what_changed: NASA closed the Goddard Information and Collaboration Center -- Goddard Space Flight Center's 100,000-volume research library, the largest in the agency -- on January 2-3, 2026, as part of a broader plan to shrink the 1,270-acre Goddard campus (home to Hubble and Webb telescope operations) by roughly 25%, decommissioning 13 buildings and more than 100 laboratories by March 2026. The library's collection included books, journals, and historical documents dating from the early 20th century through the 1950s-60s Space Race with the Soviet Union, much of it copyrighted, out of print, or never digitized. NASA said discarded holdings would undergo a 60-day review, with some materials transferred to other NASA libraries or government warehouses and the rest discarded; the Goddard Engineers, Scientists and Technicians Association (part of IFPTE) said the closure proceeded with 'extreme haste and no transparent strategy.' Administrator Jared Isaacman characterized the closure as a long-planned 'facilities consolidation' dating to a 2022 (Biden-era) master plan, projected to save $10 million per year in operations costs plus $63.8 million in deferred maintenance. IFPTE union leader Matt Biggs disputed both of Isaacman's central claims as 'misguided' and 'misleading': the 2022 master plan actually called for renovating the library building, not eliminating it, and many discarded materials were copyrighted or unique physical items unavailable in any digital form, contradicting Isaacman's assurance that researchers would retain access to needed materials. Biggs said NASA scientists and engineers 'shouldn't have to be dumpster divers to do their work.' Separately, the building closures include labs used by teams working on the propulsion subsystem for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, one of NASA's flagship missions, raising concern among employees and lawmakers about schedule and technical risk to an active, mission-critical program rather than only administrative/archival loss. Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), ranking member of the House Science Committee, sent a formal letter to Acting/Administrator Sean Duffy (predating Isaacman's confirmation) demanding NASA immediately halt the closures pending more transparency; the Maryland congressional delegation separately sought information on the closures. This entry is a companion to nasa-science-budget-workforce-collapse-2025.json, which documents the broader FY2026 NASA science-budget cuts and workforce exodus (JPL layoffs, Goddard leadership departures, Earth-science mission cancellations) -- that entry covers people and money; this one covers physical infrastructure, irreplaceable archival materials, and mission-critical lab capacity specifically.

title: Trump's Proposed NASA Budget Cut Science Funding Nearly in Half, Triggering a 20%+ Workforce Exodus and Dozens of Canceled Missions
institution: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
status: Ongoing -- the FY2026 budget remains a proposal Congress has not finalized, but the workforce reductions and JPL layoffs it triggered have already occurred; satellite decommissioning was planned to begin as soon as October 2025
date_of_action: 2025-04-10 (initial OMB budget draft) through 2025-10-14 (JPL's third layoff round)
what_changed: On April 10, 2025, the White House Office of Management and Budget sent NASA a draft FY2026 budget proposal that would cut the agency's overall funding by roughly 24% and its Science Mission Directorate specifically by nearly half -- from $7.3 billion to $3.9 billion, a 47% reduction. The Planetary Society estimated the cuts would cancel no fewer than 41 active and planned missions, including the Mars Sample Return program (billions of dollars in prior U.S. and international-partner investment already sunk) and a roughly 50% cut to the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, on which NASA had already spent nearly 90% of its projected development cost. Seven former NASA science chiefs publicly condemned the proposal. The budget cuts coincided with, and helped drive, a parallel workforce exodus: NASA opened a second round of its 'deferred resignation' buyout program in mid-2025 after roughly 870 employees took the first round; by late July 2025 nearly 4,000 employees (about 20% of the agency's roughly 18,000-person workforce) had accepted the program, shrinking NASA to about 14,000 employees. The cuts hit NASA's field centers unevenly, with Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland losing the most staff (607), followed by Johnson Space Center (366), Kennedy Space Center (311), and NASA headquarters (307). Leadership departures accompanied the buyouts: Jet Propulsion Laboratory director Laurie Leshin stepped down in June 2025, and Goddard Space Flight Center director Makenzie Lystrup announced her departure July 21, 2025, effective August 1, amid a Goddard staff dissent letter over the cuts. Separately, the White House's FY2026 budget proposed decommissioning the fully operational Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 and -3 satellites -- which measure atmospheric carbon dioxide and plant health and, per a 2023 senior review, remained in 'excellent condition' with enough fuel to operate until 2040 -- along with other Earth-science missions, with decommissioning planned to begin as soon as October 2025; scientists warned this would create a significant gap in climate-monitoring data. The workforce reductions continued independent of the budget fight: on October 13, 2025, JPL laid off approximately 550 employees (about 11% of its workforce) in what director David Gallagher called an unrelated internal 'realignment' that began in July 2025, not a response to that month's federal government shutdown -- JPL's third layoff round since February 2024.
