title: National Cancer Institute Lost Staff and $180 Million in Grants Amid a Proposed 37% Budget Cut and Dismantled Public Communications
institution: National Cancer Institute (NIH)
status: Split status, corrected 2026-08-17: the proposed FY2026 37.3% NCI budget cut was rejected -- Congress instead enacted an increase. The FY2026 Labor-HHS-Education appropriations act (P.L. 119-75, H.R. 7148, Division B, signed 2026-02-03) provided NCI $7.4 billion, an increase over FY2025 rather than the proposed cut to ~$4.53 billion. The already-executed 2025 harms this entry documents -- staff losses, $180M+ in cancelled active grants, and the dismantled public-facing communications infrastructure -- have not been reversed by the FY2026 funding increase and remain in effect.
date_of_action: 2025 (staff purges, grant cancellations, and communications dismantlement, ongoing through at least September 2025); FY2026 budget request proposing a 37% cut submitted 2025
what_changed: Separate from -- but compounding -- a proposed FY2026 budget request that would cut NCI's funding by 37.3% (about $2.69 billion, from roughly $7.22 billion to $4.53 billion), NCI had already lost hundreds of staff and had more than $180 million in active research grants cancelled as of a June 26, 2025 Guardian report, with key prevention, clinical-trial, and community-research programs being dismantled in the process. A May 2025 U.S. Senate Minority Staff report separately found the federal government had cut approximately $2.7 billion in NIH funding overall in the first three months of 2025, including a 31% year-over-year decrease in cancer-research funding through March 2025 compared with the same period in 2024 -- a distinct, already-executed reduction from the proposed FY2026 request. By September 2025, the New York Times Magazine reported NCI's public-facing website and communications functions had been 'devastatingly dismantled,' leaving patient calls for cancer information unanswered, and that labs studying specific cancers -- including pediatric brain tumors -- were being gutted, with researchers forced to suspend ongoing studies and lay off their own staff as grant funding lapsed. Analysts and cancer-research organizations warned that if the proposed 37% FY2026 cut were enacted, NCI's grant-approval rate would collapse to roughly 4% of new applications (down from historical norms several times higher), rejecting 96% of new research proposals. Update 2026-08-17: The proposed FY2026 37.3% NCI cut described above did not take effect. Congress enacted the FY2026 Labor-HHS-Education appropriations act (P.L. 119-75, H.R. 7148, Division B) on 2026-02-03, providing NCI $7.4 billion -- an increase over FY2025 funding, not the proposed $2.69 billion/37.3% cut to ~$4.53 billion. This entry's date_added (2026-08-12) came more than six months after that enactment, so the 'proposed, not yet enacted' framing had already gone stale before this entry was first written. The already-executed 2025 harms described above -- the 2025 staff losses, the $180M+ in cancelled grants, and the dismantled communications infrastructure -- are separate, already-completed actions and are unaffected by the FY2026 appropriations increase; they have not been reversed.

title: National Climate Assessment Gutted -- 400 Authors Dismissed, Reports Pulled Offline, Climate Skeptic Installed to Run the Program
institution: U.S. Global Change Research Program (USGCRP) -- National Climate Assessment
status: Ongoing and escalated -- USGCRP, now under Wielicki, published a formal proposed amendment to the already-released Fifth National Climate Assessment (NCA5) on August 25, 2026, open for public comment through September 9, 2026; the Sixth Assessment (due 2028) remains in doubt
date_of_action: 2025-04-01 (ICF International coordination contract cancelled) through 2026-07-09 (skeptic appointed to lead USGCRP)
what_changed: In early April 2025, NASA cancelled a contract with ICF International, the consulting firm hired to support the U.S. Global Change Research Program's (USGCRP) logistical coordination work across the 15 federal agencies and hundreds of volunteer authors that produce the National Climate Assessment -- a report on climate change's impacts on the United States that has been congressionally mandated every four years since the Global Change Research Act of 1990. On April 28, 2025, nearly 400 scientists and scholars who had already begun volunteer work on the Sixth National Climate Assessment (due for publication by early 2028) were informed by email that they had been 'released' while the report's scope was 'reevaluated.' By June 30, 2025, the National Climate Assessments -- including prior, already-published editions -- were no longer accessible on federal websites, with no explanation or referral to alternative sources, after globalchange.gov and climate.gov both went offline without prior notice. Officials initially announced NASA would take over hosting the existing reports to preserve public access; on July 14-15, 2025, a NASA spokesperson reversed that pledge, stating 'NASA has no legal obligations to host globalchange.gov's data... We never did and will not host the data' -- relying on the fact that the Global Change Research Act of 1990 only requires the assessments be submitted to Congress every four years, not that they be publicly hosted online, as the legal basis for declining to restore access. The move was consistent with Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation policy blueprint, whose chapter on the National Climate Assessment (co-authored with input from OMB Director Russell Vought) called for the report to be reshaped and its contributors 'better scrutinized.' The dismissal left the administration able to either skip the congressionally mandated report or pursue an alternative version. On July 9, 2026, the White House confirmed that direction: it appointed Matthew Wielicki, a former University of Alabama geochemist and prominent skeptic of mainstream climate science, to lead USGCRP -- the program responsible for compiling the assessment the administration had gutted fifteen months earlier. Update 2026-08-18: this entry's existing caveat noted that the eventual shape of any future National Climate Assessment under Wielicki's leadership was 'not yet known' as of the entry's original verification -- but work on the Sixth Assessment did not sit idle between the April 2025 author dismissals and Wielicki's July 2026 appointment as USGCRP director. Starting in December 2025, the administration invited a new group of researchers known for climate skepticism to resume work on the Sixth National Climate Assessment, months before Wielicki was named to formally lead the program. This is a distinct fact from, and should not be confused with, a separate Department of Energy effort covering similar ground: DOE Secretary Chris Wright separately convened his own five-scientist 'Climate Working Group' (John Christy, Roy Spencer, Steve Koonin, Judith Curry, and Ross McKitrick) earlier in 2025 to produce a contrarian report critiquing the existing Fifth National Climate Assessment and the EPA's endangerment finding; Wright dissolved that group himself in a September 3, 2025 letter after its report drew a rebuttal from 85+ scientists, and a federal court (Judge William Young, D. Mass., January 30, 2026) later found the Climate Working Group's secretive operation violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act. That DOE action is institutionally separate -- a different agency, a different responsible official (Wright, not the USGCRP/NASA officials and Vought documented in this entry), and a different specific action -- and is already tracked in this database's Cabinet-Level tracker (see wright-faca-violation-2026.json); it is not folded into this entry despite the thematic overlap. Update 2026-08-29: on August 25, 2026, USGCRP published a Federal Register notice announcing a proposed amendment to NCA5 -- the existing, already-published Fifth National Climate Assessment, not the still-pending Sixth -- open for public comment through 11:59 p.m. ET on September 9, 2026. The proposed amendment addresses NCA5 findings that depend materially on RCP8.5, SSP5-8.5, SRES A2, or similar high-emissions pathways, stating that those pathways should not be treated as expected, likely, baseline, business-as-usual, central, or policy-relevant planning futures, and that NCA5 findings substantially dependent on them should be labeled as resting on 'implausible high-end scenario assumptions.' This is the first concrete action under Wielicki's USGCRP leadership that reaches backward to reclassify an already-published, congressionally mandated assessment's own findings, rather than only shaping the still-pending Sixth Assessment -- resolving this entry's prior caveat that no completed or published document existed yet to assess. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 49, during the still-open comment period): the amendment's core technical premise -- that RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5 shouldn't be treated as a likely, business-as-usual future -- is not a fabricated or purely political claim; mainstream climate scientists (e.g. The Climate Brink, May 18, 2026) had already been retiring RCP8.5 as an implausible worst-case scenario for roughly a decade, independent of this administration, citing coal-reserve assumptions the scenario exceeds, clean-energy cost declines, and diverging real-world emissions trends. That same mainstream commentary explicitly separates the underlying science from what it calls a political misuse of the point: it criticizes President Trump's public framing of the scenario's retirement as an 'admission' that climate projections were 'WRONG,' and notes the irony that the administration's own climate-rollback policies (including the SO2/NOx and power-plant-GHG rollbacks tracked elsewhere in this database's Corporate Deregulation tracker) push future emissions trajectories closer to the high-end scenarios it is now dismissing as impossible. Criticism of the specific NCA5 amendment is not limited to mainstream defenders of the assessment, either: climate economist Roger Pielke Jr., who has himself long argued RCP8.5 is overused, wrote that while the administration is 'directionally correct' about the scenario's problems, the amendment 'cannot succeed' because NCA5's underlying problems are 'systemic and irreparable' -- i.e., a critique from someone otherwise sympathetic to the RCP8.5 objection that this specific fix is inadequate, not that it goes too far. No comment-period outcome exists yet since the window remains open through September 9, 2026.

primary_proponent.note: Reporting (Rolling Stone, EDF) identifies Vought -- who ran OMB during Trump's first term and co-authored Project 2025 -- as the figure who has 'long sought to bury or weaken' the National Climate Assessment, and as the architect of the Project 2025 chapter calling for a National Climate Assessment written by researchers who downplay or deny humanity's role in climate change. No single official's name was confirmed publicly as the signer of the April 28, 2025 dismissal email; Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), ranking member of the House Science Committee, addressed her formal oversight letter on the dismissals to Michael Kratsios, Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, which has institutional oversight of USGCRP.

estimated_impact.summary: The National Climate Assessment is the U.S. government's flagship, legally mandated report on how climate change is affecting the country -- used by city and state planners, insurers, farmers, and courts. Dismissing its ~400 volunteer authors, cancelling the contract coordinating the 15-agency effort behind it, and removing existing editions from federal websites leaves the statutorily required Sixth Assessment (due 2028) in doubt, and installing a climate-science skeptic to lead the program that produces it signals the administration intends to replace mainstream scientific consensus in the government's own official climate reporting rather than simply pause it.

The July 2026 Wielicki appointment is corroborated by the Washington Post, SEJ, and Eos -- and, notably, also celebrated in identical factual terms by climate-skeptic outlets (Climate Depot, Watts Up With That, CFACT) covering their own side's win, which corroborates the characterization of this as a deliberate ideological redirection rather than a framing dispute between outlets. Re-verified 2026-08-29: the proposed NCA5 amendment is corroborated directly by the Federal Register notice and NOAA's own posted PDF of the proposed text, with the same facts (scope, RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5/SRES A2 language, September 9 comment deadline) independently reported by outlets favorable to the change (Competitive Enterprise Institute, Watts Up With That, Roger Pielke Jr.'s newsletter, AEI) -- the same same-fact-different-framing corroboration pattern already used for the Wielicki appointment in this entry. Real correction, GSR recheck batch 49 (2026-09-01): the mainstream-science RCP8.5-retirement context is sourced to The Climate Brink (a climate-science newsletter run by scientists including Andrew Dessler), independently corroborating the pre-existing, apolitical scientific basis for the amendment's core technical claim while directly criticizing its political framing -- and Pielke Jr.'s critique that the amendment 'cannot succeed' is drawn from his own Substack/AEI commentary, both already cited in this entry's sourcing for other facts. Both additions describe reactions during an open comment period, not a resolved outcome. title: $362 Million in National Park Service Grants Stalled Awaiting Political Review in Burgum's Office
institution: National Park Service / Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing -- backlog reported as of early June 2026, with no reporting reviewed indicating it had been cleared
date_of_action: 2026-06 (backlog reported); consolidation of grant-approval authority into the Secretary's office occurred earlier in 2025-2026
what_changed: More than 1,400 active NPS grants worth roughly $362 million are sitting unapproved at the Department of the Interior, awaiting political review after the department consolidated grants-management sign-off into Secretary Doug Burgum's office. The stalled projects include nonprofit youth-program deployments to clear trails, work to prevent washouts during heavy rain, and wildlife surveys. Interior is managing the backlog with a significantly reduced staff, after the department shed roughly 13,000 employees (about 20% of its workforce) in 2025, including about 4,000 at NPS specifically. Update 2026-08-17: more than 70 House Democrats, led by Rep. Elfreth and Sen. Merkley already documented here. No reporting reviewed indicates the backlog has been cleared or the additional review layer removed. title: GSA/DOGE Listed 34 National Park Service Buildings for Lease Termination, Including Visitor Centers and Museums Housing Artifacts
institution: National Park Service (NPS); General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Ongoing in phases through 2026; at least two individual sites (Fairbanks, AK and Seattle, WA) reversed or found to have been included in error; the leasing-authority bill Congress introduced in response has since advanced out of committee
date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (list publicly reported) through 2026 (phased terminations continuing)
what_changed: On March 6, 2025, the Washington Post reported that GSA, working with DOGE, had targeted the leases of at least 34 National Park Service buildings for termination as part of the administration's broader federal real-estate cost-cutting push -- including visitor centers, law enforcement offices, park headquarters, and museum/archive space housing millions of cultural artifacts. GSA said terminating the leases could save taxpayers millions of dollars; terminations were structured to arrive in waves stretching from 2025 into 2026, with example dates including a planned September 30, 2025 termination for Seattle's Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park visitor center and a planned end-of-May-2026 termination for a National Park Service building in Fairbanks, Alaska. Park advocates warned the closures would degrade the visitor experience, particularly during peak summer season, threaten artifact preservation, and disrupt law-enforcement and emergency operations at affected parks. At least two individual terminations were subsequently reversed or corrected: GSA restored the Fairbanks-area Alaska Public Lands Information Center lease roughly 10 days after terminating it, following pressure from Sen. Dan Sullivan; and the Klondike Gold Rush visitor center lease in Seattle was found to have been placed on the termination list in error -- the lease had actually been extended by Historic Seattle in September 2024 through 2030, with GSA apparently unaware of the extension when it added the site to the list. Members of Congress, including Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith, formally urged GSA not to proceed with terminations affecting other specific NPS buildings; a bill, the National Park System Long-Term Lease Investment Act (S.2498/H.R.4931), was introduced in Congress during this period aimed at giving NPS more stable, long-term leasing authority, though it had not been enacted as of this entry's last verification. title: National Park Service Lost 24% of Its Permanent Staff — Internal Report Contradicts Interior's Public 'False Narrative' Denial
institution: National Park Service (NPS), Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing -- the 2025 pattern repeated into the 2026 summer season: permanent staffing losses (~24%, ~4,000 people) remain unreversed, and 2026 seasonal hiring again fell short of its own target heading into peak season
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (initial mass layoff, dubbed the 'Valentine's Day Massacre' by affected staff) through 2025-08-27 (internal operational-status report surfaces)
what_changed: On February 14, 2025, NPS laid off approximately 1,000-1,700 probationary employees just weeks before peak visitor season began across the system's 63 national parks and 370 other managed sites. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0136): a March 13, 2025 preliminary injunction from Judge William Alsup ordered NPS and five other agencies (Agriculture, Defense, Energy, Interior, Treasury, and VA) to immediately reinstate their terminated probationary employees; NPS and other named agencies complied only nominally, notifying fired staff they were reinstated but then placing them on indefinite paid administrative leave rather than restoring them to duty -- a workaround Alsup explicitly ruled violated the injunction, since it did not restore the services the order intended to restore. The Supreme Court stayed Alsup's reinstatement order on April 8, 2025 on standing grounds, allowing the administration to resume the firings; NPS's ~24% permanent-staff loss documented later in this entry reflects that the initial February terminations were not durably reversed. By March 11, 2025, reporting confirmed the administration was separately pushing for a 30% reduction in NPS's overall payroll -- a budget-driven target distinct from, and layered on top of, the February probationary firings -- expected to further reduce park rangers, custodial staff, and conservation-program capacity. By July 2025, independent analysis of Interior Department workforce data by the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) found NPS had lost 24% of its permanent staff overall (about 4,000 people) since January, while only roughly 4,500 of a promised ~8,000 seasonal positions had been filled. In April 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued Secretarial Order 3426, mandating that every park remain 'open and accessible' regardless of staffing levels -- meaning parks could not close facilities or reduce services in response to the shortages, only quietly absorb the strain. Per Order 3426's own reporting requirement, every park unit had to submit an updated operational status by July 25, 2025; an internal NPS report compiled from those submissions, first reported by the New York Times, documented widespread, specific impacts: nearly 70 parks reduced visitor center hours, 22 postponed maintenance, and 11 closed or delayed opening facilities. Specific documented examples include all 13 lifeguard positions vacant at Assateague Island National Seashore (leaving the beach unguarded) -- a shortage CBS News had already reported independently on July 5, 2025, three weeks before Order 3426's own compilation deadline, tying it to the hiring freeze and warning of elevated drowning/injury risk given the beach's millions of annual summer visitors -- the fire management team reduced to one person at Cumberland Island National Seashore, and Indiana Dunes National Park's ranger-led tours cut from 575 to approximately 100 for the year after 4 of 6 interpretive-division supervisors took early retirement. When this internal report became public, Interior deputy press secretary Aubrie Spady called the reporting a 'false narrative,' stating 'staffing levels and operations at our National Parks this summer are on par with previous years. Full Stop' -- a direct denial of findings drawn from the agency's own internal, Order-3426-mandated data collection. For the 2026 season, NPS again fell short of its own seasonal-hiring target: roughly 4,500 of a planned 5,000+ seasonal positions were filled heading into peak summer season, with reporting citing paperwork delays, background-check backlogs, and housing shortages as contributing causes -- a smaller absolute gap than 2025's (~4,500 of ~8,000 filled), but the same shortfall pattern for a second consecutive year. The ~24% permanent-staff loss and its downstream effects (documented in this entry's 2025 examples) had not been reversed as of this update. On September 2-3, 2025, nearly 600 employees at Yosemite and Sequoia & Kings Canyon voted overwhelmingly to unionize with the National Federation of Federal Employees, a direct workforce response to the mass purges and budget cuts documented above -- workers cited the strain of being stretched thin (scientists and other specialists covering basic operational duties) as a driving factor. Update 2026-07-26: the 2026 peak season brought the staffing crisis to a head -- record crowds collided with reduced capacity at parks including Yosemite, where seasonal employees reportedly went weeks without pay, scientists and hydrologists were reassigned to cleaning restrooms and staffing entrance gates, and some campgrounds closed for lack of staff to run them. NPS also removed timed-entry reservation systems at some of the busiest parks and introduced a new $100-per-person fee for international visitors, both of which affected entrance-line flow during the July 4th weekend's record crowds. On a partial-relief note, NPS was approved to refill roughly 600 staff positions -- a real but small fraction of the several thousand permanent positions lost since January 2025, not a reversal of the underlying staffing loss this entry documents. Update (2026-08-17 recheck): on April 3, 2026, the White House released its fiscal year 2027 budget proposal, requesting $2.14 billion for NPS operations -- a $736 million, roughly 25% cut from the prior year -- which NPCA and other outlets project would eliminate approximately 2,920 additional full-time positions on top of the ~4,000 permanent positions already lost since January 2025. As with the entry's existing budget-threat context, this is a proposal, not enacted law: Congress alone controls appropriations, and as of this update the FY2027 budget remained under congressional debate, with a final vote not expected before fall 2026 at the earliest. Notably, Congress rejected a comparable roughly $1 billion FY2026 NPS cut proposal in a January 5, 2026 appropriations bill, instead approving $3.267 billion in flat funding and adding a requirement that the administration notify Congress before any future mass firings or reorganizations -- a precedent for congressional pushback, though not a guarantee the FY2027 proposal meets the same fate. Update 2026-08-30: the National Parks Conservation Association organized a nationwide 'Day of Action,' running August 22 through September 1, 2026 with roughly 30 events across 20 states and Washington, D.C., calling on President Trump and Interior Secretary Burgum to invest in NPS staffing and address the workforce shortages this entry documents. NPCA -- a 501(c)(3) that states it does not endorse, oppose, or fund political candidates -- organized the events partly in response to Interior Department claims about employee political activity. The campaign's public materials also cited related administration actions not otherwise part of this entry's own documentation: separate pricing for international visitors, placement of Trump's image on the 2026 annual pass, and removal of 'disparaging' content from federal historic sites -- noted here for context but not independently verified by this entry, since they fall outside its core staffing-crisis subject. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): the FY2027 budget fight referenced in this entry's 2026-08-17 update ('not yet enacted, still under debate') had already moved by the time of that recheck -- the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies released its FY2027 bill on May 20, 2026, rejecting the administration's proposed $736 million/~2,920-position cut and instead holding NPS operations funding essentially flat at $2.9 billion (a 1.3%/~$3 million reduction from FY2026), following the same pattern as Congress's FY2026 rejection of a similar cut this entry already documents. The bill still needed full-House passage and Senate reconciliation as of the sourcing reviewed, so this is a subcommittee-level rejection of the administration's ask, not a final enacted FY2027 appropriation.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) / Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.role: DOGE directed the initial layoffs; Interior Secretary Burgum issued the 'stay open regardless of staffing' order that followed
primary_proponent.note: Burgum's Secretarial Order 3426 is the specific policy mechanism that turned a staffing shortage into a documented service-quality crisis -- by prohibiting parks from closing or scaling back in response to short-staffing, the order effectively required remaining staff to absorb the gap rather than allowing an official acknowledgment of reduced capacity. Interior's own deputy press secretary's 'false narrative' denial is difficult to reconcile with the fact that the cited findings came from data Interior itself required parks to report under Burgum's own order.

estimated_impact.summary: NPCA President and CEO Theresa Pierno characterized the situation as predictable: 'This crisis was both predictable and preventable. Gutting staff, freezing seasonal hiring, and pushing out experienced rangers was a recipe for disaster.' Beyond visitor-experience impacts, several documented examples touch public safety and resource protection directly -- the loss of fire response capacity at Cumberland Island, halted pest/disease monitoring (including zoonotic disease surveillance for plague, rabies, and hantavirus) at Grand Canyon, and unstaffed entrance stations at Glacier National Park during normal operating hours.

Congressional Republicans overseeing NPS (Rep. Ryan Zinke, Rep. Tom Tiffany, Sen. Steve Daines) expressed confidence Secretary Burgum could adequately staff parks for the season, a genuinely different assessment from Democratic members and outside advocacy groups, worth presenting as a real point of disagreement among people with access to the same underlying situation, not just a one-sided finding.

Individual park examples (Assateague lifeguards, Cumberland Island fire team, Indiana Dunes tours) are specific, named, and quantified rather than general characterizations. Re-verified 2026-07-20: no evidence the underlying permanent-staffing crisis was addressed; 2026 seasonal hiring again missed its own target, though the target itself was smaller than 2025's (5,000+ vs. ~8,000), which somewhat complicates a direct year-over-year comparison -- cite the 2026 figures as their own data point rather than implying they're directly comparable in scale to 2025's. Re-verified 2026-07-26: the Yosemite specifics, international-visitor fee, and 600-position refill approval are corroborated by CNN, RV Lifestyle, and Modern Campground reporting on the 2026 peak season. Re-verified 2026-08-17: the FY2027 budget proposal figures ($736M cut, ~2,920 positions) are corroborated across NPCA, GearJunkie, and Outside; its not-yet-enacted, still-under-debate status and the January 2026 FY2026 precedent (Congress rejecting a similar cut, approving $3.267B flat funding with a mass-firing notification requirement) are corroborated via NPCA's own reporting. Re-verified 2026-08-30: the NPCA Day of Action (Aug. 22-Sept. 1, 2026, ~30 events/20 states+DC) is HIGH confidence, sourced directly to Newsweek's reporting on NPCA's own campaign materials; the additional grievances it cited (international-visitor pricing, Trump's image on the annual pass, historic-site content removal) were left unverified and out of scope for this entry's own core subject, consistent with this tracker's stay-tight-to-the-entry's-own-subject discipline. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): the May 20, 2026 House Appropriations Subcommittee action and the $2.9 billion/1.3% figures are corroborated via direct fetch of NPCA's own reporting on the subcommittee release -- HIGH confidence on the subcommittee-level action; the bill's subsequent full-House and Senate status was not independently re-checked as of this recheck. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog cluster c0430): the Assateague lifeguard shortage is corroborated independently by CBS News reporting from July 5, 2025, predating the internal Order-3426 report by three weeks -- HIGH confidence.

A proposed FY2027 budget (April 2026) would cut NPS operations by $736M/~25% and ~2,920 more positions; not yet enacted, and Congress rejected a comparable FY2026 cut proposal in January 2026. title: Tribes Lost Over $6 Million in Non-IHS Federal Health Grants and Technical Support Staff Despite RFK Jr.'s Promise to Protect Native American Health Funding
institution: HHS agencies outside the Indian Health Service (CDC, HRSA, and others)
status: Ongoing -- a third, distinct funding threat (ACA enhanced-subsidy expiration hitting tribal marketplace-coverage programs) identified alongside the original non-IHS grant cuts and the FY2026 IHS appropriations fight; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed for any of the three threads
date_of_action: 2025-02 through 2025-06 (cumulative grant cancellations and staffing losses reported)
what_changed: Despite HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stated commitment to protect Native American health funding by shielding the Indian Health Service (IHS) itself from cuts, tribes reported losing more than $6 million in grants from other HHS agencies -- funding that paid for community health workers, vaccinations, data modernization, and other public health efforts -- according to a May 2025 letter from the National Indian Health Board to Kennedy. The administration canceled funding for programs it classified as violating Trump's ban on diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, including a program supporting Native American youth interested in science and medicine careers and a program helping several tribes increase access to healthy food. Tribal health officials also reported that federal staffing cuts across HHS agencies made it substantially harder to get technical support and administer federally funded health projects, in some cases because specific staffers tribes had worked with directly were fired. Tribal leaders highlighted the contradiction between the administration's stated chronic-disease-prevention priority and its funding cuts, with one official noting it was 'very confusing to say chronic disease prevention is the No. 1 priority and then to eradicate the support needed to address chronic disease prevention in Indian Country.' Update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): the non-IHS pattern documented above continued into 2026 -- CDC's Healthy Tribes program (culturally tailored public health initiatives) was reported terminated, and further reductions were reported at SAMHSA (Tribal Behavioral Health and Opioid Response grants, Native Connections), HRSA, the Administration for Community Living, and NIH, with the administration's FY2026 budget proposal separately seeking to eliminate roughly $128 million in Tribal set-aside mental/behavioral health funding and the Food is Medicine program. On the IHS side specifically -- which RFK Jr.'s promise covered -- Congress rejected the administration's proposed nearly-30%/$900 million FY2026 IHS cut: the enacted FY2026 appropriations package instead increased IHS funding roughly 1.1-1.3% over FY2025 (about $8.05 billion total, plus $5.31 billion in FY2027 advance appropriations), including a $41 million boost to the Special Diabetes Program for Indians (its largest in 22 years) and a $5 million increase for Urban Indian Health. This means the entry's core distinction -- IHS protected, non-IHS agencies cut -- held up and sharpened over the following year: Congress affirmatively reinforced IHS funding while the non-IHS cuts this entry documents continued and expanded. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 39): identified a third, mechanically distinct funding threat missed by the entry's prior two updates -- the December 31, 2025 expiration of enhanced ACA marketplace subsidies has directly strained tribal health organizations' insurance-assistance programs, which help Native Americans access care outside limited IHS facilities. Tuba City Regional Health Care Corp. (Navajo Nation, Arizona) reported its patient-coverage costs rising roughly 170% to nearly $38,000/month without the enhanced subsidies; Fort Peck Tribes (Montana) said it is now 'limiting who gets help'; and Blackfeet Nation (Montana) paused employer-sponsored coverage for 52 people in January 2026. National Indian Health Board CEO A.C. Locklear warned that reduced access to general primary care compounds existing health disparities. This is a third, distinct mechanism from the entry's existing two threads (non-IHS HHS grant/staffing cuts, and the IHS budget-appropriations fight) -- it affects tribal organizations' own insurance-navigation and coverage-assistance programs rather than direct federal grants or IHS appropriations, and predates but was not previously captured by this entry's 2026-08-18 update. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): identified a fourth, mitigating funding thread not previously in this entry -- the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), a $50 billion, five-year CMS grant program created by HR1 itself (the same law whose Medicaid cuts this tracker's related entries document) and announced Dec. 29, 2025, with awards to all 50 states announced starting late January 2026, includes Tribal-specific set-asides or initiatives in at least 13 states' approved applications (AZ, CA, CO, MN, MT, NE, NM, NY, OK, OR, UT, WA, WI). Oregon's application, developed with its nine federally recognized Tribes, dedicates $21.7 million of the state's 2026 RHTP award specifically to a Tribal Initiative improving healthcare access in rural and remote Tribal communities. This is a distinct, positive-mitigation development running alongside -- not a reversal of -- the entry's existing three threads (non-IHS grant/staffing cuts, the IHS appropriations fight, and the ACA-subsidy marketplace strain); RHTP funds tribal-specific rural-health infrastructure and access initiatives, not the specific non-IHS programs (Healthy Tribes, SAMHSA behavioral-health grants, etc.) this entry documents as cut, so it does not offset those losses directly.

primary_proponent.note: Publicly promised to protect Native American health funding by shielding IHS from HHS-wide cuts, while cuts to non-IHS HHS agencies serving the same tribal communities proceeded; no single official was identified in reporting as directing each individual non-IHS grant cancellation.

estimated_impact.summary: Tribes lost over $6 million in HHS grants outside the Indian Health Service, plus DEI-flagged program cancellations and technical-support staffing losses, undercutting the administration's own stated promise to protect Native American health funding and directly contradicting its stated chronic-disease-prevention priority. Separately, a new $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program created by the same HR1 law includes Tribal-specific funding set-asides in at least 13 states, including a $21.7 million dedicated Tribal Initiative in Oregon for 2026 -- a mitigating funding stream running alongside, not offsetting, the cuts this entry otherwise documents.

title: Trump Administration Moves to Remove Supercomputers From NCAR, Disrupting Weather and Climate Research for 1,500+ Scientists
institution: National Science Foundation / National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)
status: Blocked as of June 1, 2026 -- a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction halting the transfer of the NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center's stewardship from UCAR to the University of Wyoming, following UCAR's March 2026 lawsuit alleging the plan was retaliation against Colorado; a second, distinct lawsuit filed August 20, 2026 by the Environmental Defense Fund separately challenges the planned closure of NCAR's Mesa Laboratory itself under the National Historic Preservation Act; both cases remain pending with no ruling on the merits identified as of this recheck
date_of_action: 2025-12-16 (first reporting of White House plan to 'break up' NCAR) through 2026-02-13 (NSF letter confirming supercomputer removal plan)
what_changed: Reporting first surfaced in mid-December 2025 that the administration was moving to dismantle the National Science Foundation's National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado -- a 60-plus-year cornerstone of U.S. weather and climate science -- with officials characterizing it as a source of "climate alarmism." The news broke via a post on X from OMB Director Russell Vought, with no advance warning to NCAR's own funder, NSF, or to the White House's usual channels for announcing agency actions; CNN reported the announcement landed in the middle of the American Geophysical Union's (AGU) annual meeting, where climate scientist Katherine Hayhoe wrote on Bluesky that 'NCAR is quite literally our global mothership... Dismantling NCAR is like taking a sledgehammer to the keystone holding up our scientific understanding of the planet.' AGU convened an emergency town hall of hundreds of scientists at the meeting in response, and on March 12, 2026 formally submitted comments to NSF opposing the dismantling proposal, arguing NCAR's integrated, interdisciplinary structure is what makes it irreplaceable and that the rushed timeline and limited stakeholder consultation fell short of standard governance practice. That earliest reporting specifically named NCAR's Mesa Laboratory campus as a target for shutdown, described plans to eliminate research programs internally labeled "woke," and indicated only select functions such as weather modeling would be transferred elsewhere rather than preserved intact. Following a January 2026 White House announcement of intent to 'break up' NCAR, an NSF letter released February 13, 2026 confirmed plans to remove NCAR's supercomputing facility and transfer its stewardship to the University of Wyoming, per subsequent reporting identifying the specific recipient this entry had previously left unnamed. The facility supports weather forecasting models, climate simulations, and extreme-weather prediction research used by approximately 1,500 researchers across more than 500 universities; NOAA itself relies on the facility to run some of its current forecasting models. Former NCAR director James Hurrell and other prominent colleagues in the weather and climate research community warned NSF that 'any path that leads to the fragmentation or dismantling of NSF NCAR is fundamentally not in the nation's interest,' and that the move could further set back NOAA's own weather-modeling capabilities, which the researchers noted have already lagged behind international competitors. On March 16, 2026, the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) -- the nonprofit consortium of 129 universities that manages NCAR -- sued the federal agencies and officials behind the breakup plan, alleging the effort was retaliation against Colorado: specifically, that the administration was using NCAR's dismantling to pressure the state over Gov. Jared Polis's refusal to grant clemency to Tina Peters, a former county clerk convicted of tampering with voting machines in pursuit of Trump's 2020 election-fraud claims, and over the state's broader resistance to ceding authority over its own elections. OMB Director Russell Vought had publicly framed the plan as 'breaking up' NCAR because it was 'one of the largest sources of climate alarmism in the country,' and a White House spokesperson told CNN that Colorado's treatment depended on having 'a governor who actually wanted to work with President Trump.' On June 1, 2026, U.S. District Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued a preliminary injunction blocking the administration from taking further steps to dismantle NCAR, a win for the researchers and UCAR that halted the removal plan pending further litigation. Update 2026-08-31: identified the specific institution NSF planned to transfer the NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center's stewardship to -- the University of Wyoming, which had offered to take over operations of the Cheyenne facility -- corroborated across DataCenterDynamics, AIP.org, and Courthouse News reporting on Judge R. Brooke Jackson's June 1, 2026 preliminary injunction; the ruling found NSF had announced the transfer more than a month before its own public-comment deadline and that officials' prior statements 'strongly suggest[ed] the outcome was predetermined,' making the reorganization arbitrary and capricious under the APA. No appeal of that injunction was identified in this recheck. Separately, a second, distinct lawsuit was filed August 20, 2026 in federal court in Colorado by the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF), unaffiliated with UCAR's suit, specifically challenging the administration's plan to close NCAR's Mesa Laboratory building -- the 1967, I.M. Pei-designed campus this entry's earliest reporting had named as an initial shutdown target. EDF's complaint adds a legal theory UCAR's suit did not raise: that closing the Mesa Laboratory without the environmental and public-consultation review required under the National Historic Preservation Act is unlawful, arguing the building -- while not currently listed on the National Register of Historic Places -- is eligible for listing given its architectural significance and the scientific discoveries made there. EDF seeks to block the closure and compel the required historic-preservation review; corroborated across EDF's own press release, Inside Climate News, E&E News, Boulder Reporting Lab, and BizWest. No ruling on EDF's suit was identified as of this recheck.

title: NCUA Board Reduced to a Single Member After Trump Fires Both Democratic Board Members
institution: National Credit Union Administration
status: Ongoing on a fast-track briefing schedule -- the D.C. Circuit deferred ruling on Harper and Otsuka's Fed-like-protection argument pending further briefing on how the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 Slaughter and Cook decisions apply to NCUA, then set a schedule (administration's brief due September 12, 2026; Harper/Otsuka reply due October 3; government reply due October 17; oral argument after briefing concludes) that could produce a ruling by year-end 2026; the two remain off the single-member board as of this update
date_of_action: 2025-04-15 (firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling narrowed path to reinstatement)
what_changed: In April 2025, President Trump fired both Democratic members of the National Credit Union Administration's three-person board -- former Chairman Todd Harper and Tanya Otsuka -- by email, without citing cause, leaving Republican Chair Kyle Hauptman as the sole remaining board member. Harper's term was not set to expire until April 2027 and Otsuka's not until August 2029. The Federal Credit Union Act defines the NCUA board as a three-member body with staggered six-year terms, structured (according to a subsequent district court finding) to mirror the Federal Reserve's governance model and insulate credit union regulation from political turnover. With only one board member, the NCUA could continue routine supervision and enforcement but could not vote on new rulemakings or policy changes; a scheduled board meeting was canceled. Harper and Otsuka sued; in July 2025 U.S. District Judge Amir Ali ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, finding Congress had deliberately restricted the president's removal power when it added fixed terms to the statute in 1978. The two briefly returned to a board meeting before an appeals court granted the administration an emergency stay, sidelining them again. The case was held in abeyance pending Trump v. Slaughter; when the Supreme Court ruled for the administration on June 29, 2026, credit-union trade groups and legal analysts concluded the ruling 'effectively ends' the Harper/Otsuka challenge, since the Federal Credit Union Act -- unlike the Federal Reserve Act -- contains no explicit 'for cause' removal language for the NCUA to lean on. Harper and Otsuka's attorneys have since asked the D.C. Circuit to let them argue the NCUA deserves Fed-like treatment given its similar market-regulatory structure, but as of this writing they remain off the board, which continues to operate with a single member. Update 2026-07-19: in a filing with the D.C. Circuit in mid-July 2026, Harper and Otsuka's attorneys formally argued NCUA deserves Federal Reserve-like removal protection, leaning on the district court's earlier finding that Congress deliberately modeled NCUA's governance structure on the Fed's -- the same distinction that succeeded for Cook but was rejected for MSPB's Harris. No ruling on this argument had issued as of this update; the appeal remains pending. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling identified yet on Harper and Otsuka's mid-July D.C. Circuit filing arguing for Fed-like removal protection; the appeal remains pending and the board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no ruling identified on Harper and Otsuka's mid-July D.C. Circuit filing arguing for Fed-like removal protection; their reply (due August 5, 2026 per the court's prior order) was not independently located, and no further D.C. Circuit action was found as of this update. The board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member. Update 2026-08-29 (real correction): the D.C. Circuit did not rule on the removal-protection argument directly. Instead, before the August 5 reply deadline, the court deferred consideration of Harper and Otsuka's motion and ordered the administration to explain by July 29 how the case should proceed in light of the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 Slaughter and Cook decisions, with Harper and Otsuka permitted to respond by August 5. Following that exchange, the D.C. Circuit set a fast-track briefing schedule: the administration's brief is due September 12, 2026; Harper and Otsuka's reply is due October 3; the government's reply is due October 17; oral argument will follow "the first appropriate date following the conclusion of briefing." Legal press described the expedited schedule as one that could produce a ruling by the end of 2026. Harper and Otsuka's central remaining argument is that NCUA falls within the narrow financial-regulator exception the Supreme Court recognized in Cook for the Federal Reserve, rather than the broader removal-power holding in Slaughter. The board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member pending this schedule.

title: NEA Terminates Over Half of Its Open Grants in a Single Weekend
institution: National Endowment for the Arts
status: Complete for terminated grants (effective May 31, 2025); the agency's proposed full elimination was not enacted as of the last-verified date, though grantmaking priorities remain altered under new leadership. A Nov. 2025 sector-wide survey found the cumulative effect on museums specifically still ongoing.
date_of_action: 2025-05-02 to 2025-05-12 (termination notices); leadership confirmed December 19, 2025
what_changed: On the evening of May 2, 2025, hours after the administration released a preliminary FY2026 budget proposing to eliminate the NEA entirely, the agency emailed termination or withdrawal notices to hundreds of grantees nationwide, affecting more than half of its open awards, in amounts ranging from $10,000 to $100,000, effective May 31, 2025. A second round of termination notices followed on May 12, 2025. Affected organizations spanned all 50 states, Puerto Rico, and Washington, D.C., including theaters, orchestras, literary magazines, and community arts programs. Some grantees whose projects appeared to match the NEA's own newly stated priorities were terminated anyway; California Symphony, for example, lost funding for a commission specifically written to celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, one of the NEA's own listed new priorities. On May 5, 2025, ten NEA discipline directors and two members of senior leadership announced they would take deferred resignation, departing by the end of May. Mary Anne Carter, who had led the NEA during Trump's first term, was serving as senior adviser overseeing the agency at the time the terminations were issued (the previous Biden-appointed chair, Maria Rosario Jackson, had resigned on Inauguration Day); Carter was confirmed by the Senate as permanent NEA Chair on December 19, 2025. Separately, a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down a related NEA policy disfavoring grant applications the agency deemed to 'promote gender ideology' on September 19, 2025. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog cluster c0703): a November 11, 2025 American Alliance of Museums survey found NEA was among the three federal grantmakers (alongside NEH and IMLS) most commonly cited by museums reporting lost federal funding since Trump took office -- see the museum-sector-wide survey findings in aam-survey-museum-funding-cuts-2025.json.

title: Nebraska becomes first state to opt into Trump's uncapped federal private-school tax credit
institution: U.S. Treasury (federal program) / Nebraska Governor's Office (state opt-in)
status: Ongoing (program launches 2027)
what_changed: Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order on September 29, 2025 opting the state into the federal Scholarship Tax Credit program created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, making Nebraska the first state to elect to participate. Under the program, individual taxpayers can direct up to $1,700 to a qualified scholarship-granting organization (SGO) and receive a full, dollar-for-dollar federal income tax credit in return; SGOs may keep up to 10% for administration and distribute the rest to families for K-12 education expenses, including private-school tuition. Families earning up to 300% of area median income qualify (roughly $228,000-$240,000 depending on county). The program is uncapped -- no limit exists on total participation or total federal tax revenue forgone -- and takes effect January 1, 2027; Pillen's order directs state agencies to help compile a list of qualified SGOs for Treasury ahead of that date. The move comes less than a year after Nebraska voters repealed two similar state-level private-school-scholarship laws (LB 753 and LB 1402) at the ballot box in November 2024.

title: National Endowment for Democracy Funding Withheld, Partially Restored Only After Court Order
institution: National Endowment for Democracy (funded via State Department appropriation)
status: Ongoing, with a real correction to this entry's funding-status framing -- FY2026 NED funding was fully enacted at $315 million (not merely 'recommended' as this entry previously stated) when President Trump signed the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 4779) on February 3, 2026; the D.C. Circuit appeal of the FY2025 withholding (docket 25-5361) remains separately pending
date_of_action: 2025-01-22 (funding access first denied) through ongoing litigation as of 2026
what_changed: Since January 22, 2025, the executive branch withheld the National Endowment for Democracy's (NED) access to congressionally appropriated funding, according to NED's federal lawsuit. NED, a nonprofit created by the 1983 National Endowment for Democracy Act, is statutorily directed to receive annual grants through the State Department; it distributes roughly 83% of its funds directly to democracy, free-press, and anti-corruption groups in more than 90 countries. NED sued in March 2025, alleging the withholding of nearly $240 million violated the Administrative Procedure Act, the NED Act, and constitutional separation-of-powers and appropriations provisions. The funding halt forced NED to furlough 75% of its staff and, per the lawsuit, created a 'devastating' cash flow crisis affecting 226 approved grants, 124 board-recommended grants, and 53 'core institute' projects. On August 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich -- a Trump appointee -- granted a preliminary injunction, finding the administration had likely violated the NED Act by conditioning fund disbursement on alignment with 'Administration priorities,' calling that rationale 'not plausible' given repeated delays and shifting justifications. Following the ruling, DOJ released the roughly $95 million that remained withheld from NED's FY2025 appropriation. The administration appealed to the D.C. Circuit on October 9, 2025 (case ongoing as of this writing), and separately proposed eliminating NED's funding entirely in its FY2026 budget request, citing (among other claims) an allegation -- which NED's own fact sheet disputes as false -- that NED funded a Ukrainian group accused of doxing U.S. journalists. As of early 2026 court filings, the parties remained in disputes over whether and when NED's FY2026 appropriation would be obligated and disbursed. title: National Endowment for the Humanities Grants Terminated, Staff Cut, Funds Redirected
institution: National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH)
status: Partially Reversed (grant terminations ruled unconstitutional and reinstatement process underway as of mid-2026; staff cuts and Council dissolution unaffected by the ruling)
date_of_action: 2025-04-02 (initial grant terminations) through 2025-10-01 (National Council on the Humanities firings)
what_changed: Beginning April 2025, NEH terminated more than 1,000 previously-awarded, congressionally-funded grants covering fiscal years 2021-2025, informing 56 state and jurisdiction humanities councils their funding was being 'repurposed in a new direction in furtherance of President Trump's agenda.' NEH then placed the majority of its staff on immediate administrative leave, followed by formal termination notices to 65% of its ~180 employees (about 117 people) in April 2025 -- letters described the cuts as necessary to comply with a Trump executive order directing DOGE to eliminate 'waste, bloat, and insularity.' NEH Chair Shelly C. Lowe, the first Native American to head the agency, was forced out about a month before the mass layoffs. In October 2025, during the government shutdown, all but 4 of the 26 members of the National Council on the Humanities (the body that advises NEH on funding priorities) were fired by email from the White House Office of Presidential Personnel. Separately, the 2025 tax-and-spending law directed NEH to contribute $40 million toward constructing Trump's proposed 'National Garden of American Heroes' sculpture garden -- redirecting endowment funds toward a specific administration priority rather than the competitive peer-reviewed grants the agency traditionally funds. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0621): after Trump forced Chair Lowe out, he named NEH general counsel Michael McDonald acting chairman, who began issuing non-competitive 'chairman's awards' bypassing the agency's traditional outside peer-review process -- an unprecedented degree to which chairman's awards came to dominate NEH's funding agenda, per reporting. The most prominent example: NEH awarded the Tikvah Fund, a conservative think tank, $10.4 million in September 2025 for a 'Jewish Civilization Project' to combat antisemitism -- the largest single grant in the agency's 60-year history, representing roughly 10% of NEH's total budget alongside one other large grantee. Tikvah's application had originally been rejected by NEH's own advisory council (before its October 2025 dissolution, documented above) over concerns the proposal was vague and too advocacy-focused, and Tikvah was not among the 97 projects in NEH's original August 1, 2025 funding announcement -- the grant was added separately on September 15, 2025, after that rejection. Beyond Tikvah, NEH's chairman's-award pattern directed more than $75 million toward projects reflecting the administration's ideological priorities, including $10 million each to two public universities' new 'civics' schools and to an education network headquartered at a conservative think tank, with funding overwhelmingly favoring Western-civilization, 'great books,' and other conservative-aligned humanities projects. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog cluster c0703): a November 11, 2025 American Alliance of Museums survey found NEH was among the three federal grantmakers (alongside NEA and IMLS) most commonly cited by museums reporting lost federal funding since Trump took office -- see the museum-sector-wide survey findings in aam-survey-museum-funding-cuts-2025.json. Update: On May 7, 2026, U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) ruled in American Council of Learned Societies v. NEH -- brought by ACLS, the American Historical Association, and the Modern Language Association -- that the mass termination of more than 1,400 grants was 'unlawful, unconstitutional, ultra vires, and without legal effect,' violating the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment's equal-protection component, and undertaken without statutory authority. NEH has since begun a reinstatement process: starting June 30, 2026, the agency began sending affected recipients a 'Reinstatement Assurances Form' asking whether they still want the award, disclosing any personnel changes since termination, confirming continued capacity to complete the project, and specifying whether a restart period or reimbursement is needed. This is not automatic restoration -- it functions closer to a new award action, requiring a fresh institutional review of personnel, budget, subrecipient status, and timeline for each grant. The ruling does not affect the separate staff terminations or the National Council on the Humanities dissolution described above.

The underlying policy direction traces to a Trump executive order tasking DOGE with eliminating 'waste, bloat, and insularity' in federal agencies. No single named individual was identified as personally directing the NEH-specific cuts beyond this White House personnel office role -- flag as a diffuse, White-House-directed action rather than one attributable official.

Terminated projects cited by name in reporting include an oral history archive of Tulsa Race Massacre survivors (Oklahoma), an initiative digitizing North Carolina Central University's historical records, an oral history project at Kennesaw State University, and a library renovation at the University of Missouri.

title: HHS Disbanded the Advisory Committee That Recommends Which Rare Genetic Diseases Are Screened for at Birth
institution: Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children (ACHDNC), Health Resources and Services Administration, Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing -- disbanded, no reinstatement identified in sourcing reviewed as of last verification, despite advocacy-organization and congressional requests
what_changed: HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children on April 3, 2025, citing compliance with a Trump executive order to shrink the federal government. The volunteer committee -- composed of medical geneticists, pediatricians, and public health experts -- recommends which rare genetic and metabolic conditions states should add to their newborn-screening panels, the heel-prick blood tests given to virtually every baby born in the U.S. The committee had been scheduled to meet in May 2025 to vote on adding two serious, treatable-if-caught-early conditions to the national Recommended Uniform Screening Panel: metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD) estimates roughly 450 babies are born with MLD or DMD combined each year in the U.S.; early detection is clinically significant for both conditions because available treatments are far more effective when started before symptoms appear. NORD and its network of 40 affiliated Rare Disease Centers of Excellence sent HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. a letter demanding the committee's immediate reinstatement. On August 1, 2025, Rep. Kelly Morrison led a congressional letter to Kennedy pressing for an explanation of the decision and its rare-disease impact. No sourcing reviewed as of this entry's addition indicates the committee has been reinstated or that a replacement process for evaluating new conditions has been established.

primary_proponent.note: HHS, under Kennedy, terminated the committee April 3, 2025, citing the administration's government-downsizing executive order; the decision was not publicly announced in advance and was first reported by the Boston Globe and NBC News rather than via an HHS press release.

title: A Deliberate Biocontainment-Suit Sabotage Shut Down One of the Nation's Few BSL-4 Ebola Research Labs -- Which Remains Closed and Deprioritized Nearly a Year Later
institution: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) / National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Closed since a complete operational halt announced May 7, 2025; as of March 2026, Maryland's congressional delegation continues pressing the administration for answers, and reporting indicates NIAID has restructured the facility under its Division of Intramural Research and is deprioritizing biodefense/pandemic-preparedness research generally, beyond the original safety incident.
date_of_action: 2025-04-29 (initial safety stand-down) through 2026-03 (ongoing congressional pressure over the facility's status and NIAID's broader deprioritization of biodefense research)
what_changed: On April 29, 2025, HHS ordered a 'safety stand-down' halting all experimental work at NIAID's Integrated Research Facility (IRF) at Fort Detrick, Maryland -- one of a small number of biosafety-level-4 labs in the country equipped to study Ebola, Lassa fever, and other lethal high-consequence pathogens. The trigger was a violent altercation between two contract staff: one allegedly deliberately cut a hole in a co-worker's biocontainment suit during a personal dispute, compromising the suit's protective seal and creating a real risk of pathogen exposure. On May 7, 2025, newly appointed NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya -- who said he had decided to shut the facility down shortly after taking office in March 2025 -- announced a complete halt to all operations, stating the lab 'will not reopen until I am satisfied it is safe.' Testifying before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee (reported May 14, 2025), HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. confirmed the FBI had been brought in to investigate, telling Sen. Rand Paul the incident 'appears like it was a deliberate criminal act that was kind of equivalent to attempted murder.' The facility's director was placed on administrative leave. Maryland's full congressional delegation (Sens. Van Hollen and Alsobrooks, Reps. McClain Delaney and Elfreth, among others) sent HHS and NIH multiple letters beginning in June 2025 demanding a detailed accounting of the facility's status, the underlying safety failures, and the national-security implications of the prolonged closure of one of the country's few facilities capable of this research. By March 2026, the delegation was still pressing for answers, and reporting indicated NIAID had restructured the IRF under its Division of Intramural Research and was more broadly deprioritizing biodefense and pandemic-preparedness research -- developments the lawmakers characterized as extending well beyond what the original safety incident alone would require.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.; Dr. Jay Bhattacharya
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services; Director, National Institutes of Health
primary_proponent.note: Bhattacharya made the operational decision to fully halt the facility and has stated it will not reopen until he is personally satisfied it is safe; Kennedy publicly confirmed the FBI investigation and characterized the underlying incident's severity in Senate testimony. This entry's subject is the closure and its prolonged aftermath, not an allegation that either official caused the underlying safety incident -- the alleged sabotage was carried out by contract staff, not administration officials.

estimated_impact.summary: The shutdown removed the United States' operational capacity at one of a small number of BSL-4 facilities equipped to study Ebola, Lassa fever, and other high-consequence pathogens, for nearly a year and counting as of this writing, at a time global health officials were already warning about degraded U.S. disease-surveillance and outbreak-response capacity (see this database's separate entries on USAID's dismantlement and CDC/bird-flu surveillance cuts). The underlying trigger -- an alleged intentional biocontainment-suit sabotage risking real pathogen exposure -- is itself a serious biosafety failure independent of any administration policy; the accountability concern this entry documents is the prolonged, still-unresolved closure and subsequent institutional deprioritization of biodefense research that followed it, which Maryland's congressional delegation says has gone beyond what addressing the safety incident itself would require, with limited public transparency into the facility's remediation timeline or reopening criteria.

The accountability question this entry documents is narrower: the prolonged closure's duration, the limited public transparency into remediation and reopening criteria despite repeated congressional inquiries, and reporting that the facility's mission has been restructured and deprioritized in ways that go beyond addressing the specific safety failure.

title: NIH's Research Hospital Saw Patient Numbers Fall to a Fraction of Pre-Pandemic Levels Amid Staff Losses and an Immigration Crackdown
institution: NIH Clinical Center
status: Reported ongoing as of August 2025; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-01 (visitor policy change and workforce departures begin) through 2025-07 (most recent reported figures)
what_changed: CBS News reported August 19, 2025 that patient numbers at the NIH Clinical Center -- the federal government's dedicated research hospital, which treats cancer, rare-disease, bone marrow transplant, and infectious-disease patients, often as their last remaining treatment option -- fell sharply during the first months of the second Trump administration. The hospital's average daily census ran 60 to 80 patients from February through April 2025, versus roughly 80 in October 2024 and more than 110 daily before the pandemic; April 2025 alone showed a 5.7% year-over-year decline. Cancer clinical-trial enrollment was down approximately 20% by July 2025 compared to the prior year, outpatient visits were down 8.5% year-over-year through April 2025, and new patients overall fell 6.7% to roughly 3,370 people. HHS fired more than 1,200 NIH employees in 2025, with additional departures through early retirement and voluntary exits, including bioethics department leader Christine Grady and former Clinical Center CEO James Gilman, who led the hospital from 2017 until leaving in January 2025 and was succeeded by acting CEO Pius Aiyelawo. Acting CEO Aiyelawo attributed part of the enrollment decline directly to departing investigators no longer recruiting patients into trials, compounding the effect of cancelled grants and delayed research supplies documented elsewhere in this database's NIH-related entries. Separately, a new visitor policy launched in late January 2025 requiring non-citizens to register online, implemented alongside the administration's broader immigration-enforcement operations, coincided with international patients avoiding the hospital; one departing clinician told CBS News 'international patients are terrified to come,' citing fear over 'what will happen to them.'

title: NIH Let Contract-Staff Work Orders Lapse and Was Ordered to Cut $2.6 Billion (35%) in Contracts -- Hitting Nearly Half Its Workforce
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Ongoing as of last verification -- contract cancellations continued through 2025 with no reported reversal; a May 2025 Science/AAAS report puts the actual scale of contract-staff job loss at roughly 2,200 contractors NIH-wide since January 2025, resolving the entry's prior LOWER-confidence anecdotal estimate
date_of_action: 2025-01 (communication freeze begins, contract renewals stall) through 2025-04 (formal 35% contract-cut order and initial implementation)
what_changed: Starting when the Trump administration took office in January 2025, NIH allowed a growing number of contract-staff work orders to lapse without renewal, effectively ending those positions -- NOTUS reported this on March 20, 2025, noting contract staff make up nearly half of NIH's total workforce. The lapses stemmed in part from a since-lifted Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) communications freeze imposed at the start of the administration: contract renewals require NIH to communicate with the outside contracting agencies that formally employ and insure NIH's contract staff, and NOTUS found that communication remained effectively stalled even after the freeze was formally lifted in February. A contract employee at NIH's Vaccine Research Center told NOTUS they personally knew of roughly 10 colleagues whose contracts had recently expired and gone unrenewed -- an early, anecdotal data point NOTUS could not yet size against the full workforce. The lapses were followed by a formal directive: on April 3, 2025, Science reported the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had ordered NIH to eliminate $2.6 billion in contracts, requiring each of NIH's 27 institutes and centers to cut contract spending by roughly 35% by April 8, 2025 -- part of a broader HHS-wide DOGE directive (reported separately by NOTUS) to cut $13.6 billion in annual contract spending across the department. NIH contracts fund staff scientists, clinical-trial support at universities, biospecimen repositories, and long-term health studies; an NIH official told Science a 35% cut would be 'devastating' given how much of the fiscal year's contract funding had already been committed. By the time of that reporting, a DOGE-linked contract-cut tracking site showed NIH had already cut more than 400 contracts totaling about $780 million, including funding for biospecimen repositories and long-term health-study support. A May 11, 2025 Science/AAAS follow-up, reporting on the Vaccine Research Center specifically, put a number on the scale NOTUS's March 2025 reporting could only estimate anecdotally: data shared with staff at one NIH institute showed the contractor purge had reached roughly 2,200 contract workers agency-wide since January 2025 -- rivaling the ~2,500 federal staff lost to two rounds of layoffs since mid-February. At the Vaccine Research Center itself, one immunology lab had lost 40% of its workers and stopped developing antibody tests for some future clinical trials.
