title: NIH Strips DEI Requirements From Grant Applications, Then Terminates $783M in Active Grants on Disfavored Topics
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Ongoing (Supreme Court allowed the $783M in terminations to proceed Aug. 21, 2025 while the underlying guidance documents remain vacated by a lower court; NIH settled in Dec. 2025 to reconsider some frozen/denied grants, but its director said in the same period that grants already restored under court order would not be renewed; NIH continued issuing new topic-based terminations into August 2026, cancelling a further $15M combined across Emory and University of Pittsburgh Alzheimer's/discrimination research grants)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial grant terminations begin) through 2026-01 (settlement on reconsidering stalled grants)
what_changed: Starting in late February 2025, NIH began terminating active research grants tied to topics the administration classified as DEI, gender identity, LGBTQ+ health, or vaccine hesitancy, eventually withholding or terminating $783 million across dozens of active awards. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0498: among those terminated in May 2025 was a five-year grant to UC San Diego imaging scientist Uri Manor, who was born with congenital severe-to-profound hearing loss and was studying the cellular mechanisms of hearing loss to develop new treatments; Manor had qualified for the funding through a National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders program supporting researchers with disabilities, and had already spent $1.5 million of the award over two years before its cancellation forced him to halt long-running experiments and lay off lab staff. On March 25, 2025, NIH separately notified staff it was eliminating DEI-related requirements from grant and conference-funding applications going forward: applicants would no longer need to submit 'Plans for Enhancing Diverse Perspectives,' 'Recruitment Plans to Enhance Diversity,' or 'Trainee Diversity Reports,' diversity plans would no longer be evaluated in funding decisions, and training-data tables used in review were revised to drop calculations of the percentage of underrepresented minorities. On April 21, 2025, NIH went further, publishing a notice amending the civil-rights provisions of the NIH Grants Policy Statement to require institutions receiving new, renewal, supplement, or continuation awards to certify they do not operate DEI programs 'in violation of Federal anti-discrimination laws' and are not boycotting Israel, on pain of termination and clawback of funds -- a condition industry commentary (FierceBiotech) characterized as NIH asserting authority to override how recipients interpret their own obligations under the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In June 2025, U.S. District Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled the terminations violated the Administrative Procedure Act, finding NIH had unlawfully targeted research on 'disfavored' topics and populations -- including training grants meant to diversify the biomedical research pipeline -- without adequately defining what 'DEI' meant or weighing the grants' value, and calling the terminations 'racial discrimination, and discrimination against America's LGBTQ community' on the record; he ordered the funding reinstated. The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stay that order, and on August 21, 2025, the Court allowed the $783 million in terminations to proceed while the case continued, even as Judge Young's ruling vacating NIH's underlying guidance documents themselves remained in effect below. NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya (confirmed by the Senate March 25, 2025 -- the same day as the initial application-requirement change, though sworn in April 1 and not in office for the February terminations) said on December 31, 2025 that DEI-related grants restored to plaintiffs under the court order would not be renewed once their current funding cycles ended. Days earlier, on December 29, 2025, NIH separately settled a related suit by agreeing to reconsider a batch of frozen and denied DEI-related grant applications -- reported in January 2026 (Government Executive) as the administration agreeing to drop anti-DEI evaluation criteria for that specific stalled-grant backlog, distinct from the $783 million already terminated and litigated separately. Update 2026-08-17: the termination campaign continued into August 2026 -- on August 4, 2026, Bhattacharya notified the University of Pittsburgh that a five-year, $9.6 million grant to social epidemiologist Tamara Dubowitz studying cognitive aging and Alzheimer's risk among African Americans in poor Pittsburgh neighborhoods, with $7 million already spent, would be terminated in full, part of a stated shift toward 'measurable health outcomes' and away from health-disparities framing in NIH's funding priorities. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 35): the August 2026 wave was broader than the single Pittsburgh/Dubowitz grant already documented -- Bhattacharya's letters also terminated a second, separate University of Pittsburgh grant (Andrea Rosso and Ann Cohen, studying racial discrimination's links to Alzheimer's diagnosis and other sociologically-driven dementia risk factors) and a National Institute of Mental Health grant to Emory University clinical neuropsychologist Negar Fani, a five-year study (awarded December 2024) examining how racial discrimination affects white-matter brain microstructure in 220 Black volunteers via wearable devices and MRI. Fani's team had been told as recently as June 5, 2026 that its second year of funding was approved, then was notified by the end of July 2026 that the grant was cancelled. NIH's termination notice for the Emory grant stated the research's discrimination measure was 'subjective and problematic' and that studying only Black participants 'seriously limits possible comparisons and controls and does not seem scientifically justified' -- an explicit NIH rationale for why race-specific health-disparities research itself fails its new 'measurable health outcomes' standard, not just a funding-priority reshuffling. Combined, Science/AAAS and The Week/Yahoo report the Emory and Pittsburgh cuts announced in this wave total $15 million. Separately, the Supreme Court's August 2025 ruling in this case -- previously described in this entry without a case name -- is identified in legal commentary (Ogletree, Crowell & Moring, The Arc) as NIH v. APHA; the ruling itself created a jurisdictional split (Justice Jackson dissenting) under which challenges to NIH's underlying guidance continue in district court while claims seeking restoration of terminated grant funding must be filed separately in the Court of Federal Claims, a more burdensome path for affected researchers. The First Circuit heard oral argument on the broader guidance challenge in January 2026 but had not ruled as of this recheck (a separate First Circuit ruling that same month, upholding the block on NIH's indirect-cost-rate cap, is a related but distinct case and should not be conflated with this still-pending DEI-guidance appeal).

NIH's own director has stated publicly that restoration under the court order is not being treated as a durable outcome -- grants reinstated by Judge Young's order will not be renewed going forward, meaning the practical effect of the litigation win for affected researchers is temporary continuation, not a reversal of NIH's underlying policy direction.

A federal judge ruled the terminations illegal and discriminatory in June 2025 (the case is NIH v. title: NIH Halted New Foreign Subawards, Then Replaced Them With a New 'Linked Award' Structure -- Threatening Billions in International Research During the Transition
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: New 'linked award' structure required for all new international collaborations as of September 25, 2025 (replacing the halted foreign-subaward mechanism); the underlying international research relationships are not banned, but the four-and-a-half-month transition gap (May 1-September 25, 2025) disrupted ongoing renewals and new international collaborations
date_of_action: 2025-05-01 (foreign-subaward halt takes effect, per NIH notice NOT-OD-25-104) through 2025-09-25 (NIH stops accepting the old subaward structure entirely, forcing all new international work through the replacement mechanism)
what_changed: Effective May 1, 2025, NIH's grants policy office issued notice NOT-OD-25-104 barring any new, renewal, or non-competing continuation award -- to either a domestic or foreign entity -- that includes a subaward to a foreign entity, citing 'a need to maintain national security' alongside tracking and oversight concerns about how U.S. research funds flow to foreign institutions once passed through a domestic prime awardee. STAT News and Science|Business reported the halt threatened roughly $500 million a year in the foreign subawards NIH typically distributes, and 'billions of dollars' cumulatively across ongoing global-health projects, infectious-disease and cancer clinical trials, and university partnerships across Europe and elsewhere. The New York Times reported May 15, 2025 that researchers warned specific projects could be derailed, including breast-cancer research that depends on unique Danish patient-data and tissue-sample registries with no equivalent domestic source. Rather than a permanent ban on international collaboration, NIH announced in September 2025 a replacement award structure -- effective September 25, 2025, ahead of Fiscal Year 2026 -- eliminating the subaward mechanism itself: instead of a domestic principal investigator's subaward flowing on to a foreign partner, NIH now issues separate but coordinated 'linked' awards directly to each domestic and foreign principal investigator under one multi-project funding opportunity, with foreign researchers becoming prime awardees in their own right rather than subcontractors. The policy is prospective, not retroactive -- already-active awards continue unaffected unless and until they come up for renewal or a non-competing continuation -- but any project needing to renew, add a new foreign component, or start new international collaborative work during the roughly five-month gap between the May halt and the September relaunch faced a genuine funding and administrative disruption, with institutions' own research offices (UC Santa Cruz, Boston University, University of Utah, Case Western Reserve, Weill Cornell, among others) issuing guidance warning affected researchers of the gap.

institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: GAO Legal Finding Issued (nonbinding; underlying funding dispute partially reversed, full compliance unconfirmed)
date_of_action: 2025-08-05 (GAO report issued); underlying actions Feb 2025 - Dec 2025
what_changed: Following Trump executive orders in early 2025 targeting DEI and 'gender ideology' funding, NIH terminated more than 1,800 previously-awarded research grants and, separately, obligated roughly $8 billion less in new/continuing grant funding between February and June 2025 than in the same period the prior year -- a drop of more than a third. NIH also paused grant review meetings entirely from late January to early March 2025, delaying funds to hospitals and universities -- NPR reported on February 22, 2025 that this freeze alone had stalled roughly 16,000 pending grant applications worth about $1.5 billion, as the administration blocked the Federal Register notices required to schedule the review meetings. Separately, on February 24, 2025, NPR reported the administration's plan to cap NIH's reimbursement rate for research institutions' indirect costs (overhead such as facilities and administrative support) at 15%, down from a historical rate as high as 56% at some institutions -- a change research universities warned would force layoffs and halt projects even where direct grant funding remained intact, since indirect-cost reimbursement funds much of the physical and administrative infrastructure research depends on. An earlier, larger staffing figure was reported on April 28, 2025: outlets described NIH as having 1,300 staff fired by that point, with $2 billion in research grants cancelled and ongoing clinical trials for Alzheimer's, cancer, and stroke treatments halted -- a snapshot that predates and is not necessarily consistent with (may reflect a different scope or a since-revised count from) the more specifically sourced 250-employee May 6 figure below. NIH's funding contraction had a direct staffing dimension too: CBS News reported NIH issued surprise layoff notices to nearly 250 employees on May 6, 2025, including about 50 from the National Cancer Institute specifically. On June 13, 2025, more than 60 NIH employees signed a public letter, the Bethesda Declaration, condemning the administration's health policies as unethical, politically driven, and dangerous -- accusing leadership of censoring science, cutting billions from NIH's budget, halting over 1,300 grants, and endangering patients in ongoing clinical trials, an internal-dissent episode directly reflecting the funding and grant-termination pattern this entry documents. The pattern continued into the funding-mechanism itself later in the year: the New York Times reported that in December 2025, Trump ordered NIH and NSF to issue multi-year grants as upfront lump sums rather than the traditional annual-installment structure, a change that depleted available budgets faster and resulted in roughly 40% fewer new projects funded, alongside mass delays and grant cancellations reported as politically motivated by affected researchers. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan congressional watchdog, concluded on August 5, 2025 that the original 2025 funding actions violated the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which requires the executive branch to spend congressionally appropriated funds unless it follows a specific legal process to formally request a rescission -- a process NIH/HHS did not use. GAO noted HHS had taken down a public spending-tracking website, which itself hampered GAO's ability to investigate. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0520): a peer-reviewed study published in JAMA Internal Medicine and reported by AP News in November 2025 quantified the trial-level disruption this funding contraction caused -- of 11,008 NIH-funded clinical trials the researchers tracked, 383 (about 1 in 30) lost funding between late February and mid-August 2025, affecting more than 74,000 enrolled participants studying cancer, heart disease, brain disease, and infectious diseases including flu, pneumonia, and COVID-19. The disruption took several forms: some trials never began after participants had already enrolled, some participants lost access to medication or were left with an unmonitored device implant, and some completed trials never had their results published. A concrete instance of this pattern: in fall 2025, the National Cancer Institute told the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium -- a network of 16 children's hospitals -- that its roughly $4 million in annual NCI funding would end when the current award expires in March 2026; the consortium responded by halting enrollment in its six active trials, including a CAR T-cell therapy trial for ependymoma and a minimally invasive laser-ablation trial, before that expiration date. NCI's stated plan is to shift pediatric early-phase trials to a broader existing network (the Pediatric Early Phase Clinical Trials Network under the Children's Oncology Group), but the consortium's own chair said the transition would not be seamless and some patients would likely lose access to trials in the interim.

title: NIH Terminates 33+ Grants Studying Vaccine Hesitancy Amid a Growing Measles Outbreak
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Terminations themselves ruled unlawful by a district court over a year before this entry was written, with a mixed and still-unresolved appellate outcome -- not simply "finalized." On June 16, 2025, Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled NIH's grant-termination directives -- covering vaccine hesitancy, DEI, gender identity, and other disfavored topics -- "void and illegal" under the APA and ordered roughly 900 grants held by the named plaintiffs reinstated. On August 21, 2025, the Supreme Court granted a partial stay: it left intact the district court's finding that the directives themselves violated the APA, but ruled the district court likely lacked jurisdiction to order reinstatement of the grants directly (a Tucker Act/Court of Federal Claims jurisdictional question), a mixed outcome for both sides. The First Circuit heard oral argument on the preliminary injunction appeal January 6, 2026; litigation remains ongoing on two tracks (district court merits and the First Circuit appeal), with no final resolution identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update. Whether the specific 33+ vaccine-hesitancy grants this entry documents are among the ~900 plaintiff grants covered by the reinstatement order, and their current funding/operational status as of August 2026, were not confirmed in sourcing reviewed.
what_changed: NIH abruptly terminated at least 33 research grants funding studies of why people are hesitant to receive vaccines and what strategies improve vaccine uptake, with an additional 9 grants flagged for modification or further cuts, after the agency adopted a policy stating it would no longer 'prioritize research activities that focus on gaining scientific knowledge on why individuals are hesitant to be vaccinated and/or explore ways to improve vaccine interest and commitment.' Affected researchers, including one whose work had identified a genuine vaccine safety signal, were notified their studies were being cut off mid-stream, an unusual mechanism for ending federally funded research already underway. The terminations came as HHS was newly led by vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and coincided with a Texas-originated measles outbreak that had grown to over 300 cases and at least one death by the time of the cuts, drawing criticism from public health researchers that the timing undercut exactly the kind of research needed to counter vaccine-preventable disease spread. The Center for Science in the Public Interest, ACLU, and Protect Democracy Project sued NIH and HHS on April 2, 2025 over what they characterized as unlawful, politically driven grant cancellations; as of early 2026 the case was on appeal, with oral argument held January 6, 2026. Update (2026-08-17 recheck): this entry, written August 11, 2026, originally described the terminations as simply "finalized" -- but a district court had already ruled the underlying termination directives unlawful more than a year earlier. On June 16, 2025, Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled in American Public Health Association v. NIH that NIH's directives -- which the court found had terminated roughly $1 billion in grants across categories including vaccine hesitancy, DEI, gender identity, and race-related health research -- were "arbitrary and capricious" and void under the Administrative Procedure Act; Young further found evidence of racial discrimination in the terminations he called, in his 40 years on the bench, among the most "palpable" he had seen. The ruling ordered roughly 900 grants held by the case's named plaintiffs reinstated -- a subset of the estimated 2,300 grants NIH terminated administration-wide, not a reinstatement of every terminated grant nationwide. The First Circuit denied the government's request to stay Young's order on July 18, 2025. On August 21, 2025, the Supreme Court granted the government a partial stay: a 5-4 majority left intact the district court's APA conclusion that the directives themselves were unlawful, but ruled the district court likely lacked jurisdiction to order the grants reinstated directly, since grant-funding disputes may belong in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act rather than district court -- a mixed ruling that left the underlying policy void as illegal while complicating the remedy. The First Circuit separately heard oral argument on the case's preliminary-injunction appeal on January 6, 2026 (already reflected in this entry's original text); no decision in that specific appeal was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update. Note: a separate First Circuit ruling on January 5, 2026 (one day earlier) in APLU v. NIH unanimously struck down NIH's 15% cap on facilities-and-administrative cost reimbursement -- a different NIH policy dispute with a different plaintiff group; it is not the same case or ruling as the vaccine-hesitancy grant-termination litigation this entry covers, and should not be conflated with it despite the near-identical dates. Separately, under a related stipulation agreement, NIH agreed to evaluate more than 5,000 stalled or previously rejected funding applications in the "ordinary course" of its scientific review process, without applying the challenged directives. Whether the specific 33+ vaccine-hesitancy grants named in this entry are among the ~900 plaintiff grants covered by Young's reinstatement order, and whether those grants are currently funded and operating as of August 2026 or have lapsed again amid the ongoing jurisdictional dispute, were not confirmed in sourcing reviewed -- this entry should be rechecked specifically for that operational-status question when clearer sourcing becomes available. Re-verified 2026-08-29: no First Circuit ruling identified on the January 6, 2026 oral argument in the preliminary-injunction appeal. The Georgetown Health Care Litigation Tracker's most recent entry for this case is a March 19, 2026 defendants' response to a notice of supplemental authority, with briefing described as ongoing; no docket activity or ruling was identified between then and this update. The operational status of the specific 33+ vaccine-hesitancy grants named in this entry remains unconfirmed in sourcing reviewed.

title: NIH Fired 11 of Its Most Senior Neuroscience Lab Heads -- Including a Breakthrough Prize Winner -- in a Reduction-in-Force Attributed to a 'Coding Error,' Kept Them Terminated for Seven Weeks While RFK Jr. Told Congress No Scientists Had Been Fired
institution: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH/HHS)
status: Reversed -- HHS formally revoked all 30 reduction-in-force notices on May 21, 2025, before the June 2, 2025 termination date took effect
date_of_action: 2025-04-01/02 (RIF notices issued) through 2025-05-21 (formal revocation)
what_changed: On April 1-2, 2025, as part of the Trump administration's broader HHS-wide reduction in force under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., 30 employees at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) received reduction-in-force (RIF) notices, including 11 of the institute's most senior lab heads and distinguished investigators: Richard Youle, Miguel Holmgren, Steve Jacobson, Dorian McGavern, Joseph Mindell, Katherine Roche, Zu-Hang Sheng, David R. Sibley, Kenton Swartz, Susan Wray, and Ling-Gang Wu, plus senior associate scientist Silvina Horowitz. Youle, at NIH since 1978 and winner of the $3 million 2021 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for identifying a cellular mechanism behind Parkinson's disease, was among those terminated. NIH and HHS officials later attributed the firings to a 'coding error' in the RIF process that swept up senior investigators who were not supposed to be included. Despite verbal reassurances from NIH leadership, including Director Jay Bhattacharya, that the layoffs would be rescinded, the RIF notices remained formally in effect for seven weeks. On May 14, 2025, testifying before the Senate health committee, Kennedy stated, 'As far as I know, we have not fired any working scientists... our policy was to make sure none of them were lost and that that research continues' -- a claim contradicted by the NINDS scientists' still-active termination notices at the time he made it. HHS did not formally revoke the RIF notices until May 21, 2025, via email, days before the scheduled June 2 termination date. The 11 affected labs employed roughly 100 total staff, described by reporting as mainly young trainees whose research and career trajectories were disrupted during the seven-week uncertainty. After news of his firing broke, Youle received four outside job offers, three of them from institutions abroad.

what_changed: On February 21, 2025, the New York Times reported layoffs and buyouts had already cut about 20% of staffing at the World Trade Center Health Program specifically, jeopardizing research grants and delaying certifications critical to treating 9/11 responders and survivors -- a cut initially reinstated after pushback from lawmakers and veterans' groups, though the program's staffing crisis recurred and deepened in the following months as described below. Beginning February 20, 2025, Trump administration cuts began hitting NIOSH more broadly, the CDC institute responsible for occupational safety and health research. Early casualties included Patrick Montague, an investigator for the National Firefighter Registry for Cancer, fired along with colleagues in his program citing probationary status. By April 3, 2025, hundreds of NIOSH staff had been fired, including key personnel from the World Trade Center Health Program -- which provides medical care to 9/11 first responders and survivors -- and the program's longtime director, Dr. John Howard, was also removed. By April 13, the Guardian reported the WTC Health Program had been plunged into disarray, with cancer treatment, PTSD care, and other services for 9/11 survivors and first responders disrupted with no public transparency about what coverage remained available. Wired reported April 18, 2025 that the cuts had eliminated roughly two-thirds of the staff at NIOSH's Morgantown, West Virginia lab specifically, leaving thousands of biological specimens -- including human urine samples, rodent brains, and diseased lung tissue used to study black lung disease and other occupational illnesses, some requiring ultra-cold storage to remain viable -- with no clear plan for maintenance or preservation, according to laid-off researchers who warned the samples were at risk of degrading or being lost entirely, along with decades of accumulated exposure and disease data. By April 22, ProPublica reported the purge had eliminated 7 of the 8 members of NIOSH's firefighter fatality investigation team, halting major studies into firefighter cancer risk alongside the WTC-program disruption. On May 12, more than 100 current and former NIOSH employees sent a joint letter to Congress warning that mass purges were putting American workers at risk, stating more than 90% of NIOSH staff had received layoff notices and that critical programs -- the 9/11 Health Program and black lung screening among them -- had already been disrupted. By May 27, the Guardian confirmed an 85% NIOSH staff purge, with only a fraction of positions reinstated after public backlash. By early June, Reuters reported the cuts -- nearly 900 staff purged in April alone -- were forcing shutdowns of occupational-safety training programs specifically serving fishermen, farmers, and loggers, among America's most dangerous occupations, with key training centers warning they would run out of funding by summer or fall 2025. Update, 2026-08-17: two later developments clarify how this crisis evolved. First, the WTC Health Program's separate, longstanding funding-formula shortfall -- which periodically threatened the program's ability to pay for care independent of the 2025 NIOSH staffing purge -- was permanently fixed via a bipartisan provision (led by Rep. Andrew Garbarino, Speaker Mike Johnson, Rep. Brett Guthrie, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, and Sen. Chuck Schumer) in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), signed by President Trump February 3, 2026, securing funding through 2040. This resolves the funding-formula problem specifically; it does not restore the staff this entry documents being purged in 2025. Second, on the staffing side, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in April 2026 he was 'fixing' the WTC Health Program's problems, but reporting found only four job vacancies had actually been posted against the program's need. A bipartisan, bicameral letter led by Sen. Gillibrand and Rep. Garbarino, sent July 10, 2026 ahead of the September 2026 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, urged Kennedy to reappoint Dr. John Howard to a new six-year term as NIOSH director and WTC Health Program administrator, while acknowledging HHS had taken 'recent steps' on staffing shortages, delayed research grants, and pending petitions for additional covered conditions -- language consistent with the vacancy rate cited above, not with the crisis being over.

title: NIST workforce reduction and standards/research budget cuts
institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology (Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing, with a partial reversal on MEP specifically and a still-unresolved GAO investigation request -- after issuing RIF notices to the entire program's staff despite full congressional funding, NIST released a Notice of Funding Opportunity in July 2026 for 14 MEP centers (applications closed Aug. 21, 2026, outcome not yet announced) and, separately, resolved a distinct funding gap at 12 of 13 other state MEP centers by early July 2026 (Colorado still pending); NIST also launched a new $40 million MEP pilot program in June 2026 even as the elimination proposal and RIF notices this entry documents remain in effect, while the Coons-led congressional inquiry into the earlier RIF action and the Cantwell/Peters-requested GAO investigation both remain unanswered
date_of_action: 2025-02 to 2026-01 (workforce cuts); FY2026 budget proposal released June 2025
what_changed: NIST, the 125-year-old nonregulatory agency that sets the country's measurement, cybersecurity, and technology standards (including the widely used Cybersecurity Framework, the AI Risk Management Framework, and post-quantum encryption standards), lost more than 700 positions between the start of the Trump administration and January 2026 through resignations, retirements, and voluntary deferments, including roughly 500 recent hires who were let go early in 2025 while still in probationary status. A lab responsible for testing and validating the federal government's encryption implementations lost 89 staff. On March 26, 2025, the administration moved to eliminate NIST's Atomic Spectroscopy Group, which maintains atomic measurement data used as a foundational reference across nuclear fusion, astrophysics, and semiconductor-manufacturing research nationwide -- a specific, named-program elimination distinct from and in addition to the broader probationary and encryption-lab losses already documented in this entry. The administration's FY2026 budget request proposed cutting NIST's $1.2 billion budget by $325 million, eliminating the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership Program entirely (97 positions, $175 million, serving small and mid-size manufacturers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico) and cutting $125 million and 556 positions from NIST's core Scientific and Technical Research and Services program, citing cybersecurity/privacy, health and biological measurements, and physical-infrastructure research as target areas. House appropriators later rejected the steepest of these cuts and restored funding above the administration's request, but the agency has already absorbed the workforce losses and, as of early 2026, is still awaiting a formal Reduction-in-Force and reorganization plan. Congress's final FY2026 appropriation funded NIST's Scientific and Technical Research and Services program at $1.25 billion -- more than $542 million above the administration's request, and higher than even the $980 million House figure already cited in this entry -- and fully funded the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership at $175 million, rejecting the administration's proposal to eliminate it. Despite that enacted funding, NIST issued Reduction-in-Force and possible-separation notices to every MEP employee, prompting Sen. Chris Coons and colleagues to send a formal letter demanding an explanation for what they characterized as an 'unauthorized dismantling' of a program Congress had just funded. NIST's Computer Security Division also lost its division head and roughly a dozen subordinates to retirement offers, a specific loss to the cybersecurity-standards function this entry already documents as strained. Update 2026-07-26: NIST released a Notice of Funding Opportunity for 14 Manufacturing Extension Partnership centers (Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Missouri, Montana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Utah, and Vermont), with an informational webinar scheduled July 28, 2026 and applications due August 21, 2026. Trade press (Advanced Manufacturing) frames this as a real reversal after NIST's earlier funding notice for the program's next tranche of centers was delayed until December 4, 2025 -- itself more than six months behind schedule and a gap that, combined with the RIF notices, had already pushed roughly 90% of MEP centers into layoffs or hiring freezes, with some at risk of closing entirely. This doesn't resolve Sen. Coons's still-unanswered oversight letter about the RIF notices themselves, but is a concrete sign the program is continuing rather than being wound down. Update 2026-08-29: on July 3, 2026, Sens. Maria Cantwell and Gary Peters -- Ranking Members of the Senate Commerce and Homeland Security/Governmental Affairs Committees, respectively -- sent a letter to Acting Comptroller General Orice Williams Brown formally requesting a GAO investigation into whether Commerce, under Secretary Lutnick, followed the law in funding and managing the MEP program. The senators state that Commerce's own Inspector General personally confirmed to Democratic committee staff that the IG findings the Department cited as its stated justification for defunding MEP (concerning executive-compensation limits and overstated economic-impact claims) were not legal or otherwise appropriate grounds for defunding the program -- directly undercutting the administration's own stated rationale for the RIF notices this entry already documents. No GAO findings or response were identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): the MEP funding-uncertainty pattern this entry already documents (the 14-center July 2026 NOFO) recurred separately and earlier at a distinct set of 13 existing state MEP centers (Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Indiana, Maryland, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia), which were left operating without renewed federal award obligations into mid-2026; trade press reported 12 of the 13 had received their federal MEP awards by July 6, 2026, with Colorado still delayed over budget revisions. Separately, and in apparent tension with both the RIF notices and the elimination proposal this entry documents, NIST simultaneously launched a new $40 million MEP Pilot Program (Federal Register notice, May 20, 2026; public webinar June 24, 2026) committing roughly $20 million per project over two years to accelerate additive manufacturing for aerospace components and build a domestic critical-minerals supply chain, open only to existing MEP centers. No response to Sen. Coons's original RIF-notice oversight letter, and no findings from the Cantwell/Peters-requested GAO investigation, were identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update.

The $40 million MEP Pilot Program is HIGH confidence, corroborated against NIST's own Federal Register filing (2026-10105, May 20, 2026) directly, not only a trade-press synthesis -- elevated from an initial single-outlet (Manufacturing Dive) finding after that direct-source check, consistent with this sweep's standing single-source-corroboration discipline.

A specific research group maintaining foundational atomic measurement data was also eliminated. title: NLRB Loses Statutory Quorum for Nearly a Year After Trump Fires Board Member Wilcox
institution: National Labor Relations Board
status: Complete (Wilcox's removal is now considered constitutionally settled following Trump v. Slaughter, June 29, 2026, though the Supreme Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific case)
date_of_action: 2025-01-27 (firing) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court's Slaughter ruling resolves the underlying legal question); board lacked a working quorum for roughly 11 of the intervening months
what_changed: On January 27, 2025, President Trump fired NLRB Board Member Gwynne Wilcox without citing any of the statutory grounds (neglect of duty or malfeasance) required by the National Labor Relations Act, leaving the five-seat Board with only two active members, below the three-member quorum required to issue decisions. Wilcox sued on February 5, 2025. U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell ruled the firing unlawful on March 6, 2025, calling it a 'blatant violation of the law' and a 'power grab,' and ordered Wilcox reinstated, which briefly restored the Board's quorum. A three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed that ruling on March 28; the full en banc D.C. Circuit reversed course and reinstated Wilcox again on April 7; Chief Justice Roberts then issued an emergency stay removing her again on April 9. On May 22, 2025, the Supreme Court declined to reinstate Wilcox in a 6-3 emergency-docket order, explicitly not a ruling on the merits. The Board remained below quorum until regaining one in December 2025 through new Trump nominations. On January 28, 2026, the D.C. Circuit declined en banc review of the panel decision upholding Wilcox's termination. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's decision in the related case Trump v. Slaughter overruled the 90-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent underlying Wilcox's legal theory; legal analysts across firms now consider her removal constitutionally settled even though the Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific still-pending case. Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): On August 7, 2026, the Senate confirmed James Macy as a new Republican Board member (alongside the renomination of Democratic member David Prouty), giving the NLRB a full 3-1 Republican majority for the first time since Wilcox's firing. A bare quorum had technically been restored in December 2025, but this confirmation is the first point at which the Board has held the three Republican votes needed to formally overturn Biden-era precedent, not just issue decisions.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Fired Wilcox directly via a short email citing loss of confidence in her leadership, then pursued the legal theory that his Article II authority permitted the removal all the way to the Supreme Court, a position the Court substantially validated in the related Slaughter case.

estimated_impact.summary: The National Labor Relations Board, the sole federal agency responsible for enforcing private-sector labor law and adjudicating unfair-labor-practice and union-election disputes, was left without a functioning quorum for nearly all of 2025, halting its ability to issue binding decisions during that period.

Labor advocates and a 20-state coalition of attorneys general (led by California AG Bonta, in an amicus brief) argued the firing created a 'dangerous regulatory vacuum' that left workers without a functioning forum to resolve unfair-labor-practice complaints or conduct union elections for most of a year. Notably, the legal question was genuinely unsettled for over a year: a federal district court and an initial D.C. Circuit panel sided with Wilcox, before the en banc D.C. Circuit, a Supreme Court emergency stay, and ultimately the Slaughter precedent sided with the administration, reflecting real legal uncertainty rather than a one-sided dispute.

title: NNSA Nuclear-Weapons-Complex Staffing Crisis -- From Accidental Firings to a Shutdown Furlough That Halted Weapons Work for the First Time in History
institution: National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), a semi-autonomous Department of Energy agency responsible for the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile; related developments at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
status: Ongoing, with escalating severity through the year -- initial erroneous firings (Feb 2025) gave way to a documented brain-drain (Mar-May 2025), then a historic shutdown-driven near-total work stoppage (Oct 2025), followed by a policy shift that reduces regulatory oversight of new reactor construction (Dec 2025); a April 2026 Stimson Center workforce-pipeline report quantifies the structural gap underlying the crisis, finding NNSA still roughly 200 positions short of the ~2,369-person staffing benchmark a 2020 agency study identified as needed by fiscal 2026
date_of_action: 2025-02-17 (initial erroneous firings) through 2025-12-30 (Reactor Pilot Program launch)
what_changed: In February 2025, DOGE-driven federal workforce cuts mistakenly fired NNSA employees -- some working on the nuclear stockpile and on tracking nuclear threats, including in Ukraine -- and the administration then could not contact them about reinstatement because their government email accounts had already been deactivated. ABC News reported on February 21, 2025 that this confusion was not limited to NNSA: hundreds of federal employees initially terminated from agencies including NNSA, the VA, and USDA had their dismissals rescinded, but many remained unclear on their actual employment status even after the reversal, reflecting a broader pattern of chaotic, poorly-tracked terminations across the initial wave of DOGE-directed cuts. By March 2025, the New York Times reported more than 130 senior scientists, engineers, and security experts had been forced out of NNSA, jeopardizing nuclear modernization programs and safety protocols. By May 2025, USA Today reported the cuts had derailed years of hiring progress and raised new safety concerns at weapons facilities including Los Alamos, the Y-12 National Security Complex, and Pantex. The staffing erosion reached the Nuclear Regulatory Commission as well: at a September 4, 2025 Senate hearing, two of the NRC's three remaining commissioners said they feared Trump could purge them too if they resisted his push to fast-track new reactor approvals, part of a stated goal to quadruple U.S. nuclear generating capacity by 2050. The crisis peaked during the October 2025 government shutdown: NNSA warned it would furlough 80% of its workforce as shutdown funding ran out, leaving only 375 'essential' employees and placing facility contractors in 'minimum-safe' status; by October 21, more than 1,400 employees -- over 75% of staff -- had actually been furloughed, leaving fewer than 400 on duty and suspending nearly all work on the U.S. nuclear weapons program, the first time in the program's history that weapons assembly and modernization work came to a complete stop. Funding for the Office of Secure Transportation, which physically moves nuclear warheads and materials, was confirmed only through October 27 as the shutdown continued. Then, on December 30, 2025, Trump officials launched a Reactor Pilot Program fast-tracking construction of new, largely untested nuclear reactor designs, with oversight shifted from the traditionally independent Nuclear Regulatory Commission to the Department of Energy itself -- aiming to bring at least three experimental reactors online by July 4, 2026 under an aggressive political deadline and with limited public transparency. In April 2026, the Stimson Center published a report, 'Securing the Future: Building the US Nuclear Security Workforce Pipeline,' putting a structural, longer-horizon number on the staffing gap underlying the year's crisis: a 2020 NNSA study had identified a need for 2,369 personnel by fiscal 2026, but the agency's own FY2026 budget request targeted a workforce of roughly 200 positions below that benchmark. The report attributes the shortfall not just to the year's disruptive events but to durable structural competition -- weak internal career-advancement pathways compared to the private sector, and NNSA's technical talent pool increasingly drawn instead toward AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology roles.

title: NNSA Leak Crackdown Following Real Security Failures at Los Alamos and Kansas City, Amid Internal Opposition to Trump's Push to Resume Live Nuclear Weapons Testing
institution: National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), Department of Energy
status: Ongoing -- leak-crackdown memo issued; no formal order to resume explosive testing, and no confirmed disciplinary/criminal action under the memo, as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-07 (Kansas City hack) through 2025-11-22 (Williams' leak-crackdown memo)
what_changed: The November 2025 leak crackdown followed two distinct, documented threads. First, real security failures: in July 2025, foreign hackers breached IT systems at the Kansas City National Security Campus (which manufactures roughly 80% of the non-nuclear components used in U.S. nuclear weapons) by exploiting two unpatched Microsoft SharePoint vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-49704); Microsoft attributed the broader campaign to three China-linked hacking groups, though a source involved in the incident response told CSO Online a Russian actor, not a Chinese one, carried out this specific intrusion, and the security firm Resecurity suggested a Chinese-developed exploit may have been independently reproduced by Russian, financially-motivated actors. NNSA said only 'a very small number of systems were impacted' and that no classified information was compromised, though unclassified technical requirements documents -- which can reveal the level of precision required for weapons components -- were exposed. Separately, DOE's own security-enforcement records document an unauthorized disclosure of classified information to personnel lacking proper access authorization at the Kansas City campus on September 5, 2025, and recurring incidents of unauthorized controlled articles being introduced into secure areas at Los Alamos National Laboratory. Second, and simultaneously, an internal policy leak: in late October 2025, President Trump posted on social media directing the Department of Defense to begin nuclear weapons testing 'because of other countries testing programs' -- the first public suggestion of a return to explosive nuclear detonation testing since the U.S. moratorium began in 1992. Per CNN's November 14, 2025 exclusive report, NNSA officials prepared an internal memo for Energy Secretary Chris Wright and NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams outlining the agency's existing non-explosive verification methods and the timeline a return to explosive testing would require; Wright, Williams, and National Laboratory officials planned to tell the White House that resuming explosive testing was not 'tenable,' and Nevada's congressional delegation (Reps. Susie Lee and Steven Horsford) sent formal letters in early November 2025 opposing any return to testing. Against that backdrop of both real breaches and a leaked internal policy dispute, Williams sent an agency-wide 'urgent' memo on November 22, 2025: 'It saddens me that this message is necessary,' he wrote, adding that 'past actions by NNSA-affiliated personnel have undermined national leadership's confidence in our ability to safeguard classified and sensitive unclassified information related to our national security work,' and that 'any compromise of information, regardless of its perceived sensitivity, represents a direct threat to our strategic interests.' Williams listed potential consequences as 'severe and far-reaching': administrative penalties, loss of security clearance, civil liability, and criminal prosecution -- without specifying which incident(s) prompted the memo or naming any individuals. The New York Times' coverage of the memo also noted critics' concerns about Williams' own qualifications for the role: he is a former one-term GOP congressman with six years' service as a Navy nuclear submarine officer and an MBA from Wharton, confirmed September 18, 2025 as part of a 48-nominee batch Senate Republicans approved en masse along party lines (51-47) rather than through individualized vetting; Sen. Elizabeth Warren had written to Williams during his nomination warning that 'a leader without strong technical expertise and extensive experience could put our nuclear deterrent at risk and waste billions of dollars.'

estimated_impact.summary: This documents a security/secrecy episode rather than a funding or staffing cut with its own dollar figure; no cost/savings figure applies to the memo itself, though the July 2025 Kansas City breach targeted a facility making ~80% of the country's non-nuclear weapons components. The health/mortality stakes are indirect: the nuclear-testing policy dispute the leaks separately concerned carries a well-documented historical health legacy from the prior era of U.S. atmospheric testing, cited as context for why internal experts reportedly opposed a return to testing, not as a quantified harm estimate from this memo itself.

title: NOAA Climate Research Zeroed Out in FY2026 Budget Proposal, Princeton Partnership Defunded
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
status: Partially implemented, and repeating -- the Princeton funding cut took effect and the administration proposed eliminating NOAA's climate research office again in its FY2027 budget, for the second year running; Congress rejected the same elimination in FY2026 and House appropriators' initial FY2027 markup signals they are likely to do so again
date_of_action: 2025-04-08 (Princeton funding cut announced) through the FY2026 budget cycle (proposal released July 2025; Congress had not enacted it as of the last-verified date)
what_changed: On April 8, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced the termination of nearly $4 million in NOAA cooperative research funding to Princeton University, effective June 30, 2025, covering three programs including the Cooperative Institute for Modeling the Earth System, which supports Princeton's partnership with NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL), widely regarded as producing some of the world's most advanced climate modeling. The Commerce Department's official announcement stated the program 'promotes exaggerated and implausible climate threats, contributing to a phenomenon known as climate anxiety.' In July 2025, NOAA's proposed FY2026 budget was reported to contain a literal line reading 'Total, Climate Research: $0,' along with the proposed elimination of the entire Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), NOAA's research arm, and defunding of all of OAR's climate and weather cooperative institutes nationwide, including CIRES at the University of Colorado Boulder, which houses the National Snow and Ice Data Center. The overall proposal called for cutting NOAA's budget by more than 25% and its ~13,000-person workforce by roughly 17%, along with a 44% reduction in planned investment in next-generation geostationary weather satellites. Congressional spending panels rejected the FY2026 budget request as proposed, but the administration proceeded with some of the changes administratively regardless, including terminating contracts for planned satellite instruments in August 2025 as what agency officials described to staff as a 'down payment' on the broader proposed cuts. The administration's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, again proposes eliminating the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) -- the same office Congress rejected eliminating in the FY2026 cycle -- along with more than $1 billion in additional NOAA program cuts, including defunding the network of global monitoring laboratories and 14 other climate laboratories nationwide. At an April 2026 budget hearing, NOAA officials defended the cuts while members of both parties on the relevant committee pushed back. The House Commerce-Justice-Science Appropriations subcommittee's initial FY2027 markup was reported as favorable to NOAA's weather enterprise, suggesting Congress may again decline to enact the full elimination, consistent with the FY2026 outcome. The administration's separate FY2026 budget request also proposed eliminating all $43.5 million in federal support for NOAA's Integrated Ocean Observing System, a real-time data source used by harbor pilots, weather forecasters, and military operations, according to AP reporting in May 2025. By September 2025, the Washington Post reported the cuts had moved beyond budget proposals into concrete instrument shutdowns: the administration was closing down climate-monitoring satellites, shutting off carbon-tracking instruments, and scrapping sensors used to monitor water contamination and greenhouse gases, with internal budget documents directing NOAA to focus solely on 'weather-only' tools -- consistent with Project 2025's earlier call to dismantle federal climate research capacity. One consequence of NOAA's shrinking disaster-tracking function became visible that fall: NBC News reported in October 2025 that after the administration effectively shut down NOAA's billion-dollar disaster-cost-tracking database, a group of former NOAA scientists rebuilt an equivalent tracker independently through the nonprofit Climate Central -- their reconstruction found the costliest six-month stretch of U.S. weather disasters on record, with 14 separate events each exceeding $1 billion in damage, led by the Los Angeles wildfires at more than $61 billion.

estimated_impact.summary: A federal agency responsible for the data and modeling underlying weather forecasting, hurricane prediction, and climate research had its dedicated climate research funding line proposed at zero and lost a 57-year research partnership with one of the world's leading climate modeling laboratories.

Critics, including former NOAA research director Craig McLean, argue the cuts amount to dismantling the scientific basis for hurricane and severe-weather forecasting, and ProPublica reporting noted that Secretary Lutnick's former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, had itself described climate change in prior public materials as 'the defining issue of our time' and warned it would be 'disastrous and life threatening' if unchecked, a contrast critics cite as evidence the funding decision reflects political priorities rather than a reassessment of the science. It is also important to note the FY2026 budget eliminating NOAA's climate research entirely is a proposal, not enacted law: congressional appropriators in both parties have been reported as skeptical of the scale of the cuts and have not approved the request as written, even though the administration has moved ahead with some individual actions, such as satellite contract terminations, independent of congressional approval.

Strong for the FY2026 budget proposal and OAR elimination plan, independently corroborated across NPR, Colorado Public Radio, Eos, Science/AAAS, PBS NewsHour, and ProPublica, with the important caveat clearly noted that this remains a budget proposal Congress has not enacted as of the last-verified date. title: DOGE/GSA Listed the Support-Office Lease for NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory -- Home of the Keeling Curve -- for Termination, Then Quietly Resolved It
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Monitoring Laboratory -- Mauna Loa Observatory; General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Resolved -- NOAA confirmed in July 2025 the lease matter was settled before the August 31, 2025 expiration, without specifying how; the observatory continued operating and was reported in 2026 to be expanding, not closing
date_of_action: 2025-03-11 (lease publicly reported as targeted) through 2025-07 (NOAA confirms resolution)
what_changed: In March 2025, Reuters and other outlets reported that DOGE/GSA had listed the lease for an eight-person NOAA support office in Hilo, Hawaii (suite 102, Kilauea Financial Plaza) among the federal office leases slated for early termination as part of the administration's real-estate cost-cutting push. The office is the ground-support base for the Mauna Loa Observatory, established in 1956 on the mountain's northern flank, which holds the world's longest continuous record of atmospheric carbon dioxide measurements -- the Keeling Curve -- and was already operating under strain from the loss of its only road access after Mauna Loa's 2022 eruption, making the Hilo office's remote-support role especially load-bearing. The lease was set to expire August 31, 2025. As of a late-August 2025 report, no resolution had been announced and Hawaii's congressional delegation -- Sen. Mazie Hirono and Reps. Jill Tokuda and Ed Case -- introduced a formal resolution expressing concern and reaffirming support for the observatory, with Hirono calling the threatened closure 'yet another attack on science.' NOAA subsequently confirmed to reporters that the lease matter was resolved in July 2025, before the deadline, without detailing the mechanism (renewal, relocation, or reversal of the termination decision). By mid-2026, reporting described the observatory not merely surviving but being rebuilt and expanded, with measurement programs that had been curtailed since the 2022 eruption road closure increasingly restored.

primary_proponent.note: No named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for including this specific office; this is the same GSA/DOGE lease-termination sweep documented separately for the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory's Hilo office, a different agency and mission housed in a different Hilo building, targeted in the same week -- see [[doge-volcano-observatory-lease-terminations-2025]].

estimated_impact.summary: One of the eight-person support offices keeping alive the world's longest-running atmospheric CO2 record was briefly listed for lease termination with no documented contingency plan, at a moment when the observatory's summit instruments were already isolated by 2022 eruption damage and dependent on this office's remote-support role -- an example of a blanket real-estate cost-cutting sweep reaching a scientifically irreplaceable, decades-long dataset without an apparent case-by-case review.

NOAA's own account of the resolution mechanism is vague ('resolved') rather than specific, and no source reviewed states whether the termination decision was formally reversed or the office was relocated on the same footprint.

title: DOGE Cuts Gutted NOAA's Space Traffic Coordination Office, Then FY2026 Budget Sought to Eliminate Its Core System Entirely
institution: NOAA Office of Space Commerce (Commerce Department)
status: Mixed and recurring -- the February 2025 staffing cuts stand and were never fully reversed. The FY2026 threat to eliminate TraCSS funding entirely was rejected by Congress in enacted law (P.L. 119-74, signed 2026-01-23, $52.5 million against an $11 million request), but the same fight restarted for FY2027: the administration's April 3, 2026 budget request again proposed just $11 million with no dedicated TraCSS funding, and the House Appropriations Committee again restored funding (to $50 million, approved May 13, 2026) with report language explicitly supporting TraCSS. The FY2027 appropriations cycle was not yet finalized as of this update. TraCSS itself remains operational and growing, with 70 pilot users representing 11,345+ satellites onboarded as of August 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02-27 (initial firings) through 2026 budget cycle (proposed elimination of TraCSS funding)
what_changed: On February 27, 2025, DOGE-driven cuts hit NOAA's Office of Space Commerce (OSC), a roughly 25-person office, on a few hours' notice -- about a third of the office's staff, including the chief of the Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), Dmitry Poisik. TraCSS is the civilian satellite traffic coordination system OSC has been building since 2018 (under Space Policy Directive 3, signed in Trump's first term) to warn commercial and government satellite operators of potential collisions as low Earth orbit becomes increasingly crowded. The cuts also hit OSC's Commercial Remote Sensing Regulatory Affairs Division, which licenses commercial imaging satellite companies; affected licensees received an email stating 'no senior personnel remain in the office' and warning of 'significant delays' processing licensing actions. Since the initial layoffs, three staffers in leadership roles were brought back, but congressional Democrats (Reps. Valerie Foushee and Zoe Lofgren among others) continued to warn about the office's reduced capacity. In 2026, the administration's budget request went further, proposing to cut OSC's budget by 85% and eliminate 18 positions, while eliminating federal funding for TraCSS entirely -- a group of space-industry organizations wrote to House and Senate leaders warning the cuts would put both commercial and government satellite operators at risk of collision. Update, 2026-08-17: the FY2026 defunding threat this entry describes as an unenacted budget proposal was resolved -- and rejected -- in enacted law before this entry was even written. The House Appropriations Committee's FY2026 Commerce-Justice-Science bill (approved May 2026) funded the Office of Space Commerce at $50 million against the administration's $11 million request; the Senate Appropriations Committee proposed $60 million; the final enacted figure, signed into law as part of P.L. 119-74 on January 23, 2026, settled at $52.5 million -- preserving TraCSS rather than eliminating it, following sustained pressure from a coalition of 450+ space, satellite, and defense companies. As of July 2026, TraCSS had 68 pilot users representing more than 11,290 satellites in orbit onboarded to the system, though work is reportedly proceeding more slowly than the pre-budget-threat schedule that had targeted full operational capability by January 2026. This funding resolution does not address the February 2025 staffing cuts themselves, which this entry's original reporting describes as only partially reversed (three leadership-role staffers reinstated of the roughly one-third of the office cut). Update, 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 29): the defunding fight recurred for FY2027. The administration's FY2027 budget request, released April 3, 2026, again proposed only $11 million for the Office of Space Commerce with no dedicated TraCSS funding -- industry sources described it to SpaceNews as 'another attempt by the White House Office of Management and Budget to cancel or severely curtail TraCSS,' the same pattern as the FY2026 request a year earlier. The House Appropriations Committee's FY2027 Commerce-Justice-Science bill, approved May 13, 2026, again restored funding, to $50 million, with report language explicitly supporting continued TraCSS work. As of this update the Senate had not yet completed action and no FY2027 appropriations bill had been enacted (the federal fiscal year begins October 1, 2026), so this remains an unresolved, recurring threat rather than a settled one. Separately, TraCSS's pilot-user base grew modestly since the prior update, from 68 to 70 pilot users representing over 11,345 satellites in orbit.

title: NOAA-Wide Staffing Collapses by Roughly a Quarter in Six Weeks, With Disaster Training Cancelled and Privatization Floated
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), agency-wide (distinct from this database's separate, NWS-specific weather-balloon and staffing-loss entries)
status: Implemented and escalating across the documented period
what_changed: Over a roughly three-week span in March 2025, multiple outlets documented an escalating wave of NOAA-wide staffing cuts, distinct from the NWS-specific weather-balloon suspensions and 600-person NWS staffing loss already tracked in separate entries in this database. On March 12, the Associated Press reported plans to cut another 1,000 NOAA jobs, amounting to a 10% agency-wide workforce reduction affecting weather forecasting, ocean research, and fisheries management. The same day, The Hill reported the administration had cancelled disaster-response training for NWS meteorologists specifically due to staffing shortages and travel-budget cuts, with employees blocked from booking travel and some forced to cancel trips they had already booked. On March 13, ABC News reported NOAA was preparing mass layoffs affecting over 1,000 employees, describing a cumulative 25% workforce reduction since January as the agency was forced to eliminate entire functions rather than trim personnel within existing ones. On March 15, FedScoop reported NOAA had fired 800 probationary employees, on top of roughly 500 additional departures under the agency's deferred-resignation program, with former officials warning the combined losses endangered NOAA's weather forecasting, climate monitoring, and hurricane-tracking capabilities. On March 26, ABC News reported the administration was considering privatizing the National Weather Service entirely, a proposal tracing to Project 2025's recommendation that NOAA be 'broken up and downsized' and that NWS 'fully commercialize its forecasting operations.' By April 2, The Guardian reported NOAA was 'reeling' from the cumulative effect of more than 1,000 staff cuts, with some critical roles (including hurricane trackers) hastily rehired after the initial firings, and separately reported the agency's switch to an unsecured email server had left remaining staff flooded with spam. Mother Jones reported May 27, 2025 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0356, added 2026-09-10) that the cuts also hit the National Geodetic Survey (NGS), the small NOAA office responsible for maintaining the nation's official spatial reference system -- the precise measurements of latitude, longitude, elevation, and gravity underlying mapping, infrastructure, and disaster-response work -- jeopardizing a major planned upgrade to the national geospatial datum; one expert described the office's largely invisible but foundational role as being comparable to oxygen -- something nobody notices needing until it is gone. This entry treats NGS as one more named office within the broader NOAA-wide collapse already documented above rather than a separate action, since only one outlet's reporting on NGS specifically was identified.

title: Interior Suspended Air-Quality Monitoring at All 63 National Parks Under a DOGE Oil Executive's New Authority -- Then Reversed Course Within Days of Exposure
institution: National Park Service / Department of the Interior
status: Reversed within days of Washington Post reporting; contracts were paused, not permanently canceled, and Park Service spokeswoman Rachel Pawlitz confirmed the stop-work orders would be lifted and contractors notified immediately. No sourcing reviewed indicates the pause recurred outside the October-November 2025 government shutdown, which separately disrupted the same monitoring networks agency-wide.
date_of_action: 2025-05 (stop-work orders issued and reversed within the same reporting window)
what_changed: In early May 2025, the Interior Department ordered contractors to stop air-quality monitoring across all 63 U.S. national parks, per an internal email obtained by the Washington Post. The affected program tracked ozone, particulate matter, and other pollutants at monitoring sites in and around park units nationwide -- data used to inform permitting decisions for nearby industrial projects and to track 'regional haze,' the human-caused visibility impairment the EPA has required states to reduce in national parks and wilderness areas since 1999. The pause came shortly after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum granted sweeping administrative authority over the department -- including funding decisions, hiring/firing, and policy-setting across the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, and Bureau of Indian Affairs -- to Tyler Hassen, a former oil-field-services executive (ex-CEO of Basin Energy) serving as a DOGE-affiliated assistant secretary for policy, management and budget. After the Post's reporting and the leaked stop-work email became public, Park Service spokeswoman Rachel Pawlitz said in an email that the orders would be reversed and 'contractors will be notified immediately'; the agency confirmed monitoring had resumed. Former National Park Service directors and career leaders separately published an open letter and op-ed urging Burgum to reverse course on this and related park policies.

estimated_impact.summary: A nationwide pause of the air-quality monitoring network across all 63 national parks -- reversed within days once exposed publicly -- briefly removed data used to track pollutants linked to heart attacks, strokes, asthma, and premature deaths, and used to support industrial-permitting decisions and regional-haze/visibility-protection requirements near parks. Because the pause was reversed quickly and contracts were paused rather than canceled, no sourcing reviewed identifies a specific data gap or measurable health/permitting consequence that resulted before the reversal.

title: NRC Commissioner Fired Without Cause, Agency Independence and Staffing Cut Under DOGE Reorganization
institution: Nuclear Regulatory Commission
status: Ongoing (Hanson's firing remains final and unlitigated; the commission remains at its full five members under Chairman Ho Nieh; the DOGE-directed reorganization and regulatory rewrite are continuing on EO 14300's original schedule, with NRC targeting completion of its organizational restructuring by the end of September 2026 and a new rulemaking-procedure rule published August 11, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-05-23 (executive order) and 2025-06-13 (Hanson firing)
what_changed: On June 13, 2025, President Trump fired NRC Commissioner Christopher T. Hanson, effective immediately, via a two-line email from the White House Presidential Personnel Office. It was the first removal of an NRC commissioner since the agency's creation in 1974; Hanson's term was not set to expire until 2029, and no cause was cited beyond a White House spokesperson's comment that 'all organizations are more effective when leaders are rowing in the same direction.' Hanson, originally appointed by Trump in his first term and later chaired the commission under Biden, said he was terminated 'without cause, contrary to existing law and longstanding precedent regarding removal of independent agency appointees.' The firing left the five-member commission at a 2-2 partisan split with one vacancy, and came three weeks after Trump signed Executive Order 14300, 'Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission' (May 23, 2025), which directs the NRC to reorganize and undertake reductions in force in consultation with its DOGE Team, shrink the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards to the statutory minimum, and complete a 'wholesale revision' of its safety regulations and guidance documents within 18 months, with rulemaking routed through OMB Director Russell Vought's office -- a process not previously applied to this traditionally arms-length safety regulator. EO 14300 also directed NRC to reconsider its reliance on the decades-old linear no-threshold (LNT) radiation-exposure model in favor of "determinate" limits, and the NRC's resulting February 2026 proposed rulemaking (the "wholesale revision" already documented below) would replace the longstanding As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) principle -- which requires operators to keep exposures below the legal limit whenever practicable -- with a "graded approach," while raising the allowable radionuclide emissions standard for a hypothetical resident at a plant's property line from 10 to 25 millirem per year. NRC Chairman Ho Nieh said the change removes "ambiguity" and does not alter worker or public exposure limits themselves, but the Union of Concerned Scientists' Edwin Lyman warned some proposals could let actual exposures rise closer to the maximum caps that ALARA's separate, more conservative practice had kept them well below. Career staff departures followed; NRC's No. 2 career operations official, a 32-year veteran and self-described two-time Trump voter, retired in May 2025 partly in protest of political operatives being embedded in senior leadership positions with what he called potential to 'significantly influence decision-making.' Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0447: The Hill named that embedded political operative on July 14, 2025 as Adam Blake, a staffer detailed from the Department of Energy (not NRC itself) placed in charge of implementing EO 14300 at the commission, including overseeing the required reductions in force and structural changes meant to accelerate reactor licensing. Because Blake was detailed from DOE rather than hired by or accountable to NRC, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse called his presence 'a Department of Energy hostile takeover of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.' At a May 2025 meeting, a DOGE representative told the NRC chair and top staff that the agency would be expected to give 'rubber stamp' approval to new reactors already tested by the Energy or Defense Departments -- a directive that would bypass NRC's own independent safety review for those reactors. The DOGE-directed reorganization required by EO 14300 has proceeded on the order's own timeline: the NRC issued its notices of proposed rulemaking for the 'wholesale revision' of safety regulations by the February 2026 deadline, and in mid-2026 launched a major organizational restructuring -- consolidating around new-reactor, operating-reactor, and materials/waste business lines, and creating two new offices (Office of Advanced Reactors; Office of the Chief Nuclear Reactor Inspector) -- targeted for completion by September 2026, with final rules due under the EO's 18-month deadline (November 2026). Investigative reporting in March 2026 (Sludge) revealed Blake had by then also become Energy Secretary Chris Wright's 'de facto proxy' inside the NRC while simultaneously sitting on the board of KCRise Fund, a venture-capital firm funded by nuclear-industry investors -- a direct financial tie between the DOGE operative directing NRC's deregulatory restructuring and the industry that restructuring benefits, not previously disclosed when Blake's role was first reported in July 2025. No update on Hanson's own removal was found; it remains final and unlitigated as of this recheck. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0354): on June 24, 2025, nearly 30 former NRC officials and staff, organized around former NRC Chairman Stephen Burns, sent a letter of protest over Hanson's firing, warning it "endangers the independence of the NRC as it raises the specter of political considerations carrying greater weight than public health and safety" and that compromising that independence "can only reduce the effectiveness of nuclear regulation in the United States as well as around the world, increasing the likelihood of a costly accident." CORRECTION 2026-07-26: this entry's prior recheck (2026-07-20) still described the commission as sitting at a 2-2 partisan split with one vacancy from Hanson's June 2025 removal -- that vacancy was actually filled months earlier, when Doug Weaver was sworn in December 22, 2025, restoring the commission to its full five-member statutory complement. Separately, on January 8, 2026, Trump designated Commissioner Ho Nieh -- a Republican who previously ran NRC's Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation from 2018-2021 -- as the NRC's 20th chairman, succeeding David Wright, who continues serving as a commissioner. The commission's current composition includes Republicans Nieh and Wright alongside Democratic commissioners Matthew Marzano and Bradley Crowell. Hanson's own removal remains final and unlitigated as of this update; the leadership-composition correction here is about the vacancy his firing created, not about the firing's legality. Extending the deregulatory push, the NRC voted in April 2026 to phase out its own agency-led 'force-on-force' security drills at nuclear power plants -- mock attack exercises historically run and evaluated by NRC inspectors to test each plant's defenses -- shifting to a model where plant operators run their own exercises and NRC staff only observe. Reuters reported the change came as Trump pressured the NRC to speed reactor approvals for a major nuclear-capacity expansion tied to AI, data-center, electrification, and crypto-mining electricity demand. Update 2026-08-17: the reorganization continued on schedule, with NRC reaffirming a target of implementing its new organization chart by the end of September 2026. On August 11, 2026, NRC published a Federal Register rule, 'NRC Modernization: Rulemaking Procedure, Federal Advisory Committee Act Alignment, Access, and Security,' extending the regulatory rewrite already documented in this entry into a formal rule governing how the agency itself makes rules and manages its federal advisory committee. No update on Hanson's own removal was identified in sourcing reviewed; it remains final and unlitigated.
