title: RFK Jr. Pushes FDA to Fast-Track Psychedelic Drug Approvals After 2024 MDMA Rejection
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA); Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing policy shift as of July 2025 -- no psychedelic drug had received full FDA approval as of the sourcing reviewed; Kennedy stated a hope for approval within roughly 12 months without specifying which drug or a formal review-timeline change
date_of_action: 2025-07 (Kennedy's public fast-track statements; Texas's ibogaine appropriation)
what_changed: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2025 that he hoped a psychedelic pharmaceutical -- most likely MDMA-assisted therapy -- would receive FDA approval within about 12 months, framing psychedelics as a top HHS priority, without specifying which drug or what formal change to FDA's review process would make that timeline possible. The push followed a real prior FDA setback: in August 2024 (under Biden), the FDA had rejected Lykos Therapeutics' MDMA-assisted-therapy application, citing significant concerns about clinical-trial design, blinding, and missing safety data. Kennedy's embrace effectively reopens that door administratively rather than through a new completed rule or approval; AP News and other outlets reported the administration's posture had shifted the agency's stated priorities toward psychedelics generally, though no source reviewed identified a formal, published change to FDA's safety-review standards or timelines specific to this drug class. Separately, and as a concrete, completed government action, Texas approved $50 million in state funding to research ibogaine -- a Schedule I hallucinogen, on the same restricted-drug list as heroin, not yet approved for any medical use -- as a treatment for opioid addiction, PTSD, and other conditions, reportedly the largest such government research investment of its kind. The funding passed with public backing from former Texas Governor and Trump-administration DOE Secretary Rick Perry and from combat veterans advocating for ibogaine access. Researchers and clinicians in the psychedelic-medicine field expressed mixed reactions: some welcomed the political momentum, while others -- per CNN and Scientific American reporting -- worried that Kennedy's specific, personally-driven advocacy risked discrediting the field if a drug appeared to be rushed to market or became too closely associated with him personally, especially given Kennedy's documented history of promoting scientifically unsupported health claims elsewhere in this database's coverage.

estimated_impact.summary: No drug had received approval as of this entry's sourcing, so no direct patient-safety harm has yet materialized from the federal fast-track push itself; the concrete, quantifiable action is Texas's $50 million state appropriation to research a Schedule I hallucinogen with no established medical-use approval, a real financial commitment whose safety and efficacy outcomes remain to be determined by the research it funds.

title: RFK Jr. and Sen. Ron Johnson Pressured a Scientific Journal to Justify Retracting a Flawed Vaccine-SIDS Study
institution: HHS / Toxicology Reports (Elsevier journal)
status: Ongoing -- journal given a deadline to respond as of this entry's sourcing
date_of_action: 2026-06 (Kennedy's letter) through 2026-07 (Johnson's follow-up letter to Elsevier made public)
what_changed: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sent a letter dated June 11, 2026 demanding the editor of Toxicology Reports explain the journal's retraction of a single-author study by vaccine critic Neil Z. Miller, which had used Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) data to claim 75% of reported SIDS cases occurred within seven days of a vaccination. The journal's April 9, 2026 retraction notice cited serious methodological flaws in the paper's use of VAERS data to infer a vaccine-SIDS correlation and warned of 'potential implications for medical practice' if the flawed conclusions were relied upon. Kennedy called the retraction notice 'woefully insufficient' and demanded the journal explain, by June 25, how the retraction decision was reached and what experts were consulted. Sen. Ron Johnson separately sent a letter dated June 29 (made public July 13) directly to both the Toxicology Reports editor-in-chief and Elsevier's CEO, demanding release of all internal records related to the retraction decision. Miller's study had previously been cited to support CDC/ACIP childhood immunization schedule changes made under Kennedy. Update 2026-08-17: no reporting reviewed shows the journal's response to Kennedy's June 25 deadline or any change to the retraction decision itself -- editor-in-chief Lawrence H. Lash's original determination that Miller's response failed to 'satisfactorily address' the identified methodological flaws appears to still stand as of the most recent sourcing found. The pressure campaign itself continues to be the documented impact, not a reversed outcome. CORRECTION 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 51): this entry's own confidence_note stated 'no public response from Toxicology Reports or Elsevier was identified' -- that was incomplete. Elsevier did respond, on the record, before Kennedy's letter was even sent: on June 8, 2026 (three days before Kennedy's June 11 letter), an Elsevier spokesperson told The Epoch Times, 'We stand by the decision that the recommendations and conclusions presented in the paper may pose potential risks to public health and could potentially be applied in clinical practice resulting in harm to patients.' No further Elsevier or Toxicology Reports statement responding directly to Kennedy's or Johnson's letters (as opposed to this pre-existing June 8 statement) was identified in sourcing reviewed.

title: RFK Jr. Diverted CDC Staff to Compile Measles Data, Blocked Briefings, Spread Vaccine Disinformation -- CDC Chief Medical Officer Resigned in Protest
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
status: Reported as a completed episode during the 2025 outbreak; Houry's resignation was final as of summer 2025. Update 2026-07-27: the Washington Post reports the U.S. recorded 2,295 measles cases in 2026 as of late July -- the highest annual total since 1991 -- with more than five months remaining in the year, which public health experts attribute to declining vaccination rates and sustained outbreaks across multiple states. Update 2026-08-05: Utah's outbreak, part of the sustained 2026 transmission WSJ and CIDRAP report has continued since early 2025, has reached 679 cumulative cases (197 in 2025, 482 in 2026) with measles detected in every health jurisdiction in the state; the CDC has said the U.S. is at risk of losing its measles elimination status -- unbroken since 2000 -- if any transmission chain remains continuous for a full year, a threshold Utah's outbreak is approaching. Utah's kindergarten MMR vaccination rate (78.5% in 2023-2024) is well below the ~95% threshold public health officials say is needed to prevent sustained spread.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Corry's resignation) through Houry's resignation in summer 2025, with the broader outbreak-related pattern continuing into 2026
what_changed: Communications turmoil under Kennedy surfaced early: Thomas Corry, HHS's top communications official, resigned without explanation on LinkedIn in early March 2025, just two weeks after taking office and shortly after Kennedy downplayed the severity of the West Texas measles outbreak and misstated the number of deaths -- a resignation The Hill and CBS News both linked to internal frustration over canceled vaccine-advisory meetings, stalled research funding, and Kennedy's mishandling of the unfolding public health crisis, months before the more widely reported resignation of CDC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Debra Houry described below. Former CDC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Debra Houry said that while CDC staff were actively responding to the largest U.S. measles outbreak in decades -- more than 2,000 cases nationwide in 2025, including two child deaths linked to a West Texas outbreak cluster, with 93% of cases involving people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status -- HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his aides requested 15 years of historical data on every individual measles case, including comorbidities among the deceased. Separately, on April 18, 2025, CDC cancelled a planned program to help Texas schools assess and improve ventilation systems to help manage the state's measles outbreak, after notice that the CDC engineer leading the initiative would be terminated by June -- a concrete program loss amid the broader staffing purges affecting outbreak response described throughout this entry. Houry said the requests diverted CDC staff time and attention away from active outbreak management, stating publicly that 'the active measles response has to take priority,' and characterized the data requests as 'not based on science or reality, but trying to answer an agenda that was already in place.' Houry said Kennedy separately declined briefings from CDC's top medical officials on the measles epidemic despite CDC's offers to provide 'correct statistics, correct information,' spread false claims about vaccines (including the MMR vaccine) that CDC experts were prevented from countering, and relied on advisers she said lacked medical, scientific, or government background. Houry resigned in protest in summer 2025, saying she could no longer protect the agency's scientific integrity and citing measles, whooping cough, and flu deaths she witnessed: 'I couldn't stand behind that.' Her resignation followed Kennedy's June 9, 2025 removal of all 17 members of CDC's vaccine advisory committee (ACIP, tracked separately in this database), whose replacements included members with ties to lawsuits against vaccine makers -- notable given that Kennedy himself had collected referral fees from such lawsuits before becoming HHS Secretary. By the eighth week of 2026, CNN reported measles cases had already surpassed 1,100 nationally -- roughly six times the total typically seen in a full year -- with 96% of infections among unvaccinated people and health officials warning deaths would likely rise, putting the U.S. at risk of losing its measles elimination status -- a designation held since 2000 -- for the first time. A Reuters analysis of Michigan state data found the state's childhood vaccination series-completion rate fell nearly 3 percentage points, to 66.5%, between January 2025 and January 2026 -- about 13 times the average annual change over the prior 18 years. Reuters found the decline had different drivers across communities: Kennedy's vaccine-skeptic messaging was the primary influence among white families, while the administration's ramped-up immigration enforcement led Latino families to avoid public clinics and other activities outside the home for fear of deportation, after their vaccination rates had partially recovered post-COVID. A related disease is also reappearing: NBC News reported in late March 2026 that doctors were warning that Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) -- a bacterial disease once nearly eradicated in the U.S. through vaccination -- is resurging as childhood vaccination rates decline, with cases still low in absolute terms (8 cases reported nationally as of March 21, 2026) but rising, including severe recent infections and at least one reported death in an unvaccinated infant. A parallel state-level story, reported the following month, shows the same dynamic playing out through exemption law rather than data or messaging: Informed Consent Action Network (ICAN) -- a private anti-vaccine advocacy group whose founder Del Bigtree is a longtime Kennedy ally -- sued and won a court ruling restoring broad religious exemptions from Mississippi's previously strict school vaccine mandate, celebrating it as 'the right to medical choice for the citizens of Mississippi.' Mississippi Today/The Guardian reported that in the following year, the state's whooping cough (pertussis) cases reached their highest level in at least a decade, and in September an infant died of the disease -- Mississippi's first pertussis death in 13 years. More than one in five kindergarten religious exemptions issued that year came from newly-eligible families, and Kennedy allies were reported to be using the Mississippi outcome to push similar exemption rollbacks in other states. This entry documents ICAN's lawsuit and its allied framing, not a direct HHS or federal action -- distinct from the federally-driven measles-data-diversion and ACIP-panel actions above, though part of the same broader vaccine-skepticism ecosystem this entry tracks. Update 2026-08-13 (round 4 batch 29, cluster c0170): ProPublica reported that in the same March 2025 window, the CDC blocked release of an internal forecast modeling high measles-transmission risk in areas with low vaccination coverage; the agency had originally planned to use the forecast to underscore the importance of vaccination, but instead issued a public statement echoing Kennedy's framing, describing vaccination as 'a personal choice' rather than a public-health recommendation -- a second, earlier instance of HHS leadership overriding a CDC scientific product, predating the 15-year historical-data request Houry later described. Update 2026-08-13 (round 4 batch 29, cluster c0171): the same period produced a documented physical-harm consequence of Kennedy's vaccine-skepticism messaging -- CNN reported Covenant Children's Hospital in Lubbock, Texas treated multiple unvaccinated children for vitamin A toxicity after parents gave them unsupervised high-dose vitamin A supplements, following Kennedy's public promotion of vitamin A as a measles treatment; vitamin A does not prevent or treat measles. ABC News reported the national case count had reached 483 across 19 states as of the same week (most among unvaccinated children, the West Texas outbreak the epicenter), an early data point predating the 2,000+-case 2025 total already documented above. Update 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit ec8078a, which marked 28 discovery-backlog records folded into this entry in candidates.json but never actually wrote their content here): Kennedy's vaccine skepticism predates his HHS tenure -- during a 2015 multi-state measles outbreak he dismissed public concern as 'hysteria,' blamed vaccine manufacturers for pushing legislation to end personal-belief exemptions, and promoted the debunked vaccine-autism link (Mother Jones, reporting in April 2025). During the 2025 outbreak itself, Kennedy made several further specific public claims that contemporaneous reporting showed were false or misleading, beyond the general pattern Houry later described: in April 2025 he asserted on social media that the Texas outbreak's growth curve was 'flattening' thanks to CDC reinforcements and vaccine distribution, a claim ABC News reported was contradicted by Texas's own state data showing infections still rising and spreading into new counties; in a nationally aired Dr. Phil interview on April 29, 2025, he said vaccines are not properly safety-tested and urged parents to 'do your own research' (New York Times); and around May 1, 2025 he revived the long-debunked claim that the MMR vaccine contains 'aborted fetus debris' (Reuters). Case counts climbed steadily through the spring, passing 700 (mid-April, USA Today), 800-900 (late April, ABC News), and topping 1,000 for the first time in five years by mid-May 2025 (Reuters), with Texas's Gaines County the single-county epicenter (405 of the state's 717 cases); the New York Times reported on April 23, 2025 that the CDC had designated the Texas-Oklahoma-New Mexico spread a single unified outbreak, the largest since the 2000 elimination declaration. Michigan's outbreak first surfaced in this same window -- its first in six years, three cases in Montcalm County and seven statewide (ABC News, April 18, 2025) -- an early data point in the same Michigan story whose 2026 vaccination-rate collapse (69.4% to 66.5%) is already documented above via Reuters' March 2026 analysis. By early July 2025 the national total had climbed further to roughly 1,280 cases -- the worst since 2000 -- centered on an unvaccinated Mennonite community in West Texas and spread to 39 states (Newsweek, Guardian, Reuters), with Reuters reporting Kennedy had by then fired CDC vaccine experts and installed anti-vaccine allies to help rewrite immunization policy. Separately released CDC kindergarten-vaccination data in early August 2025 showed national measles coverage had fallen to 92.5% for the 2024-25 school year, with exemptions rising in most states (Reuters) -- a national vaccination-rate data point distinct from, and predating, the Michigan-specific decline already documented above. A CBS News investigation published August 31, 2025 reported that Trump administration interference with CDC communications and staffing had paralyzed the agency's outbreak response -- internal reports censored, experts sidelined, staff purged -- leaving Texas local health officials feeling 'all alone' as the outbreak spread across six states and into Mexico; the same investigation put the cumulative toll at that point at roughly 4,500 cases and at least 16 deaths, a figure substantially higher than, and not reconcilable with, the 2,000-2,295-case U.S. national totals documented elsewhere in this entry -- this discrepancy is unresolved in sourcing reviewed for this backfill and the 4,500/16 figures are flagged rather than adopted as a corroborated national total; the qualitative claim of CDC communications/staffing paralysis corroborates Houry's account already documented above. The Utah-Arizona border outbreak documented above (679 cumulative Utah cases as of August 2026) began smaller: NBC News reported 65 confirmed cases across southwestern Utah and Mohave County, Arizona as of September 27, 2025, concentrated among unvaccinated children in communities where some schools reported MMR coverage as low as 7%. A previously undocumented South Carolina outbreak emerged in parallel that autumn and grew into one of the largest legs of the national outbreak: NBC News reported South Carolina and Minnesota outbreaks had quarantined at least 270 unvaccinated students by mid-October 2025; South Carolina's own count reached 16 cases by October 19 (USA Today), traced in part to Global Academy, a charter school with only 17% student immunization that placed over 140 students in quarantine; the national total reached 1,563 cases across 41 states by mid-October, with officials warning the true total could exceed 5,000 (NPR); further NBC News and AP reporting through December 2025 tracked continuing quarantines across South Carolina, Ohio, Utah, and Arizona and a national total approaching 2,000 cases by year's end. South Carolina's outbreak then accelerated sharply into 2026: CNN reported it had surpassed 200 cases by January 22, 2026; Reuters put it at 434 cases (up 124 in roughly two weeks) by January 29, concentrated in Greenville and Spartanburg counties and hitting children ages 5-17 hardest; and PBS NewsHour reported nearly 600 additional cases in a single month brought South Carolina's total to 789 by early February 2026, centered in Spartanburg County -- a county-level total that had by then surpassed the entirety of Texas's 2025 outbreak. The outbreak's international dimension was reported separately from this domestic case-count tracking: the Guardian reported in October 2025 that measles had resurged across the Americas, with more than 11,000 cases in ten countries -- 4,800 in Mexico alone -- as U.S.-originated anti-vaccine messaging spread through Latin America; and the WHO reported in December 2025 that global measles infections had topped 11 million across 59 countries, warning that collapsing immunization coverage was also priming resurgences of polio, diphtheria, and whooping cough, with the U.S. (over 1,700 cases at the time of that report) among the affected countries. The CDC's own year-end tally for 2025, reported by ABC News on January 5, 2026, put the final total at 2,000+ cases across 43 states and 50 separate outbreaks with roughly 93% of cases among unvaccinated people or those with unknown status -- the same figures already cited above via CBS News' later July 2026 reporting, now traced to their original CDC source and reporting date. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0216): a Stanford Medicine-led modeling study, published in JAMA on April 24, 2025, projected the longer-term consequence of the declining vaccination rates this entry documents: even at 2025's actual vaccination rates, the simulation found measles could become endemic in the U.S. again within two decades, producing more than 850,000 cases, 170,000 hospitalizations, and 2,500 deaths over the next 25 years; a further 50% decline in vaccination coverage would produce an estimated 51.2 million cases over the same period, while a modest 5% increase in coverage would keep the disease safely below endemic thresholds. title: Trump, RFK Jr., and FDA Promoted an Unproven Tylenol-Autism Link and Fast-Tracked Leucovorin, Drawing Global Regulator Pushback
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS, FDA)
status: Contested and partly walked back -- global regulators and U.S. medical bodies continue to reject the acetaminophen-autism causal claim; the FDA's leucovorin approval was ultimately narrowed to an ultra-rare genetic condition rather than the broad autism indication originally promised
date_of_action: 2025-09-05 (initial report) through 2026-03-11 (FDA's final, narrowed leucovorin approval)
what_changed: News that HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. would link autism to acetaminophen (Tylenol) use during pregnancy first broke on September 5, 2025, ahead of any official announcement, triggering an immediate stock selloff in Kenvue, Tylenol's maker. The report also previewed a related claim: that folinic acid (a folate derivative) could ease autism symptoms. On September 22, 2025, President Trump, Kennedy, and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary held a White House event formalizing both actions. Trump told pregnant women Tylenol 'is no good' and to 'fight like hell' to avoid it, tying acetaminophen use in pregnancy to autism despite the FDA's own prior conclusions, reached as recently as August 2025, that the evidence does not support a causal link; the FDA nonetheless began the process of a label change and issued a physician notice. Separately, Makary announced the FDA intended to approve Wellcovorin (leucovorin) -- an existing chemotherapy-support drug -- to treat autism symptoms, predicting 'hundreds of thousands of kids' would benefit, and stating this would proceed based on a systematic review of published literature and case reports rather than a randomized controlled trial. Medical organizations, including the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the American Academy of Pediatrics, and the Autism Science Foundation, immediately rejected the causal claim as unsupported by the evidence and warned that discouraging fever/pain treatment in pregnancy carries its own documented risks. Global regulators followed within a day: on September 23, 2025, the European Medicines Agency, the UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration, and the World Health Organization all publicly stated the evidence does not support an acetaminophen-autism link, with UK Health Secretary Wes Streeting saying he trusted 'British doctors, British scientists... over President Trump.' Physicians reported a surge of anxious patient questions from pregnant women in the announcement's immediate aftermath. On October 17, 2025, Kenvue formally petitioned the FDA to reject a citizen petition (filed by the Informed Consent Action Network) seeking an autism warning on Tylenol's label, calling the request 'unsupported by the scientific evidence and legally and procedurally improper'; the FDA had reaffirmed as recently as August 2025 that the data do not support a causal association. On October 28, 2025, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Kenvue and Johnson & Johnson, alleging the companies deceptively marketed Tylenol as safe in pregnancy while concealing an autism risk -- the first state lawsuit following Trump's September claims, though independent of the FDA/HHS action itself. The next day, October 29, 2025, Kennedy partially walked back the administration's own claim, telling reporters the evidence was 'suggestive' of a link but that a causative association 'is not sufficient to say it definitely causes autism,' calling for further caution rather than certainty. The leucovorin approval itself was ultimately far narrower than promised: FDA's final decision, reported March 11, 2026, cleared Wellcovorin only for cerebral folate transport deficiency in patients confirmed to carry a specific genetic variant -- a condition documented in fewer than 50 people nationwide -- not the broad autism indication Makary had described to 'hundreds of thousands' of children five months earlier; agency officials said they went into the review considering a broader autism approval but could only find sufficient evidence for the ultra-rare genetic condition.

The underlying scientific question (whether any acetaminophen-autism association survives adjustment for genetic/familial confounding) remains actively studied and is presented here as contested, not resolved in either direction beyond what FDA, ACOG, AAP, and international regulators have themselves concluded.

title: RFK Jr. Directs CDC to Contradict Its Own Vaccine-Autism Guidance and Launches Multi-Agency Reexamination of Debunked Vaccine-Autism Link
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (CDC, FDA, NIH, NIOSH)
status: Ongoing and escalated -- CDC website guidance remains changed and softened; the confirmed CDC director declined to commit to reversing it; and an August 10, 2026 executive order formally directs the reinstated Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines to restructure the federal vaccine schedule within 90 days, a major expansion beyond the reexamination effort this entry originally documented
date_of_action: 2025-05-16 (Reuters first reports NIH autism-research funding cuts) through 2026-07 (CNN reports on the broader dismantling effort)
what_changed: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0340, antecedent context): before the CDC webpage changes documented below, Kennedy's HHS had already been cutting the legitimate autism research this reexamination claims to prioritize. A Reuters review of federal spending data published May 16, 2025 found NIH autism-research spending down roughly $31 million (26% below the prior four-year average) for January-April 2025, with grants canceled or held up specifically because they involved diverse populations, studied gender differences in autism, or were based at universities under separate Trump administration scrutiny -- among the eliminated grants Reuters identified by name: a $509,000 study of genetic factors in mental health and gender diversity among 10,000 autistic and non-autistic people, a $211,000 grant on improving mental health outcomes for autistic adults, and a $548,000 study of autism risk among children of women exposed to childhood abuse. A ProPublica investigation published August 20, 2025 found the cuts extended further: Kennedy eliminated the entire NIOSH division of researcher Erin McCanlies, who had spent nearly two decades studying how parental chemical exposure affects children's autism risk, shutting down her lab just three weeks before she finished her fourth major paper on the subject; ProPublica's own review of federal data found more than $40 million in NIH autism-research grants canceled and more than 50 autism-related studies defunded under Kennedy's tenure -- directly undercutting his own repeated public pledge to find autism's environmental causes. On November 19, 2025, the CDC's vaccine-safety webpage was changed from stating 'vaccines do not cause autism' to instead claim that assertion isn't 'evidence-based' -- a change that bypassed the agency's normal scientific-clearance process and was made without the involvement of the CDC office that manages the page, according to NPR and STAT News. Kennedy confirmed on November 21, 2025 that he had personally directed the change. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. personally directed the CDC to update its website to contradict the agency's longtime public guidance that vaccines do not cause autism -- a position supported by decades of scientific consensus and numerous large-scale studies, and one independent researchers across seven countries have tested in more than 40 high-quality studies covering over 5.6 million people. Kennedy tasked Stefanie Spear, one of his closest advisers, with leading an HHS effort to search for evidence of a vaccine-autism link. HHS separately reinstated the Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, a body disbanded in 1998, to reexamine childhood immunization safety. A broader multi-agency initiative, reported by the New York Times, involves researchers across several federal agencies comparing long-term health outcomes between vaccinated and unvaccinated children and revisiting questions about vaccine ingredients including thimerosal, a mercury-based preservative removed from most childhood vaccines decades ago -- millions of dollars in federal funding have been redirected toward this effort. A concrete instance of the redirected funding: on September 11, 2025, the CDC announced a $362,493 sole-source (no-bid) contract to Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute to investigate a vaccine-autism link, a move autism researchers called unnecessary given decades of settled science; Kennedy said in a statement 'families have been left without answers or options as autism rates have soared.' Update 2026-08-02: The scientific basis Kennedy has relied on to justify this reexamination has itself been collapsing under independent scrutiny. At least three studies frequently cited by Kennedy to promote vaccine-safety doubts -- a 2021 Neil Z. Miller paper in Toxicology Reports linking vaccines to SIDS, a 2020 Miller/Brian S. Hooker paper in Sage Open Medicine claiming vaccinated children had higher rates of developmental delays and asthma, and a 2010 Carolyn Gallagher/Melody Goodman paper in the Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health linking early Hepatitis B vaccination to autism -- have all been removed, retracted, or placed under additional scrutiny by their publishing journals within a roughly two-month span reported in June 2026. Kennedy relied on two of these three studies in a 2023 book he co-wrote arguing unvaccinated children were healthier than vaccinated children. Separately, Kennedy demanded a different vaccine-aluminum study be retracted; the journal declined. Update 2026-08-17: on July 23, 2026, the CDC's vaccine-autism webpage was softened again, this time in the opposite direction -- adding a footnote stating 'Scientists have not identified the root causes of autism. HHS continues to support rigorous scientific research and will update this page as reliable new evidence becomes available.' The change came as a negotiated concession to Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), an HHS critic of Kennedy's vaccine views and chair of the Senate HELP Committee, in exchange for his support of the administration's CDC director nominee, Dr. Erica Schwartz; the Senate HELP Committee voted 13-10 to advance Schwartz's nomination on July 30, 2026. The page's original 'Vaccines do not cause autism*' header was not removed -- HHS officials told Cassidy it would remain per their agreement -- and the page continued to cite at least one already-retracted study as of late July 2026 reporting, drawing renewed criticism from public-health groups even as the footnote nominally reaffirmed that autism's causes remain scientifically unresolved rather than tied to vaccines. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 43): three developments, one of which predates and was missed by the 2026-08-17 update. First, the missed development: the full Senate confirmed Schwartz as CDC director on August 5, 2026 by a 51-44, largely party-line vote (Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., crossed over in favor) -- the entry's prior update only reached the July 30 committee vote and never recorded the actual confirmation outcome twelve days before its own last-verified date. During her July confirmation hearing, Sen. Bernie Sanders pressed Schwartz on whether she would remove the CDC's vaccine-autism webpage; she acknowledged 'overwhelming evidence' that vaccines don't cause autism but did not commit to removing the page. Second, NOTUS reporting (July 24, 2026) identified by name the specific retracted study the page continued citing, which this entry's own update already referenced without naming: a 2010 Gallagher/Goodman paper on hepatitis B vaccination and autism, retracted in May 2026 after an independent statistical reviewer found 'fundamental methodological flaws' and an 'overstated conclusion' -- the CDC page cites it alongside a 2014 HHS review that had deemed it 'reliable,' a characterization the retraction has since undercut. Third, and most significant: on August 10, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14420, 'Delivering Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations for Americans,' which directly escalates the reinstated Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines this entry already documents. The order gives the Task Force 90 days to present plans to (a) offer core childhood vaccines, starting with MMR, as single vaccines rather than only in combination form, (b) reassess the timing and sequencing of the full childhood schedule and adjust the federal schedule accordingly, (c) develop alternative adjuvants to aluminum and conduct comparative safety/efficacy studies, and (d) continuously reevaluate vaccine risk/benefit profiles. The order is separately grounded in an HHS scientific assessment claiming the U.S. recommends more childhood vaccines, and more than twice the vaccine doses of some European peer nations, than any peer country -- and per the White House's own fact sheet, reduces the diseases recommended for universal childhood vaccination from 18 (84 doses in 57 shots, by the fact sheet's count) to 11, with the remaining vaccines shifted to 'shared clinical decision-making' between parents and doctors rather than a universal recommendation. Public-health reporting (KFF) criticized the single-MMR-vaccine directive specifically, noting historical precedent that countries which abandoned combination MMR vaccines saw increased measles, mumps, and rubella outbreaks, and that Trump has separately and inaccurately called MMR 'quite lethal.' This converts the Task Force from a reexamination body into one with an explicit mandate and deadline to rewrite the federal vaccine schedule, with the process bypassing the CDC's own Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), the body that has historically set U.S. vaccine recommendations. title: SAMHSA Banned Federal Grant Funding for Fentanyl and Xylazine Test Strips, Reversing Harm-Reduction Policy
institution: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Final guidance in effect as of April 24, 2026; no reversal identified as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-07-24 (executive order) / 2025-07-29 (initial SAMHSA Dear Colleague letter, with a test-strip carve-out) through 2026-04-24 (SAMHSA guidance eliminating that carve-out) and 2026-05 (reporting on the resulting funding losses)
what_changed: Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0504: this April 2026 test-strip ban was itself an escalation of a broader harm-reduction defunding policy that began roughly nine months earlier. Following President Trump's July 24, 2025 executive order on 'Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets,' SAMHSA issued a Dear Colleague letter to states on July 29, 2025 stating that federal funds could no longer support activities labeled 'harm reduction,' including technical assistance for syringes, pipes, safer-smoking kits, or syringe exchanges, because such programs 'advocate for policies that are incompatible with federal laws and inconsistent with this administration's policies'; the Washington Post reported August 6, 2025 that this raised the possibility SAMHSA itself could eventually be dissolved into a restructured HHS agency. At that time, SAMHSA explicitly exempted naloxone, drug-checking supplies (including fentanyl test strips), and sharps disposal kits from the funding ban, carving them out as still-eligible lifesaving tools -- the carve-out this entry's April 2026 guidance later eliminated by extending the funding ban to test strips specifically, completing a policy arc from 'harm reduction' broadly to the one tool SAMHSA had initially preserved. On April 24, 2026, SAMHSA issued guidance prohibiting federal grant funds from being used to purchase 'substance test kits, including fentanyl test strips and xylazine test strips,' as well as test strips for medetomidine, a veterinary sedative increasingly found contaminating the illicit drug supply -- reversing the prior (Biden-era) policy that had funded harm-reduction organizations' distribution of these low-cost testing supplies. Test strips cost approximately $1 each and allow drug users to check street drugs for the presence of fentanyl, xylazine, or medetomidine before use, a widely-used harm-reduction measure. The Kentucky Harm Reduction Coalition, one specific organization affected, learned it would lose a $400,000 federal grant that had supported distribution of 48,465 fentanyl test strips in the first quarter of 2026 alone; organizations nationally that relied on SAMHSA grants for this purpose now face cutting services or finding alternative funding.

primary_proponent.name: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration leadership, under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: SAMHSA issued the guidance; HHS Secretary Kennedy oversees SAMHSA as part of his broader restructuring of federal health agencies
primary_proponent.note: Reporting reviewed attributes the guidance to SAMHSA as an agency rather than to a single named individual signer; it fits the broader pattern of harm-reduction and public-health-infrastructure rollbacks documented elsewhere under Kennedy's HHS.

estimated_impact.summary: The policy arrives as overdose deaths have declined roughly 19% nationally since their August 2023 peak, a reduction public health experts substantially credit to expanded harm-reduction measures including widespread test-strip distribution -- cutting funding for this specific, low-cost tool risks reversing recent progress at a moment overdose deaths, while declining, still number in the tens of thousands annually.

title: HHS Abruptly Cancelled $2 Billion in Addiction/Mental Health Grants, Then Reversed Within 24 Hours
institution: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Reversed within 24 hours, but the episode itself caused documented real-world disruption before the reversal
date_of_action: 2026-01-14 (termination notices sent) through 2026-01-15 (grants reinstated)
what_changed: On January 14, 2026, SAMHSA sent termination notices to an estimated 2,000-2,900 grantees, immediately cancelling close to $2 billion in federal grants supporting addiction treatment and mental health care nationwide, including funding for overdose prevention, naloxone distribution, and other substance-use-disorder services. The termination letters cited generic, non-specific reasons such as 'adjusting its discretionary award portfolio' or 'non-alignment with SAMHSA priorities,' without program-specific explanations. Providers reported overnight layoffs and service shutdowns as the cuts took effect. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was responsible for the termination. Facing swift bipartisan backlash from behavioral-health advocates and members of Congress -- including Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), ranking member of the Senate's Labor-HHS-Education Appropriations Subcommittee, who said there had been an 'intervention' at the White House to halt the cuts -- the administration reversed the terminations and reinstated the grants within 24 hours, by January 15, 2026. No public explanation was given for either the original decision or the reversal, and no official was identified as personally accountable for the initial termination beyond Kennedy's role as HHS Secretary.

estimated_impact.summary: Even though the cuts were reversed within 24 hours, the abrupt termination caused real, documented disruption -- providers reported immediate layoffs and program shutdowns -- illustrating that a policy 'undone' within a day still has real-world consequences for services like overdose prevention and naloxone distribution where even brief interruptions carry acute health risk.

title: SAMHSA Lost More Than Half Its Staff and All Ten Regional Offices Amid Push to Dissolve It Into a New HHS Agency
institution: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing -- staff losses not reversed; SAMHSA's independent structure is being folded into the Administration for a Healthy America (AHA); a permanent administrator has been nominated but not yet confirmed as of this update
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (first RIF wave) through 2025-10-30 (STAT News' most recent staffing count)
what_changed: On February 14, 2025, HHS dismissed roughly 10% of SAMHSA's approximately 900-person workforce in the first of what senators were warned at the time would be a much larger reduction. Through the spring of 2025, further reductions-in-force cut SAMHSA's staff by more than half: by October 30, 2025, STAT News reported fewer than half of the roughly 900 employees on staff in January remained, including just 5 of the agency's 17 most senior leaders. All 10 of SAMHSA's regional offices were closed, eliminating the on-the-ground staff who administered grants and oversaw state and local substance-use and mental-health programs; a group of Senate Democrats led by Sens. Michael Bennet and Alex Padilla wrote HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on March 31, 2025 that two regions in particular (Regions 4 and 5) had been left with no staff at all, cutting off 14 states from regional officials who help run local grants and life-saving programs. Other eliminated units included SAMHSA's external management team, Office of Minority Health, Office of Behavioral Health Equity, and an internal policy lab. The cuts came alongside a Kennedy-announced HHS reorganization plan to dissolve SAMHSA as an independent agency and merge its functions into a newly created entity, the Administration for a Healthy America (AHA), alongside HRSA and parts of other agencies -- senior SAMHSA staff working on that merger were themselves among those laid off. By June 2025, the Washington Post reported SAMHSA -- the federal agency responsible for the nation's response to the addiction and mental health crisis -- was itself in institutional crisis, with remaining staff describing disrupted school-based mental health programs, youth suicide-prevention work, community recovery supports, and substance-use treatment guidance. Senators' letters throughout 2025 specifically warned the cuts endangered the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which SAMHSA administers -- a line that had by then fielded roughly 12 million contacts since its 2022 launch; a national survey of the network's state-run call centers found 71% understaffed and 89% lacking the funds to hire, even before accounting for the SAMHSA-level cuts documented here. As of STAT's October 2025 reporting, the White House had not nominated a permanent SAMHSA administrator, leaving a low-profile deputy in charge; more than 30 current and former SAMHSA officials, congressional aides, lobbyists, and behavioral-health leaders described remaining staff as demoralized and fearful the 33-year-old agency was on the brink of collapse. In September 2025, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary Kennedy publicly warned of a U.S. mental health crisis, even as the same administration was cutting billions from the federal mental health programs -- including SAMHSA initiatives and NIH mental-health research -- described throughout this entry. Update 2026-08-17: on July 14, 2026, the White House quietly sent the Senate a nominee for the assistant secretary for mental health and substance use post that also heads SAMHSA -- Timothy Westlake, an emergency-medicine physician and SAMHSA's own chief of staff -- without a formal announcement. As of this update his nomination had not been confirmed, meaning SAMHSA had gone without a permanent, Senate-confirmed leader for the entire period since Trump's January 2025 inauguration.

title: Small Business Administration Cuts 43% of Staff
institution: Small Business Administration
status: Complete (reorganization announced and implemented in 2025); a related plan to hand SBA the federal student loan portfolio was separately blocked in court and abandoned
date_of_action: 2025-03-21 (announced); implemented through 2025
what_changed: On March 21, 2025, the SBA announced it would eliminate approximately 2,700 active positions out of a workforce of nearly 6,500, a 43% reduction, through voluntary resignations, the expiration of COVID-era and other term appointments, and a limited number of formal reductions in force. The agency described the goal as returning to staffing levels from the first Trump administration. The same day, President Trump separately announced that the SBA would immediately take over the Education Department's roughly $1.6-1.7 trillion federal student loan portfolio, a move announced on the same day as, and in apparent tension with, an executive order to begin dismantling the Department of Education. A federal judge blocked the loan-portfolio transfer in May 2025 on the grounds the SBA lacked statutory authority to administer student loans under the Higher Education Act. The administration ultimately abandoned the SBA option and, in March 2026, signed an interagency agreement to move the loan portfolio to the Treasury Department instead. Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): separately, the administration's FY2027 budget proposal calls for cutting SBA's total discretionary budget from roughly $1 billion to $329 million (a 67% reduction) and eliminating 15 of the SBA's 16 entrepreneurial development programs, which the proposal's critics say would affect services to nearly 1 million small businesses annually. This is a proposed FY2027 appropriations request, not yet enacted, distinct from the already-completed 2025 workforce reduction documented above.

what_changed: Margaret Ryan, Director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement, abruptly resigned on March 16, 2026 after only about six months in the role, with the SEC's own announcement providing no explanation. Multiple outlets subsequently reported Ryan had clashed with SEC Chairman Paul Atkins and other senior officials over the handling of cases touching Trump- and Musk-linked figures: she reportedly wanted to pursue fraud and other charges against crypto entrepreneur Justin Sun and against Tesla/X CEO Elon Musk, but faced internal resistance. title: White House-directed content review and exhibit alterations at the Smithsonian
institution: Smithsonian Institution (Washington, DC museums, via White House Domestic Policy Council/OMB)
status: Ongoing and escalated -- President Trump signed a second executive order, 'Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution' (E.O. 14416), on July 24, 2026, directing agencies to use funding/contract leverage to compel compliance and ordering NPS-installed warning signage outside the National Museum of American History; a bipartisan Senate letter (Murkowski/Merkley, Aug. 6, 2026) is now seeking implementation details on the signage directive; second-phase museums beyond the original 8 still not announced as of this update
date_of_action: 2025-03-27 (executive order) through 2026-07 (findings report)
what_changed: President Trump's March 27, 2025 executive order 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History' directed Vice President JD Vance, who sits on the Smithsonian's Board of Regents, to work to 'remove improper ideology' from Smithsonian museums, and instructed OMB and the Vice President to condition future appropriations on exhibits not 'degrading shared American values' or 'dividing Americans based on race.' In August 2025, White House aide Lindsey Halligan, Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley, and OMB Director Russell Vought sent a letter to Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch launching a formal review of eight flagship DC museums (including the National Museum of American History, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, and the National Portrait Gallery), demanding exhibition texts, future exhibition plans, internal curatorial guidelines, staff manuals, and organizational charts, with a 120-day deadline for museums to begin 'content corrections' replacing 'divisive or ideologically driven language.' The National Museum of American History removed references to Trump's two first-term impeachments from a display in July 2025 as part of an internal content review the Smithsonian undertook under White House pressure; the references were restored about a week later after public criticism. The Smithsonian's Office of Diversity was closed. National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet resigned in mid-2025 after Trump publicly said he was firing her, calling her 'a highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI' (the Smithsonian said only Secretary Bunch could make that personnel decision). Artist Amy Sherald canceled a planned exhibition of her work at the National Portrait Gallery in late July 2025 following a dispute over a painting depicting a transgender Statue-of-Liberty figure. In July 2026, the White House Domestic Policy Council published a report titled 'Saving America's Story' accusing the National Museum of American History of 'extreme political activism' and faulting it for not having created a dedicated exhibit on the Founding Fathers, the Declaration of Independence, or the Revolutionary War even in the 250th-anniversary year. The White House's July 2026 report -- formally titled 'Saving America's Story: How Ideological Capture at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History Erases Our Heritage,' issued July 4, 2026 by the Domestic Policy Council -- specifically accused the museum of 'anti-white,' 'illegal alien,' and transgender-related 'activism' in addition to underemphasizing the Founding era. Secretary Bunch responded publicly on July 8-9, 2026, writing that the report 'is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History' and that the institution 'remain[s] focused on what grounds us: a steadfast commitment to scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy and integrity' -- a direct, specific, on-record rebuttal to this particular report, distinct from his earlier general September 2025 independence statement already cited in this entry. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- no announcement identified yet of which museums comprise the review's second phase. Update 2026-08-17: on July 24, 2026 -- two days before this entry's prior 'no material change' recheck, which missed this development -- President Trump signed Executive Order 14416, 'Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution,' formalizing the July 2026 'Saving America's Story' findings report into a directive. The order instructs the Secretary of the Interior, the OMB Director, the GSA Administrator, and the Domestic Policy Council to 'identify and utilize any and all available authorities' to push compliance, explicitly including funding and contract conditions -- an escalation from review and public criticism to stated administrative/financial leverage. It also directs the National Park Service to install temporary signage along the public sidewalks/walkways leading to the National Museum of American History warning visitors that the museum reflects 'ideological capture' per the findings report and directing them to alternative sources for 'accurate' history, and mandates temporary outdoor counter-exhibits focused on the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence timed to the 250th-anniversary Semiquincentennial. No announcement of which museums comprise the review's second phase was identified as of this update. Update 2026-08-30: on August 6, 2026, Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Jeff Merkley (D-OR) sent a bipartisan letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and NPS Director Jessica Bowron questioning the E.O. 14416 signage directive's legal basis, seeking the total number, size, placement, content, and manufacturing/installation cost of the planned signs, the funding source within Interior, the number of DOI/NPS staff assigned, and where visitors would be directed for 'accurate' information and who compiles it; no response from Interior/NPS was identified as of this update. Still no announcement of which museums comprise the review's second phase.

primary_proponent.role: Special Assistant to the President and Senior Associate Staff Secretary, White House
primary_proponent.note: Co-signed and helped lead the August 2025 letter to Secretary Bunch launching the formal Smithsonian museum review, and, per legal analysis, has 'sought to influence the Smithsonian's decisions, including by instigating a curatorial review of the museum,' despite being a non-Senate-confirmed executive branch appointee with no formal authority over the historically independent institution.

estimated_impact.summary: A White House-directed content review, backed by the implicit threat of withholding congressionally appropriated funds, has already produced at least one exhibit alteration, contributed to the departure of two museum leaders, and led to the cancellation of at least one planned exhibition, at an institution that hosted nearly 17 million visitors in the prior year.

title: 770,000+ Children Lost SNAP Benefits in the Year After Trump's Domestic Policy Law, Despite Promises Children Would Be Protected
institution: USDA / Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
status: Ongoing and worse than first measured -- ProPublica's original 12-state analysis (776,134 children) was superseded in scope by a 19-state CBPP analysis (1.06M+ children, 44% of all losses) reported July 23, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed) through 2026-06 (ProPublica analysis published)
what_changed: Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit d9a0f29, which marked these records folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): The child-enrollment losses documented below are the downstream result of a monthslong 2025 legislative process. House Republicans first unveiled SNAP restrictions in May 2025 -- stricter work requirements, limits on aid to citizens and green-card holders, and a proposal to shift 5-25% of SNAP benefit costs plus 75% of administrative costs onto states starting in 2028 -- as part of a broader tax-and-spending bill (New York Times, May 12, 2025; Washington Post, May 13, 2025). CBO estimated in late May that more than 3 million people could lose SNAP monthly under the House bill's roughly $300 billion in proposed cuts (New York Times, May 22, 2025); by June, Reuters (June 11, 2025) reported the $22 billion state cost-shift alone could push over 4 million people off food aid, and the Wall Street Journal (June 2025) cited a CBO distributional analysis showing the wealthiest 10% would gain an average of $12,000 while the poorest households would lose about $1,600 from the combined Medicaid/SNAP cuts. On June 24, 2025, the Senate parliamentarian ruled that this flat-percentage state cost-shift proposal violated the Byrd rule, forcing Republicans to drop the roughly $128 billion savings mechanism from the bill entirely (AP, June 24, 2025); the state cost-sharing mechanism that ultimately survived into the final law was tied instead to each state's administrative payment error rate rather than a flat percentage (see below and this tracker's separate Arizona SNAP error-rate entry) -- though no record reviewed here states explicitly that one mechanism was designed as a direct replacement for the other. Added 2026-09-09 (same backfill): Through late June and early July 2025, reporting described the reconciliation bill's combined scope as it neared passage: roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts alongside the SNAP changes, together projected to strip healthcare from about 11 million people (New York Times, June 26, 2025); one estimate put combined Medicaid/SNAP/ACA-subsidy cuts at $1.4 trillion against $3 trillion in tax cuts, disproportionately benefiting the wealthiest households (Guardian, July 3, 2025); and the expanded work requirements, covering parents of children as young as 7 and adults aged 55-64, were projected pre-passage to threaten aid for up to 8 million people (Guardian, June 28, 2025) -- a figure the CBO later refined, post-passage, to 2.4 million people actually stripped of benefits by the work-requirement expansion alone (Guardian, August 12, 2025). Following the bill's July 4, 2025 signing, Politico (July 6, 2025) reported food banks warning the SNAP cuts could eliminate up to 9 billion meals a year, and the New York Times (July 4, 2025) reported Democratic governors warning that federal emergency funds were inadequate to cover states' new cost burden; the Wall Street Journal (mid-July 2025) reported food banks nearing collapse as pandemic-era aid ended and federal food deliveries were canceled on top of the new work requirements. Added 2026-09-09 (same backfill): The state cost-sharing mechanism took its final, enacted form by September 2025: the New York Times (September 20, 2025) reported the law requires states to fund a share of SNAP benefits for the first time in roughly 60 years, with each state's required contribution tied to its SNAP payment error rate -- a mechanism Arizona (tracked separately in this database) responded to in part by tightening enrollment. On October 1, 2025, the law's elimination of SNAP-Ed -- federal nutrition-education funding that also supported food banks -- took effect; the Guardian (September 30, 2025) called the combined cuts 'the largest SNAP cuts in U.S. history' and warned 4 million people a month would lose benefits amid grocery prices up nearly 18% since 2022, while the law's cancellation of the USDA's hunger survey drew criticism for obscuring the cuts' impact. States began absorbing the administrative burden immediately: the New York Times (September 30, 2025) reported Colorado counties taking on new enforcement costs for the law's expanded Medicaid/SNAP work requirements, part of a $386 billion combined Medicaid/SNAP decade-long cut. A ProPublica analysis published June 17, 2026 found at least 776,134 children stopped receiving SNAP benefits in the 12 states that report participation by age, in the year following Trump's signing of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025 -- legislation that cut roughly $186 billion from SNAP over a decade, the largest cut in the program's history, imposed new work requirements on older adults and parents of teenagers, and shifted billions in administrative and benefit costs onto states. Children made up nearly half of everyone cut from the program across the states studied. The impact was highly uneven: Arizona alone lost 205,223 children from its SNAP rolls since July 2025, a 55% decline (driven in part by the state's own error-rate-penalty response, tracked separately in this database), while Louisiana recorded the second-steepest child decline at 22%. Republicans had promised during the law's passage that children and other vulnerable groups would be shielded from its effects. A subsequent Center on Budget and Policy Priorities analysis, reported by Newsweek on July 23, 2026, extended the picture across 19 states (versus the original ProPublica analysis's 12) and found more than 1.06 million children had lost SNAP benefits since the law's enactment, with children accounting for 44% of all enrollment losses in those states -- a materially larger scope than the 776,134/12-state figure this entry was originally built around, though the two analyses use overlapping but not identical state samples. Update 2026-08-30: NPR/member-station reporting published August 3, 2026 places the child-specific figures already in this entry within the total program's collapse: national SNAP participation fell from 42 million to 37 million recipients (11%, roughly 4 million people) between July 2025 and April 2026, with over 1 million children losing benefits across the same 19 states CBPP examined. Arizona -- already this entry's steepest-decline example -- lost more than 400,000 total participants and saw enrollment fall to about half its year-earlier size, with more people visiting food banks monthly than remained enrolled in SNAP for the first time on record; Texas separately lost roughly 500,000 participants, a state not previously named in this entry's state-level breakdown.

title: SNAP Cuts Threaten 27,000 Small Grocers, Many in Rural Trump-Voting Areas
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture; SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program)
status: Ongoing -- OBBBA's SNAP cuts and eligibility/work-requirement changes were enacted July 4, 2025 and are phasing in; no source reviewed confirmed a national count of actual grocery-store closures attributable to the cuts as of this entry's sourcing
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (OBBBA enactment) through 2025-07-19 (Politico's dedicated reporting on rural-grocer impact)
what_changed: Politico reported July 19, 2025 that OBBBA's deep SNAP cuts -- described by multiple outlets as the largest cuts to the 86-year-old program in its history, affecting more than 42 million recipients nationwide -- were poised to hit independent grocery stores especially hard, including in many rural and small-town communities that voted for Trump. Small, independent grocers that operate on thin profit margins and depend heavily on SNAP purchases to stay viable are frequently the only full-service supermarket serving a given rural area; their closure would force residents to travel 30 or more miles for groceries. Separately, the Urban Institute projected 22.3 million of the 42 million SNAP-reliant families would lose some or all of their benefits as a result of the law's combined eligibility restrictions and administrative changes -- a demand-side reduction in SNAP purchasing power that directly reduces revenue for the retailers CAP identified as most exposed. title: SNAP Benefits Withheld During 2025 Government Shutdown
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service
status: Resolved (shutdown ended, full funding restored through Sept. 2026) but litigation exposed underlying legal violations
date_of_action: 2025-10-31 through 2025-11-13 (peak crisis); shutdown began Oct. 2025, was the longest in U.S. history
what_changed: During the government shutdown, the Trump administration initially announced SNAP benefits (food stamps for ~42 million Americans, about 1 in 8 people in the U.S.) would not be paid in November 2025 at all, breaking from the precedent of prior administrations tapping a contingency fund to keep benefits flowing during shutdowns. After lawsuits, a federal judge in Rhode Island (John McConnell) first ordered partial funding (~65% of normal benefits) from the contingency fund, then found the administration's partial-payment approach itself 'arbitrary and capricious' and ordered full funding by a set deadline. Some Democratic-led states issued full benefits before the Supreme Court intervened with a temporary stay blocking the order, creating a chaotic situation where some recipients got full benefits and others got partial or none, based on which state they lived in and how quickly that state's officials acted. USDA then ordered states to 'immediately undo' full benefit issuances already made. The dispute was ultimately mooted when Congress passed a bill ending the shutdown with SNAP funded through September 2026. Re-verified 2026-07-26: one additional litigation detail worth noting -- the administration itself moved to drop its own First Circuit appeal of the Rhode Island judge's order, rather than the appeal being denied on the merits, consistent with this entry's existing framing that the dispute was ultimately mooted by the funding CR rather than resolved by any appellate ruling. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change to this entry's own claims. (A separate, related case -- Rhode Island State Council of Churches v. Rollins, over work-requirement waiver terminations rather than the contingency-fund payment dispute this entry documents -- was dismissed by joint stipulation in early 2026 after the waivers in question expired on their own terms; noted here only to distinguish it from, not as new information about, this entry's tracked dispute.) Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit d9a0f29, which marked these records folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): earlier in the same crisis, in late October 2025, USDA had told states it could not use the contingency fund because the money was 'not legally available' for regular monthly benefits, per an internal USDA memo reported by AP, and separately directed states not to process November benefits with their own state funds without federal approval -- blocking at least three states (Louisiana, Vermont, Virginia) that had said they would try to keep aid flowing on their own. More than 200 House Democrats sent USDA a letter urging use of the contingency fund; House Speaker Mike Johnson publicly backed the administration's decision not to tap it, while the House remained out of session during the standoff. Two senior USDA Food and Nutrition Service officials -- FNS administrator James Miller and senior adviser Babs Hough -- resigned in late October, days before the November lapse, leaving the agency's SNAP leadership vacant during the crisis. As litigation escalated in early November, Trump publicly said SNAP would resume 'only when the Radical Left Democrats open up government,' appearing to threaten defiance of the court order then in effect, before his press secretary said hours later that partial payments would go out after all; separately, in appealing Judge McConnell's full-funding order, administration lawyers argued they could not 'find $4 billion in the couch cushions.' AP also reported some beneficiaries being turned away at grocery stores during the partial-payment period as merchants grew wary of reimbursement uncertainty tied to the shifting court orders.

title: OBBBA's SNAP Cost-Shift Collided With ALEC-Backed State Income-Tax Cuts, Risking Total Program Termination in Some States
institution: State governments (budget offices, human-services agencies) / USDA SNAP program
status: Ongoing -- the cost-shift and work-requirement phase-in runs 2027-2029, so most states' actual fiscal exposure has not yet hit; the crisis described here is a documented near-term risk based on state officials' own projections, not yet a confirmed nationwide program collapse.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OBBBA signed, states begin absorbing early administrative costs) through 2025-12 (ProPublica investigation into the tax-cut/cost-shift collision) and ongoing through the 2027-2029 phase-in
what_changed: Even before OBBBA's reconciliation bill passed, its scope blindsided states that had already finalized fiscal-year budgets: the Associated Press reported July 1, 2025 that 46 states had already begun their new fiscal year under budgets locked in before the bill's Medicaid/SNAP cuts and first-ever state SNAP cost-sharing requirement were finalized, forcing states to scramble with whatever reserve cushions they had on hand. State budget experts David Adkins (Council of State Governments), Brian Sigritz (National Association of State Budget Officers), and Erica MacKellar (National Conference of State Legislatures) described the timing as uniquely disruptive since Medicaid alone accounts for roughly 30% of average state spending. Specific state reserve positions varied widely going in: New Mexico capped a $2 billion trust fund; Virginia (Gov. Glenn Youngkin) built a roughly $900 million cushion via May 2025 vetoes; Missouri (Gov. Mike Kehoe) vetoed/froze $500 million; Florida held a 25%-of-revenue reserve requirement (roughly $750 million/year); Hawaii held a $200 million contingency; Vermont set aside $110 million ($50 million immediate, $60 million for future years); Montana's legal framework triggers a formal study if cuts exceed $50 million or losses exceed $100 million; Maryland requires a report if losses exceed $1 billion; and North Dakota's part-time legislature, constrained by an 80-day biennial session limit, had only 6 session days left to respond. The AP noted this SNAP/Medicaid cost-shift arrived alongside separate federal clawbacks of broadband and transit grants and threats to defund sanctuary cities, compounding the same states' fiscal exposure from multiple directions at once. A ProPublica investigation published December 9, 2025 (reporter Eli Hager) identified a distinct and more severe structural problem than states simply lacking a large enough reserve: many of the states now facing OBBBA's SNAP/Medicaid cost-shift had already hollowed out their own tax bases through a decade-plus of ALEC (American Legislative Exchange Council)-backed income-tax cuts, engineered as slow multi-year 'path to zero' triggers specifically designed to delay fiscal pain and avoid the kind of immediate public backlash that hit Kansas's 2012-2017 tax-cut experiment. At least 26 states cut income taxes since 2021 -- 23 cut their top marginal rate, 8 adopted flat taxes -- per Tax Foundation analyst Jared Walczak. North Carolina, which eliminated its corporate income tax as part of this wave, now faces a roughly $420 million/year SNAP administrative-cost penalty against an estimated $1 billion in revenue already lost to its own prior tax cuts, plus a separate $535 million Medicaid hospital-funding impasse. West Virginia (House Deputy Speaker Matt Rohrbach, R) faces $400 million-plus in projected deficits, with SNAP caseworkers already carrying 947 cases each. Missouri's own 2023 tax cut delivered a roughly $43,000 annual benefit to a millionaire household versus about $80 for an average earner (state Sen. Dave Rader, R, and critics cited this disparity directly). Georgia -- per a GAO finding -- spent roughly twice as much on administrative overhead as on actual benefits once Medicaid work-requirement rules took effect there. ALEC's own Joshua Meyer, along with Americans for Prosperity, defended the tax cuts as pro-growth; state fiscal-policy researchers Jason Bailey (Kentucky Center for Economic Policy), Wesley Tharpe (Center on Budget and Policy Priorities), Geraldine Miranda (Arizona Center for Economic Progress), and Craig Beck (OpenSky Policy Institute, Nebraska) instead described an 'administrative death spiral': tax cuts hollow out caseworker staffing, understaffed offices miss audits and process errors, missed audits and errors raise a state's SNAP payment error rate, and a higher error rate raises that state's required cost-share contribution under OBBBA's error-rate-tied cost-sharing formula (the same mechanism this tracker's snap-770000-children-lost-benefits-2026.json entry documents being finalized in September 2025) -- compounding the fiscal hole further. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0428: the error-rate-tied cost-sharing formula's final shape reflects a specific legislative carveout secured during passage. To win Sen. Lisa Murkowski's (R-AK) deciding vote, OBBBA's final text delayed the cost-sharing requirement by up to two additional years for the 10 SNAP jurisdictions with the highest FY2024 error rates -- Alaska, D.C., Florida, Georgia, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, and Oregon -- exempting them from the formula this entry documents until FY2029 rather than its earlier effective date for other states; critics noted this rewards the worst-performing states' error rates rather than incentivizing improvement. The same negotiation also doubled a rural-hospital relief fund from $25 billion to $50 billion over five years (with Alaska projected to receive at least $200 million of it) and made Alaska eligible for waivers from OBBBA's new SNAP work requirements for able-bodied adults without dependents. Ohio and Wyoming officials told ProPublica they were evaluating whether to terminate their state SNAP programs entirely rather than absorb the new costs; the October-November 2025 federal government shutdown, which briefly disrupted SNAP payments nationally, was cited by multiple state officials as a preview of what full program collapse would look like for beneficiaries. Officials in several states warned that balanced-budget mandates would force offsetting cuts elsewhere -- state college tuition hikes, frozen public-employee salaries, and canceled road projects -- to cover the new SNAP/Medicaid cost-share obligation once the 2027-2029 phase-in takes full effect.

primary_proponent.name: Congressional Republicans / state legislatures pursuing ALEC-model tax cuts
primary_proponent.role: Enacted OBBBA's state SNAP cost-sharing mechanism; separately, over a decade-plus, enacted the state income-tax cuts (in NC, WV, MO, OK, KY, MS, AZ, and others) that ProPublica's reporting ties directly to states' inability to absorb that new cost
primary_proponent.note: This is a two-part causal chain documented across two levels of government: OBBBA's cost-shift mechanism was a federal congressional action (documented in detail, including the Byrd-rule fight over its original design, in this tracker's snap-770000-children-lost-benefits-2026.json entry); the state income-tax cuts that left many of the same states unable to absorb it were separate, state-level Republican legislative actions over the preceding decade, coordinated in significant part through ALEC model legislation per Tax Foundation and multiple state-level policy researchers cited by ProPublica.

estimated_impact.summary: States that had already cut their own tax bases through ALEC-modeled 'path to zero' income-tax reductions now face hundreds of millions of dollars each in new, federally-mandated SNAP/Medicaid cost obligations they structurally cannot absorb without either terminating benefit programs outright or cutting other state services (tuition, salaries, infrastructure) -- a risk state officials in Ohio and Wyoming say they are actively evaluating, not merely a hypothetical.

title: Trump's Tax and Spending Law Stripped SNAP's Categorical Work-Requirement Exemption for 1.2 Million Veterans
institution: USDA / Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
status: In effect since November 1, 2025 -- veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth up to age 24 are no longer categorically exempt from SNAP's 3-month Able-Bodied Adult Without Dependents (ABAWD) work-requirement time limit; a veteran can still qualify for a different exemption (a disability that limits work, caring for a child under 14, or being 65 or older), but the veteran-specific blanket exemption itself is gone.
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed) through 2025-11-01 (nationwide compliance deadline, exemption removal took effect)
what_changed: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, eliminated the categorical ABAWD work-requirement exemptions that the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act had granted to veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth up to age 24 -- populations Congress had specifically carved out of SNAP's work-requirement time limit two years earlier. The same law also raised the ABAWD age ceiling from 54 to 64, sweeping in a larger population of older near-retirees. Effective November 1, 2025, all three previously-exempt groups must now prove at least 80 hours per month of work, job training, or volunteering to keep SNAP benefits beyond three months, unless they qualify for a different exemption (disability, caregiving for a child under 14, or age 65+). Per the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, an estimated 1.2 million veterans live in households that receive SNAP nationally, with state-level breakdowns including roughly 115,000 in California and nearly 100,000 each in Florida and Texas; state agencies implemented the change directly -- Pennsylvania's Department of Human Services, for example, explicitly notified recipients that veterans of any branch would lose their exemption as of October 31, 2025. National SNAP enrollment fell sharply in the months surrounding the November 1 compliance deadline, though national data does not break the decline out by exemption category (veteran vs. homeless vs. former-foster-youth vs. newly-covered-by-the-raised-age-cap), and some portion of the drop reflects administrative/paperwork friction during a large, fast-moving rule change -- a caseworker not yet processing a submitted exemption before a deadline passed -- rather than every case being a permanent loss of eligibility.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law July 4, 2025, which eliminated the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act's categorical SNAP work-requirement exemptions for veterans, homeless individuals, and former foster youth, effective November 1, 2025.

estimated_impact.summary: Roughly 1.2 million veterans nationally live in SNAP-participating households and are now subject to proving 80 hours/month of work, training, or volunteering to keep food assistance beyond three months -- a documentation burden advocates say falls hardest on veterans with PTSD, other service-connected conditions that fall short of a qualifying disability exemption, or limited civilian work histories. Food insecurity is independently well-documented among veterans as linked to worse physical and mental health outcomes, including elevated risk of depression and suicidal ideation, particularly among veterans with a history of PTSD or military sexual trauma -- this entry does not attribute any specific health outcome to this policy change directly, since no source reviewed ties a mortality or morbidity figure to this exemption removal specifically, but the general food-insecurity/veteran-mental-health link is independently established research.
