title: African Development Foundation Reduced to Near-Nothing Before Courts Fully Reverse Takeover
institution: U.S. African Development Foundation and Inter-American Foundation
status: Reversed (final federal court orders in 2025-2026 fully vacated the takeovers at both agencies)
date_of_action: 2025-02-19 (executive order) through 2026-03 (final court order restoring USADF)
what_changed: On February 19, 2025, President Trump issued an executive order directing USADF, the Inter-American Foundation (IAF), the U.S. Institute of Peace, and the Presidio Trust to be reduced to 'the minimum presence and function required by law.' Peter Marocco, a State Department official who also oversaw the dismantling of USAID, moved to take control of both USADF and IAF within days. At IAF, Marocco held a one-person 'board meeting' outside the agency's locked headquarters on February 28, 2025, after being unable to gain entry, and declared himself acting CEO and president in a notice entered into the Federal Register. At USADF, staff denied DOGE personnel direct access to internal systems, citing privacy and security requirements, while Marocco announced by email that he would chair the agency's board. On March 11, 2025, District Judge Richard Leon initially found that a large reduction in USADF's staff and funding could itself be legal, declining at that stage to block leadership changes, while ordering DOGE staff to explain how they would maintain the agency's minimum required functions. By early April 2025, the government acknowledged in court that IAF had been reduced to a single employee and a single active grant. On April 4, 2025, Judge Loren AliKhan ordered the indefinite reinstatement of ousted IAF president Sara Aviel and blocked Marocco from serving on IAF's board, unwinding his actions including frozen grants. On July 1, 2025, Judge Leon ruled that Trump had violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act by installing Marocco at USADF without Senate confirmation, voiding the staff terminations and grant cancellations Marocco had directed. A final order in Rural Development Innovations Ltd. v. Marocco fully blocked the USADF dismantlement, and by March 2026, USADF staff were allowed back into their offices for the first time in months.

Court rulings distinguished between two separate legal questions along the way: Judge Leon's initial March 2025 ruling found that a large reduction in USADF's staff and funding could itself be legal, meaning the scale of cuts was not automatically unlawful, while his later July 2025 ruling found the specific mechanism used, installing Marocco without Senate confirmation, violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, voiding the actions taken under his leadership. This is a genuine reversal story: both USADF and IAF ultimately had their takeovers fully undone by final court orders, with USADF staff physically returning to their offices in March 2026, though Devex reporting notes the agency's reentry into the foreign-aid sector 'seems to be just beginning' after a year of program cancellations and funding freezes, and separately references newer, unrelated corruption charges connected to the agency as of that report.

title: USAID DRC mission closure and CDC global-health staffing cuts hampered detection and response to 2026 Ebola outbreak
institution: USAID (dissolved into State Department) / CDC global health security programs
status: Ongoing -- outbreak remains the deadliest DRC Ebola outbreak on record as of late August 2026 reporting (5,794 cases/2,786 deaths as of Aug. 27); a vaccination campaign began Aug. 27, 2026, but UN officials warn response funding will run out within weeks against a ~$679M humanitarian funding gap; USAID's DRC mission and broader global-health staffing cuts remain in effect, unreversed
date_of_action: 2025 (USAID DRC mission closure, CDC global-health staffing cuts) -- outbreak detected April 2026, still growing as of July 2026
what_changed: A Bundibugyo-strain Ebola outbreak, first detected in April 2026 in DRC's Ituri province, grew into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, reaching 3,442 confirmed cases and 1,521 deaths in the DRC by late July 2026, with additional cases and deaths in neighboring Uganda; WHO and Africa CDC declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. USAID's DRC mission had been shuttered in 2025 as part of the agency's broader 83% program-termination and dissolution into the State Department (see this tracker's usaid-dismantlement entry); the International Rescue Committee said the resulting reduction in country-level surveillance capacity contributed to delayed detection, and Bloomberg's public-health commentary and multiple outlets identified reduced CDC staffing and USAID/WHO funding cuts as having limited the surveillance, laboratory, and response-team capacity available to catch and contain the outbreak early. The disease is reported to have spread undetected for several weeks before health authorities officially confirmed it on May 15, 2026. Update 2026-08-17: the outbreak has continued to accelerate sharply. By August 15-16, 2026, DRC's public health institute reported 4,945 confirmed cases and 2,325 deaths, surpassing the 2,299-death toll of the 2018-2020 DRC outbreak to become the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history, and the second-largest and fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record globally. The single deadliest week so far (August 3-9) saw 579 new cases and 304 deaths. The outbreak has spread from Ituri into five additional DRC provinces (North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, and Bas-Uele) and to Uganda's capital, Kampala. Uganda itself declared its own linked outbreak over on July 28, 2026. Update 2026-08-30: the outbreak has continued accelerating and the international funding response remains critically short. By August 27, 2026, DRC's public health institute reported 5,794 confirmed cases and 2,786 deaths (up from 4,945/2,325 in mid-August). WHO's own August 14, 2026 situation report separately confirmed Uganda's 42-day enhanced-monitoring period tied to its last imported case (discharged July 16) was set to conclude August 27, 2026 -- a formal WHO confirmation distinct from, and following, Uganda's own earlier July 28 declaration that its linked outbreak was over. The DRC's Ministry of Public Health launched the outbreak's first vaccination campaign on August 27, 2026, using the ERVEBO vaccine in Kisangani, targeting the affected Tshopo, Bas-Uele, and Haut-Uele provinces; WHO approved 70,000 doses, with roughly 50,000 for frontline/health workers and 20,000 allocated to a clinical trial testing the vaccine's efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain specifically, since ERVEBO's proven effectiveness is against a different, more common Ebola strain. The UN's senior Ebola coordinator, Julien Harneis, said in late August 2026 that existing response funding 'will run out within weeks' and that the outbreak is spreading 'faster and wider' than previously documented; OCHA's $60 million Central Emergency Response Fund allocation falls well short of a nearly $679 million humanitarian funding gap, and Africa CDC and WHO issued a joint appeal for an additional $518 million. More than 160 healthcare workers have been infected and 43 have died, amid over 260 attacks on health workers in the preceding six months. This funding-shortfall reporting extends this entry's core claim beyond pre-outbreak detection capacity to the ongoing emergency response itself, which independent reporting directly ties to the same underlying USAID/CDC/WHO funding and staffing cuts already documented in this entry.

title: USAID Dismantled and Absorbed Into the State Department, Despite Being a Congressionally-Independent Agency
institution: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)
status: Operationally dissolved (July 1, 2025) but legally unresolved -- USAID was made an independent agency by Congress in 1998 and can only be formally abolished by an act of Congress, which has not occurred. Since mid-2026 the State Department has resumed nearly $2 billion in humanitarian and global-health funding by channeling it through multilateral organizations (Gavi, WFP, UNICEF, the Global Fund, and others) rather than restoring USAID itself, with political conditions attached.
date_of_action: 2025-01-24 (foreign aid freeze ordered) through 2025-07-01 (official dissolution and merger into State Department)
what_changed: On his first days in office, Trump ordered a near-total freeze on foreign aid, and within weeks the administration placed most USAID employees on administrative leave. By March 10, 2025, Secretary of State Rubio announced 83% of USAID's programs (roughly 5,200 contracts) had been terminated following an internal review; on March 28 he formally notified Congress that USAID would be dissolved and its remaining functions absorbed into the State Department -- ABC News reported the dissolution notice came just hours after a federal appeals court lifted a lower-court ruling that had been blocking the shutdown, meaning the announcement followed directly on the litigation clearing rather than preceding it. USAID officially ceased independent operations on July 1, 2025, after 63 years. On that final day, former Presidents Obama and Bush both publicly condemned the dismantlement -- a rare bipartisan former-presidential rebuke -- calling it a 'tragedy' and 'colossal mistake,' per CNN. Staffing was reduced from over 10,000 employees to fewer than 300. USAID's own Inspector General issued a report warning the spending pause and staff furloughs limited the agency's ability to ensure funds didn't reach terrorist-linked recipients, and separately warned that $489 million in humanitarian food aid risked spoiling due to the furloughs; the White House Office of Presidential Personnel fired that Inspector General less than 30 minutes after the report's publication -- despite a federal law requiring 30 days' advance notice to Congress before removing an inspector general. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0272): FedScoop reported that on April 24, 2025 USAID's IT office told departing employees -- an agency source said the decision could affect roughly 10,000 people -- that their government-issued iPhones, iPads, and laptops would be remotely wiped and marked disposed from IT asset inventories around each employee's reduction-in-force date, rather than returned; staff could then simply discard the hardware themselves. The agency framed this as reducing burden on departing employees, but it departs from federal agencies' standard practice of auctioning or reassigning surplus equipment rather than wiping and discarding it. Added 2026-08-10: The New York Times reported in early March 2025 that the freeze had already crippled global disease-prevention programs on the ground -- leaving dangerous pathogens unsecured, halting inspections for Ebola and mpox, and stopping screenings at international checkpoints -- with scientists warning that outbreaks once contained by U.S.-funded efforts now posed a greater risk of spreading worldwide, including to the U.S.; this is an earlier, contemporaneous data point on the same disease-surveillance capacity loss later linked (see below) to the 2026 DRC/Uganda Ebola outbreak, not a separate action. Update 2026-08-13 (round 4 batch 30, cluster c0178): the freeze's on-the-ground consequences extended beyond disease surveillance to disaster response. When a 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Myanmar on March 28, 2025 -- killing more than 1,700 people initially, a toll that continued climbing past 3,300 by early April and eventually surpassed 3,700, and displacing millions amid an ongoing civil war -- a three-person USAID assessment team that had just arrived in the disaster zone received termination notices on April 4, 2025 as part of the broader agency-wide cuts already documented above; CNN and BBC reported the notices arrived within days of the team's arrival, and that the three were advisers, not rescuers. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0199): NBC News independently corroborated the same terminations, reporting the laid-off workers were left sleeping on the streets alongside earthquake survivors while China and Russia expanded their own aid presence. The United States' overall response was limited to roughly $2 million in aid channeled through humanitarian groups already operating in Myanmar, a fraction of the scale China and Russia rapidly deployed. CSIS characterized the episode as the first real-world test of the administration's emergency-aid cuts; sweeping USAID reductions had already left the agency with over $2 billion in unpaid debt to humanitarian organizations, contractors, and international partners operating in Myanmar and elsewhere, forcing partner organizations to scale back operations independent of the earthquake itself. A significant, largely unresolved legal question underlies the entire action: USAID was reorganized by Congress as an independent agency in 1998 specifically to give it statutory protection, and per that same statute can only be formally abolished by an act of Congress -- which has not happened. USAID therefore legally still exists even though it has been operationally dissolved. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0519: a separate, earlier litigation track over the funding freeze itself reached the D.C. Circuit first. A coalition of international aid organizations sued over the funding freeze on February 10, 2025, and U.S. District Judge Amir Ali issued a preliminary injunction in March 2025 ordering the administration to resume disbursing billions in already-appropriated foreign assistance funds. On August 13, 2025, a divided D.C. Circuit panel reversed that injunction 2-1 (Judges Karen Henderson and Gregory Katsas in the majority, Judge Florence Pan dissenting), holding that only the Government Accountability Office's Comptroller General -- not private grant recipients -- has standing to sue under the Impoundment Control Act; the panel did not reach the underlying constitutional question of whether withholding congressionally appropriated funds was itself lawful. Judge Pan's dissent said the majority's standing ruling ignored the funding cuts' threat to 'the rule of law and the very structure of our government.' The Supreme Court later built on this standing theory, ruling 6-3 on September 26, 2025 to let the administration withhold roughly $4 billion in foreign aid via a 'pocket rescission' -- letting a rescission request expire unacted-upon at the fiscal year's end so the funds lapse without an up-or-down congressional vote -- a separate but related mechanism for withholding the same category of appropriated foreign-assistance funds this entry documents being frozen and terminated administratively. On the litigation front, the D.C. Circuit held oral argument on April 23, 2026 (before Judges Srinivasan, Pillard, and Pan) on the appeal of the core USAID dismantlement case; no ruling had issued as of this update. In a related case, briefing continues on a schedule running into summer 2026, with the government's reply brief due July 31, 2026. Separately, a federal court in Maryland denied efforts to block depositions of Elon Musk and other DOGE-linked officials in a class-action suit over USAID's shutdown (Does 1-26 v. Musk, D. Md.); that case is proceeding through discovery. Update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): the Musk-deposition framing above is now stale -- the Fourth Circuit reversed that February 4, 2026 order on March 4, 2026, blocking Musk from being compelled to sit for a deposition, at least for now (whether the reversal is final or merely delays the deposition question depends on how the broader suit progresses). The underlying constitutional claims (Appointments Clause, separation of powers) remain unresolved and the case continues in the district court, with a related preliminary-injunction appeal still in abeyance at the Fourth Circuit since June 2025. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling identified yet from the D.C. Circuit panel (Srinivasan, Pillard, Pan) that heard oral argument April 23, 2026; the appeal remains undecided and USAID's operational/legal status is unchanged from the prior update. Added 2026-07-27: former USAID Administrator Samantha Power said in a Bloomberg interview that she does not believe the Ebola outbreak spreading across the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda -- which has killed more than 400 people -- would be spiraling as it has if USAID had not been dismantled, citing the loss of the agency's early-warning disease-surveillance systems and cold-chain infrastructure (whose degradation contributed to delayed detection, since transported swab samples were no longer reliably preserved). The administration's separate withdrawal from the World Health Organization compounded the effect by removing another layer of international outbreak-response coordination. This is presented as a concrete, on-the-ground consequence of the dismantlement documented above, not a new or separate action. Update 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0116): added the Johns Hopkins University layoff figures (2,222 positions, $800 million in lost contracts), independently corroborated across CNN, Higher Ed Dive, The Daily Record, and CBS News, all citing the university's own March 2025 announcement. Added 2026-08-10: Rubio's 'no one has died' claim was not the only official denial contradicted by the record -- Mother Jones reported in June 2025 that internal State Department cables reviewed by the outlet documented lifesaving HIV treatment programs in Lesotho and food-aid programs in Malawi being cut as a direct result of the dismantlement, with diplomats warning of resulting deaths, hunger, and trafficking risk. That reporting directly contradicts Elon Musk's own public claim, made while leading the DOGE effort that drove the cuts, that 'zero people have died' as a result. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0129): the foreign-aid freeze also abruptly halted a $300 million, 10-year USAID commitment to clean up dioxin contamination from Agent Orange at Vietnam's Bien Hoa air base -- the largest remaining Agent Orange hotspot in the country. Work on the site, underway since 2019, stopped in March 2025, leaving exposed pits of contaminated soil at risk of washing into nearby communities during the rainy season; the same freeze also halted a related USAID-funded program clearing unexploded American munitions and landmines, a rehabilitation program for Vietnamese war victims, and work on a museum exhibit documenting U.S. remediation efforts. Following USAID's July 2025 dissolution, funding responsibility for the Bien Hoa cleanup shifted to the State Department, but U.S. diplomats and outside experts have warned that halting a dioxin remediation project mid-cleanup is more dangerous than never having started one, and that the suspension has strained relations with Vietnam, a strategic U.S. partner in the region -- an on-the-ground consequence of the funding freeze documented above, not a separate action. Update 2026-08-13 (round 4 batch 29, cluster c0172): added the appeals-court timing detail on the March 28 dissolution notice and the Obama/Bush bipartisan condemnation on USAID's July 1, 2025 final day, both minor corroborating/color additions to the already-extensively-documented dissolution timeline -- not new substantive claims. Update 2026-08-13 (round 4 batch 30, cluster c0178): added the Myanmar earthquake response episode, corroborated across CNN, BBC, CSIS, and CFR, all reporting the same three-person team's termination notices days after arriving in the disaster zone and the roughly $2 million U.S. aid figure -- a concrete, dated, on-the-ground consequence of the funding freeze/dismantlement already documented above, not a separate action. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0470): a Reuters investigation published July 19, 2025 -- based on interviews with 17 sources -- identified 21 unfinished water and sanitation infrastructure projects across 16 countries left half-built after funding was canceled, with hundreds of millions of dollars in cancellations since January 2025; workers abandoned holes half-dug and building supplies unguarded. Documented examples included an abandoned irrigation canal under construction in Kamleza, Kenya, and defunct USAID water kiosks in eastern Congo now used by children as play areas rather than functioning water infrastructure. Re-verified 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): the D.C. Circuit's AFGE v. Trump appeal (No. 25-5290, argued April 23, 2026 before Srinivasan, Pillard, and Pan) remains undecided -- no material change to the core dismantlement litigation's status since the prior update. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0780): the origin point of the multilateral-funding restructuring described in the following update. On December 29, 2025, the State Department and the U.N.'s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA, led by Tom Fletcher) signed a first-of-its-kind Humanitarian Reset agreement in Geneva, anchored by a U.S. pledge of $2 billion to 18 country-based and crisis-level pooled funds -- a pledge administration officials themselves said was down from $8-10 billion in annual U.S. voluntary humanitarian funding in recent years (other reporting cited a $17 billion 2022 peak). A State Department statement accompanying the announcement warned that individual U.N. agencies would need to adapt, shrink, or accept elimination, tying the reduced funding to consolidation demands, efficiency/accountability standards, and tighter U.S. control over how the money is spent. Update, 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 29): since June 2026 the State Department has resumed nearly $2 billion in humanitarian and global-health funding, routed not through a rebuilt USAID but through multilateral organizations directly -- $600 million to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance; $800 million to the World Food Programme for malnutrition response in Ethiopia, Myanmar, and Ukraine; $218 million to UNICEF for child health, nutrition, water, and sanitation programs; $661 million to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; $203 million to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies for disaster response; $100 million to the public-private Operation End Starvation initiative; and $50 million to an Ebola vaccine/pandemic-preparedness coalition, alongside separate DRC-focused Ebola response funding. The funding carries explicit political conditions: reporting describes prohibitions on directing funds to Afghanistan and Yemen, reduced assistance to Sudan, and a ban on climate-change-related humanitarian programming. This does not reverse USAID's dismantlement or restore the agency itself -- it is the administration routing a substantial, but conditioned and narrower, share of prior USAID-level funding through international intermediaries instead, a materially different mechanism worth distinguishing from the entry's dismantlement narrative rather than treated as a reversal of it. The D.C. Circuit appeal remains undecided as of this update. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0266): CBS News reported April 23, 2025 that the domestic fallout extended well beyond Johns Hopkins and EnCompass -- an estimated 19,187 American jobs had been lost across 46 states as of that reporting, with FHI 360 terminating 480 U.S. employees (140 at its North Carolina headquarters) and Georgia alone losing 44 USAID-funded programs worth an estimated $257.9 million. Most remaining USAID employees were slated to lose their jobs on July 1 or September 2, 2025, per that same reporting. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47): a second, distinct ~$2 billion funding tranche was announced August 10, 2026, this one routed to faith-based and community organizations under what the State Department calls the 'America First Global Health Strategy' -- a different mechanism from the multilateral-organization funding (Gavi, WFP, UNICEF, etc.) already documented above (see estimated_impact.figures for the breakdown). A State Department official told reporters the funding does not restore any previously cut program: 'there are not programs we cut that are now going to be funded again.' Separately, Boston University researcher Brooke Nichols' 'Impact Counter' -- a running, modeled estimate distinct from the Lancet's forward-looking 2030 projections already documented above -- put actual deaths in the year since the cuts began at over 700,000, including more than 500,000 children, a figure NPR reported July 17, 2026 alongside three additional named child-death cases beyond the Nigeria case already documented in this entry's primary_proponent field. On PEPFAR specifically, reporting reviewed found roughly $3 billion of a $6.045 billion FY appropriation remained withheld as of mid-2025, and Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) said July 22, 2026 he had received administration assurances that $1.3 billion of the frozen PEPFAR funds would be released; a July 2026 IAS conference presentation found 1,700 PEPFAR-supported sites closed and 77,000 fewer children receiving PEPFAR-supported treatment as a result of the disruption.

primary_proponent.name: Marco Rubio
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of State
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the program terminations, the dissolution notice to Congress, and USAID's final closure, writing on Substack: 'As of July 1st, USAID will officially cease to implement foreign assistance... This era of government-sanctioned inefficiency has officially come to an end.' Rubio told a congressional hearing in May 2025 that 'no one has died because of USAID [cuts]' -- a claim directly contradicted by subsequent peer-reviewed research (see below) and by on-the-ground reporting, including one documented case of a child in Nigeria who died after the USAID-funded clinic he depended on for urgent care was closed. This action is closely related to, but categorically distinct from, the separately-tracked State Department reorganization entry in this database -- USAID's elimination is the dismantling of an entire congressionally-independent agency, not an internal State Department restructuring.

estimated_impact.summary: A peer-reviewed study published in The Lancet (one of the world's most established medical journals) estimated USAID funding prevented more than 91 million deaths globally between 2001 and 2021, including a 65% reduction in HIV/AIDS mortality and 51% reduction in malaria mortality in the countries it funded. The same study projected that, absent a reversal, the 2025 cuts could contribute to more than 14 million additional preventable deaths by 2030, nearly a third of them children under 5 -- a scale the study's authors explicitly compared to 'a global pandemic or a major armed conflict,' while noting this crisis would stem from 'a conscious and avoidable policy choice.' A follow-up Lancet study one year later, incorporating a full year of real data rather than projections, estimated a somewhat lower but still severe 9.4 million-death figure by 2030 if funding trends continue -- researchers who reviewed the modeling told CNN the precise numbers should be treated with some caution but that the overall conclusion (large-scale, avoidable death) is likely correct. Domestically, the closure eliminated an estimated 19,187 American jobs across 46 states as of April 2025 reporting, spanning USAID staff and its contractor/NGO ecosystem -- one contractor, EnCompass, lost over 400 jobs in under a month, and FHI 360 terminated 480 U.S. employees. The largest single documented example was Johns Hopkins University, the country's top university recipient of federal contracts: after losing $800 million in USAID-funded contracts, Johns Hopkins announced in March 2025 what a university spokesperson called the largest layoff in its history -- 2,222 positions cut (1,975 international staff across 44 countries plus 247 U.S.-based positions), spanning its Bloomberg School of Public Health, Center for Communication Programs, and affiliated nonprofit Jhpiego, with roughly 100 additional workers furloughed to reduced schedules.

section_summaries.what_changed: USAID was operationally shuttered and absorbed into State after a near-total funding freeze shrank its staff by more than 97% -- though legally, only Congress can abolish it, and hasn't. Disease-screening and outbreak-prevention programs were disrupted almost immediately, and former Administrator Samantha Power has since linked the dismantlement to a worsening Ebola outbreak in the DRC and Uganda. Since mid-2026 the State Department has resumed nearly $2 billion in humanitarian/health funding, but routed through multilateral organizations with new political conditions attached, not through a rebuilt USAID.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: A peer-reviewed Lancet study credited this funding with preventing tens of millions of deaths and projected millions more by 2030 if the cuts hold, calling the toll avoidable, not inevitable; a running BU model estimates 700,000+ actual deaths in the year since the cuts began. A 2026 Ebola outbreak (400+ deaths) and a PEPFAR disruption (1,700 sites closed, 77,000 fewer children treated) are cited as concrete real-world instances of that lost capacity. A combined ~$4B in resumed funding since mid-2026 -- ~$2B via multilateral organizations and a second, distinct ~$2B via faith-based/community organizations -- is a partial, conditioned offset, not a restoration of USAID's own infrastructure; officials themselves say it does not fund previously cut programs.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Exceptionally strong sourcing, including two independent peer-reviewed medical studies and the agency's own Inspector General; official statements and the death-toll research genuinely disagree -- present both. The Ebola link is attributed expert opinion, well-corroborated but not an adjudicated causal finding. The 2026 multilateral funding resumption is well-corroborated on dollar figures; its specific political conditions rest on single-outlet sourcing. The BU Impact Counter's 700,000-death figure is a running model estimate, not a peer-reviewed final count.

title: Bird Flu Response Hampered by USDA's Accidental Firing of Response Staff, Plus Broader Funding Freezes and a Federal Communication Blackout
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA); Department of Health and Human Services / CDC
status: Reversal attempted on the USDA firings specifically -- USDA moved to rehire the affected employees shortly after the error was reported; the broader funding-freeze and communication-blackout effects on the wider bird-flu response were not confirmed as resolved in sourcing reviewed for this entry
date_of_action: 2025-02-15 through 2025-02-21 (reported)
what_changed: Over the weekend of February 15-16, 2025, USDA mistakenly terminated several employees whose work was critical to the federal government's response to the ongoing bird flu (avian influenza) outbreak, including staff in food-safety and inspection roles. NBC News reported USDA moved afterward to try to reverse the firings and rehire the affected workers, characterizing the terminations as an error made amid the broader probationary-employee purge underway across federal agencies at the time, rather than a deliberate targeting of bird-flu-response staff specifically. Separately, The Hill reported that the same period's broader pattern of mass firings, funding freezes, and a federal communications blackout had stalled the wider federal bird-flu response beyond just the USDA staffing error -- as egg prices surged nationally, the CDC struggled to provide timely public updates, leaving local health officials navigating a patchwork of delayed federal information during an active outbreak. The staffing losses continued beyond the February episode: around April 2, 2025, roughly 140 staff were fired from the FDA's Center for Veterinary Medicine, which had been overseeing the federal response to the ongoing bird flu outbreak in poultry and dairy cattle. By April 10, 2025, three key employees in USDA's National Animal Health Laboratory Network -- the lab-coordination staff responsible for bird flu testing -- were also leaving their positions, further thinning response capacity amid what was, at the time, the worst avian flu outbreak in U.S. history.

title: USDA Canceled the $3.1B Climate-Smart Commodities Program, Rebranding It Without the Climate Focus
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)
status: Implemented -- program canceled and replaced April 14, 2025, using existing (not new) funding
what_changed: Internal emails later obtained by NOTUS show that in February 2025, Gavin Kliger -- a 25-year-old DOGE staffer on unpaid leave from AI firm Databricks, with no USDA role or formal authority -- directed USDA's climate-grant elimination effort ahead of the program's public cancellation. On February 19, 2025, USDA Deputy CFO Lynn Moaney asked Kliger to approve agency-wide guidance identifying climate funding that did not 'demonstrably directly or indirectly benefit farmers or producers'; Kliger requested an extension while telling Moaney he hoped they would 'hopefully exceed our 120m goal significantly' by reviewing all USDA climate grants, and coordinated directly with Secretary Rollins on formalizing the resulting memo, with staff internally describing the compressed timeline as difficult to meet. On April 14, 2025, Rollins announced the cancellation of the Biden-era Partnerships for Climate-Smart Commodities (PCSC), a $3.1 billion initiative funding carbon-reducing farming practices, which USDA had already frozen funding for earlier in the administration. USDA said a line-by-line review found many of the Biden-era partnerships had high administrative overhead, with some projects passing less than half of their federal funding directly to farmers; Rollins has separately made clear she does not support climate-change-focused programs. Rather than simply terminating the program, USDA said existing grant recipients could continue under a new initiative, Advancing Markets for Producers (AMP), which drops the climate framing and requires that at least 65% of each grant's federal dollars go directly to farmers; USDA said it would honor expenses incurred before April 13, 2025, and that the AMP transition uses only existing program funding, with no new money appropriated. Missouri alone had roughly $1.2 billion in Climate-Smart Commodities funding at stake, according to state-level reporting.

estimated_impact.summary: A $3.1 billion program supporting carbon-reducing farming practices was eliminated and replaced with a rebranded initiative that drops the climate framing entirely, though existing grant recipients retain a path to continued funding if they meet new farmer-payout criteria -- a redirection of the same money's purpose rather than a straightforward funding cut.

title: USDA Canceled All Food for Progress Foreign Food-Aid Grants, Then Partially Reversed Course Days Later

what_changed: USDA canceled all existing grants under its Food for Progress program, which sends American-grown commodities -- including milled rice, soybean meal, wheat, and yellow soybeans -- abroad to support agricultural development and food security in developing countries, according to an internal email reviewed by Reuters. what_changed: On March 6, 2025, USDA notified members that it had terminated the National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods (NACMCF, established 1988) and the National Advisory Committee on Meat and Poultry Inspection (NACMPI, established 1971), consistent with a February 20, 2025 termination date reported by trade press, as part of the administration's broader elimination of federal advisory committees under Executive Order 14217. title: USDA Cancels 30-Year Household Food Security Survey as 4.7 Million Lose SNAP Benefits
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture
status: Complete -- survey terminated; Democratic members of Congress have introduced bills to reinstate it, not yet enacted
date_of_action: 2025-09-20 (survey termination announced)
what_changed: In September 2025, USDA terminated its annual Household Food Security Survey, which for 30 years had been the government's primary tool for measuring whether American households have reliable access to enough food, and which researchers and policymakers widely regarded as the 'gold standard' for understanding food access nationally. USDA's own press release described the survey as 'redundant, costly, politicized, and extraneous.' The cancellation followed passage of Trump's tax and spending law (HR1/OBBBA) in July 2025, which shifted significant SNAP funding responsibility to states and expanded work requirements; since then, roughly 4.7 million people -- about 11% of prior participants -- have lost SNAP benefits, with further losses expected as states continue implementing the changes. Food-security researchers said the survey's elimination will make it substantially harder to measure whether hunger is increasing as a result of the SNAP changes, since no comparable federal data source currently exists. Democratic members of Congress have introduced legislation to reinstate the survey; it has not been enacted as of this entry. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0593): days after the September 20, 2025 cancellation announcement, USDA placed about a dozen Economic Research Service staff behind the survey -- including Acting Administrator Kelly Maguire, her chief of staff, and the food economics division head -- on indefinite leave, citing an investigation into 'unauthorized disclosure' of non-public information; the affected employees had all attended the internal meeting announcing the report's cancellation. They were escorted from their offices and had their laptops seized, though USDA said the leave was not disciplinary. The agency did not specify what was disclosed or to whom, and AFGE, the employees' union, said USDA offered no further clarification; critics characterized the move as retaliation against researchers who had resisted burying the survey's data.

title: USDA Cancels $1 Billion in Local Food Purchasing Programs for Schools and Food Banks
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)
status: Finalized; not restored as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-03-11 (cuts publicly reported) through 2025-05-31 (continued downstream reporting)
what_changed: USDA canceled two Biden-era programs that funded schools and food banks to buy fresh food directly from local farmers: the $660 million Local Food for Schools (LFS) Cooperative Agreement Program and the roughly $500 million Local Food Purchase Assistance (LFPA) Cooperative Agreement Program, together over $1 billion in annual funding. Both programs had opened a new funding round on December 10, 2024, and many states and school districts had already signed new agreements before USDA ended them in March 2025, as part of the administration's broader effort to shrink federal spending. The School Nutrition Association estimated the cut would pull local, fresh-food purchasing away from an estimated 12 million students nationwide. By late May 2025, downstream reporting from North Carolina documented concrete on-the-ground effects: schools and small farms losing funding mid-agreement, farm layoffs, reduced fresh-produce access for students, and food banks bracing for increased demand amid a worsening hunger crisis, since the LFPA program specifically supported food-bank purchasing alongside the school-focused LFS program. title: USDA Mass Firings Gutted Food-Safety and Import-Inspection Staff, With a Reinstatement Order Not Immediately Followed
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) -- Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) and Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS)
status: Complete (initial probationary firings reversed under court order, USDA confirmed compliance May 2025; second, larger resignation wave was not reversed)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (probationary firings begin) through 2025-05 (15,000+ cumulative deferred-resignation departures, USDA confirms reinstatement-order compliance)
what_changed: Beginning in February 2025, USDA terminated at least 5,692 probationary employees as part of the government-wide firing wave, including roughly 200 inspectors in APHIS's Plant Protection and Quarantine (PPQ) program -- the unit that screens agricultural imports at ports of entry and detects invasive pests and diseases before they can spread domestically. (A separate, narrower incident the same month -- USDA's accidental firing of bird-flu-response staff, later reversed -- is tracked in its own entry in this database.) On March 13, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California issued a preliminary injunction ordering the immediate reinstatement of the terminated probationary employees; the Ninth Circuit denied USDA's request for a stay and upheld the injunction on March 17. Reinstatement did not happen immediately: on March 25, Rep. Jill Tokuda and 32 House colleagues sent USDA a letter urging urgent rehiring of the terminated agricultural inspectors, warning the delay heightened the risk that unscreened imports could introduce invasive pests and diseases into U.S. agriculture. USDA did not confirm compliance with the reinstatement order until May 2025, when it sent formal written notices to the affected probationary employees. By then a second, much larger wave of departures was already underway: more than 15,000 USDA employees -- over 15% of the department's workforce -- accepted deferred-resignation buyouts across two rounds (roughly 3,900 in the first round, 11,300 more confirmed by May 5, 2025), including hundreds of food-safety inspectors and technical experts. A subsequent analysis of USDA's own workforce data found FSIS (which inspects meat, poultry, and egg products) lost about 8% of its staff and APHIS (import and pest inspection) lost about 20% of its staff between January and March 2025 alone, with departing staff averaging 16-21 years of experience and 63% of FSIS separations specifically inspectors. Facing internal warnings that the departing employees' work was 'essential to securing the safety of the American food and agriculture system,' USDA reversed course on the ongoing buyout campaign in an April 23, 2025 email urging employees who had already accepted resignation offers to 'reconsider,' calling the work 'vital, mission critical' -- but the reconsideration window applied only to the second round of departures still in progress, not to employees who had already left the agency.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Agriculture
primary_proponent.note: Oversaw both the probationary firings and the deferred-resignation buyout programs, while publicly stating 'If you are FSA or frontline or with the farmers, you are not eligible to take early retirement' -- a claim in tension with the hundreds of frontline food-safety and import-inspection staff who did depart through the programs she ran, and with the department's own April 2025 email urging 'vital, mission critical' staff to reconsider resigning.

estimated_impact.summary: The cuts hit the specific functions responsible for stopping unsafe food and invasive pests before they reach the public: import screening at ports of entry, meat/poultry/egg plant inspection, and pest/disease detection. USDA's own workforce data, reviewed by an agricultural-policy nonprofit, documented double-digit staffing losses at the agencies responsible for import and pest inspection within the cuts' first two months, and advocacy groups warned of growing inspection gaps at small and mid-sized processing plants.

title: USDA Shuts Down $420 Million Nationwide Program That Aided Small Farms and Food Businesses
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Marketing Service
status: Terminated -- USDA stated it would continue honoring existing commitments on more than 450 already-awarded grants, but the program itself, including its 12 regional centers' broader technical-assistance and coordination work, was shut down
what_changed: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced the termination of the Regional Food Business Centers (RFBC) program on July 15, 2025. USDA had launched the program in 2022-2023 with $420 million in American Rescue Plan Act funding, establishing 12 regional centers -- covering all 50 states, plus a dedicated national tribal center and centers targeting Colonias (U.S./Mexico border counties) and persistent-poverty areas -- to provide small and mid-sized farms and food businesses with technical assistance, grants, and help navigating federal, state, and local resources to access new markets. Rollins criticized the program's structure directly: 'The Biden Administration created multiple, massive programs without any long-term way to finance them. This is not sustainable for farmers who rely on these programs, and it flies in the face of Congressional intent.' USDA said it would continue honoring more than 450 already-awarded grants to farmers and food businesses so in-progress planning decisions on the farm could proceed, but ended the centers' broader ongoing technical-assistance and coordination role. Local reporting through mid-2025 and into 2026 documented concrete downstream effects: Civil Eats reported the program had already been caught in the administration's earlier funding freeze months before its formal termination, and KCUR reported in August 2025 on a Midwest small grower who said losing the program's support put her farm's continued operation at risk; This Is Reno reported small Nevada farms and food businesses stood to lose roughly $3 million in USDA support tied to the program specifically in that state.

title: USDA's SNAP Recipient-Data Demands and a Threatened Mass Reapplication, Backed by Unreleased 'Massive Fraud' Claims, Drew a 21-State Lawsuit and Two Federal Court Losses
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service
status: Ongoing litigation. USDA's proposed mass-reapplication requirement for all SNAP recipients was walked back in December 2025 in favor of existing state recertification procedures, but the underlying fight over USDA's demand for recipients' personal data continues: a federal court blocked USDA from withholding SNAP funding over states' data refusal (Feb. 2026), and USDA/DOJ escalated in June 2026 by directly suing four non-compliant states to compel them to turn over data.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (executive order directing 'unfettered access' to state program data) through 2026-06-26 (DOJ sues four non-compliant states)
what_changed: In March 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to obtain 'unfettered access' to state-held program data. USDA subsequently demanded that all states turn over comprehensive SNAP applicant and recipient records -- names, Social Security numbers, addresses, and financial information -- threatening to withhold SNAP funding from states that refused. In July 2025, California Attorney General Rob Bonta led a coalition of 21 states and the District of Columbia in suing USDA (State of California et al. v. Rollins), arguing the data demand violated the SNAP Act's data-security-protocol requirements and the Administrative Procedure Act; a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction in October 2025 blocking USDA from withholding funding or pursuing noncompliance proceedings against the plaintiff states. USDA responded by sending a new data-demand letter to the same 21 governors in November 2025, characterizing it as a separate action not covered by the injunction and again threatening to withhold benefits from non-compliant states. On November 19-20, 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced that all of the program's roughly 41.7 million recipients nationwide would be required to reapply for benefits, citing what she called 'massive fraud' -- without USDA releasing the underlying data publicly. In subsequent media appearances (including a NewsNation interview), Rollins cited specific figures -- 186,000 dead people receiving benefits, 500,000 Americans receiving benefits twice, and more than 120 arrests for SNAP fraud -- as evidence, though USDA did not make the underlying data available for independent verification. By December 1-5, 2025, facing criticism that ordinary payment-error rates were being mischaracterized as fraud, USDA walked back the universal-reapplication plan, with a spokesperson saying the agency would instead rely on states' 'standard recertification processes' -- the periodic (typically six-to-twelve-month) eligibility updates already required under existing law. Rollins simultaneously previewed broader plans to 'completely deconstruct' SNAP, including new work requirements, continuing to cite the unreleased fraud data as justification. On February 2026, Judge Maxine Chesney of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California again ruled for the plaintiff states, permanently blocking USDA from withholding SNAP funding over the data-sharing dispute -- finding the relevant statute requires data disclosure 'subject to data and security protocols agreed to by the State agency and Secretary' (a negotiation requirement USDA had bypassed) and that USDA's proposed data-sharing protocols would likely violate separate statutory privacy safeguards; the judge also rejected USDA's request to stay the ruling pending appeal. By mid-2026, 28 states and Guam had turned over data voluntarily; USDA cited that data as showing 'billions of dollars per year' in overpayments and fraud, again without releasing it for independent review. On June 26, 2026, the Justice Department escalated by directly suing four states that had refused to comply -- Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Minnesota -- seeking a court order compelling them to turn over five years of SNAP applicant data, with Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and Secretary Rollins accusing the states of 'shamelessly' defying federal law.

estimated_impact.summary: No SNAP household is confirmed to have lost benefits specifically from this episode -- the universal-reapplication plan was walked back before implementation -- but the fight put all ~41.7 million SNAP recipients' benefits under a public threat for several weeks based on fraud figures USDA never released for independent verification, and the underlying data-privacy dispute (recipients' Social Security numbers, addresses, and financial records) remains an active federal court fight into mid-2026, with USDA/DOJ shifting from defending against a states' lawsuit to affirmatively suing states to compel data turnover.

title: USDA Canceled $500 Million in Supplemental Emergency Food Assistance Funding, Scrapping 94 Million Pounds of Food Deliveries to Food Banks Nationwide
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service / Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC)
status: Rescinded and not restored as of last verification. The $500 million was supplemental funding on top of TEFAP's regular annual appropriation, which remains in place; this entry covers only the canceled supplemental tranche.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (cuts begin) through 2025-11-19 (NPR reporting on continued post-shutdown food-bank demand)
what_changed: In October 2024, the Biden administration's USDA announced $500 million in supplemental funding for The Emergency Food Assistance Program (TEFAP), drawn from the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC) -- on top of TEFAP's regular annual appropriation -- adding to nearly $1 billion in similar CCC-funded supplemental commitments announced in September 2022. Beginning in March 2025, the Trump administration's USDA canceled this supplemental funding, halting roughly 4,300 planned deliveries of USDA-purchased meat, dairy, eggs, and produce -- about 94 million pounds of food -- before they reached food banks nationwide, per a ProPublica investigation that tracked the cancellations 'down to the number of eggs.' USDA characterized the canceled funding as a 'Biden-era slush fund,' telling reporters: 'The Biden Administration inflated statutory programs with Commodity Credit Corporation dollars without any plans for long-term solutions.' National-scope reporting emerged first: The New York Times reported April 28, 2025 that food banks nationwide were already serving diminished, less-nutritious meals as a result of the cuts -- including one West Virginia food bank forced to substitute crackers, dried cranberries, and vegetable soup for previously USDA-supplied ingredients while preparing meals for 40 seniors -- citing Feeding America's estimate that the Trump administration's combined food-aid cuts (spanning both this TEFAP/CCC rescission and the separately tracked LFS/LFPA program cuts) totaled roughly $1 billion. Early, regional effects were documented by the Washington Post in May 2025: food banks in Virginia, Washington D.C., and Maryland reported losing more than 1.4 million meals combined, compounded by separate USDA cuts to local-food-purchasing programs (see the related, separately tracked usda-local-food-schools-food-banks-cut-2025 entry) and senior nutrition programs -- with rural areas such as Virginia's Blue Ridge region reporting record need even as national unemployment remained low. By September 2025, the strain was also squeezing hunger-relief networks that depend on unpaid labor: NPR and The Maine Monitor reported that Maine's food pantries -- more than 75% of which run entirely on volunteers, many in their 70s and 80s -- had seen their supply from Good Shepherd Food Bank, the state's only food bank, cut by half or more since March. Good Shepherd began allowing pantries running low on food to turn away visitors who didn't live nearby, reversing its longstanding "food for all" policy (one pantry director, Phylis Allen of Neighbor's Cupboard in Winterport, refused to comply); Minnesota's Second Harvest Heartland, the country's second-largest food bank, had to turn away thousands of pounds of donated food in early September for lack of volunteers to sort it. The same reporting noted charitable food networks were separately bracing for $186 billion in SNAP cuts enacted via OBBBA that summer. By the time of ProPublica's October 2025 investigation, the national scope was clear: food banks across the country reported empty warehouses and were forced to cut rations, with state-level examples including Louisiana food banks losing more than $400,000 in aid and Louisiana recipients going months without meat in their food distributions. The cuts landed during a period of food insecurity at its highest level since the Great Recession, and coincided with the largest food-stamp (SNAP) funding reduction in the program's history, enacted via OBBBA the same summer. Demand kept climbing into November 2025: NPR reported the Greater Boston Food Bank, the San Antonio Food Bank, and West Virginia's Facing Hunger Food Bank all describing record strain -- inventories running at less than half of normal, staff working weeks without a day off, and one West Virginia mobile pantry reduced to splitting a single bag of potatoes between two families -- as a spike in need from the government shutdown's SNAP disruption (see the separately tracked snap-shutdown-funding-freeze-trump2 entry) had not abated even after most SNAP payments resumed, compounding with the OBBBA SNAP cuts and expected reductions to Medicaid, housing assistance, and health-insurance subsidies. Feeding America president Linda Nageotte and Harvard public-health researcher Sara Bleich both likened the mounting pressure to a slow-building crisis, with Bleich predicting a "tsunami" effect with "a generational impact." A USDA spokesperson said the SNAP cuts were meant to curb "proven cases of waste, fraud and abuse" and make the program "sustainable for future generations."

title: USDA Terminated Nearly $300M in Farm and Land-Access Grants, Abruptly Ending Already-Underway Tribal Projects on Blackfeet and Chippewa Cree Land

what_changed: USDA terminated nearly $300 million in farm and land-access grants as part of the administration's stated anti-DEI purge, AP News reported. title: DOGE Ordered Lease Terminations at 25 USGS Water Science Centers That Support Flood Warnings and Drinking-Water Safety
institution: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Department of the Interior
status: Partially reversed -- GSA renewed 2 of the 25 leases (New England and South Atlantic Water Science Centers) in June 2025; the remaining terminations stood as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-04-29 (reporting on the lease terminations) through 2025-06 (partial reversal)
what_changed: DOGE, then led by Elon Musk, ordered the termination of leases at 25 USGS Water Science Centers nationwide, with 16 of the leases set to expire by August 31, 2025. These centers collect the streamflow, groundwater, and water-quality data that the National Weather Service and FEMA use to issue flood warnings, that states use for drought declarations and water-rights enforcement, and that regulators use to detect aquifer contamination from pollutants including PFAS ('forever chemicals'). The decision to terminate the leases was reported to be based on lease-expiration timing rather than any scientific review of the centers' value. In June 2025, facing criticism from scientists, state water managers, and advocacy groups, the General Services Administration partially reversed course, renewing the leases for the New England Water Science Center and the South Atlantic Water Science Center; the remaining terminated leases were not reported as reversed as of this entry's creation.

title: DOGE Takes Over U.S. Institute of Peace by Force; Building Later Renamed for Trump
institution: United States Institute of Peace
status: Ongoing (a federal district court ruled the takeover unlawful, but a stay pending appeal keeps the administration in control as of this update; USIP moved July 2, 2026 to lift the case's abeyance and schedule oral argument now that Trump v. Slaughter has been decided, the government opposed that motion July 8, 2026, and the D.C. Circuit had not yet ruled on it as of this update)
date_of_action: 2025-02-19 (executive order) through ongoing appeal; headquarters renamed December 3, 2025
what_changed: On February 19, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing USIP, a congressionally chartered independent nonprofit created under President Reagan in 1984, to be eliminated 'to the maximum extent consistent with applicable law,' incorrectly characterizing it as a government entity. On March 14, 2025, Trump fired most of USIP's 15-member bipartisan board without stating a reason, leaving only Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and National Defense University President Peter Garvin, who then removed acting president George Moose and installed DOGE-affiliated Kenneth Jackson. After being turned away once, DOGE staff forced entry into USIP's headquarters on March 17, 2025 using a physical key taken from a former security contractor, with help from D.C. police, following a standoff in which USIP staff had locked the building. Court filings alleged DOGE personnel accessed and disposed of financial records marked 'SHRED' and enlisted a former USIP IT employee to help bypass the institute's cybersecurity to gain full system control. On March 28, 2025, the administration terminated more than 200 remaining USIP staff overnight via personal email and messaging apps, after employees had already lost access to work systems, and headquarters ownership was transferred to the General Services Administration. On May 19, 2025, U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell ruled the board removal was unlawful and declared all subsequent actions, including the staff firings and building transfer, 'null and void,' ordering reinstatement. USIP retook physical control of its headquarters on May 22, 2025; acting president George Moose said the building had been 'essentially...abandoned for many weeks,' protected only by a 'woefully insufficient' security and cleaning presence, and staff found extensive damage from the roughly two-month DOGE occupation: water leaks and water damage throughout, missing ceiling tiles in multiple locations, a damaged garage door, non-operational vehicle security barriers, weeds growing in the rooftop cooling tower, and an infestation of rats and roaches. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0376: TechCrunch's coverage, corroborated by the security chief's own account, described the building's interior as resembling 'a zombie movie.' On June 27, 2025, the D.C. Circuit granted the government a stay pending appeal, citing related Supreme Court precedent allowing presidents to remove independent-agency leaders while litigation proceeds and finding USIP 'exercises substantial executive power,' which returned practical control to the administration. The D.C. Circuit denied USIP's motion to partially lift that stay on November 26, 2025, and held the case in abeyance pending the Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter ruling, issued June 29, 2026. On December 3, 2025, the State Department renamed the institute's headquarters the 'Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace,' while the administration's FY2026 budget request eliminated federal funding for the organization entirely. Update 2026-07-19: with Trump v. Slaughter now decided, USIP filed a motion on July 2, 2026 to lift the D.C. title: Trump Repeatedly Floats Merging USPS Into Commerce Department; New Postmaster General Pledges to Preserve Independence
institution: U.S. Postal Service
status: Ongoing -- as of the most recent reporting reviewed (Feb-March 2026), the merger remains 'under consideration' but has not been formally implemented; new Postmaster General David Steiner has publicly pledged to preserve USPS's independence
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Trump first floats the merger) through 2025-07 (Steiner appointed, pledges independence)
what_changed: Starting around March 2025, Trump repeatedly said he was considering merging USPS into the Commerce Department, describing it as 'a form of a merger' (NPR, Supply Chain Dive, March 2025). Under a 1970 postal reorganization law, USPS is an independent executive-branch agency governed by an 11-member Board of Governors (nine presidentially nominated) and overseen for postage rates by an independent regulator, insulated from direct day-to-day political control. Democratic senators, including Gary Peters, said an attempt by Trump to seize control of USPS or fire its Board of Governors outright would be illegal under that statute. Around the same time, longtime Postmaster General Louis DeJoy -- Trump's own favored pick during his first administration -- announced he would step down and asked the Board to identify a successor; the Board named David Steiner, a former FedEx board member, as his replacement. On July 17, 2025, Steiner publicly pledged to keep USPS operating as an independent agency despite the merger talk, a stance drawing skepticism from postal unions given his FedEx background and the administration's continued interest in the merger idea (Reuters, July 2025). As financial context for why the merger idea has traction, USPS has lost more than $100 billion cumulatively since 2007, and the agency has separately been in talks with UPS and other private carriers about better leveraging its delivery network -- a strategy Steiner's team pursued as an alternative to a Commerce takeover.

title: USPS Suspended Employer Pension Contributions Amid Cash Crisis
institution: United States Postal Service
status: Ongoing -- suspension began April 10, 2026 as a stated temporary cash-conservation measure; as of a June 2026 update, USPS no longer expects to exhaust cash reserves in early 2027, but warns the suspension only delays, not resolves, its long-term financial position
date_of_action: 2026-04-09 (announced); 2026-04-10 (suspension began)
what_changed: The USPS Board of Governors suspended the agency's biweekly employer contributions to the Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS), covering roughly 99% of career postal workers, beginning April 10, 2026. The move defers roughly $200 million every two weeks (about $400 million/month, an estimated $2.5 billion for the fiscal year) that would otherwise fund employee retirement benefits, redirecting it to preserve operating cash. USPS stated this was necessary because it faced a severe cash crisis, with projections at the time showing it could run out of cash as early as February 2027 absent action; employee-side FERS payroll deductions continue to be withheld and forwarded to OPM as normal, and USPS says current employees' and retirees' benefits are not immediately affected. USPS separately sought a 4-cent stamp price increase around the same time. Reporting attributes the underlying cash crisis to multiple compounding factors: two decades of declining first-class mail volume, growing competition from private carriers (including Amazon's own delivery operations), a 2006 law requiring USPS to pre-fund 75 years of retiree health benefits within 10 years, a $634 million first-quarter FY2026 spike in workers' compensation costs, and -- per multiple outlets -- the effects of the administration's global tariffs, high inflation, and gasoline-price spikes on USPS's own costs and mail volume. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 39): the 4-cent stamp price increase this entry documents as 'sought' took effect July 12, 2026, raising the First-Class Mail Forever stamp from 78 to 82 cents, per USPS's own pricing announcement and multiple outlets' coverage of the change taking effect. No resumption date for the suspended FERS contributions has been announced; no material change to the underlying cash-crisis narrative or the FY2031-2035 shortfall projection already documented in this entry's estimated_impact was found in sourcing reviewed.

title: RFK Jr. Fires USPSTF Vice Chairs, Repeatedly Postpones Meetings, Leaves Vacancies Unfilled Following Supreme Court Ruling Confirming His Authority
institution: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (HHS)
status: Ongoing -- the July 10, 2026 meeting (fourth postponement) was rescheduled to 'late August 2026,' with HHS preparing to announce eight new members ahead of it per July 2026 reporting, but as of this recheck (which falls on the announced deadline itself) no independent reporting confirms the meeting occurred or that new members were actually named; vice chair vacancies and expired-term member seats remain unfilled, and no USPSTF recommendation updates have been issued since August 2025
date_of_action: 2025 (meeting gap already underway, per Feb. 2026 reporting) through 2026-08 (fourth postponement rescheduled to 'late August 2026')
what_changed: Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit ec8078a, which marked these 3 records folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): the disruption this entry documents had an even earlier flashpoint than the February 2026 NBC News reporting below. In late July 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported Kennedy planned to remove all 16 sitting USPSTF members, reportedly viewing the panel as too 'woke' over its use of inclusive language and its acknowledgment of systemic racism in health disparities. The American Medical Association urged Kennedy to abandon the plan on July 27, 2025 -- both the Guardian and Reuters covered the AMA's warning, which explicitly cited Kennedy's prior replacement of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee (ACIP, documented separately in this database) as the pattern it feared USPSTF would repeat. Even before the Supreme Court ruling below, NBC News reported in February 2026 that USPSTF had not held a formal meeting in nearly a year and was operating with fewer members, as Kennedy reshaped federal health advisory committees more broadly -- establishing that the panel's disruption predates and is not fully explained by the subsequent Kennedy v. Braidwood ruling. In June 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Kennedy v. Braidwood that the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force -- the independent panel that determines which preventive services (cancer screenings, HIV prevention, diabetes tests, and more) insurers must cover under the ACA without cost-sharing -- was constitutionally structured, while also confirming that its members serve at the HHS Secretary's discretion. Effective May 11, 2026, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissed the Task Force's two vice chairs, drawing condemnation from the American Medical Association and other public health organizations. Kennedy also declined to fill member seats whose terms expired in December 2025, and indefinitely postponed the panel's last three scheduled meetings, including its July 10, 2026 meeting, without providing a rescheduled date -- HHS cited an 'unprecedented number of nominations' still under review as the reason for the fourth postponement. HHS has also blocked public access to records concerning the panel's nomination and vacancy-filling process. Healthcare organizations have publicly drawn a parallel to Kennedy's earlier dismissal of all 17 members of the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), which he replaced with a smaller panel including members who have expressed anti-vaccine views, raising concern that USPSTF will undergo a similar politically-driven overhaul. Reuters reported the stalled panel has specifically delayed pending updates to guidance on cancer screening, HIV prevention, and heart disease -- three of the major preventive-care areas the panel's recommendations directly govern insurer coverage requirements for. Update 2026-08-17: Avalere Health Advisory reported the postponed July 2026 meeting was rescheduled to 'late August 2026,' with HHS again citing the backlog of new-member nominations as the reason. New members had originally been expected to begin serving in June 2026 following the Task Force's April 2026 nomination call, but that timeline also slipped. Avalere separately noted no new USPSTF recommendation updates have been issued since August 2025, though existing recommendations remain in effect and evidence reviews reportedly continue in the interim. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47): a bicameral, 19-senator letter (Sens. King, Murray, Warren, Schumer, Sanders, and 14 others), sent March 24, 2026 and not previously documented in this entry, demanded answers by April 15, 2026 on the meeting cancellations and additionally revealed that USPSTF failed to submit its statutorily required annual evidence-gaps report to Congress for the first time since the requirement took effect, and flagged concern that the Task Force might be directed to re-examine its PrEP (HIV prevention) recommendation; no HHS response to the letter or confirmation the annual report was subsequently filed was found in sourcing reviewed. Separately, at an April 21, 2026 House Ways and Means Committee hearing, responding to Rep. Vern Buchanan (R-FL), Kennedy called USPSTF 'lackadaisical and negligent for 20 years,' said he intends to appoint new members 'with a clear mission,' and predicted the reconstituted panel would hold 'much more frequent meetings' and, 'for the first time, transparency' -- his own on-record rationale for the vice-chair firings that followed three weeks later, though he gave no specifics on either claim. NOTUS reported July 7, 2026 that HHS was preparing to announce eight new members ahead of the late-August meeting, which would be the panel's first in 17 months, with a backlog of anticipated votes including prostate cancer screening, adult weight-loss counseling, cervical cancer screening (already finalized but unpublished), perinatal depression, alcohol misuse, and fall prevention; former USPSTF member Mike Silverstein compared the approach to Kennedy's ACIP purge but 'in slow motion.' A subsequent WebSearch synthesis claim that eight vaccine-critic members were already appointed could not be corroborated against a primary source and is not included here.

title: VA Briefly Implemented, Then Fully Rescinded, a Rule That Could Have Cut Disability Ratings Based on Treatment Effectiveness
institution: Department of Veterans Affairs
status: Fully rescinded as of late February 2026, following veteran advocacy backlash and congressional pressure
date_of_action: 2026-02-17 (guidance issued) through late February 2026 (fully rescinded)
what_changed: On February 17, 2026, VA directed its medical examiners to evaluate a veteran's level of impairment as it presents while the veteran is taking medication or undergoing other treatment, rather than rating the underlying condition's raw severity -- a methodology change that veteran advocacy groups warned would open the door to reducing or eliminating disability benefits for veterans whose symptoms are medically controlled but not cured (e.g., PTSD or chronic pain managed by medication rather than resolved). The change was made without traditional notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures. Veterans flooded a government feedback website with objections, and Democrats on the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs committees sent VA Secretary Doug Collins a letter demanding confirmation the rule was dead, a full withdrawal timeline, and an explanation for bypassing normal rulemaking. VA initially paused implementation amid the backlash, and Secretary Collins ultimately announced the rule's full rescission days later.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Collins
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Veterans Affairs
primary_proponent.note: Collins rescinded the rule himself following the backlash, distinguishing this from cases where a rollback stands despite objections.

estimated_impact.summary: The rule, during the roughly two weeks it was in effect or under implementation, threatened to reduce disability benefits and healthcare access for potentially millions of veterans whose service-connected conditions are managed through ongoing treatment rather than cured -- a population advocacy groups say makes up a substantial share of VA disability recipients.

title: DOGE Purge Removes VA.gov's Cybersecurity Lead, Leaving Veterans' Benefits Portal Without a Full-Time Security Chief
institution: United States Digital Service / Department of Veterans Affairs
status: Implemented as of February 2025 reporting; the Lavingia AI-contract-review episode ran March-May 2025, ending with his DOGE termination
date_of_action: 2025-02-22 (cybersecurity lead fired) through 2025-05 (Lavingia terminated from DOGE)
what_changed: DOGE's mass workforce purge included the firing of Jonathan Kamens, the cybersecurity lead for VA.gov -- the primary online portal veterans use to access benefits and manage sensitive personal and medical data. Wired reported the firing left the site without a full-time security lead, raising concerns about the protection of millions of veterans' personal and medical information going forward. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0201): weeks after that gap opened, a DOGE staffer with no government or health-care experience gained privileged access to VA systems and used it to build an AI tool that cancelled hundreds of VA contracts. Sahil Lavingia, a startup CEO listed as an adviser to the VA chief of staff, was sworn in March 17, 2025; on March 25, 2025 Wired reported VA tech staff and contractors were alarmed to discover him pushing changes to VA.gov's code inside the agency's GitHub instance, and that he had been given a 'zero account' granting privileged system access alongside attempts to deploy the AI coding tool OpenHands to write VA code directly. ProPublica's June 2025 investigation, obtaining the tool's actual code and prompts, found Lavingia finished a first version of an AI contract-review tool on his second day on the job, instructing it to flag anything not 'directly supporting patient care' for cancellation; the tool ran on older OpenAI models via the VA's own systems and judged entire contracts using only their first ~2,500 words of sparse summary text. It flagged more than 2,000 VA contracts as cancellation targets, of which roughly 600 were actually cancelled -- including gene-sequencing devices used in cancer-treatment research and nursing-care-quality measurement tools. Lavingia was terminated from DOGE after about 55 days, following a Fast Company interview in which he discussed his work; NPR reported the firing June 13, 2025. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0383: ProPublica's investigation, which obtained the tool's actual code, found the prompts labeled cancellation-recommended contracts 'munchable' without clearly defining that term or others like 'core medical/benefits,' and separately instructed the model to flag DEI-related programs without defining what qualified as DEI, leaving those judgment calls to the model itself. One documented misfire: the tool flagged a VA hospital-internet-service contract as 'munchable' even though the VA plainly needs internet connectivity, a product of the model's vague and internally conflicting instructions rather than any judgment that the service itself was wasteful. The tool also sometimes returned an incorrect dollar figure when a contract's text contained multiple dollar amounts, an error experts said was avoidable since the correct figure was available in public contract databases. Lavingia acknowledged to ProPublica the model was flawed but said all contracts it flagged as 'munchable' were subsequently vetted by other people before cancellation. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0418: Sens. Richard Blumenthal (Ranking Member, Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee) and Angus King called on the VA's Office of Inspector General to investigate the cancellations, citing ProPublica's reporting; their own preliminary analysis of more than 650 VA contracts terminated 'for convenience' between January 20 and May 30, 2025 found a majority appeared to be for services directly supporting veterans or critical VA operations, including safe health-care delivery. VA Secretary Doug Collins refused multiple requests from Blumenthal, King, and other congressional Democrats to send Congress a complete, updated list of contracts canceled or proposed for cancellation.
